stories.title: The Tide Will Have Her Answer
stories.prompt: A disgraced shipwright is crowned the town’s god for a joke—but when the sea obeys her, she has fifty-seven minutes to decide whether she will allow the ritual to make her mortal again.
stories.body:
# The Tide Will Have Her Answer

“A fair wind for our god!” someone called, and the whole quay laughed because Bruna Elt had built ships that could not be trusted with one.

They made her kneel in the dead-low basin, where green weed lacquered the immersion steps and stranded crabs ticked among the stones. The crown was plaited rush, broad as a basket, with seven old copper scales tied around it. Each scale bore the dent of some former season’s fool. The fishmonger settled it over Bruna’s cropped gray hair and pushed until the reeds scratched her ears.

“We bow our heads,” the crowd recited, bowing with elaborate groans, “and grant you the harbor’s keeping. Its depths attend you. Its tides take your word. Its creatures know your shadow. For fifty-seven minutes, we obey.”

The last line drew the loudest laughter. Nobody in town had obeyed Bruna for three years.

At the top of the steps, a glass water clock began dripping into a copper bowl. Fifty-seven marks had been scratched inside the bowl. When the last mark filled, tradition said, the fool-god must wade from the old step and surrender crown and immortality to the returning tide. Children loved the word *immortality*. Adults loved choosing the person who had to pretend to lose it.

Bruna rose. The numb fingers of her left hand caught in the rushes, and pain climbed from the other knuckles into her wrist. She saw Pavo Drin beside the careening posts, a coil of towline on one shoulder. He had not come to watch. He was inspecting a workboat’s scraped hull while the town inspected her.

Someone cried, “God, send us a whale for supper.”

“God, turn the mud to beer.”

“God, build us a ferry that floats.”

That one left a neat little hollow in the laughter.

Bruna looked from the speaker to the basin. Six fishing boats rested on their bilges along the central run, as they did at every dead low water. Beyond them, a skin of tide still shone between the harbor bar and the open sea. She had once stood above a hundred workers and made a launchway clear with three words. The words came back before prudence did.

“Sea,” she said, “stand clear.”

The harbor emptied.

Not with a wave. The remaining water drew itself flat, shivered like cloth pulled from a table, and ran backward through the bar. Silver fish struck mud. Mooring ropes fell slack. Beyond the outer shoal, the retreating sea rose in a dark blue ridge that climbed without breaking.

Every joke stopped at once.

Bruna felt the water depart as if a hand had been drawn down the length of her spine. Then the sensation opened. The ridge beyond the bar leaned against her awareness with its whole stored weight. She knew the drag of sand beneath it, the cold threads turning below the sun-warmed face, the press of saltwater inside every hull seam it still touched. No yard plan had ever given her such a clean account of loads. No timber had ever spoken so plainly under the adze.

The pain in her right hand was gone. So was the ache in the left fingers, though their old numbness remained. She put two fingertips below her jaw.

Nothing beat there.

“Four marks,” Pavo said.

He had come down from the posts. Mud blackened his boots to the ankle. He did not bow.

The banked water beyond the bar climbed another handspan.

“Bring it all back,” Bruna said.

Pavo caught her wrist. “How much, and where?”

At the first shape of her intention, the blue ridge bulged toward the entrance. Its shadow swept across the bar. Bruna closed her mouth. The water held, quivering.

Pavo released her as if her skin had burned him. “The sea moved. It didn’t vanish. You piled it somewhere.”

“I can see that.”

“You used to see a bad cut and call it fair.”

The remark landed where he meant it. Three years before, Bruna had cut the after hook of a ferry’s keel scarf half a thumb too shallow. She had packed the hollow with an oak slip, sealed it under pitch, and signed the joint herself. The ferry had broken in a late storm. Not at the scarf alone—the inquiry had found poor ballast, an overworked pump, weather no owner should have challenged—but a deckhand had died in the water, and Bruna’s hidden cut had become one cause nobody could argue away.

Pavo had found the slip in the wreckage. Pavo had laid it on her bench and stood there until she stopped lying.

Beyond the bar, something knocked twice against the stored tide.

Bruna turned toward it. The contact ran through her without crossing skin: a hull’s bluff bow, its starboard bilge, a propeller cage buried in silt. An outer workboat lay canted on the seaward flat, stranded when her order stripped the last water from beneath it. Three people clung to the high rail. The returning ridge would roll the boat before it floated.

“There’s a crew on the outer flat,” she said.

Pavo followed her gaze but could see only the black line of hull beyond the bar piles. “Then don’t bring it all back.” He looked at the water clock. Nine marks had filled. “The old words. Do you remember the end?”

“A dip and a soaking while everyone sings.”

“Freely into the tide from the old step before the fifty-seventh drop. ‘Water takes the mantle; blood takes up its labor.’ That is how you become mortal again.”

Bruna flexed her painless hand. “Again.”

“That was always the joke.” His attention stayed on the workboat. “Put a channel to them. No more than the boat needs.”

She almost told him to stop giving orders on her launch. The old irritation rose brisk and familiar. But this was no launch, and the thing waiting on her word was far more obedient than any crew should be.

“A tongue of water,” she said toward the wet edge beyond the bar. She saw the dimensions as she spoke them. “Six feet wide. Two feet deep. From the eastern shoulder of the ridge to the workboat’s stern. Move at walking pace. Spill nothing beyond its banks.”

Water separated from the ridge. It did not arch grandly or shine with festival light. It shouldered into a channel of its own making, brown with lifted silt, carrying bladderweed, three cork floats, and a terrified shoal of finger-long fish. One fish shot over the edge and flapped on the mud.

Pavo scooped it up and tossed it back. “The other stranded ones.”

Bruna could feel them now: scores of small lives beating in warm puddles across the basin. She set a thumb’s depth of water creeping among them, linked by narrow rills to the channel. Gulls descended, discovered their breakfast had acquired walls, and screamed objections.

At the fifteenth mark, she and Pavo went out across the mud.

Bruna no longer grew winded. Her boots dragged, but her thighs did not burn. The crown sat cold and absurd above a body that had ceased making the small complaints by which she had measured every day. Beside her, Pavo breathed hard and used his towline as a staff.

They reached the workboat with forty marks left to fill. Its hull leaned twenty degrees to starboard, keel sunk unevenly. The three adults aboard stared down at Bruna. One had a bleeding scrape along his temple; another held a boathook in both fists.

“Can you lift us?” the one at the rail called.

“The sea can,” Bruna said.

“Same question,” Pavo muttered.

She crouched by the exposed forefoot. Old habits put her hand to the planking, though touch was no longer necessary. The thin channel kissed the rudder and gave her the hull from within: every fastening as a point of interrupted pressure, every warped seam a faint escape. The starboard garboard had softened. A sweeping lift would push through it.

“Two blocks under the quarters,” she said.

Pavo turned the broad command into the questions he had asked as an apprentice. “How broad?”

“Four feet each.”

“How hard?”

“Enough to take weight, not enough to stove her.”

“That isn’t a measure.”

“It is if you can feel the planks.”

He looked at her then—at the crown, perhaps, or the stillness in her throat. “I can’t.”

Bruna revised the pressure down until it would have supported half the boat’s burden on ordinary launching cradles. Water crawled under the hull in two dark rectangular masses. The workboat shuddered. Mud released the keel with a long belch.

“Starboard is rising faster,” Pavo said.

“I know.”

“You always knew.”

She cut the port block deeper and let the other spread rather than climb. The deck leveled by degrees. The crew’s hands loosened on the rail.

The water was not timber. It had no grain to split, no hidden rot, no contrary spring. It took any bearing surface she imagined and reported every ounce of strain back to her. Yet it was full of inconvenient life. Crabs burrowed from her pressure. Weed clogged the temporary run. The cork floats she had carried inland jammed beneath the workboat’s propeller cage until Pavo waded thigh-deep into the narrow channel to wrench them free.

“Release around his legs,” Bruna ordered.

The water dropped away from Pavo so sharply that he staggered onto one knee.

“Gradually,” he snapped.

“I kept you upright.”

“No. You decided I would stay upright, and the rest was luck.”

She could have held him. She could have made the channel clasp his calves, brace his hips, carry him ashore like cargo. The possibility was exquisitely simple.

Instead she said, “A foot of slack around Pavo. Match his movement.”

Water eased back. He stood without taking the hand she offered.

At twenty-six marks, the first water block began sliding shoreward. Bruna moved it one foot, paused to feel the hull settle, then brought the second alongside. It was a launch backward and uphill: keel first through a channel barely wider than the boat, stored sea meted under it in supports. The workboat advanced with sucking sounds while its crew shifted loose gear away from the weakened side.

Halfway to the bar, a buried cable tightened across the channel. The moving water caught it and pulled. Far inside the basin, a moored fishing boat jerked sideways on the mud; one bilge prop toppled.

“Stop,” Pavo said.

Bruna stopped the blocks. The workboat halted so cleanly that its bow wave fell straight down.

She felt along the cable to the mooring it had fouled, then sent a shallow pulse beneath it. Mud let go. Pavo guided the freed length over a post while Bruna held thousands of tons of water waiting on the other side of her thought.

“You hid the oak slip because the owner would have taken the launch from you,” he said, hauling the cable.

“Is this when you want to discuss it?”

His answer came faintly from behind her as well as beside her: *Is this when you want to discuss it?* The words whispered from every salt puddle and wet hull seam in the basin. People on the quay turned. One of the stranded crew swore; the same oath came back in a hundred watery voices, thin as gossip through a wall.

Pavo stared at the channel. “Nothing private over water, then.”

Bruna should have been horrified. Instead a laugh broke out of her, and it too ran shoreward from puddle to puddle. The crowd heard their god laughing and did not join in.

Pavo set the cable down. “You were afraid to lose the work.”

“I lost it.”

“After you made sure no one else could judge the joint.”

Bruna looked at the flawless supports beneath the workboat. “I can judge this.”

“That is what frightens me.”

At thirty-nine marks, the workboat passed between the bar piles. Bruna widened the channel by inches where old stone narrowed it, lifted the softened starboard plank clear of a broken stake, and laid the vessel into protected water. The crew climbed onto the quay without ceremony. One clasped Pavo by both shoulders. None touched Bruna.

The ridge still waited outside, higher now than the harbor wall.

She returned it in stages. First a braided foot of water along the central run, slow enough to fill hollows rather than seal air inside them. Then enough beneath the fishing boats to meet their bilges evenly. She felt each hull accept buoyancy: weight passing from mud to water, ropes drawing taut, rudders waking in their pins. At the forty-third mark, the last boat righted itself. She let the rest of the stored tide cross the bar in low terraces that dissolved one into another without a breaker.

The harbor rose to its expected height. Only Bruna knew how much the west wall pressed against its footing, where a leaking dinghy drank through its seams, how warm runoff feathered across colder salt. The town had once been a scatter of jobs she could no longer do. Now it was a single structure resting in her hands.

People came down the steps and bowed without mockery.

“Keep the water off my cellar,” one said.

“My brother’s skiff is still outside.”

“Wash the silt from the north slips.”

“Leave it. The shellers need the mud.”

They spoke over one another, then quieted whenever Bruna looked their way. Nobody laughed at the crown. Their fear had given the old words fresh weight; their requests kept giving it weight. Worship was not affection. Authority was not trust. Neither distinction loosened the cold rush band around her brow.

Pavo pointed toward the old immersion step. “Fourteen left.”

They walked along the upper quay. The crowd followed until Pavo turned and told them the closing rite required no witnesses. The lie, if it was one, worked because they had begun to fear doing a god’s ritual incorrectly.

At the fiftieth mark, he and Bruna descended behind the net sheds. The path forked ahead. One branch curved back to the immersion step, now washed by the restored tide. The other followed a drainage channel between high stone walls and did not rejoin the basin for half a mile.

Pavo kept toward the step.

Bruna said, “If I go in, what comes back?”

“Your pulse, I suppose. Your sore hand. Hunger. Age.”

“My yard?”

He stopped. Water dripped from his clothes into the channel, each drop a bright point in her awareness.

“No,” he said.

“You might work with me again.”

“No.”

“You trusted me out there.”

“I trusted you to feel the hull. I trusted you after I checked every measure I could.” He rubbed mud from his towline with one thumb. “The deckhand stays dead. The hidden cut stays hidden until I dragged it into daylight. Getting that crew home does not put your bench back where it was.”

Bruna had imagined mortality as a door into some smaller, sounder version of her former life: not the old yard, perhaps, but honest repairs; not forgiveness, perhaps, but Pavo’s respect earned plank by plank. She had made the rescue bear that hope because a load, once named, could be placed.

Pavo would not help her place it.

“Then why are you taking me to the step?” she asked.

“Because I am afraid of needing you.” He looked toward the harbor, where every wet stone carried their words away. “I’m afraid of anyone who can turn a mistake into an order the world obeys. I’ll tell you the rite. I’ll stand there while you do it. I won’t call that forgiveness.”

Five marks remained.

The rescued boat was safe. The banked tide was released. No necessity remained for Bruna to shelter behind.

She put her left hand against the drainage wall. The two numb fingers still gave her nothing. Divinity had not repaired the old nerve damage. It had simply drawn a greater body around it, cold and immense, with currents for tendons and hulls for joints. She wanted its precision. She wanted to wake tomorrow without pain. She wanted fifty-seven years more, and fifty-seven after that, to learn what pressure did to every shape people dared put into water. She wanted an obedient material, though obedience had already made a monster of one flawed joint.

“I want it,” she said. The words traveled down the channel and out across the basin. “Not because they need me now. I want the sea-sense. I want the time. I want my hands steady.”

Pavo lowered his eyes to the towline and picked mud from a splice he had already cleaned.

“Then say that,” he said. “When they ask.”

Bruna turned into the drainage channel.

It was not a dash made in the last dripping seconds. The old step lay behind her, close enough to reach if she turned at once. She walked the other way with four drops remaining, then three. Pavo did not follow. With two left, she heard his boots retreat along the upper path.

When the fifty-seventh drop struck the copper bowl, the crown tightened cold against her living skin.

Bruna stood ankle-deep where the drainage channel met the tide. She told the harbor, carefully, to resume its ordinary course until she spoke again. Water slipped past her legs, inattentive in its eddies, exact in its obedience. From the wet edges of the basin came the town’s voices, faint and simultaneous: requests, thanks, accusations, a prayer already practiced into confidence.

She gave them no answer. She waited through the time in which her next breath should have come, then pressed two fingers below her jaw.

Her heart did not beat.

stories.title: The Star That Followed the Bells
stories.prompt: A shepherd finds an injured living starship grazing on an aurora above the summer pastures. It cannot remember its destination, has lost the small satellites it calls its flock, and assumes the shepherd’s bells are an offer to guide it home.
stories.body:
# The Star That Followed the Bells

She counted the flock twice every evening: once with her eyes while the light held, and once with her ears after the slope had taken the sheep from sight.

The second count was usually the easier. The old ewe with one folded ear wore a squat iron bell that said *tonk* even on level ground. The three sisters answered one another in thin brass notes. The young wether's bell had a crack down its lip and buzzed whenever he trotted, which was often and seldom toward anything useful. Fifty-three animals made fifty-three moving sounds, each fitted to a body, a temper, and a place on the summer pasture.

That evening she reached fifty-three, tucked the tally cord into her sleeve, and heard another bell answer from above the upper slope.

She listened again. The folded-ear ewe tore grass beside a boundary stone. The sisters had gone behind the stony rise but chimed in their ordinary quarrel. The wether was nosing at a thistle. None of them had made the long, low note that rolled down from the sky.

There should not have been an aurora in the warm part of the year. Yet green light lay over the pasture in broad pleats, low enough to silver the seed heads. Violet gathered along its lower edge. When the wind bent the grass, the colors appeared to brush it.

The extra note came a second time. It was too deep for a sheep bell and too deliberate for thunder: a call, a pause, the same call again.

She set the flock moving uphill. If something wanted to be found, she still preferred to keep fifty-three other somethings where she could hear them. The sheep followed because the night's grazing was good and because she had the salt pouch. Their bells spread over the slope while she climbed ahead with her crook.

At the crest she first saw the wound.

It hung above the next hollow, longer than the ridge was wide. Torn white fibers trailed from a dark seam along one side, twitching whenever the aurora touched them. Around the fibers, seven empty hollows pulsed in the green light, evenly spaced, as if bodies ought to have occupied them. The rest of the creature was a deep blue so dark it kept the last stars in its skin. Along its broad underside, thousands of translucent cilia combed through the aurora. Each stroke drew color inward. Cold green droplets gathered at the cilia's tips and fell into the grass.

The sheep noticed the droplets before they noticed the creature. They crowded forward to lick them from the stems.

"Leave that," the shepherd said, though she bent and touched one drop with her own tongue. It tasted of iron and salt. "You'll spend all morning refusing clean water."

The folded-ear ewe ignored her. The thing above them gave its long note.

Every bell on the slope trembled. The little bells carried the high edges of the sound, the iron bells its weight, the cracked bell a roughness like a throat hurt by speaking. From all those separate cups came words.

"Moving harmonics. Guide present."

Several sheep looked accusingly at their own necks.

The shepherd tightened her grip on the crook. "Can you understand me?"

The bells gave a brief, uncertain shuffle. "Sound source local. Meaning sufficient."

"Are you a ship?"

The dark body shifted. A fin she had taken for cloud drew close against its injured side. More green drops fell.

"Living carrier. Wounded. Feeding is poor."

"You came down for the lights."

"I came down because I could no longer stay up."

That answer was too plain to mistake for weather. She lowered the crook. The sheep had begun grazing in a crescent beneath the great body, content now that the impossible thing had proved edible.

"Where were you going?" she asked.

The long note shook through the bells, but no words formed. Above her, the seven hollows in the aurora brightened and emptied again.

"Destination absent," the ship said at last. "Injury severed the bearing fringe. My flock dispersed. Seven small lives. Seven route-bearers. No answers."

"Your flock are ships too?"

"Small. Living. Mine to keep near. Each steers itself."

The shepherd looked back at the sheep, where the young wether had found a patch of green dew and was licking with great concentration. "That is a flock. Where did you last hear them?"

"At the wound. Before descent. After descent, only moving harmonics."

"Those are my bells."

"Yes. You offer guidance."

She should have heard the question hidden inside the certainty. Instead the sisters were splitting around the stony rise, the wether was pushing deeper under the ship, and the light was failing over the track to the lower fold. On these slopes, a sheep left to choose its own way often chose the gully. She answered before the ship could do the same.

"Follow me," she said.

All fifty-three bells answered at once.

The ship drew in its cilia. The green hollows folded around it. With a slow turn that covered half the sky, it aligned its long body over the flock.

"Guidance accepted."

The shepherd started down.

For the first hundred paces, she thought she had solved the immediate problem. The sheep knew the track. The ship followed their moving music, keeping high enough that its shadow passed softly over the grass. Its cilia dipped now and then to graze the aurora, and the wound stayed closed. They might reach the fold before full dark. Then she could settle her own flock and consider what one fed a ship after the sky ran out.

"Your small ones," she called. "Do they stray often?"

"They range. They return. This is not straying."

"Mine would say the same if I let them talk through bells."

"Your flock is poorly clustered."

"They prefer grass."

"Mine prefer distance."

"That seems badly arranged."

The bells considered this. "Usually it is not."

Then the track bent hard around the head of a gully.

The lead sheep took the turn. Their bells swung left, followed by the middle of the flock, while the stragglers still chimed from the higher line. The ship tried to match both directions. Its nose yawed over the gully; its tail remained above the ridge. The air tightened. Wool lifted along every sheep's spine. Pebbles clicked uphill, rose an arm's length from the path, and hung there.

"Keep high," the shepherd shouted.

The ship descended.

Its lower cilia touched the tops of the rowan shrubs. Frost flashed over the leaves, summer green gone white in an instant. The torn side flexed as the ship corrected. A line of blue light opened inside the wound, and the white fibers snapped taut.

The sheep broke downhill. The three sisters went together, which was a mercy, but the wether plunged toward the gully and half the flock followed his cracked, urgent buzz.

The shepherd ran across them, planted the crook, and slapped its shaft against the ground. "Away! Away from there!"

They checked, bunched, and milled. Above them the ship lowered another body-width, seeking the strongest line of bells.

She dragged a handful of carded wool from the pouch at her belt and caught the folded-ear ewe first. A twist around the clapper silenced the iron bell. She plugged the sisters' bells, then the cracked bell when the wether blundered within reach. The practiced leaders stopped chiming. The flock's motion lost its shape.

The ship stopped following.

For one hopeful instant it hung still. Then its whole dark length sank.

The aurora pressed flat across its back. Cold prickled the shepherd's face. Stones rose from the path and tapped against the ship's underside. The sheep, unable to hear their familiar leaders, spread in every direction.

"Guide vanished," the remaining bells said. Their words came lower now, stretched by the ship's failing height. "Flock vanished. Reduce altitude. Search near last signal."

"No, you great fool."

"Procedure preserves lost lives."

"It will flatten these ones."

She ripped the wool from the folded-ear ewe's bell. *Tonk*, said the bell. She freed the sisters, three bright notes nearly together, and finally the wether's cracked cup. He shook his head and produced a furious buzz.

The ship arrested its descent so sharply that air rolled out from beneath it. The shepherd went to one knee. Sheep staggered against sheep. The torn seam widened another handspan, leaking blue light across the white fibers before the fin clamped down.

Pebbles dropped from the air. Bells settled against wool. Even the wether stood quiet.

The shepherd got up. Her palms were scored with bell rust and wool grease. "I have told you wrong."

Every bell became quiet except for the small sounds of sheep breathing.

"You offered guidance," the ship said.

"I told you to follow. I meant down to my fold, where I could keep my flock from the gullies. I don't know your destination. I don't know one star from the next."

The bells struck a harsh chord. The flock flinched as one body.

"Then destination offer was false. Following caused damage."

"Yes."

She wanted to say she had meant well. The wound above her made that useless.

"Withdraw guidance," said the ship.

"Withdrawn."

The dark body rose a little, enough to clear the shrubs, and held there by labor she could see in the shiver of its cilia.

"I can still help look for your seven," she said. "Only that. You stay high enough for the sheep. I make no promise past finding them."

"Your prior search signal led away from the injury site."

"Those bells lead sheep. They weren't searching for your flock."

"They moved in a path. A guide signal is a path."

Before she could answer, the folded-ear ewe went uphill after the thicker green dew. The rest followed unevenly. At the stony rise, half went left and half right. Their bells opened across the pasture, a slow arc of iron and brass with no single front.

The shepherd listened. On the narrow track, the bells had made an arrow. Here they made weather. A sound could come from any edge and meet other sounds in the middle.

"Hold where you are," she said.

The bells gave one low stroke. "Is this guidance?"

"No. It is the first part of looking. Hold there and call your flock. Let my bells carry it. If something answers, you listen instead of following."

The ship's cilia spread into the thinning aurora. Its fin eased a fraction from the wound.

"Assistance bounded to gathering," it said. "Accepted. I will hold and call."

The shepherd took the salt pouch and walked across the upper pasture. She rattled a pinch onto stones where she wanted the leaders to linger, then pushed the eager sheep onward before they could bunch. She sent the sisters toward the high end of the slope and turned the wether below the rise. The flock stretched sideways, fifty-three small wanderings held in a broad crescent. Her sore hands knew when to tap a rump with the crook, when to stand in a gap, when to do nothing and let greed for green dew accomplish the work.

When the crescent was as wide as she dared make it, she lifted one hand.

The ship called.

It did not use words. A low current entered the iron bells and climbed through brass, bell after bell taking up a different part. The cracked cup supplied a raw pulse that made the shepherd's teeth ache. Above them, violet gathered from the aurora and ran along the ship's torn fringe. The call went over the pasture, beyond the ridge, and into the clear dark.

For a while there was only grazing.

Then a thin answer sounded beyond the high end of the crescent, no louder than a needle tapping a bowl.

The ship's cilia lifted. "One."

It did not move.

The answer came again, nearer. A small dark shape slipped beneath the aurora. Small was the ship's word for it; the shepherd judged it the size of her fold. It had three translucent fins, one bent close to its body. It approached in short, suspicious glides, answering the great ship's call only after each pause.

"It can see you," the shepherd whispered. "Let it choose the last distance."

"It always chooses."

The satellite circled once, then settled into one of the green hollows around the wound. Its good fins spread. Light passed between it and the ship, and a new direction rippled through the bells.

"Route sector refreshed," said the ship. "Destination remains absent. Six lives absent. Call may narrow."

The next answer came from below the ridge. That satellite arrived spinning, checked itself before the crescent, and entered its place tail-first. The third dragged a veil of green sparks and would not join until the first moved aside to give it room. The fourth came high, a clean black seed against the stars, though a pale scar crossed its underside. With each return, the great ship's call grew less diffuse. Its flock gave back pieces of a route they maintained among themselves: a curve past one darkness, a correction near a brightness, an approach whose end still had no name.

The fifth satellite skimmed so low that the sheep ran from its shadow. The shepherd spent precious minutes rebuilding the crescent, scolding both flocks without favor. The sixth answered from directly overhead. It descended with one fin furled and took station near the ship's torn seam. Together, the six cast crossing bands of violet around the wound. The white fibers stopped snapping in the wind.

The eastern edge of the sky had gone gray.

"Six," the ship said. "Bearings sufficient to travel. Destination insufficient. One life absent. Feed ending."

The shepherd stood among sheep wet to the knees with green dew. They had eaten until their bellies bulged. Their bells made small, irregular sounds as they cropped the last sweet stems.

"Call again."

"Three calls unanswered in final sector."

"My count was wrong before because there was an extra sound. It may be wrong again."

The ship sent the call. The aurora was so thin now that the answer seemed to pass through bare dawn. Bells sounded all along the crescent. Fifty-three sheep shifted, tore grass, nudged one another, and stepped around stones. Beneath them ran the ship's great note and the six smaller replies.

There was something else.

She walked to the lower end of the flock. The sound weakened. She crossed above the stony rise; it strengthened, but the sisters' bells crowded it. She pushed them ten paces east. Their three notes moved with them.

The faint sound stayed where it was.

It was almost the same pitch as the wether's cracked buzz. Almost. He trotted after a mouthful of salt, carrying his noise sideways, while the other tone remained fixed beyond the lower ridge.

"There," she said. "Past the gully. Low. One sound that doesn't move with a sheep."

The ship's nose began to turn.

"Hold," she shouted.

The turn stopped. For an instant the bells carried no words, only strain.

"I can call toward a bearing without following," the ship said.

"Do that."

The directional call struck the bells like a gust. Beyond the gully came a fragile answer.

Once. Silence. Then twice.

The seventh satellite rose by degrees from behind the ridge. One of its fins hung in strips. It climbed a little, rested on the charged air, and climbed again. The six around the ship answered in separate notes. The injured satellite paused outside the formation, trembling.

The great ship held its place. Its cilia bent toward the struggling shape, but its long body did not advance.

At last the seventh crossed the remaining distance. It entered the final hollow beside the wound, where the others shifted to receive it. Violet bands passed from body to body. The torn white fibers gathered between them, supported in a cage of light. The small ships flew in their own places, each adjusting by separate degrees as the wound steadied.

The bells filled with a chorus too intricate for words. The shepherd heard turns and distances, corrections tested and returned, seven routes becoming one road because each carried a part the others had refreshed. The great ship's dark skin brightened until the last stars vanished from it.

Then the bells spoke.

"Destination restored. Flock complete. Travel wound supported."

The shepherd gave the settling whistle. The sheep were exhausted enough to obey. One after another they folded their legs beneath them. The three sisters stayed up to nose for salt, so she caught their brass cups in one hand until they too settled. At last every bell rested against wool.

"No guide signal," she said. "Tell me what you do now."

The ship and its seven satellites hung above the slope in their violet frame.

"We depart by the route we carry," it said. "We do not follow you."

"Good."

After a pause, the cracked bell gave a small buzz. "Your flock-work was hazardous."

She looked at the frost-burned shrubs, the scattered stones, and the young wether lying on the wrong side of everyone else. "So was yours."

"Assessment shared."

The seven satellites tilted outward. Their light drew the wound closed enough for travel. The great ship rose without haste, cilia combing the last green strands from the sky. It passed above the ridge and became a dark stroke across dawn, attended by seven smaller strokes. Then all eight turned toward a point the shepherd could not distinguish from any other brightness and went on.

By sunrise, the sheep had eaten every bead of green dew they could find. At the lower trough they sniffed the water and refused it exactly as she had predicted. The young wether's bell had warped under the ship's call; its old buzz now ended in a squeak. She would have to mend it before evening.

She counted at the fold wall, wanting breakfast.

Fifty-two.

This time no impossible note answered from the sky. After a moment, the folded-ear ewe's familiar *tonk* came from the wrong side of the downhill path.

The shepherd took up her crook and went after it.

stories.title: The Upward Rain
stories.prompt: Once in a lifetime, a coastal region’s rain reverses and carries the sea into the sky, exposing the ocean floor for a single day. Two rival explorers descend expecting the ruins of a legendary drowned kingdom.
stories.body:
# The Upward Rain

The last drop fell upward between Tressa Vahl and Rudek Sohl.

It trembled on the black lip of the coast, round as a lens, holding a tiny upside-down image of both explorers. Then it sprang into the air and joined the rain streaming toward the sky.

Tressa stepped onto the seabed.

So did Rudek.

Their boots struck the wet sand close enough to splash each other.

"You broke the count," Tressa said.

"You were counting my feet."

Above them, Caudren Reach had become impossible.

The rain had reversed before dawn. First it lifted from roof tiles and gutters, then from cisterns, reeds, and the backs of startled animals. At the shore, ranks of silver cords began climbing from the waves. By sunrise the whole coastal sea was rising in broad, braided sheets. It hung now high over the Reach: a dark, moving ceiling miles across, swollen with currents. Fish passed through it in glittering schools. Their shadows rushed over land that had not felt the sun in centuries.

The newly exposed floor sloped away from Tressa's boots, gray-brown and shining. Pools frothed in the hollows. Weed lay flattened in the direction of vanished tides. Beyond the first terraces, the drowned shelf descended toward a basin hidden by pale mist.

Namarre waited somewhere below. Or its proof did.

Tressa tightened the amber shutter over her recording case. The naked light under the suspended sea would bleach an optical plate in minutes. She checked her slate, her rubbing cloths, the narrow trowel at her hip, and the cord of ceramic route markers clipped to her pack.

Beside her, Rudek drove a sighting pin into the sand and took the first angle of the descent.

"That pin marks my first station," he said without looking up.

"It marks where I began."

"Fortunately, metal accepts more than one interpretation."

He slung his level across his back and started down. Tressa let him gain three strides before following. Being seen to race was almost as bad as being second.

The coast behind them diminished quickly. The cliffs turned blue through vapor, though Tressa could still make out the mouths of the high shelters cut into them. The water would return by evening. Nobody claimed to know the hour. The first ordinary downward drops at the rim were the only warning worth trusting, and by then the exposed basin would already have begun to fail.

It was failing in small ways now. Air entered seams long pressed shut. Mud sighed under their weight. A brine hollow beside Tressa suddenly opened a dozen bright mouths as stranded burrowers pushed up to inspect the day. Rudek detoured around it. Tressa did the same, though she chose a route one pace higher.

The moving sea cast bands of light across them. Once, the magnified shadow of a ray sailed over the slope so vast and swift that Tressa crouched before she could stop herself. Rudek glanced back.

"Only a shadow," he said.

"I saw it."

He grinned and kept going. They had been preparing for this day since before either had gray in their hair. Tressa had assembled the surviving Namarrean fragments: three route verses copied into a prayer book, a tax mark on a foundation stone reused inland, nine signs preserved in a sailor's song whose tune was much younger than its words. Rudek had crossed the Reach in every season, sounding ridges through fifty fathoms of water and publishing maps with infuriating blank spaces exactly where Tressa wanted certainty. Each had lectured that the other mistook a method for the world. Neither had expected the upward rain to come while both were still fit to descend.

On the third terrace they found a straight ridge beneath the weed.

Rudek cleared a strip with the side of his boot. Two parallel rows of fitted stone appeared, the space between them packed with crushed shell. "Road."

"Avenue," Tressa said.

"It has a grade of one in seventeen."

"Kings can climb."

"Carts prefer not to."

Twenty paces on, a marker leaned from the mud. Tressa knelt and washed its face with water from a trapped pool. Four signs emerged, their strokes softened by time. The first was the stepped enclosure used for an important precinct. The second might have been *upper*, or *first*. Below them ran a damaged compound she had translated in other contexts as *bearing*, though the same strokes could mean *load brought to account*.

She pressed rubbing cloth into the cuts and worked charcoal across it.

"Well?" Rudek asked.

"The upper precinct."

"And the lower line?"

"Eroded."

He watched her fold the rubbing. His face was not built for belief, but he said only, "The grade stays constant past the turn."

That should have troubled her. Ceremonial roads respected walls, courtyards, views. This one respected effort. Tressa clipped a white route marker beside the stone and followed the ridge east, where the first route verse placed the royal precinct after the third ascent.

Rudek remained at his level. "My soundings put the largest stone mass west."

"A reef."

"Your song puts a palace east."

"It is not a song."

"Then we can each be disappointed in private."

He turned west. Tressa nearly called him back. Not because she wanted his company. His contour sheets would have been useful, and if he found the palace first he would describe it as a fortunate bump beneath his keel. But the third sign on the marker had been clear enough: a direction toward the stepped precinct. She had twenty years of context behind that reading.

She went east alone.

The avenue led through a field of low shapes. At first the shapes looked like walls buried to their footings. Tressa uncovered one, then another. They were not walls. They were sockets: squared depressions where dressed blocks had been seated and later lifted out.

She stood among the absences and forced herself to see a district. Doorways could be inferred from gaps in the sockets. A channel ran along one side, its stone lining gone but its bed stained dark. A scatter of green glass beads lay fused where a workshop furnace must have stood. In a drain, Tressa found the base of a cup still marked with a common measure. People had lived here. That was no palace, no temple composed to flatter a visitor. It was a row of workshops stripped almost to the ground.

She moved upslope, searching for collapse. A city drowned suddenly ought to have left walls fallen beside their foundations, roof tile in corners, broken columns too heavy for waves to roll far. She found chips. Every chip lay on the uphill side of an empty socket.

On the fifth foundation, repeated notches had been cut beside the missing blocks. Three bars, then a hooked sign. Four bars, then the same hook.

Counts, she thought. Or mason's marks. She photographed them under the amber hood, opening the shutter only long enough for the plate to drink the strange green light. When she covered it again, the enormous sea above shifted. A shoal scattered, each fish flashing separately, and their light ran over the empty foundations like a net being hauled.

Tressa consulted the route verse. It promised seven gates around the house that governed tides. She had found no gates. There were not even seven openings aligned with one another.

A dull crack traveled beneath her boots.

The saturated slope dropped the width of her hand. Mud folded across the avenue behind her, swallowing two of her white markers. A farther section slumped with a wet, gathering roar.

Tressa ran downhill before the sinking ground could take her sideways. She crossed a belt of weed, vaulted a narrow brine cut, and stopped where firmer shell beds broke the slope. Someone's red route cord crossed in front of her.

"I wondered when your palace would throw you out," Rudek called.

He stood below a bare rise, mud to his knees and a block of fitted black stone cradled against his chest. Behind him rose a natural reef armored along one edge with three courses of masonry.

"You found a royal barnacle," Tressa said.

Rudek set the block down carefully. "Breakwater facing. Deliberate work, wrong hill. Your district?"

"Human. Later stripped."

"Later than what?"

"Its construction."

"A magnificent conclusion."

She looked at the block. It was small enough to carry and cleanly jointed on two faces. "Planning to take that?"

"Planning to return with something heavier than an opinion."

"Its position is the evidence."

"Its position was the edge of a reef. I measured it."

"You measured what you understood."

"And you translated what you wanted."

The accusation landed because the damaged compound on the road marker pressed against her ribs inside the folded rubbing. Tressa took it out.

"The lower line may refer to bearing loads," she said.

Rudek held out his hand. "May?"

"The verb carries both senses."

"That stone ridge is a load road. Constant grade from the old shoreline. It cuts across every contour a ceremonial approach would use."

"You called it a road."

"I wanted to know how long you'd keep calling it an avenue."

She almost folded the rubbing away again. Instead she spread it across his contour sheet. Rudek pinned both to the black block. His penciled line from the reef and her eastward ridge met lower on the slope, where several shallow channels converged into one.

Not channels, Tressa saw. Two grooves ran along each, too even and too nearly parallel to be drainage. The supposed route to the upper precinct crossed the old city's orientation, but it held the easiest grade toward land.

"A hauling network," Rudek said.

"Possibly."

"Your favorite word at last."

"Leave the block."

He glanced upslope at the long return climb, then at the slope below. "If this ends in another cup base, I am taking it on the way back."

They followed the paired grooves down.

Namarre appeared by subtraction. Every hundred paces gave them less to admire and more to read. A dwelling foundation had numbered sockets around a central hearth. A long workshop court retained grooves worn deep where blocks had been dragged through its own doorway. At a crossway, three haul traces joined in a fan aimed toward the drowned shore. Rudek measured their width, pace, and grade. Tressa uncovered tally marks beside the stripped thresholds.

They disagreed without separating. Rudek called a broad footprint a storehouse because carts could turn inside it. Tressa called it a meeting court because a fragmentary sign mentioned witnesses. When they found iron wedges rusted into a sill, he claimed them aloud and she entered them on her slate before he could. At a kiln scar, she identified the written sign for roof tile; he pointed out there was no tile anywhere downslope.

The conclusion accumulated in the gaps between their claims: nothing here had been smashed, and nothing large had been left.

Near the basin floor the land softened into blue clay. The sea ceiling seemed lower there, though Tressa knew it was only the basin's depth and the swollen lensing of the water. Boats still caught in the suspended sea passed far overhead, their hull shadows stretched to black needles. One crew had lowered a line into open air, apparently to see whether it would hang upward or down. The weighted end swung uselessly above the seabed, nowhere near the explorers. Rudek laughed once, and the sound went a long way across the emptied world.

Then the grooves ended at a rectangular foundation so large that Tressa forgot the boats. The place lay at the center of the basin. Six stairways entered it. On the western side, sockets marked a hall wider than any building footprint above. The surviving route verse had placed the house that governed tides below seven gates, at the meeting of roads. It had made a palace of those words. Standing there, Tressa could not say the verse was wrong. She could not say there had ever been seven gates.

Rudek paced the western edge while she searched the stair footings. Most stones had been extracted cleanly. One cracked slab remained facedown in clay, discarded a short distance from its socket. Its underside formed a thin dark cavity. When Tressa pushed her trowel beneath it, the blade struck incised stone.

"I have writing."

Rudek did not run to her. He finished setting a pin, read the angle, and entered it on his sheet. Only then did he kneel opposite her.

Together they cleared a trench along the slab's lower edge. The writing ran in small, orderly rows protected against silt and centuries of water. Tressa read the first signs silently. Then again.

"Say it," Rudek said.

"Hold the lamp lower."

"You do not need a better lamp."

She wanted another minute in which the words belonged only to her. The want was ugly, familiar, and useless: the slab continued beyond the trench, and beyond the slab Rudek's sighting pins marked facts she did not possess.

Tressa read aloud. "Namarre." The city's name was complete, unmistakable, followed by the administrative sign she knew from the tax stone. "Then: west court, twelve stone loads, complete. River stair, eight loads, complete. Archive foundation, twenty-one loads, complete."

Rudek lowered the lamp to the next row. "And that?"

"Hall of measures. Sixteen loads made ready. Then a missing sign. Then *carried* or *removed*."

"Direction?"

"The edge is broken."

They cleared farther. More buildings. More counts. Each line ended in the same square sign: complete. The final legible row named the great central foundation beneath them. Its number matched the extraction notches Tressa had passed upslope.

Rudek opened his route sheet beside the trench. His mapped grooves entered the central footprint at the missing stairways, paired and evenly worn. From there, the traces climbed through the stripped districts, joined the constant-grade road, and pointed toward the former shore.

"They dismantled it," he said.

Tressa pressed two fingers to the city's name, careful not to touch the ancient cuts. She had imagined Namarre drowned with banners on its towers, its rooms interrupted, its people surprised by the sea. The fragments had seemed to promise catastrophe because catastrophe preserved grandeur. Instead, someone had counted the stair stones.

"Before the water," she said. "An inventory made as the buildings came down."

"Loads went landward."

"The scars do. The text does not say where."

"Stone doesn't care what your text says."

"Stone can be moved after a flood."

Rudek scraped his thumbnail down the exposed edge of one groove. Below lay dark, scoured clay; above it, pale marine sediment rested in unbroken layers. "The sled passed on dry ground. The overlying bed seals the scar. Nothing cut down through it later."

She saw that he was right, as far as the ground could carry them. The city had not waited intact beneath the first deep water. Its principal buildings had been taken apart, load by numbered load. Perhaps the people had moved them. Perhaps conquerors had. Perhaps stone had gone to walls still standing somewhere inland under other names. The slab would not give them a destination merely because they wanted one.

A faint tapping reached them from far upslope. Rudek looked toward the rim. Dark points appeared in the pale exposed sand, widely spaced at first. Downward drops. Ordinary rain.

"We take the slab," he said.

"It weighs half a ton."

"A fragment. The named edge."

"And lose its relation to the tally? We would spend our margin breaking it."

"A rubbing of a hole in the ground will not survive an argument."

"A stolen corner proves only that someone carved Namarre on a stone. I need the full lines."

"You do not have time for full lines."

The tapping became a hiss along the upper terraces. Above, the suspended sea darkened as its lower skin loosened into rain.

Tressa pulled four sheets of copying cloth from her case. "Rows one through nine. A rapid trace, no restorations."

"Two sheets."

"Three. You make a fixed-point plate sequence from the western pin to the slab, and key every frame to the grooves."

"Your trace enters my station numbers."

"Your plate labels enter my line letters."

Rudek looked at the long slope, calculating. "Eight minutes."

"Nine."

"Eight, and we leave the stone."

They worked. Tressa's stylus raced over the cloth as the incisions rose beneath it. She did not pause at broken signs. At each margin she wrote Rudek's station and bearing exactly as he called them. Rudek moved between pins with his recording case under its amber hood, uncovering each plate for a measured exposure. Before every shutter click he set Tressa's lettered scale beside the visible line.

Rain reached the basin while Tressa copied the last row. Drops struck the clay and punched tiny craters into Namarre. One landed on the slab, filling the city name with bright water.

"Eight," Rudek said.

She lifted the cloth. They packed without taking the stone.

The outward route did not survive them. Halfway up, a whole strip of blue clay released and slid across the paired grooves. Tressa's white markers vanished under it. The shortest path now climbed a smooth bank already twitching with cracks.

Rudek studied the slope through the downward rain. "West. Around the shell bed."

"That returns us to your reef."

"It returns us to ground with bones."

"The second road marker should be above that dark channel." Tressa wiped rain from her eyes and searched. Fish shadows wheeled over the mud. The sea was descending by degrees, its lower surface shredding into long curtains. "There. The broken cap. I marked the sequence: cap, twin sockets, shell bed."

Rudek sighted along her arm. "Then we cross below the cap, not above it. The upper face is ready to go."

They angled west. Tressa found the markers in their remembered order; Rudek chose the weight-bearing lines between them. Neither thanked the other. Gratitude would have consumed air they needed for climbing.

At the reef, Rudek passed his black block without slowing. Water streamed down now. Brine hollows overflowed. The tiny burrowers had withdrawn, leaving their bright mouths to fill. Tressa's legs shook on the final terrace, and the cliff shelters blurred behind silver rain. She fixed her eyes on Rudek's red route cord. When he chose a traverse that seemed to turn away from safety, she followed it. When her last surviving white marker showed through a sheet of runoff, he followed her.

They reached the high opening as the first broad fold of the sea came down.

The shelter's stone shutter took both of them to swing closed. Water struck outside with a weight beyond thunder. Darkness jumped around them. The chamber trembled; grit sifted from the ceiling; then the roar settled into the immense, familiar labor of an ocean occupying its bed.

For a while they sat on the floor among their wet packs. Tressa held the copied sheets beneath the shelter lamp. Three rapid traces. Blurred at the edges, incomplete, but legible. Rudek counted his plate cases twice before he allowed himself to lean against the wall.

Between them lay a blank report slate. Tressa picked it up. "During the exposure of the Namarrean capital—"

"Site named Namarre," Rudek said. "You cannot make it a capital from a route verse."

She scraped the line clean. "At the exposed site of Namarre, an inscribed removal tally establishes that its principal structures were dismantled before inundation."

"My grooves establish the removal. Your tally counts loads."

"Your grooves cannot say what they carried."

"Your verbs cannot say where they went."

Outside, the returned sea rolled stones over the road they had taken, the workshops, the empty central foundation, and the slab they had left in place. Tressa could feel each wave through the slate resting on her knee.

She began again. "At the exposed site named Namarre, the inscribed tally and the landward haul traces, considered together—"

"Considered is doing a great deal of work," Rudek said.

Tressa did not stop writing. "You may object to *together* in the second sentence."

"Leave space after it."

"For your qualification?"

"For what neither of us found."

She left the space.

stories.title: The Unfinished Sunset
stories.prompt: The white-haired ronin returns to the village she abandoned twenty years ago, only to find it trapped beneath the same sunset—and everyone inside still waiting for her to finish the duel she fled.
stories.body:
# The Unfinished Sunset

The road had learned to hide from Hisae.

Twenty years ago it had run straight between millet fields to the village. She had run the other way, fast enough to lose one sandal, with Jinsaku shouting behind her and the evening wind cold in her mouth. Now alder roots buckled the old wheel ruts. Pines stood where the lower fields had been. Twice she followed deer tracks into bramble and had to turn back.

She marked both wrong turns anyway. Habit made an escape route out of every mistake.

The new post road lay a day's walk east. She had left it at dawn with a surveyor's map rolled in her pack and an ache under her right kneecap. At an inn three weeks earlier, the surveyor had complained that old tax rolls placed a village in a tract no one could enter. He meant to leave it off his next map. Hisae had bought the flawed sheet before he finished his cup.

By late afternoon, ordinary dusk had begun to blue the woods behind her. Ahead, through the cedars, the old sunset still burned.

It had not reddened or thinned. The sun rested against the same broken ridge tooth, half a finger above it, copper light flooding the same patch of sky. Hisae remembered that light on Jinsaku's cheek and along the edge of his descending sword. She had seen it whenever she shut her eyes on a westward road. She had told herself memory was a crueler jailer than any village.

Memory, at least, moved.

She reached the boundary before the road emerged from the trees. The first marker was a cedar post wrapped in faded braids of rice straw. Moss furred the shaded side, but the straw itself was bright and dry, every cut end still showing fresh gold. Beyond it, a gnat hung above a puddle. Water bulged soundlessly over a stone in the millrace without falling. A thread of cookfire smoke leaned across a roof and ended as cleanly as a brushstroke.

Hisae walked the boundary north, then south. She found the slope where a child might scramble out, the ditch beneath the west fence, and the gap where the stream entered under split rails. At each place the fixed copper light met the woods' gathering gray in a plane too straight for weather. When she pressed a twig through, the tip stopped. It did not snap or bend. It simply refused the next inch.

At the old road she set down her pack outside the straw-wrapped post, straps facing her, sword side uppermost. If she had to seize it while running, she would lose no time turning it. Then she looked into the threshing court.

The court occupied the village edge, a hard circle of packed earth bordered by bundled rushes. Chaff hung above it, hundreds of pale husks arrested in the act of settling. The witnesses stood just beyond the ring: a woman with both hands raised to her mouth, a boy leaning so far forward that he should have fallen, three field workers still dusty from harvest. No one had aged a breath.

Jinsaku waited among them, though waiting was not the shape of him. He was halfway through a cut.

His sword slanted down toward the place where Hisae had been. His front heel had not yet touched earth. His black hair, tied too loosely as always, swung beside his jaw. He wore the indignant concentration of a man of twenty-seven who had discovered that skill did not guarantee obedience from the world.

Hisae was forty-eight. The hair beneath her traveling hat had gone white from the temples back. Her knee had been opened by a spear butt in a quarrel that was not hers. Two of her lower teeth belonged to a battlefield ditch. She had spent twenty years learning how to answer the cut now hanging in front of her.

She picked up her sheathed sword and stepped between the posts. The village struck her all at once.

Water slapped the mill wheel. A dog barked. Chaff fell. Jinsaku's heel landed, and his blade came down with all the speed it had carried twenty years before.

Hisae drew into the cut. Steel met steel above her left shoulder. The shock ran to her elbow and nearly tore the sword from her hand. She turned the edge, slid away, and felt Jinsaku's blade pass close enough to stir the white hair at her cheek.

The woman beyond the rushes finished her gasp.

Jinsaku finished his shout. “—think you can turn your back on us?”

He recovered into guard. His eyes found Hisae's face, and his sword point dipped.

“What happened to your hair?”

Hisae had prepared answers in winter camps, ferry queues, rented rooms, and once during three fevered days under a cart. All of them began with an account of why she had needed to leave. None survived his question.

“Twenty years,” she said.

Jinsaku frowned. “What?”

“I was gone twenty years.”

Behind him, the boy who had been falling caught himself on both hands. Someone laughed once, sharply, as if she had made a poor joke. The woman lowered her hands and stared at Hisae's hair.

“You were gone one breath,” Jinsaku said.

The sun had not moved. It remained pressed above the ridge, pouring the same light across his young face.

Hisae lowered her sword. “Not outside.”

The field workers began talking over one another. One hurried toward the road, perhaps to see what could turn black hair white between one cut and the next. At the boundary he stopped so suddenly his chest struck empty air. He shoved both hands forward, then recoiled.

“The posts are holding,” he said.

“Of course they are.” Jinsaku did not look away from Hisae. Anger had steadied his point again. “The bout isn't finished.”

She had hoped, until that moment, that her return itself might be enough. It was the kind of hope she favored: a door mistaken for an answer.

“I came back,” she said. “If the working wanted me, here I am.”

“In the ring, with your sword out.”

“You don't understand what has happened.”

“I understand that you agreed before witnesses.” His voice carried the old clipped patience he used when repairing a gate after someone else had hung it badly. “If I disarmed you, you would stay one winter and train whoever the village chose. If you put me beyond the rushes, we would give you rice, salt, new sandals, and no one would ask you to stay again. The loser had to name the winner. You crossed the boundary instead.”

The gathered villagers had gone quiet. Hisae remembered their faces turned toward her on that other side of the same heartbeat. Her lord had died that spring, leaving armed men without wages and villages without protection. She had returned home wanting them to admire the freedom she had not chosen. Jinsaku had asked her to spend one winter teaching them how to keep raiders from their grain.

She had made the wager because she believed she could not lose it.

“The lord I served was dead,” she said. “I would not trade his claim for yours.”

“One winter wasn't your life.”

“It was mine to refuse.”

“Then you should have refused before you shook my hand.”

The words reached a place her rehearsed defenses did not cover. Hisae glanced toward the road. Her pack waited two strides beyond the post, every strap arranged for flight. Evening had deepened around it. Inside the village, chaff drifted down through copper light and seemed to slow before touching earth.

The woman who had gasped took a clay bead from a cord at her wrist. She tossed it toward the boundary. It stopped in the air just short of the post.

“Finish it,” she said. Not to Hisae alone.

Jinsaku stepped back to the center and lifted his sword. “Do the twenty years make you unable?”

Hisae flexed her right knee. Pain sat deep in the joint, watchful but not yet awake.

“No,” she said.

That answer, at least, she had not practiced.

They saluted. Jinsaku's was curt. Hisae's was exact enough to irritate him; she saw it in the set of his mouth.

He came forward at once.

The first exchange told her what time had kept and what it had stolen. Jinsaku was faster than any memory. His strength arrived through the blades without warning, young wrists behind young shoulders, each cut linked to the next before Hisae's older body had finished absorbing the first. But he was also the man she had fought for an hour. He still raised his left shoulder before changing lines. He still pressed hard into a bind and trusted his feet to save the opening.

Hisae gave him no pressure to use. She yielded half a step, turned his point, and tapped the flat of her sword against his knuckles. He hissed and withdrew.

“You got stingy,” he said.

“I learned to stop wasting motion.”

“Took you twenty years?”

“Some teachers were slow.”

He cut for her ribs. She caught it close to the hilt, where his leverage failed, and drove his blade aside. The witnesses shifted around the ring. They were not a single body now. The boy cheered Jinsaku. One field worker muttered that Hisae's heel was too near the rushes. Another told him to be quiet. Their voices made the court feel smaller.

Jinsaku feinted high and swept low. Hisae lifted her damaged leg just in time. The movement pulled a bright thread of pain through her knee. She set the foot down carefully, hiding the hitch in a retreat.

He noticed. He had always been better at reading her than she liked.

“Twenty years,” he said again, circling. “You could have come back after one.”

Hisae watched his hips, not his face. “I heard the road had gone strange.”

“After two?”

“Yes.”

“And?”

He forced her into a high guard, then struck twice below it. She took the first on her blade and escaped the second by an inch.

“I was in the north,” she said.

“After five?”

“At sea.”

“Ten?”

“Fighting.”

“You always find somebody else's winter.”

She answered with a thrust that made him give ground. It was meant to end the conversation, but Jinsaku grinned without pleasure. He had found the wound and did not need to strike it again.

Their blades touched, separated, touched. Hisae let the rhythm settle into her bones. Outside this fixed evening she had fought men with longer reach, women quicker than Jinsaku, desperate farmers who swung tools without any school's warning. She had learned from all of them. A shoulder could lie; weight rarely did. Eyes sought victory; feet revealed fear.

Jinsaku's feet revealed none. He believed the ring belonged under him. He believed a bargain could still mean what it had meant a breath ago.

Hisae drew him clockwise, away from her weak side. He resisted, then tried to reverse their places with the same hard bind he had used twenty years before. She slipped beneath it. The flat of her sword touched his sleeve before he spun clear.

A murmur went through the witnesses.

Jinsaku's jaw tightened. He advanced with three cuts, rising, crossing, rising again. Hisae knew the fourth before his elbow turned. The descending stroke had followed her across every road of her life. In dreams it cut her down. Awake, beside cooking fires, she had answered it with broom handles, sticks, empty hands. She had perfected six counters and discarded five.

She stepped closer instead of back.

His sword fell. Hisae caught it at an angle, turned beneath his arms, and guided his force past her shoulder. Her hilt struck his guard. Before he could recover, she was at his side with her point commanding the space ahead of his chest.

Jinsaku retreated. One step. Two. His heel landed on the bundled rushes.

The court erupted in warnings.

Hisae saw surprise in his face. Behind it she saw the boy who had climbed the storehouse roof with her, the young man who had asked for only one winter because asking for more would have made refusal easy. She also saw the edge of the ring beneath his heel. One clean drive and she would win. Rice, salt, sandals, silence. The village would owe her release after she had cost it twenty years.

He shifted his weight to spring left.

Hisae lunged to close the path.

Her mind measured the distance with a twenty-eight-year-old body. Her right knee locked halfway through the step.

The court tilted. Her sword point dropped. Jinsaku moved left as she had known he would, but knowledge without a leg under it was only another way to fall. He caught her blade against his guard, turned his wrists, and used the momentum she could not stop.

Hisae's sword spun from her hand. It crossed the bundled rushes and struck the packed earth beyond with a hard, final sound.

She landed on one knee. Pain swallowed the lower half of her body. Jinsaku stood over her, breathing fast, his point lowered but not touching her.

No one spoke.

Hisae looked at her sword outside the ring. Then she looked past it to the road.

Her pack was still within reach. The boundary had admitted her once. She did not know whether it would let her out, but her body had never required certainty before choosing an exit.

She pushed upright and took one step toward the post.

Behind her, the mill wheel's splash stretched thin. The witnesses' breathing faded. A husk of chaff stopped a handspan above the ground.

She took a second step.

“Hisae,” Jinsaku said.

He did not order her back. That would have been easier to resist. He stood in the ring with the winning sword and waited for her to decide whether his victory existed.

The copper light sharpened along the road. Hisae saw herself cross it: seize the pack, run through dark woods, find the new road before dawn. Behind her, Jinsaku would remain twenty-seven. The woman would keep her half-finished breath. The boy would balance forever on hands that never reached the earth. Hisae could grow old carrying all of them, and they would never gain so much as another instant in which to hate her.

She turned around.

Crossing the court hurt more than the lunge had. Jinsaku watched her limp back between the rushes. Hisae stopped in the center, where every witness could see her empty hands.

“Jinsaku won the bout,” she said. Her voice came out rough, so she said the rest without trying to mend it. “I owe the village one winter.”

For a heartbeat, nothing changed.

Then the sun fell.

Darkness rushed across the court. All the chaff came down at once, filling mouths and hair. The mill wheel slammed through the water waiting beneath it. Somewhere a kettle shrieked and boiled over; someone cursed as hot water reached a fire. A loose roof tile completed its fall and shattered in an alley. The boy sneezed so violently that the field worker beside him began to laugh.

The laughter stopped when they saw the stars.

No lamps had been lit. People stumbled toward their houses, calling for flint, children, buckets. The cookfire smoke, freed from its straight line, flattened beneath the night breeze. It smelled of supper. Bowls abandoned during the duel still held warm rice.

Jinsaku sheathed his sword. He did not offer Hisae a hand.

She retrieved her own blade from beyond the ring and wiped dirt from it with her sleeve. The boundary post stood where it had stood, but the air beside it no longer had a surface. The clay bead lay in the road.

The first lamp showed faces turned toward her.

“Tell them,” Jinsaku said.

Hisae gave the date.

Denial came before questions. One man insisted she had counted wrongly. The woman with the clay beads gripped Hisae's sleeve and asked about the farm where her married daughter lived. A field worker demanded to know who had harvested the upper terraces. Someone asked whether the old bridge still stood. Someone else named the dead lord, then named three neighboring headmen Hisae had not thought about in years.

She knew two were dead. She did not know about the third. The bridge had gone down in a spring flood. The upper terraces were pines now. The nearest market had moved east to meet the post road. She answered until every answer uncovered two more losses.

At last Jinsaku cut through them. “Enough. She doesn't know every grave between here and the sea.”

His anger had not cooled; it had changed tools. He sent people to check the wells, the storehouses, the animals, the west footpath. He ordered lamps kept away from the roofs until they knew what twenty dry years had done outside the held ground. Some obeyed. Some continued staring at Hisae. The woman released her sleeve and walked toward the boundary without waiting for permission.

Hisae found the apology she had carried through twenty winters.

“Jinsaku.”

He was examining the broken tile by lamplight. “What?”

“I am sorry.”

He set the pieces aside. “That isn't the winter.”

“I know.”

“Do you?” His face was the face she remembered, but the question in it had aged. “You had years to make that sentence. I haven't had an hour.”

Hisae let the apology remain where it had landed. “What do you need before morning?”

Jinsaku looked toward the dark road. Three villagers stood beyond the post now, touching trees grown thick in what they remembered as a field. Their voices carried fear back through the open boundary.

“A way to the new road,” he said. “News we can trust. We need to know who owns the lower land, whether anyone will call us thieves for waking in our own houses, and where to send those who go looking for kin.” He rubbed the back of his sword hand, where Hisae's earlier tap had raised a red mark. “Sword lessons can wait a day.”

“My maps are outside.”

“Of course they are.” His gaze found the pack positioned for a quick departure. “Bring them in.”

Hisae crossed the post and lifted the pack. It seemed heavier than it had at sunset. The straps held food for six days, oilcloth, a whetstone, two shirts, and every careful provision for leaving again.

She carried it back into the threshing court.

On the boards beside the first lamp, she unrolled the surveyor's map. It did not show the village. A blank stretch of hills lay where its fields and houses should have been. Jinsaku stared at that absence while people gathered behind him, asking which roads remained and which names on the paper meant anything.

Hisae put one finger on the old road beneath their feet and another on the new road to the east.

“At first light,” she said, “I will lead whoever you choose from here to here. Then we start finding the rest.”

Jinsaku studied the distance between her fingers. He did not forgive her. He nodded once and began choosing who would walk with them.

stories.title: The First Kingdom Was Late on Taxes
stories.prompt: An entire mountain village goes to sleep beneath a strange aurora and wakes millions of years later inside an archaeological excavation. The future knows them only as the mythical First Kingdom; the villagers know themselves as an unimportant trading stop with overdue taxes, mediocre beer, and no idea how to get home.
stories.body:
# The First Kingdom Was Late on Taxes

The tax of Kelpass was overdue by eleven days because Ulven Korr had brewed three casks of beer nobody wanted.

This was not the official reason. Dema Vask had tried writing *washout on the south road*, *late wool train*, and *abnormal spoilage*, all of which were true and none of which made the figures agree. The three casks remained in Ulven's back room, their iron hoops sound, their contents afflicted by a smoky bitterness that caught behind the teeth. Until they became coin, the village owed the province more than the village possessed.

“Call it temple beer,” Ulven suggested. He leaned over Dema's ledger and left a damp ring beside the column for bridge tolls. “Travelers pay twice for anything blessed.”

“By whom?”

“You have neat handwriting.”

Dema moved the ledger out of his reach. Beyond the tavern's open door, the last light lay blue across the pass. Kelpass occupied the broadest shelf between two steep mountains: forty-three houses, a weighhouse, a smithy that had lost half its roof, Ulven's tavern, and a shrine too small for the god whose name had worn off its lintel. The north road carried salt and dyed cloth upward. The south road carried wool and complaints down. Nobody conquered Kelpass because there was nowhere worth going after it except somewhere else.

That evening, light began to climb the sky.

It rose behind the northern peak in green folds, then spread violet streamers from ridge to ridge. Pots cooled on tables. Dice stopped in cups. One by one, people stepped into the street, including Dema, though the quarterly return still lacked thirty-two silver crowns and an explanation suitable for a clerk who disliked invention.

The aurora made no sound. It polished every slate roof and puddle. Its green lay in Ulven's open casks like a second, better beer.

“Snow sign?” somebody called.

“Not in autumn,” somebody else answered, as if the sky respected schedules.

Dema remembered that she had left the duplicate tax roll in the weighhouse. She also remembered the little iron pin she had dropped that afternoon near the north marker while fastening a split hoop around the documents. She had meant to retrieve it before dark.

The light folded once, very slowly, above Kelpass.

Dema's last order was to leave the tavern door open in case the two late salt wagons arrived. Then her cheek met the ledger, and the village slept.

She woke to a brightness with no flame in it.

Her neck hurt. The same damp ring marked the same page. Around her, Ulven and fourteen customers lifted their heads from tables or pushed themselves off the floor. Outside, a goat began screaming with the steady outrage of a creature that had missed no meal but suspected it might.

Dema counted the people in the tavern before she asked what had happened. Sixteen, including herself. Nobody injured. Two mugs broken, one chair overturned, one tax return stained with beer.

Above the roofs, pale objects drifted against a sky too white to be morning. They were smaller than fists, soft-edged, and each cast a fan of lines across the street. Wherever those lines met an iron nail, hinge, buckle, or cask hoop, they bent away. The tavern appeared inside a lacework of light with dark holes punched through it.

Figures stood on a platform higher than the old shrine roof. They wore close-fitting gray clothes and clear masks. One was pointing at Dema. Another had dropped something long and silver.

“Raiders?” Ulven asked.

“Raiders don't label doors.”

Small plaques had been fixed beside several thresholds. Each bore cramped symbols that changed when Dema tried to focus on them. A cord ran from the tavern eaves to a scaffold that should have been impossible, because beyond it there was no mountainside.

Dema looked away from that absence. “Count households. Street by street. Wake everyone. Nobody climbs anything, and nobody touches the floating lights.”

The habit of obeying a tally-keeper during flood, fire, and tax collection served Kelpass well. By the time the brightness above had shifted the width of a hand, Dema had one hundred and ninety-two people: one hundred and eighty-three residents and nine guests from the roads. Every person known to have slept inside the village boundary answered. So did the oxen, mules, goats, dogs, chickens, and Ulven's old cat, though the cat answered to no one and had bitten a masked figure who ventured too near the north lane.

Beyond the last houses, there was no answer at all.

The masked people descended by a stair that clung to empty air. They stopped whenever their floating lights swerved from a nail or buckle. At last a woman approached along a path marked by strips of orange cloth laid by hand. She had removed her mask. Her hair was cropped almost to the scalp, and one cheek bore a pattern of tiny silver dots.

She spoke three words. A small disk at her throat repeated them as, “Sovereign Keeper of Tribute?”

“Tally-keeper,” Dema said. “There is no sovereign here. Who are you?”

The woman answered. Her disk paused long enough to suggest disapproval, then said, “Yevrin Caul. Field reader. Vastor Cut. I request stillness from all sacred citizens.”

“They're counting chickens in the east lane. You may request around them.”

Yevrin looked toward the lane, where three children were pursuing a hen through the luminous survey lines. Her expression changed twice before settling on professional alarm. She spoke rapidly into the disk. Above them, the floating objects rose out of the children's reach.

Then Yevrin looked at the tavern. She did not glance. She studied every soot mark and warped board with the hungry attention of a buyer who had found gold under paint.

“The royal habitation,” her disk said.

“Tavern.”

Yevrin pointed to the weighhouse at the end of the square. “Seat of seals.”

“Weighhouse.”

“Coronation mark.”
