You cannot say what the sky looked like from below.

The observation is obvious enough to irritate you: exactness has an altitude.

The next caption calls the accounts “fragmentary but invaluable,” which is the first phrase in the wing you would not amend. One message contradicts the driver’s timing. Another was copied decades after the event from a damaged original. A route tally has been added wrong by one. Their limitations are printed below them in calm museum language. The small records are allowed uncertainty. Only the queen has been polished until nothing partial remains.

At the end of the case, a final panel asks whether Sol-*steece* Evening Bell was truly alone.

The text offers the Twelve as an answer. It calls them possible ghosts, symbolic companions, or later inventions meant to soften the terrible solitude of heroism.

You were the only living combatant over the Bay. That matters. No other person could take a position beside you, warn you of a needle flight, catch you when a bell-step ended in sleet. The twelve could not speak or choose. Calling them companions would invent life where none was stored.

Calling you unaided would erase their choices.

And below, beyond your attention, drivers carried civilians east. Dispatchers emptied roads. Weather observers kept instruments running under a sky they could barely read. They did not fight the host. They made it possible for a battle over an evacuated shore to remain one.

On the plaque, *alone* has to cover the sky, the crown, and every road below. It cannot.

You read the source note. Then the image credit. Then the donor acknowledgment for the case. Your promise was every caption, and museums hide their most revealing claims in small print.

The remaining wall takes forty-three minutes.

You learn which governments have lent facsimiles, which alloys were guessed for the unrecovered frames, which poet first placed a sword in your hand, and how many schoolchildren voted for the reconstructed crown’s color. You read a sanitation notice on the touch table. You read the label beneath a bench explaining that its wood came from storm-felled trees planted long after the battle.

Closing tones begin while you are bent over the fire-capacity plate beside the exit. You straighten too quickly and cross two floor triggers. The audio bead overlays a solemn account of your “final sword form” with instructions to return the device at reception. For several seconds your mythical weapon is available in six languages and must not be placed in a pocket or waste bin.

You laugh. It surprises you enough that the two tracks end before you move again.

The testimony alcove stands beyond the exhibition proper, a padded recess with one stool and a recording lens. A sign invites family stories, inherited traditions, and first-hand witness accounts. You nearly pass it. The categories have the soft, posthumous air of everything in the wing. They are built for grandchildren carrying a box of letters, not for the grammatical subject of the plaques.

The screen brightens as you approach.

**TELL US YOUR CONNECTION TO THE BATTLE OF THE BAY.**

You sit.

The form asks for your life story first. It offers prompts about childhood, coronation, grief, and the burden of survival. You skip them. It asks whether you possess an artifact for scanning. You select no. It asks what proof of identity you can provide.

You leave the field empty.

The recording lens opens. In its small black surface, you look less like the glass silhouette than the tired visitor you are: plain coat, museum bead, hair flattened on one side where the clip has pressed for hours. You could authenticate yourself in a dozen spectacular ways, none of which would prove a count. A bright seam through the wall would establish only that you could make one.

You press record.

“My name is Solstice Evening Bell.” You say it slowly, correctly, without giving the machine a performance to admire. “I am the person your exhibition calls the First Monarch. I was present above the Bay. I am recording four corrections limited to what I witnessed and what I carried.”

The red mark beside the lens holds steady.

“The host consisted of 131,072 nonliving autonomous frames: eight wedges of 16,384. I counted them through royal hearing. I did not carry a sword. The crown did not contain twelve spirits, minds, or persons. It contained twelve final spells, freely made by twelve adults whose souls and minds had passed on. Those works required my living agency, and all twelve were destroyed during the battle.

“I was the only living combatant above the Bay. I was not unaided. I cannot testify to the evacuation as it was experienced from the shore, and I do not authorize the museum to treat my account as a complete history of the event.”

You stop there.

The form asks if you would like to add the donors’ names. No. It asks permission to extract clips for promotional use. No. To preserve the raw recording for research and accession review: yes. To quote the four corrections, unaltered and with the limits you stated: yes. To synthesize or revoice your speech: no.

Relationship to the subject offers seven choices. Descendant. Family. Scholar. Community custodian. Eyewitness. Other.

At the bottom, perhaps included for people recording about themselves in more ordinary exhibitions, is **SELF**.

You select it.

The automatic transcript appears. It has spelled the number correctly. It has turned *Bell* into *Belle* and supplied *Sol-steece* as a pronunciation note beside your name.

An edit button waits.

You leave the text attached to the raw voice. The accession status reads **UNVERIFIED — PENDING REVIEW**. You submit before the screen can offer another prompt.

At reception, you return the audio bead. As you cross the outer hall, another visitor steps into the painted lane behind you.

“Sol-*steece* Evening Bell,” the guide begins, “stood alone against countless invaders—”

You continue through the doors before it reaches the sword.

stories.title: The Wolf in the Mirror
stories.prompt: You were fully prepared to watch over your cursed partner while they transform into werewolf on the full moon. What you were not prepared for was them chasing their tail for 2 hours and then barking at themselves after walking in front of mirror.
stories.body:
# The Wolf in the Mirror

The bite-resistant coat was for getting Teague off me without losing an arm. The plywood panel was for dividing the room if they became territorial. The canvas straps were for restraint, but only if the alternative was a broken window, an open door, or a throat.

The spray bottle was water. The air horn was noise. The first-aid kit was obvious.

At eight forty-three, with moonrise twenty-six minutes away, I sat cross-legged on the padded floor of our spare room and assigned every object its catastrophe.

Teague leaned in the doorway, holding two mugs of tea. “What’s the towel for?”

I looked down at the folded towel beside the emergency kit. It had somehow escaped my list.

“Blood,” I said.

“Charming.” They passed me a mug. “Could it be for tea instead?”

“If we spill tea, we’ll have a towel.”

“There. You’re adapting already.”

They were trying to make the room look less like a place we had built in case love failed under pressure. It did not work. We had taken the bed apart and stacked the frame and mattress in the hall. I had covered the baseboards with foam pipe insulation, screwed a temporary brace across the window, and laid interlocking gym mats wall to wall. The mirrored closet doors wore an old gray sheet, fastened at the top with six black clamps. Everything scented had gone: soap, laundry powder, the cedar blocks Teague kept in their sweaters. I had cleaned with hot water and the unscented liquid we used for the dishes.

The room smelled of rubber mats, weak tea, and the plastic backing of medical tape.

Teague stepped inside and shut the door. “Last check.”

We had done the check twice. I put down my mug.

They pointed to the straps. “Only if I’m going to get out or seriously hurt one of us.”

“Yes.”

“You don’t put yourself between me and the door.”

“I use the panel.”

“And if the panel doesn’t work?”

“I leave, lock the door behind me, and call the number on the fridge.”

“You don’t come back in because I sound upset.”

That was the part they always watched my face for.

“I don’t come back in.”

They nodded. Their tea trembled once against the rim of the mug. “The bruises last month were mostly on my shoulders. Scratches on my legs. Nothing that looked like a bite.”

“You told me.”

“I know. I’m telling myself.” They set the mug outside in the hall. “I remember the change. After that, pieces. A smell like wet concrete. Waking up under the workbench. I don’t know what I did in between.”

The last three full moons, Teague had locked themself in the detached garage of the house we rented. They had refused to let me watch until the bruises became too numerous to dismiss and one fingernail came back split to the quick. This month, they had drawn the room plan. They had chosen the barriers, approved the straps, and made me rehearse the lock.

Now they held out their hand. “Still willing?”

It was not a question about courage. It was permission renewed while they could give it, and an offer to stop.

I took their hand. “Yes.”

“Stay where I can see you, then.”

At nine-oh-six, I locked the door.

The change began before I had returned the key to the zippered pocket inside my coat.

Teague made one startled sound and dropped to a knee. I reached for them, remembered the plan, and stopped with my hand in the air. Heat rolled off their skin. Their fingers spread against the mat as the nails darkened and thickened. Their shoulders drew high; their shirt split at one seam, then vanished beneath a rush of coarse brown-black fur.

No part of it was neat. Their body worked furiously against a shape it had known all day. Bones shifted under skin. Breath became panting, panting became a growl too low for the room, and the room seemed to shrink around it.

I had prepared for teeth. I had not understood the size of the animal that would carry them.

When it was over, a wolf stood where Teague had knelt, taller at the shoulder than the plywood panel was wide. Their paws pressed divots into the gym mats. Their claws clicked once when they adjusted their weight. One amber eye caught the ceiling light; the other remained in shadow.

The coat suddenly felt decorative.

“Teague,” I said.

Their ears turned toward me.

Then their head swung back toward their hindquarters.

I took hold of the panel. A feint, I thought. Predators watched one direction and moved in another. I had read that somewhere in the frantic, useless week when every search for *first time supervising cursed partner* had given me either folklore or advertisements.

Teague’s tail flicked.

Their eyes fixed on it.

The tail flicked again.

Teague pounced.

They missed by the length of their muzzle. The tail escaped to the left. Teague wheeled after it, hind paws skidding on the mats, and completed one astonished circle.

They stopped. The tail swayed behind them.

I lowered the panel by an inch.

Teague turned their head slowly. The tail moved out of reach.

They lunged after it again.

By the fifth circle, I understood what I was seeing. By the tenth, I accepted that understanding it did not tell me how to stop it.

“Teague.”

Their ears twitched as they passed me, but their feet did not slow.

“Enough.”

That was our stop word. Human Teague had chosen it because, in their opinion, panic made subtle vocabulary irresponsible. Wolf Teague showed no respect for its design.

I set the padded panel in their path.

They dodged it. This was encouraging for half a second. Then the dodge carried them into a tighter turn around me, and they accelerated as if I had introduced rules to a game.

I raised the panel and backed toward the wall. “No. Not a course. This is not a course.”

Teague’s tongue appeared at one side of their mouth. Their forepaws drummed the floor. Each lap brought the thick sweep of their shoulder closer to my knees.

I retreated behind the equipment pile and began moving everything out of the circle.

The straps went onto the windowsill. The first-aid kit followed. I was shifting the emergency water when Teague cut too close and clipped the spray bottle with one rear paw. It spun across the floor. They chased that for three strides, decided it was beneath consideration, and rediscovered the tail with renewed delight.

At nine-fourteen, I opened the incident log.

*Transformation complete approximately 21:11,* I wrote. *Subject began continuous clockwise circling at approximately 21:14. Appears focused on own tail.*

I stared at the sentence. Filling in the log kept my hands from interfering, so I added: *Has not caught it.*

At nine-twenty, Teague’s orbit widened enough to graze the wall. Their tail struck the foam-covered baseboard with a soft, regular thump. I wedged the towel into the corner where their hind paw kept slipping. Blood had not touched it. Neither had tea.

At nine-twenty-seven, I tried water. I slid the metal bowl into the outer edge of their path when they seemed to be slowing.

Teague stepped in it.

Water sheeted across the mats. The bowl shot under the closet door. Teague stopped so abruptly that their back legs folded. For one hopeful moment, they sat in the puddle and panted at me.

“Good,” I whispered. “Stay.”

Their tail flopped against the wet floor.

Their head snapped around.

“Don’t.”

The chase resumed counterclockwise.

I updated the log.

At nine-thirty-nine, their nose passed near the open emergency kit. Teague recoiled as if struck. Their muzzle wrinkled; their whole body gathered around one tremendous sneeze that slammed their chin into the mat.

They stared at the kit. So did I.

Inside the top compartment, under the gauze and tape, was a foil packet of citrus cleaning wipes I had bought months ago and forgotten.

“Sorry.”

Teague sneezed again. I bagged the packet, zipped it inside a second bag, and sealed both inside the lidded waste bucket. While my back was turned, Teague found their tail again.

By ten o’clock, the room had been reorganized around the chase. Every hard object except the water bowl was outside the orbit or flat against a wall. I had looped the straps through the window brace so no paw could tangle in them, used the blood towel to pad the skid corner, and refilled the bowl with less than an inch so Teague could drink in the rare pauses without flooding the floor.

They drank twice. Both times, their tail moved before they had finished. Both times, they abandoned the bowl mid-lap and sprayed water from their muzzle across my trousers.

I did not laugh.

This felt important at the time.

Teague feared the curse. They feared what happened in the missing hours and what I might see there. They had trusted me to guard them, not to gather a private supply of amusing stories. So I kept my mouth set and my pen busy while an enormous werewolf spun past me with a look of radiant determination.

At ten-seventeen, the chase slowed from a gallop to a determined trot. At ten-thirty-six, Teague lay down, captured the tip of their tail between both front paws, and tried to bite it. The tail escaped. They sprang up with a grunt and began again.

At ten-fifty-two, I noticed that the upper-left clamp on the closet sheet had shaken loose. The sheet sagged enough to show a thumb-wide strip of mirror. Reaching it meant crossing the circle. I decided a sliver of glass was safer than a collision and wrote *replace clamp when movement stops* in the log.

At eleven-oh-five, concern finally did what fear had failed to do and made me sensible. Teague was panting hard. Their steps dragged at the end of each turn, and the pads of their paws had begun to squeak on the rubber. I wanted to stop them. Every method I had prepared depended on aggression or escape: block, startle, restrain, withdraw. None accounted for a partner who was hurting themself with enthusiasm.

I put away the air horn. I took off the heavy forearm guards because their buckles could catch fur if Teague fell against me. Then I sat outside the circle with the water bowl between my boots and waited for the tail to lose its argument.

At eleven-fourteen, exactly two hours after the first complete turn, Teague stopped.

Momentum carried their hindquarters another quarter circle. Their front paws attempted a correction, crossed, and folded. They landed on their chest with a floor-shaking *whump*.

I was up before I remembered not to rush them.

“Teague?”

They stood on the second try. Their legs were sound, though they placed each paw as if the floor had developed opinions. They drank the whole shallow bowl. Then they wandered toward the closet, swaying gently.

The loose clamp fell.

The sheet peeled from the mirror in a slow diagonal, exposing a second exhausted wolf and a pale person in an oversized protective coat.

Teague froze.

The reflected wolf froze.

Their ears rose. The other wolf’s ears rose too.

Teague barked.

The sound hit the walls hard enough to sting my face. The wolf in the mirror barked back without delay.

Teague jumped sideways, struck the dented water bowl, and barked again. Their reflection performed the same assault. Teague lowered their head and showed their teeth. The other wolf knew that trick.

“Teague.”

No response.

“Enough.”

They barked over me.

“Back.”

They advanced on the glass. I snatched up the panel, but when its edge appeared in the mirror, Teague wheeled toward it with a growl. I let it drop. The impact made them whip back to the rival.

Every answer made the question louder. Bark, recoil, bark. Claws scraped the mats as Teague charged and checked themself short of the glass. The mirror held, but the closet doors shuddered in their frame.

I looked for the angle that would let me reach the fallen sheet. Instead I saw what Teague saw: two wolves squared in a bare padded room, with two ridiculous wardens behind them. My coat reached nearly to my shins. One sleeve was soaked. A strip of silver tape clung to my hip. My hair stood upright where the helmet had pressed it, and I was holding an empty spray bottle like a ceremonial weapon.

Two hours of swallowed laughter escaped at once.

It was not graceful laughter. It started as a snort, broke in the middle, and became the helpless wheeze Teague claimed sounded like a screen door losing a fight.

The barking stopped.

Teague turned from the mirror.

Their ears eased sideways. Their mouth remained open, showing every tooth I had spent a week imagining, but the growl was gone. They looked at me for three panting seconds. Then their tail struck the floor once.

Still laughing, quieter now, I moved sideways along the wall. I kept myself out of the space between Teague and the glass. Their eyes followed me. When I reached the fallen corner of the sheet, I crouched, caught it, and drew it across the mirror from the side.

The rival wolf vanished.

Teague inspected the cloth. They sniffed the place where the other animal had been, sneezed once in what I chose not to take personally, and leaned their shoulder against my boot.

Their weight nearly tipped me over.

I sat. After a moment, Teague lowered themself beside me with a groan. I unzipped the coat so they would not rest against the hard fasteners. They put their muzzle across my ankle, hot and heavy, and closed their eyes.

I stayed awake until dawn, watching the sheet.

The return was no kinder than the change. When Teague’s paws became hands again, I covered them with the coat and waited until they could speak before I touched them. Their first word was water. Their second was my name. Their third was “Damage?”

“You’re sore. Your paws were intact before the change back. There’s a scrape on one knee now.” I helped them sit against the wall and handed over the bottle. “No bites. No broken glass. No escape attempt.”

They drank, winced, and examined me over the rim. “You?”

“Bruised dignity.”

“From me?”

“Mostly the coat.”

We waited until they could stand before leaving the room. I made toast while Teague showered and dressed. By breakfast, they had the incident log beside their plate and the suspicious expression they used when instructions omitted a step.

“You skipped from transformation complete to no one got hurt.”

I buttered the same corner of my toast for too long.

“I gave you the important part.”

“You gave me the medical part.” Teague tapped the log. “What happened for the rest of it?”

I had considered editing the account. Not lying; only choosing the details that preserved the gravity of the night. But Teague had not asked me to preserve their gravity. They had asked me to watch.

“You chased your tail,” I said.

They waited.

“For two hours.”

“Two hours?”

“I rearranged the whole room. You reversed direction once. There was a citrus-wipe incident.”

Teague covered their eyes with one hand.

“Then the mirror covering fell.”

Their hand lowered. “Oh no.”

“You barked at yourself.”

“Once?”

“It became a disagreement.”

They looked toward the hall, where the spare-room door remained locked. Embarrassment warmed their face, but they did not look away from me. “How did you stop it?”

“I laughed.”

Teague absorbed that. “And?”

“You looked at me. I covered the mirror. You lay down.”

They pulled the log closer and read every entry, including *Has not caught it.* I did not apologize for that line. They did not ask me to.

“Next month,” they said at last, “we keep the barrier.”

“Definitely.”

“Two water bowls. Heavy ones.”

“Agreed.”

“Clear the whole middle before we start. Better clamps on the sheet. And you’re allowed to laugh if I’m not injured or trying to eat you.”

“That is a difficult standard to assess in real time.”

“Put it in the plan.”

I took the pen. Teague reached across the table and stopped my hand before I could write.

“Wait,” they said. “Did I ever catch it?”

“No.”

Their relief arrived first. The laughter followed, hoarse from barking and careful of their aching side, but entirely their own.

stories.title: Thirteen Years Borrowed
stories.prompt: You can posses people for a day. For the past thirteen years, you have been looking for your original body.
stories.body:
# Thirteen Years Borrowed

The tooth is mine.

I know before I have finished taking the body. The right incisor catches the
inside of the lower lip, a tiny hooked edge where I chipped it on an apricot
stone at sixteen. Then the rest of the body closes around me: sight, weight,
the drag of a canvas bag on one shoulder, the cold brass knob beneath my hand.
I settle into the bones as into a house seen after a fire and rebuilt without
the plans.

The left fourth toe aches in the rain. I broke it kicking a bed frame and lied
about the limp for a week. The right arm reaches farther than I expect because
I have spent thirteen years measuring reach in other people's proportions.
The jaw is heavier. The lungs are shallower. The heart bangs hard enough to
blur the dim hallway.

Mine, every beat says. Mine, mine, mine.

*Get out,* says a woman inside my attention.

I let the hand fall from the apartment door. Beyond the stairwell window,
morning is a gray strip between buildings. The watch on the wrist reads 6:17.

*Now.*

My relief has nowhere to go. It shakes the knees instead. I lean against the
wall and press my tongue to the broken tooth again, as if certainty needs a
second witness.

"My name is Eamon Huxley," I say with a voice deeper than the one I remember.
"This is my body."

The woman goes quiet for three heartbeats. I feel none of her thoughts, only
the silence where her chosen words would be. A person possessed stays awake.
They feel everything I make their body do and remember the whole day, but I
cannot rummage through memory. It was the first mercy I found in the thing
that happened to me, and later the most useful excuse.

*My name is Nadira Whitlock,* she says. *You have stolen my hands in my own hallway.
Get out of me.*

I have left people after seconds when a scar was wrong, a knuckle too broad,
an old fracture absent. I have also stayed when doubt required more looking.
Whatever body I enter throws me out after twenty-four hours. Between bodies I
am almost nothing: direction, pressure, the faint wash of nearby voices. I
cannot see my way across a room. For thirteen years, the day has been a prison
and a promise.

"I need to know if it keeps me."

*You know the tooth. Congratulations. Leave.*

"The toe too. And the shoulder blade has a flat place on the left. There'll be
a white scar under the ribs, curved like a comma."

The body's mouth closes under my control. Nadira cannot stop it. By the time she
answers, I have clenched the jaw hard enough to make it ache.

*There is,* she says. *I still want my hands.*

"At 6:17 tomorrow, maybe the choice won't be mine."

*And until then?*

I look down at the unfamiliar coat, the ink stain on one cuff, the keys looped
around two fingers. The left wrist wears a black brace. These things feel like
evidence I have not yet sorted.

"Until then, I stay."

Inside the apartment, Nadira makes me remove my shoes before she will say another
word. I nearly laugh. She feels it in the chest and tells me not to.

The rooms are small and exact. A plant turns broad leaves toward the kitchen
window. Awls and brushes stand in jars on a worktable against one wall, though
Nadira informs me that the real bench is downstairs. Three pairs of reading
glasses wait where different tasks require them. The body knows none of this
for me. My hand reaches toward the wrong drawer for a spoon, and only Nadira's
sharp *left* keeps me from opening a box of powdered pigments.

In the bathroom I find the scar under the ribs. I lift the pajama shirt beneath
the day clothes and stare at its pale curve in the mirror. A pan handle did
that when I was eleven. I find the mole behind the right knee and the shallow
dent at the crown of the skull. Each recognition loosens something that has
been clenched in me for years.

But there are additions. A silver line crosses the base of the thumb. The
fingertips are rough in patterns I never earned. A tendon shifts painfully
beneath the wrist brace. There are two small holes in one earlobe, a missing
molar, faint creases bracketing the mouth. I put on the glasses Nadira directs me
to, and the labels on the medicine cabinet snap into focus.

*You are holding my neck at a ridiculous angle,* she says.

I straighten. The right shoulder still complains.

"What happened to it?"

*A press slipped last winter. I caught the platen because the alternative was
letting it crush a nineteenth-century prayer book.*

"You saved a book with my shoulder?"

*I injured my shoulder at work.*

The mirror gives us one face and no way to divide the expression. I stop
looking.

Nadira has porridge in the refrigerator and insists the body needs food before
coffee. I taste the jam before spooning it into the bowl. Sourness bites the
sides of my tongue.

*That jar is sweet,* she says.

"Not while I'm here. Sweet and sour trade places."

*That's absurd.*

"It's consistent."

*You prefer absurdity with records.*

I open the refrigerator and take out a jar of pickled onions to prove it. The
brine coats my mouth like warm syrup. Nadira tastes the same mouthful normally
and swears so vividly that I choke.

"I usually eat plain food."

*You usually do this?*

The question waits while I rinse the onion taste away. "I usually have to eat."

Nadira directs me to oats, salt, and a banana. My hand reaches automatically for
the sugar bowl, not from her habit but mine, then stops. I cannot trust the
tongue to season for the person feeling it with me. We eat the porridge plain.

At the table she asks where I was thirteen years ago.

There have been so many versions of this account, spoken to frightened
strangers and skeptical healers and one old man who tried to sell me a glass
body. In this mouth the facts feel indecently simple.

"A public washroom near the bus depot. I was washing ink off my fingers. I
blinked and I was outside, in a man waiting by the ticket machines. He started
screaming in my head. When the day ended, I fell into a woman on a bench. Then
someone on a bus. I couldn't get back inside the washroom without taking
someone who was going there. By the time I managed it, this body was gone."

Nadira does not answer at once. The refrigerator hums; rain ticks against the
window. When she answers, each clause is neat and bloodless, as if she has
pared away anything I might mistake for a plea.

*My first memory is sitting on the floor of a public washroom,* she says. *My
hands were wet. There was ink in the sink. I knew how to speak and read. I knew
what buses were and that I should not be barefoot in a public building. I did
not know my name, where I lived, or why the face in the mirror made me expect
someone else.*

The body's fingers have curled around the bowl. I make them release it.

"The date?"

She gives it. The same date. I ask the time, but she never found out. I ask
whether she saw anyone leave, whether there was a sound, a light, a smell of
ozone, a missing hour. Her answers shorten until they become one answer.

*I don't know.*

I have spent thirteen years believing that enough physical detail would lead
to an explanation. Here is the body, every private mark intact, and the cause
is no closer than when I was blind beside the ticket machines.

"Why did you leave?"

*Because a custodian was knocking. Because there were identification cards in
the wallet with a name I did not recognize, and the address had been emptied.
Because after three days of asking people to tell me who I was, I understood
that none of them could.*

"So you chose Nadira Whitlock."

*Eventually. I chose breakfast first.*

Dry laughter moves through the body before I decide whether to permit it. It is
hers in timing and mine in muscle, and the distinction troubles me more than
the scar did.

At eight, Nadira tells me we have to go downstairs.

"No."

*I promised a repair by noon.*

"Tell them you're ill."

*You have my voice, not my judgment. I prepared everything yesterday. The
collector only needs to find the package in the front cabinet.*

"Then it can sit there unfinished."

*If you intend to occupy my body all day, you can at least refrain from
damaging my business while you do it.*

I want to bolt the door, strip, and map every old hurt against my memory. I
want to walk until the gait becomes mine again. Instead I follow her directions
to a narrow workroom on the ground floor, because hiding in her apartment
would require ignoring the life around the body, and I have become less able
to do that than I was an hour ago.

The room smells of paste, leather, and damp paper. A press squats beside the
bench. Shelves hold books in stages of undress: boards removed, spines exposed,
pages lifted into careful fans. On the bench lies a school atlas with its cover
off. A torn map at the front has been flattened beneath glass. Along one margin,
a child's pencil has added a sea monster with six worried eyes.

*Wash your hands. Cold water. Dry them on the linen, not the blue rag.*

"I know how to wash hands."

*Those hands? So far I have seen no evidence.*

I obey. Nadira talks me through removing the glass and lifting the mended page.
The sheet is so thin it flutters when I breathe. Beside it waits a strip of
toned paper, nearly invisible against the torn margin.

"I remember being good with my hands," I tell her.

*You may have been. Pick up the folder.*

I choose the flat steel tool.

*The bone folder.*

"That is bone?"

*It has been a common tool longer than either of us has used these fingers.
The cream-colored one.*

I set the wrong tool down. The folder fits the palm with intimate unfamiliarity.
Nadira tells me to test the grain of the repair paper. I bend it one way, then the
other, feeling no difference.

*Again. Smaller bend.*

"It feels the same."

*It is not.*

I reach for the knife.

*Stop.*

The word strikes so hard I freeze with the blade above the paper.

*If you cut across the grain, it will pull the page when the humidity changes.
Put it down.*

"You said the collector comes at noon."

*Then we have time to do it slowly.*

The hands are mine by bone length, Nadira's by every useful callus, and presently
good at nothing. I put down the knife.

We begin again. She has me lift an edge, bend it, listen as well as feel. Across
the grain the paper gives a faint dry resistance. Along it, the curve comes
easily. Once I catch the difference, I cannot understand how I missed it.

That thought is dangerous. I cut too confidently, and the wrist twinges beneath
the brace.

*Rest the heel of the hand,* Nadira says. Her anger has changed shape. *Let the
knife travel. Do not make the wrist pull it.*

I adjust. The blade whispers through the strip.

The work takes the morning. Nadira gives instructions in distances smaller than I
can see without the strongest glasses. I mix paste too thin, then nearly ruin
the second batch by tasting a dab and reaching for salt.

*Paste is not soup.*

"It tastes sweet."

*It tastes sour because it has spoiled. Throw it away.*

We start a third batch. I learn the brush is rolled, not dragged, and that a
page can be damp enough to relax without looking wet. When the shoulder burns,
Nadira has me lower the stool. When my impatience makes the brush jump, she stops
speaking. After twelve quiet seconds, I set it down.

By eleven thirty, the repaired map lies flat. The join is visible only when I
tilt it toward the lamp. I paste new cloth to the spine, fit the cover, and set
the atlas between boards in the small press. We turn the screw together only
in the loosest sense: Nadira counts half-turns while I supply the force.

The body does not remember her craft for me. No hidden skill flows up through
the fingers. Yet when I wipe the bench, she tells me which flecks are dried
paste and which pale marks belong to the wood. The collector's key sounds in
the front door just after noon. I retreat upstairs before we can be seen.

*You put the package in the correct cabinet,* Nadira says as we climb.

"High praise."

*Do not become dependent on it.*

The afternoon narrows into maintenance. We change the wrist brace after I
sweat through the first one. We stretch the shoulder against a doorframe. I
sleep for forty minutes because the body needs it and wake in terror that I
have lost three more years. Nadira waits through the panic without soothing me.

I notice the body dislikes raw apple now. A knee clicks on the stairs. The hair
has begun to silver above both ears. Nadira has learned to turn one hip sideways
past the workroom press; I bruise it because I do not. None of these facts
disproves my claim. That is what makes them hard to bear.

At dusk, she asks how many people I have possessed.

"I stopped counting after four hundred."

*How many asked you to leave?*

I clean paste from beneath a thumbnail. "Most."

*And you did?*

"If I knew quickly."

*That was not my question.*

Rainwater crawls down the window in crooked tracks. My reflection floats over
the dark glass, older than the face I carried out of that washroom in memory.

"Sometimes I needed the whole day. A scar could have been removed. A bone could
have healed badly. People lie when they're frightened."

*Did you learn their names?*

I think of a baker whose hands I kept checking for an old burn, a student who
missed an examination while I searched her scalp, a father who begged me not
to speak to his children with his mouth. For years I treated those details as
noise. Names made the exits harder.

"Not if I could avoid it."

Nadira says nothing. The body is tired in ways I cannot separate into hers and
mine.

At 5:20 the next morning, we return to the workroom. Neither of us slept much.
The repaired atlas has dried square beneath its weights. I lift it out at Nadira's
direction and open it gently to the mended map. The six-eyed sea monster has
survived.

*Leave it on the felt,* she says.

There are fifty-seven minutes left. I sit on the stool with both hands flat on
my thighs. The room has become familiar enough that I can find the water glass
without instruction. That seems an obscenity, so I wait for Nadira to tell me.

"If the body throws me out," I say, "will you let me come back? Just to talk."

*When I have control, we can speak about that.*

"I might not find you again. I can't see well between people."

*You found me once.*

"After thirteen years."

*I will not make promises while you are wearing the only mouth I have.*

I grip the knees, then make the fingers loosen. "If it keeps me, what would you
lose?"

Her reply is immediate. *This morning's delivery. A friend who expects me for
dinner tomorrow. The lease renewal in my desk. Six books I have taken apart
and not yet put back together. Small things, if you don't have them.*

"And if it throws me out, I lose this."

*Yes.*

No consolation. No claim that one loss weighs more. The press, the shelves,
the rain-muted street beyond the high window all remain stubbornly ordinary.

At 6:10, the old signs begin. Or I think they do. A coldness behind the eyes.
Pins and needles under the tongue. In other bodies, sight tightens to a bright
tunnel in the final minute, then snaps. I tell Nadira what to expect. She asks me
to leave the hands open on the bench so she will not wake with the nails in the
palms.

At 6:16, I obey.

The second hand crosses the face of the watch. I count its small mechanical
clicks. The chipped tooth rests against the inner lip. My broken toe lies quiet
inside the shoe. Every sensation I lost thirteen years ago is here, along with
the wrist pain, the glasses pressing the nose, the dry paste on one knuckle.

The watch reaches 6:17.

Sight does not narrow. The room does not release me.

I wait through another click, and another. Then I lift the right index finger
from the bench.

It rises because I tell it to.

Nadira's silence is not empty now. It has weight. I could stand, lock the door,
and keep the body until death. The certainty arrives without flare or voice,
as plain as the pressure of the floor beneath both feet. Every other body kept
the day's limit; this one has not. It recognizes me, or admits me, or merely
fails in a new way. I do not know. I may never know.

*Take tomorrow,* Nadira says at last. Each word is placed carefully. *Let me tell
people I am going away. Let me finish the books that cannot wait. Then we will
decide.*

"We?"

She does not answer.

I imagine tomorrow evening. She will ask for one more visit, one more repair,
one more meal with her friend. I will call each extension kindness because she
offered it. Her offers will improve as she learns what I need to hear. I could
wait until she says yes without trembling and pretend the mouth was hers when
it said it.

The old evidentiary hunger rises in me. One more day could reveal why the body
keeps me. A week might restore the gait. A month might make the mirror stop
looking occupied.

I press the tongue to the chipped tooth for the last time.

"No," I say. "Tomorrow would be worse."

I release the hand first. Nadira gasps through it, one finger jerking against the
bench. Then I let go of the arm, the shoulder, the muscles between the ribs. I
withdraw without the familiar force of ejection. Sight dims from a room to a
smear of warmth. Taste vanishes. The body's heartbeat recedes until it is only
a rhythm sensed nearby.

Nadira folds over the bench and breathes with her own timing. She flexes the left
hand, winces, and adjusts the brace. Before she says anything to me, she drinks
the glass of water.

"You are still here," she says aloud.

I gather myself at the edge of her attention, close enough to hear, not close
enough to move her.

"If I ever invite you in," she says, "you leave when I ask. Not at the end of
a day. Not when you have finished looking. When I ask."

I touch the outside of her attention as lightly as I can and shape one word.

*Yes.*

stories.title: The First Wound
stories.prompt: The therapist enters his memories and follows the trauma back his memories, only to discover its source: a battle fought 25000 years ago.
stories.body:
# The First Wound

Before I entered Tammel's memory, I asked him to stop me.

He sat in the joining chair with his sleeves rolled above his elbows, watching the empty frame between us. The frame was an oval of gray ceramic set with pulse glass and nothing else. It could measure the distance between our heartbeats, break the circuit if either of us let go, and ring for the attendant. It could not open a memory. For that, there had to be two living people, one willing to remember and one willing to attend.

"Choose a word," I said. "Something that does not belong to what happened."

His intake form gave his age as *unknown*. He looked about forty-five, though the skin at his eyes had the stillness of a person accustomed to letting other people guess and tire of it.

"Spoon," he said.

"Use it now."

"Spoon."

I removed my fingers from his wrist. The frame dimmed at once.

"Again, once we're joined. If speaking becomes difficult, press your thumb twice against my fingers. If you can't do that, withdraw your pulse. Don't slow it. Don't hold your breath. Simply stop reaching for mine."

"And you'll come out?"

"We both will."

He looked past the frame to the blue walking rail fixed along the wall. Two soft cups waited on the recovery table. Mine stood on the right beside a green wrist band; his stood on the left beside an amber one. Every practical precaution in a recall room looked faintly childish until someone came back with another person's balance.

"I don't want to watch it," he said. "I want you to find where it starts and take it out."

"I can't cut a memory away. I can follow what you let me follow, and help you stay present while we do."

"Then find the source. Don't make me look."

Joined recall gave me no private route past him. I could witness what his attention made accessible; I could not search his mind as if it were an unattended archive. "I won't move your attention for you."

He put his left forearm through the frame. A pale scar crossed the base of his palm, straight as a crease made by folded paper. I laid two fingers over his pulse. He found mine with his right hand. We took three ordinary breaths, then a fourth together.

The clinic vanished at the speed of a door falling.

I was under a service lintel with cold rain on the back of my neck. A sheet of corrugated metal rattled downward in front of me. Someone on the other side struck it once, twice, three times, four. Each blow came through the floor and up my shins. My left hand closed so hard that my nails bit the palm, though there was nothing in it.

The terror arrived before the scene could explain itself. My body tried to throw us flat. Tammel's remembered knees struck wet concrete; my present knees twitched against the joining chair. The frame sounded a low corrective note somewhere far above us.

"The clinic," I said. My voice belonged to no mouth in the rain. "Gray frame. Amber band on your left wrist."

"I know."

He stood beside me and also knelt beneath the falling door. In joined recall, the remembered person often appeared twice: the body whose senses carried us and the present attention deciding where to look. His present attention was less substantial than the rain, a man-shaped refusal turned toward the wall.

The metal door hit the ground. A delivery worker outside shouted that the chain had slipped. Nothing had trapped us. No one was dying. The four blows had been a warning from someone who saw Tammel under the door.

His remembered heart did not believe any of that. It battered at the old pace.

"Where does the fourth blow lead?" I asked.

"Here."

"No. Here is where you woke last week. Find the earliest edge you can reach without leaving this scene."

He turned his head a fraction. The service yard drained of color. Rain became ash. The corrugations in the metal broadened into black bars descending through orange air.

"There," he said, with something like relief. "That one."

We fell six centuries.

Heat pressed against my teeth. We were running along a ditch outside a burning settlement, one among hundreds who had abandoned carts and bundles to reach the inner earthworks. The people around us wore glass scales sewn onto cloth. I understood their shouts only as Tammel had understood them then: *keep low, leave it, faster*. Behind us, roofs made of some pale ribbed material buckled without flame.

A gate of charred timber and iron descended ahead. Tammel's left hand reached for its lower edge. The scar across his palm was already there.

He looked exactly as he did in my clinic.

Not a father whose sensations he had inherited. Not an old story dressed in his present body. The reach was his reach, a slight inward turn of the elbow he had made when testing the exit signal. His lungs knew precisely how far they could run. His tongue found the gap behind the same back tooth.

"How long ago?" I asked.

"It doesn't matter."

The gate struck the ground. Four people on our side drove their shoulders into it, and the impact ran through his empty fist. Tammel jerked our attention away before I could see who had been shut outside.

The burning ditch returned. Then the rain. He pushed at both memories as if trying to arrange screens between us and something deeper.

"Five hundred and eighty years," he said. "Approximately. You wanted sequence."

"I wanted footing."

"You have it. That's the source."

It could have been. Later wounds do not become counterfeit because an earlier one resembles them. The remembered heat had substance; so did his desperation at the gate. If he had asked to return then, we would have returned with honest work ahead of us.

But his left hand remained closed around an absence.

"What are you holding?" I asked.

The burning settlement split down the middle.

We stood in a white-walled shelter while dust hissed over its roof. The air tasted of hot coins. Tammel, unchanged, braced beneath a circular hatch as four locking dogs slammed home above him. On the far side of the seal, a child's bracelet flashed once through the narrowing gap. He let me feel the bite of the hatch rim across his scar, then pulled us away before the fourth lock finished turning.

That memory was more than three thousand years old. He gave me the number as a direction: farther than the ditch, short of the river. He would not tell me who had worn the bracelet.

The next layers came as torn lengths rather than rooms. We ran an evacuation path paved with springy black blocks while a warning spoke in a language his present self no longer knew. We crouched under a woven dome as metal descended on chains. We tasted river silt in winter and felt the scar pull tight around the shape of a handle that vanished whenever I attended to it.

Four impacts. Falling metal. The fist with nothing inside.

With each descent, the world lost names before it lost sensation. Fastenings changed. Soles thinned, thickened, disappeared. One people built in sheets that rang underfoot; another sealed their doors with grown ropes that recoiled from smoke. Tammel's body persisted through them, not untouched but recognizably his. The scar was younger in one fragment, red at its edges. I could not discover how he had lived so long by looking at the place where he feared he had failed.

The frame's warning entered as a blue flare at the edge of every memory.

"Fifty-two minutes," I said.

"Forty-nine."

"You are reading my clock hand."

"Your left one is louder now."

In the clinic, I knew, my right hand was on his pulse. Inside the recall I felt it as my left. Motor bleed had begun. Soon I would stop knowing which body had initiated a step; after that, even an uncomplicated return could leave us vomiting on the floor or unable to stand.

I stopped following.

We settled in no single memory. Rain passed through ash, and under both lay the mineral smell of a river. Tammel faced away from the lever-shaped hollow in his attention.

"The path continues," he said.

"Yes."

"You're stopping."

"Yes."

He made a small, angry motion with his left hand. Around us, three doors tried to fall at once.

"You asked me to find the source without making you look at it," I said. "Every time I ask what your hand is holding, you take us earlier."

"Isn't that what you're here for? Earlier?"

"Earlier is not the same as truer."

The rain thinned. He could have broken contact. I made sure he could feel my fingers around his present wrist, the steady pressure of the chair beneath his legs, and the ridiculous safe word waiting unused.

"How far?" I asked.

For the first time since we entered, his attention turned toward me. His face held none of the age on his form and all of it.

"I counted by the calendars I could keep," he said. "Then by the ones I could reconstruct. About twenty-five thousand years."

The frame gave a second warning. I had perhaps twelve useful minutes before it broke the join for us.

"We can return now," I said. "Or you can show me what you have been taking us around. If we go on, you stay in charge of the exit. I won't call what we see complete history, and I won't decide for you what it means."

"You think you already know."

"I think your hand was on a lever."

The half-memories convulsed. For an instant the remembered self was outside every closing door, striking to be let in. Then Tammel pressed his thumb once against my fingers and held it there. One more press would end the join. He could feel the choice under his hand; so could I.

"It works," he said.

"It works."

He closed his eyes. "Stay until I say."

The river took us.

It was broad but not placid. Silt made the water yellow beneath a sky the color of hammered tin. We stood inside a gate post built into an earthen wall, close enough to the machinery that its vibration buzzed in our molars. Through the front slit I saw an embankment crossing the flood basin. People were running toward us along its narrow crown.

Tammel's remembered left hand rested on a wooden lever polished dark by use. The palm scar caught against a split in the grip.

I knew only what he had known from that post. A line of his rearguard came over the embankment in broken groups, carrying shields of hide and lacquered cane. Beyond them, another force advanced behind low rectangular screens. I could not see faces, banners, or the shape of the battle outside the slit. Below the embankment, in the lower channel, civilian barges strained downstream under patched square sails. One carried animals packed so closely that their backs made a shifting brown floor. Another sat low with people.

A horn sounded upstream: one long note.

In the remembered body, the sound had a precise use. The first post had fallen. The retreat was still open.

"There were supposed to be two of us here," Tammel said beside me.

The remembered man glanced once at an empty hook where a second lever-key should have hung. No commander waited to give him an order. Dust lifted behind the approaching screens.

A second horn sounded.

The barges had not cleared the mouth of the lower channel. If the enemy reached that bank, the people aboard would be pinned against the bend. If Tammel released the defensive water now, the stored head of the river would pour through the spill cuts on both sides of the embankment, tearing away the narrow crossing. The lowered road gate would keep the surge from the post.

Several of his own rearguard were still beyond it.

The third horn came ragged, its note breaking in the middle.

The frame's warning flashed blue across the river. My present right foot could no longer find the floor. I said, "We need to begin back."

"Not yet."

"Tammel."

"You said you would stay until I said."

It was not permission without a limit, and he knew it. The ceramic frame would end the contact soon whether either of us wished it or not. But the fourth horn had not sounded. His remembered hand had not moved. He was asking for seconds, not surrender.

"I'm here," I said.

The people on the nearest barge turned their sail. Wind filled it, failed, then filled it again. Its stern crawled between two black marker posts at the channel mouth. On the embankment, two defenders carried a third between them. The approaching screens drew close enough that short projectiles began to skip from the road. One struck a runner's shield and spun him sideways. He rose.

The fourth horn sounded.

Tammel pulled the lever.

His whole weight went into it. Wood grated over stone. Below our feet, a catch released with a crack, and an iron counterweight plunged through the gate post. The falling metal seemed to take my stomach with it. Chains ran. The road gate dropped across the inner end of the embankment as the spill doors heaved open.

For one breath, nothing happened.

Then the basin stood up.

Yellow water struck the embankment from both sides. It carried reeds, roof pieces, a dead tree twisting root-first. The opposing screens disappeared. So did the far end of the road. The last running figures staggered toward the descending gate. I could not count them. Tammel had not counted them then.

The barges slipped past the bend.

Something hit the outer face of the road gate.

Once.

Twice.

The remembered man kept both hands on the lever although it no longer needed him.

Three times.

On the fourth blow, the gate post shook. The scar in his left palm opened against the splintered grip. He looked down at the blood instead of through the slit.

The memory had preserved every grain of silt between his fingers. It had not preserved the number of people outside.

"I chose the barges," Tammel said. His present voice was almost lost beneath the water. "I left my own people beyond the gate."

The remembered man was still staring at his hand, arranging the world so that the falling metal had trapped him too.

I did not tell him the choice had been necessary. I did not tell him it had been unforgivable. From the gate post there was no honest view large enough for either sentence.

The blue warning became a continuous field. "What do you need me to carry out?"

He watched the last edge of the embankment dissolve.

"That I pulled it," he said. "That there were people I couldn't count. That it was twenty-five thousand years ago, and I remember."

His thumb touched my fingers in the buried clinic.

"Spoon."

I drew us upward on the line of our joined pulse. The gate became the white shelter hatch; the hatch became timber burning over a ditch; iron bars narrowed into a service door shining with rain. I named none of them. Names would have made stopping places. I kept the present around us instead: gray frame, two chairs, green band, amber band, my fingers on his wrist, his fingers on mine.

The service door struck concrete. Four harmless warning blows chased us through it.

Then I was sitting in the clinic with my left hand clamped around empty air.

The frame dimmed. Tammel had let go.

We did not speak for several minutes. He leaned to the right, compensating for a balance that was temporarily mine. I reached left-handed for my cup and knocked it over. Its soft lid kept the water in. Tammel stared at it, then gave one brief, exhausted laugh.

"That's why they're soft," I said.

"I assumed it was because your patients throw things."

"That too."

We touched the colored bands on our correct wrists and stood with the rail between us. He passed the walking check on his second try. I needed three. By then the room had stopped listing toward his stronger side, and he could close his left hand without mine answering.

Back in our chairs, I said, "What I witnessed was accessible memory, not a historical record. I can't tell you the larger battle, whether the barges survived the next bend, or what another person at that gate would say."

"There isn't another person at that gate."

"No."

He studied the amber band. The service-door panic would not vanish because we had found an older shape beneath it. The burning settlement and the sealed shelter had happened too.

I stopped before explanation became another way of keeping him in the room.

"If you come back," I said, "where should we begin?"

He flexed the scarred hand once.

"At the lever."

Then he looked directly at me and said, "Spoon."

The appointment was over.

stories.title: Nobody Spends Her Name
stories.prompt: Everyone thinks becoming the city’s youngest crime boss means money, power, and respect, but between preventing gang wars, managing corrupt officials, and keeping her own crew from betraying her, she hasn’t slept in three days—and tonight, someone has left proof that her empire is collapsing from within, it's time to take action.
stories.body:
# Nobody Spends Her Name

Rain lacquered the brim of Elspeth Kedri’s fedora and sharpened every crease in her black suit. She came into the office at twelve minutes past one with a western boss cursing through her phone and three nights awake grinding behind her eyes.

“My brother is on a slab,” the man said. “You gave me a ceasefire. What the fuck is this?”

Elspeth shut the door on the guards outside. The office smelled of stale cigars, whiskey, and the untouched line of cocaine someone had cut on her desk as a kindness. Beyond the windows, the river quarter drowned by inches and kept selling drinks.

“Your brother killed one of mine outside a card room,” she said. “Mine killed him back. That account is closed.”

“I decide when my blood is answered.”

“You decide what happens west of the river. Until I call, no western gun crosses east.”

The man laughed once. He had been a boss before Elspeth had breasts, as he had once told her at a dinner where she later took two of his routes. “And what holds my people?”

“My name.”

One of her guards was pouring whiskey. He stopped with the bottle tilted, amber liquor ticking against the rim. He was fifty-seven, scarred across the scalp, and had strangled a man with telephone wire before Elspeth was born. He did not spill a drop.

The western boss went quiet. “That name cost your family plenty.”

“Then you know it isn’t cheap. Wait for me.”

She ended the call.

A gray envelope sat in the center of her blotter.

The guards had swept the room before she entered. The windows were latched. The private stair was bolted from inside, and only four people had keys. One of them was missing.

Elspeth put on thin leather gloves and opened the envelope. The first photograph showed Olek Velcor in the rear booth of a restaurant, his heavy hand around Councillor Dastin Axholm’s wrist. Not friendship. Measurement. The second showed Axholm passing him a municipal folder. The third was a page headed with a time, 4:15, and the address of the condemned abattoir by the river.

Beneath that lay a police cordon map, a list of cars, and an execution sheet. Her name came first. Odette Naverin’s came second. The western boss and three of his captains followed.

The last photograph had been folded around a strip of white silk soaked dark red. Elspeth recognized the silk. She had torn that blouse open with her teeth six months ago, before Odette stopped sleeping in her bed and started carrying two guns.

Her guards saw the recognition. The older one’s eyes dropped to the silk and rose without comment. She folded it away.

“Olek has six men at the north garage, four at the old customs shed, and whoever he bought from us,” she said. “No calls until I say.”

The older guard looked at the execution sheet. “You think Naverin wrote this?”

“I think she stole it.”

He waited. Elspeth let him wonder whether that meant treason.

Olek answered on the second ring, voice calm and paternal. “You should have stayed at the card room. The west is boiling.”

“Odette left me a confession.”

Silence, quickly covered by a sigh. “What kind?”

“The kind with your picture in it. She says you’ve been selling routes to Axholm.”

“Then she’s frightened and inventive.”

“I want her alive.”

“That may be difficult.”

Elspeth pressed the bloody silk between finger and thumb. The blood had cooled. No smell remained except wet paper. “Bring her to the abattoir. I’ll pass sentence myself.”

“You shouldn’t come alone.”

“I didn’t ask what a girl should do.”

He disliked hearing his own favorite word returned to him. She heard it in the breath he took. “Four o’clock, then. The peace meeting has moved.”

The paper said 4:15. He had just stolen fifteen minutes from his own ambush.

“Olek.”

“Yes?”

“If anyone touches her before I get there, I’ll make you eat the hand.”

His low chuckle almost hid the relief. “There’s the boss I remember.”

After the call, Elspeth gave her guards their work: two with her, the rest to hold the office and quietly reach captains who had not yet stopped answering. She did not tell them the entire plan. Olek had built his coup from people who knew too much about how she moved.

In the elevator down, she called the western boss again.

“I know who killed your brother,” she said. “Olek Velcor ordered it. He wants your captains at the riverside abattoir before dawn. Police will close both ends of the road and leave him whoever crawls out.”

“You have proof?”

“Enough to keep you alive, not enough to make you forgive me.”

“Try money.”

“Olek has a narcotics load coming through the river depot before four. Take it. I’ll also sign over the two disputed blocks south of your clubs.”

Her older guard turned his face toward the brass elevator door. Those blocks collected from every bar, bookie, and dealer between the tram line and the water. The cocaine alone represented months of bribes and funerals.

“What do you want?” the western boss asked.

“Stay west of the iron bridge until sunrise. No shooters at the abattoir. No revenge east of the river tonight.”

“Your uncle offered me safe passage once.”

Elspeth watched the floor numbers descend. A stainless table. Her uncle’s signet ring in a gutter of blood. Olek pounding on a locked freezer door from the other side. The images came apart before they made a memory.

“My uncle offered it in my name,” she said.

“And then broke it.”

“Once.”

“They say you opened him from throat to belly on his own killing table.”

“People say it prettier every year.”

“Did you?”

The elevator opened. Three armed men in the lobby saw Elspeth and discovered urgent interest in the rain outside.

“The load and the blocks,” she said. “Those are my terms.”

“If your word fails tonight, I take four blocks and everyone in them.”

“If my word fails, there won’t be enough of me left to argue.”

The western boss breathed into the phone. “Done. Until sunrise.”

The hotel suite occupied the top floor of a building where elected men went to become appetites. Elspeth left the driver below and took her two soldiers up the service lift. Music pulsed behind the double doors. When the older soldier knocked, a naked man in his thirties opened with a champagne bottle in one hand and white powder crusting one nostril.

Elspeth walked past him.

The mirrored sitting room held five other adults in various states of undress. Two women sprawled across a velvet sofa with an adult zoning aide between them, her city lanyard the only thing she had kept on. A young man knelt at the glass table, sorting cocaine with Axholm’s gold credit card. The councillor stood near the bedroom in silk trousers, barefoot, his chest slick with someone else’s lipstick.

His bodyguard came out of the bathroom drawing a pistol.

Elspeth shot him through the cheek.

The back of his head struck the mirror first. Blood and bone stippled six reflections of the room. He slid down, leaving each version of himself wearing the same red ruin.

The kneeling man screamed. One of the women snatched the cocaine from the table before she ran. The zoning aide crawled after her on hands and knees, still wearing the lanyard.

Axholm stared at his bodyguard. “You fucking animal.”

“Put your shirt on.”

“This is an official residence.”

“It has a mirrored ceiling.”

“That man had a family.”

“You paid him to draw first.”

Her soldiers cleared the bedroom and bathroom. Nobody else had a gun. Elspeth kicked Axholm’s shirt across the carpet.

He dressed with badly controlled hands. “Do you know what follows if I disappear?”

“Yes. You return smelling like perfume, and your wife believes a smaller lie.”

“You’re exhausted.” He found his cuff links, dropped one, left it on the carpet. “You were reckless at nineteen too. I saw you at the abattoir table after your uncle died. Olek was the only man in that room who kept his head.”

Elspeth put the muzzle under his chin and lifted until he met her eyes. “Call your vice commander.”

Axholm’s phone trembled between his fingers. At Elspeth’s direction, he moved the predawn cordon away from the abattoir and sent the unit to Olek’s north garage on a civic phrase about an imminent weapons threat. He used the bloodless tone of a man adjusting sanitation crews. The commander did not question him.

“Keep the line open,” Elspeth said.

“That will sound irregular.”

“The corpse in your mirror sounds worse.”

While one soldier wrapped Axholm’s wounded vanity in a raincoat, Elspeth looked toward the window. Her eyes closed. They did not close for long. She knew because the song was still on the same filthy chorus when she opened them.

Axholm’s right hand had been inside the robe. Now it was empty.

She searched him again and found no second phone. She hated the missing seconds more than she hated him.

They put Axholm between Elspeth and the younger soldier in the back of the sedan. The older soldier took the front passenger seat. Their driver pulled into the rain. The vice commander remained a small, tinny voice inside Axholm’s coat, reporting that his unit was turning north.

The highway ran above the flooded market streets, concrete on both sides and black river beyond. A delivery van came up fast on the left. Elspeth noticed its lights vanish in the mirror.

“Down,” she said.

The van struck their rear quarter. Metal screamed. Gunfire stitched the driver’s door, crossed his spine, and took most of his jaw into the windshield. His hands locked on the wheel. The sedan climbed the barrier and dropped back hard enough to smash Elspeth’s teeth together.

The older soldier folded over three dark holes in his chest. The younger one fired through the rear window as the van struck them again.

Axholm shoved Elspeth toward the broken glass and clawed for the door. She drove her pistol into his mouth. “Try it.”

Another car blocked the lane ahead. Their dead driver’s foot kept the sedan pushing forward, engine howling against twisted metal. A shooter reached through the shattered rear window and caught Elspeth by the hair.

For one exhausted second she fought the hand and forgot there would be a body attached.

The man’s knife entered above her hip. Heat flooded her side. She trapped his wrist, dragged his face through the teeth of glass, and fired beneath his jaw. His skull emptied across the roof liner. The hand in her hair loosened one finger at a time.

The younger soldier climbed over Axholm and kicked the door open. He shot the second attacker beside the barrier. The man went down with his teeth scattered in the rain and did not move again.

Silence arrived as engine noise and wet breathing.

The older soldier was still alive in the front, barely. Blood bubbled between his fingers. The driver was beyond prayer. Axholm had a bullet through the meat of his shoulder and a second square black phone beneath his thigh.

Elspeth took it. The last sent message read: SHE HAS ME. RIVER ROAD.

Axholm began, “I can explain.”

She struck the wound with two fingers. His scream filled the wreck.

The younger soldier looked at her bleeding side. “We need a doctor.”

“After the abattoir.”

“We have one car that runs, and it belongs to them.”

“Then tonight it belongs to me.”

A stranger had stopped behind the wreck and was calling emergency services. Elspeth left the older soldier with him while Axholm, and the still-open vice-unit line in his coat, went with her. Whether police saved the soldier or finished Olek’s work was a debt she could not pay while Odette’s blood sat inside her coat.

The condemned abattoir crouched beside the river, windows bricked and loading doors rusted half open. Olek had chosen the place for the story it told before anyone spoke. Four years earlier, Elspeth had entered by the same loading hall as her uncle’s silent niece. She had left through the front office in his coat.

Tonight the younger soldier drove the captured car inside. White security lamps snapped on.

The loading hall was thirty yards long. Cracked tile climbed the walls. Overhead rails ended in black hooks that moved faintly in the draft. Olek stood behind a steel inspection table near the north doors with seven gunmen spaced along the room. Odette was tied to a chair beneath the eastern rail, face swollen, blouse red to the waist. One eye opened when Elspeth stepped from the car.

“You look like shit,” Odette said.

“You always liked the suit.”

“I liked taking it off.”

The words came dry and cold, the shape of intimacy after someone had weaponized it.

Olek smiled. “She broke into my office, stole my photographs, and killed one of my men getting that envelope to you. I caught her coming back for the rest. Loyal, if we use the word generously.”

Odette spat blood onto the tile. “Your man died stupid.”

“Did she tell you why she came back?” Olek asked. “Or did you decide the wet blouse meant love?”

Elspeth pulled Axholm out of the car. The councillor sagged against her, raincoat black with blood.

One gunman lowered his weapon an inch. Another looked toward Olek for an explanation. The official shield had arrived at Elspeth’s muzzle instead of in police cars.

Axholm saw the shift and began selling. “Mr. Velcor, this woman murdered my protective officer and abducted me. The city can still recognize the stable party here. Put down Kedri, release me, and I can contain the response.”

Olek studied him. “Can you restore the cordon?”

“The unit can be recalled.”

“No,” Elspeth said. “They’re raiding your north garage.”

Olek’s smile thinned.

Her phone rang. The western boss.

Elspeth answered on speaker. “Tell him.”

“We have the river load,” the older man said. Engines and shouting crowded his voice. “My people are west of the bridge. At sunrise, the two blocks are ours.”

Olek stared at her. “You gave him the product?”

“And the ground under two of your clubs.”

“That load carries us through winter. Those blocks pay thirty families. They’re not yours to give.”

The gunman nearest Odette spoke without looking away from Elspeth. “She said they were.”

Olek rounded on him. “She’s a sleepless cunt in a hat.”

The gunman’s mouth tightened, but he did not raise his weapon.

Axholm tried again. “Olek. We can characterize the garage action as a controlled seizure. The councillor’s office can protect an orderly transition.”

Elspeth shot him through the mouth.

The bullet broke teeth, exited beneath his ear, and painted the white tile behind Olek with a fan of red. Axholm remained standing for a strange second, lips working around nothing, then collapsed over the inspection table. His open call skittered across the floor. The vice commander’s voice asked what had happened.

“There’s your protection,” Elspeth said.

Olek looked at the councillor’s blood on his coat. “This is why she cannot lead you. She spends everything. Routes. Officials. People who love her.”

Odette’s good eye found Elspeth. Neither woman looked away.

“I built the organization she stole,” Olek said to the room. “I built her. When her uncle’s trick failed in this hall, she was nineteen and shaking so hard she couldn’t hold the knife. I opened the exits. I put her in his chair because I thought she could learn.”

Odette laughed, then coughed blood down her chin.

Olek pointed his gun at her. “Something funny?”

“You locked yourself in the gut room.”

The skin went white around Olek’s mouth.

“She opened the south gate,” Odette said. “Told the western survivors which door her uncle’s shooters were using. He’d promised them passage in her name, then set the hooks for them.”

“I gave her the knife,” Olek said.

“You dropped it when he started screaming.”

The old images locked into place around the present room: her uncle on the steel, asking who had taught her ingratitude; western men bleeding toward the open south gate; Olek’s fists hammering from inside the refrigerated room because he had mistaken hiding for patience.

Odette pulled one wrist against her binding. Elspeth saw the sliver of metal in her bloody palm and understood that she had been cutting herself free throughout the conversation.

“She killed her uncle for spending her name,” Odette said. “Paid the western debt in streets before breakfast. Then she kept you because a coward who thinks he made you is easy to watch.”

Olek shot at Odette.

She dropped sideways with the chair. The bullet tore through her upper arm instead of her chest. The younger soldier fired from behind the captured car and hit the gunman nearest the north door.

The loading hall exploded.

Two of Olek’s men fired toward the car. Glass burst inward. Elspeth dropped behind the engine block as the younger soldier took a round through his throat. His blood hit her cheek hot enough to feel alive. He kept firing until another bullet opened his neck and emptied him onto the floor.

The gunman posted over Odette stepped in to finish her. Her loosened hand came free. She seized his ankle, pulled him off balance, and drove her metal shard into the soft place beneath his jaw. He kicked against her until she took his pistol.

Elspeth shot one man crossing toward Odette. His knee burst backward. When he fell, she put another round through his face.

A second came around the west side of the car. Elspeth heard his shoes, turned toward them, and forgot the side door.

The man at the side door struck from there. His bullet plowed along her ribs and spun her against the hood. She fired too early. He caught her wrist and hammered it into the metal until the pistol dropped. His breath stank of whiskey and rotten meat.

She drove her forehead into his nose. Cartilage collapsed. He struck her wound; the room whitened. She found the attacker’s knife still lodged at her hip, ripped it free, and put it twice into the gunman’s belly. He tried to hold himself closed. Elspeth shoved him onto the broken windshield and left him sawing his palms against the glass.

Odette fired from the floor. A man above Elspeth jerked and fell between them, the back of his skull missing.

“Still like the suit?” Elspeth shouted.

“Less every minute.”

At the inspection table, Olek dragged Axholm’s body upright as cover and moved toward the old cutting room. Two of his men remained. One fired wildly at Odette. The other, the man who had said Elspeth gave the blocks, backed against the wall and let his gun fall.

Elspeth pointed at him. “Stay down and you drive.”

He went to his knees.

The last loyal gunman rushed Odette. She shot him in the stomach, missed the next shot, and he kicked the pistol away. He caught her by the throat and lifted her against the rail.

Elspeth crossed the open floor with blood filling her shoe. Olek fired from the cutting-room door. The round grazed her shoulder. She did not stop. She buried her knife behind the gunman’s ear and felt the point strike teeth from the wrong side.

He dropped Odette. Olek vanished into the cutting room.

Odette’s kicked-away pistol lay on the tile between the rail and the cutting-room door. Elspeth scooped it up; it still held rounds.

Elspeth followed.

The room beyond was smaller, tiled green, with drains like black mouths and the old stainless table bolted to the center. Olek waited behind it. He fired once and missed. The pistol clicked empty on the second pull.

“Three days without sleep,” he said. “Half your people gone. Axholm dead. The west owns your powder and your streets. Look at what you saved.”

“My chair.”

He threw the gun down and spread his hands.

Elspeth stopped across the table. Blood ran from her side, down her wrist, from somebody else’s face across her shirt. Behind her, Odette crawled into the doorway and held the wall.

Olek’s voice softened. “You always give terms. That’s what your name means. Give me a car and an hour. I disappear.”

Her phone rang again. Elspeth answered without looking away from him.

“We’re clear,” the western boss said. “No one crossed the bridge. Your two blocks are being marked now.”

“They’re yours,” Elspeth said. “The load too. My word stands.”

Olek listened. Hope entered his face because he still thought a rule that bound her must protect him.

“You heard him,” he said. “Your name buys mercy.”

“No. My name means I keep what I offer.” She stepped around the table. “I never offered you shit.”

“Elspeth.”

“You spent it anyway.”

She shot him at arm’s length. The first round broke his breastbone and folded him against the table. The second entered above his eye. He slid beneath the steel where her uncle had died, his hand smearing the leg on the way down.

Odette watched without satisfaction. “I left the envelope because I knew he’d use me to bring you here.”

“You did bring me here.”

“I also cleared the room for you.”

“You call this clear?”

Odette looked across the bodies. “I’m concussed. My standards are flexible.”

Outside, sirens multiplied along the river road.

The gunman who had surrendered drove. Elspeth sat in the back of the captured car with Odette’s head against her thigh and a pistol against the driver’s seat. The rear window was gone. Dawn rain blew in, cold on their blood.

Elspeth called a doctor who treated wounds without asking how they happened. Then she called the western boss and repeated the terms on a line with two of her surviving captains. The blocks were gone. The narcotics were gone. Nobody was to interfere before sunrise. Each word reduced what she owned and strengthened the one thing Olek had failed to steal.

Odette opened her good eye. “Don’t make the envelope into a declaration.”

“I wasn’t planning to.”

“I chose you. Tonight. Don’t get greedy.”

Elspeth put the gray envelope back inside her ruined coat. “You came back for the rest of the proof.”

“I hate unfinished work.”

“That’s why I fucked you.”

Odette’s mouth twitched, then tightened with pain. “Liar.”

The city ahead was turning gray. Police lights moved toward the river in long blue chains. Behind them waited a dead councillor, a dead operations chief, two loyal bodies, a third loyal man bleeding in a wreck, Olek’s scattered crews, and enough evidence to start a war inside city hall. Ahead waited captains who had spent the night deciding whether twenty-three was old enough to die for.

Elspeth called every one of them at once.

“Noon,” she said when the line filled. Her voice sounded scraped raw, but it carried. “Come to the west hall unarmed. Pick whose name you answer to. Anyone who stays away belongs to Olek, and I’ll hunt them before Axholm’s people hunt me.”

The surrendered gunman flinched as she pressed the pistol harder into his seat. The car drove east through rain and sirens. One by one, the men on the line answered, “Noon.”

stories.title: The Fourth Blood
stories.prompt: You're a sorcerer in the mountains, trying to unlock the secret of immortality thru blood magic. Instead, you're starting to figure out that humans have blood types.
stories.body:
# The Fourth Blood

I peeled Quenril's labels from the six cups before the gum had dried.

They watched me from the other side of the stone table, pen halted over their ledger.
