"I will not make another. This one comes off now, while neither of you is in transfer."

"No."

Ordran had expected the princess. The second refusal surprised him.

"No," Dovra repeated. Their voice came slowly, each word carried on a shallow portion of breath. "You will not cut it without telling Basma what follows."

"She can be told after you are out of range."

"There is no out of range. The harness learned her fire from my body. If I fly while it is awake, it will pull through distance until one of us breaks."

Ordran knew that. He had built no such reach into it, but nine months of repeated transfer could teach silver habits its maker had not intended. He disliked magic most when it resembled law: precedent accumulating where mercy had once been.

"I can deaden it first," he said. "Quietly. You could be through the west window before anyone knows."

Dovra studied him. "I offered Basma one night. I offered because she was burning and afraid. I did not offer to vanish while she slept and leave her to wake burning again."

Basma knelt beside the dragon's head. "You see? Dovra wants to stay."

The dragon's transparent wing edge clicked as it shifted. "I want you to live. I wanted to stay one night. I endured the second because you were still ill. On the sixth morning I asked for the catch to be opened. Your mother called the locked buckle her mercy. Two hundred and seventy-one temporary mornings have passed since then."

Basma's hand stopped a finger's width from Dovra's cheek.

Ordran looked at the crown stamped upon the brass housing. His own catch could not have taken that casing; its hinge had been sawed out and a longer tongue riveted through the silver. The work was careful. Official.

"You altered it," he said to Ivara.

"I ordered the armorer to do so."

Basma stood. "You told me Ordran had changed his mind."

"You had nearly died. Dovra was still uncertain. I believed one more day without argument would let everyone recover."

"And then?" Ordran asked.

"Then Basma would not surrender the key."

The princess drew her hidden hand forward. A brass key hung from her fist on a red cord. "Do not put this all on me now. You locked it. He built it. Dovra kept saying yes until suddenly the yes had footnotes. None of you has standing to judge what I did to stay alive."

It was an excellent defense because nearly all of it was true. Ordran felt the old pleasure of a clean incision nonetheless.

"Dovra's lack of violence was not agreement," he said. "It was care you found convenient."

The bulb in Basma's other hand softened.

Ordran saw it sag between her fingers. He saw the copper vanes on Dovra's collar turn toward her as flower heads turn toward the sun. Then Basma doubled over with a sound of shocked anger, and a red thread raced under her skin from wrist to throat.

The harness closed.

Dovra's head struck the carpet. Light flooded the clear rims of their scales, rushing inward. The brass housing began a steady metallic ticking.

"Don't touch it," Basma gasped. "Let it finish. It is always worse if you interrupt."

Ordran tore open his case. His wedge would sever the silver in one blow, but during transfer the stored heat would recoil through both linked bodies. He used the soft copper instead, looping it behind the royal housing and twisting until the metal bit his fingers. One tick faltered. On the next, he drove his file between the clasp's teeth.

The mechanism jammed halfway.

Dovra dragged in a breath. Basma screamed.

Flame ran up her arms in wavering bands, bright but not yet feeding on cloth. The room's damp hangings began to steam. Around Dovra, half-formed glass shells dropped from their mouth and shattered against the hearthstone.

"What have you done?" Ivara seized Ordran's shoulder.

"Returned half your daughter's illness to her. Bought the dragon minutes. The clasp will force itself past my file if we leave it loaded."

"Then take it out," Basma said through clenched teeth.

"No."

The word was his this time. He had said it too quickly and liked the sound too much.

Water would not quench Basma's fire, but stone and evaporation could spare her lungs and the palace. He remembered the old bath chamber behind the tiled wall, abandoned when a roof beam had cracked. Its upper smoke vent opened toward the marsh. If it still opened at all.

"Can you walk?" he asked Dovra.

"If the floor is clear."

Ivara was already hauling cushions out of the way. She kicked aside the rolling bulbs, then caught one in her hem and went hard onto one knee. For once she did not ask anyone to lift her. She rose, shoved a table against the wall, and shouldered open the bath door.

Cold damp breathed through.

They moved badly and together. Dovra crawled with wings clamped close so the glassed edges would not strike the doorframe. Ordran walked beside the collar, keeping both hands on the file as the harness tried to chew through it. Basma followed with one arm around her mother, leaving scorched footprints on the tiles. Each time her knees failed, Ivara took more of her weight.

The baths were a sunken square of blue stone under a ribbed ceiling. The pools had been drained, but rainwater stood in the channels. A copper wheel controlled the vent high above them. Its chain was furred with green.

"Cloths," Ordran told Ivara. "Soak them. Pack them at Basma's neck and under her arms. Keep them wet."

Ivara lowered her daughter onto the shallowest step and obeyed. Basma slapped the first cloth away. The queen picked it up, soaked it again, and held it where it would cool the blood without covering her daughter's face.

Ordran cut the vent chain free of its corrosion. The wheel groaned. Two shutters opened a hand's breadth, spilling a blade of night across the floor. Not enough for Dovra. He braced a shoulder under one spoke.

Behind him the harness ticked against the file.

"When I pull the wedge," he told Dovra, "brace your forefeet against the pool rim. On three, force your throat upward. Basma, turn your face from the collar. Your Majesty, hold her wrists."

"Physician," Dovra said.

"There is no time. One."

"Why are you still giving orders over my body?"

His hand remained on the wedge. The answer that came first was because I know better. It had carried him through fever tents and birthing rooms and battle yards. It had also built a catch for one desperate night and then left a dragon wearing its consequence for a season.

The harness ticked again.

Ordran released the wedge. "If I cut it while the transfer is active, the heat may strike both your hearts. If Basma opens the royal lock before the clasp forces past my file, the draw will end and I can remove the harness safely. If we wait, the file will fail. If you take another full transfer, I expect you to die. I cannot promise Basma will survive without you."

Dovra's throat worked against the silver. "Then I choose no more heat. Can you help her?"

"I can cool the blood at her neck and groin. I can keep her airway open if the smoke thickens. I can try."

Basma twisted away from her mother's hands. Fire showed at the roots of her hair now, a fine restless gold. "Dovra. One last time. Please. Let him plan after. Let me learn after. You have borne so many that this one cannot matter more."

"It matters to me," Dovra said.

"One smaller draw, then. Only until the pain stops."

"No."

"Not forever. Not even until morning."

"Basma. No."

The princess stared at them. Terror stripped the courtliness from her face. Ordran had seen that look nine months before, when she woke in a bed of smoking feathers and found a dragon drinking death from her lungs. It would have been easy to call her selfish from across a cool room. Here the heat lifted blisters on his knuckles.

The red cord around her wrist began to smolder.

"Mother," Basma said. "Order them."

Ivara's hands tightened on the soaked cloth. "I have given that order once."

"Then give it again!"

"No."

The clasp gave a sharp internal snap. Ordran's file bent.

Basma cried out and dragged the key over her head. For a moment Ordran thought she meant to throw it into the empty pool. Instead she thrust it into the brass housing at Dovra's throat. Her fingers shook too hard to turn it.

Ivara reached toward her, then stopped short of touching the key.

Basma set her other hand over the first. The skin along both wrists was reddening. She turned.

The royal housing sprang open. The copper vanes went slack.

Basma flung the key at her mother. "Keep it, since you like deciding what mercy is."

Ivara let it strike her breast and fall. She did not reach for it. She gathered Basma against her instead as the next wave of fire lifted from the princess's body.

The harness was inert under Ordran's hands. His cutters bit through the altered hinge. Silver peeled away from Dovra's throat, taking three small scales and no more. The dragon lurched free.

"The vent," Dovra said.

Ordran ran to the copper wheel. It had opened only a hand's breadth before. He planted both boots against the pool rim and hauled until the chain skipped a tooth and the shutters spread wide enough for the long head, the narrow shoulders, the glass-edged wings. Cold rushed into the room. It struck Basma's flames sideways and filled the baths with white steam.

Dovra climbed the slanted pool wall. One hind foot slipped. The clear rim of a wing struck tile and chimed, but did not break. Ordran caught himself reaching to guide the leg and lowered his hand.

The dragon paused with their head in the night.

"Dovra," Basma said. Her voice was small beneath the hiss of wet cloth. "Will I see you again?"

Dovra did not turn. "I do not know."

Then they pulled through the opening.

For three wingbeats Ordran thought the glassed edges would not hold. Dovra dropped below the sill, out of sight. A pale shape rose beyond the wall, caught the low wind, and flew toward the cold black spread of the marsh. No one called after them.

Basma's fire crested before the shape disappeared.

Ordran returned to the pool. He made Ivara move the cloths in sequence, never leaving one long enough to trap heat. He kept Basma on her side when the coughing began. The princess cursed him, then Dovra, then her mother in language precise enough to reassure him. When she clawed at the scorched skin of her arms, Ivara held her wrists against the tile and accepted every word.

"How long?" Ivara asked.

"I don't know."

"You always know."

"You always preferred that I sound certain."

So they worked without certainty. Steam pearled the queen's crown. Basma shook until her teeth knocked together, though heat still shimmered above her skin. Ordran treated the two burns that worried him and left the smaller ones alone. Beyond the open vent, the sky thinned from black to iron gray.

At last the red under Basma's skin faded to the ordinary flush of fever. Her pulse slowed. She opened her eyes and found her mother's face above hers.

"Get away from me," she whispered.

Ivara eased her grip but stayed kneeling in the rain channel, one hand beneath Basma's head so it would not rest on stone.

Ordran checked the princess's throat and listened to her lungs. Painful breaths, shallow but clear. She would scar at both wrists. She would live through this morning. Beyond that, he would not counterfeit knowledge.

"You will come tomorrow," Basma said.

"If you ask me tomorrow."

Her eyes narrowed at the condition. For a moment he saw the familiar machinery of rank searching for purchase. Then another tremor took her, and she closed her eyes. "Come tomorrow. Bring no harness."

"I will."

The marsh wind flowed through the bath, cold enough now that Ivara covered her daughter with her own cloak. Far out above the reeds, Dovra had become a pale mark against the growing light. The dragon flew unevenly, favoring the left wing, but each stroke carried them farther.

Ordran watched until he could no longer distinguish Dovra from the morning. He kept his mouth closed. Beside him, the queen remained on her knees, one hand cradling her daughter's head above the stone.

stories.title: Coiled Together
stories.prompt: Everyone knows the serpentfolk lure travelers into their caves and devour them. When you wake wrapped tightly in the coils of one of their most feared queens, however, she seems less interested in eating you than in keeping you—and insists that you were the one who begged her not to let go.
stories.body:
# Coiled Together

The first thing I knew was warmth. The second was that it had muscles.

Something thicker than my chest lay across my thighs. Another length circled my waist, pinned my left arm to my side, crossed my ribs, and rose behind my shoulders in a wall of dark gold scales. When I tried to sit up, the whole arrangement tightened with quiet, effortless attention.

I stopped moving.

My clothes were still on. My shirt was torn at one shoulder and wet to the skin, but my belt remained buckled, my boots laced, and nothing hurt except my skull. That should have been reassuring. It was difficult to feel reassured when I could not move from shoulders to ankles.

A woman's face leaned over mine.

Black hair hung loose around bronze-brown cheeks. Her eyes caught the cave's amber lamplight and returned it in narrow green slits. From the waist up she might have passed for a court beauty dressed in hammered-gold ornaments and a wrap of gray silk. From the waist down she filled half the chamber.

I knew those scales from bounty sketches. Every caravan scout did.

“The Gilded Hunger,” I said. My voice scraped.

Her mouth curved just enough to show the tips of two teeth. “Humans do favor the name they gave me over the one I possess.”

“Sivareth.”

“Better.”

At thirty-two, I had survived a bridge collapse, two border skirmishes, and an ox maddened by bluefly fever. I had never expected to die in bed. The bed, I noticed, was a broad nest of furs tucked into a hollow of the Hushvault. Clay lamps burned in wall niches. Beyond them, the chamber ended at a black cleft from which water hissed far below.

I tested the coil across my chest. It yielded less than stone.

“If you're going to eat me,” I said, “do I get to stand first?”

“You may stand when the glass-rain weakens.” Her gaze traveled over my face with an attention that felt worse than hunger. “I am not eating you.”

“Forgive my lack of gratitude.”

“I already have. You were more courteous while unconscious.”

I twisted again, sharper this time. The loop around my ribs flexed. Not tighter, exactly. It followed me, allowing no gap.

“Let me go.”

Something changed in her expression. Not anger. Disappointment, perhaps, which was more unsettling.

“You asked me not to.”

“I am asking now.”

“You are fevered, your last hour is broken, and six armed humans wait above the eastern throat.” She spoke as if listing rain, altitude, and poor road stone. “I made you a promise.”

“I don't remember making you one.”

“You did not. You begged. I promised.”

Outside the chamber, the storm hurled a fistful of glass against rock. The sound went on and on, a thousand tiny blades skittering down the mountain. Our caravan had made camp below the ridge before dawn. Captain Halvek Prynn had sent me ahead to find a sheltered way through. He had tied a charm around my neck, touched two fingers to it, and said even serpentfolk disliked the smell.

After that, I had only scraps: a yellow gleam under stone, my boot sliding, a drop where the floor should have been.

I swallowed. “Free my right arm.”

Sivareth studied me. “Why?”

“Because I asked.”

The upper coil lifted at once.

Cold air struck my wet sleeve. I pulled my arm free, half expecting the loop to snap shut and break it, but she settled her weight beneath my elbow instead. I touched my face, throat, ribs. No blood. No punctures. A tender stripe crossed my palms, as if a cord had burned through them. My knife was gone. So was the small pack I wore when scouting.

The charm's leather thong remained around my neck. It had been cleanly cut below the knot.

“You took it.”

“I removed a lure.”

“A ward.”

“Is that what the man with the red scarf called it?”

Halvek's scarf had once been crimson. Six dusty seasons had reduced it to the color of old brick. I had not mentioned him.

Sivareth reached to a stone shelf without shifting the coils around me. Between two claws she held a copper cage no longer than my thumb. Inside it gleamed a bead of cloudy resin. She had split the cage lengthwise. Even from the bed I caught its scent: hot metal, sweet rot, and the heavy musk that had followed us up the ridge.

I had blamed the pack mules.

“Your kind made this,” she said. “Copper drawn through a square plate. Hide glue boiled with pine gum. The cord was knotted by a right hand missing the tip of its smallest finger.”

Halvek had lost that fingertip to frostbite.

“You expect me to accept that because you can describe a trinket?”

“No. I expect you to be stubborn until the truth has bitten you somewhere tender.”

I reached for the cage. She let me take it.

The copper edges had been filed with a pattern of shallow nicks. Not serpent marks. Caravan marks, used to tell sealed parcels apart in darkness: two, pause, three. Halvek's private stores. I pressed a thumbnail into the resin. Its skin broke, releasing another breath of musk, and the room seemed to tilt.

Rain cut my cheeks. A ledge shuddered beneath my boots. Someone shouted from above, not in warning but with furious impatience: *Go farther in.*

Then the shelf fell.

I came back with my hand clenched. The copper cage had bitten my palm.

Sivareth's hand hovered near my wrist without touching. “That poison coaxes heat from a body and muddles the newest memories. It makes prey bright to my senses. It also makes the prey wander.”

“You sound familiar with it.”

“Three hunters used it last spring. Two fled when I found them. One reached the clutch passage.” Her teeth showed again, without humor. “The stories told about me are not all lies, Kerric Alver.”

Hearing my full name in her mouth chilled me more than the rain. “How do you know that?”

“You told me while I held you over the chasm. You also told me you were too old to die for Halvek Prynn's bad judgment.”

“That sounds like me.”

“Then perhaps some of your judgment survived.”

She shifted beneath me. Scale slid over scale with the soft scrape of dry leaves, and my treacherous body relaxed into the renewed warmth before my mind could stop it. Sivareth noticed. Her gaze softened in a way I did not trust.

“Do not mistake that for permission,” I said.

“I mistake nothing.”

“You're holding me after I told you to let go.”

Her coils went very still.

“You said it while afraid and ill.”

“I am still allowed to mean it.”

She looked toward the dark cleft. “And I am allowed to prevent a fevered man from walking into a barbed net.”

“A healer can prevent him. A queen can advise him. A captor decides his answer does not count.”

The thin membranes at her temples flared, then flattened. She had ruled the Hushvault for seventy winters, according to road tales, and killed challengers older than my grandfather. I had managed to offend her before breakfast.

Instead of squeezing, she unlooped the length across my ribs.

“Look,” she said.

Set into the wall opposite us was a sheet of pale mineral, thin as horn and veined with gold. Sivareth lifted one lamp from its niche and snuffed it between finger and thumb. The mineral dimmed. Then cloudy blooms appeared across it: one large amber shape around the bed, my smaller red-gold heat nested inside; six pale smudges in a hooked line above the eastern passage.

No, seven. One stood farther back near the mouth, broad at the shoulders.

“Stone remembers warmth for several breaths,” she said. “The wall is thin there. It cannot tell me why they wait. It tells me one carries a bow, two hold the corners of something wider than their bodies, and your red-scarfed friend remains where the rain cannot touch him.”

One of the smaller blooms vanished. A moment later it returned beside another.

“It can't show a bow,” I said.

“It shows a warm arm held away from a warm chest.”

“Could be a shovel.”

“Then he means to garden in the dark.”

Despite myself, a laugh escaped me. It hurt my head. Sivareth's smile widened, pleased and proprietary, and the sound died in my throat.

She touched the mineral. The vast coil around my legs shifted closer.

“You are safe here,” she said. “I will keep you until the hunters are gone.”

“Until when?”

“Until you are safe.”

“That's not a time.”

“Safety is not governed by clocks.”

“Nor by queens, however much they might prefer it.” I pushed at the last loop across my waist. “Release me completely. Give me my knife and pack. I will see the entrance myself.”

Her claws curled against the fur.

“No,” she said.

“Then you are keeping a prisoner, not a promise.”

Water thundered through the lower cave. The heat-shapes on the mineral held their positions.

Sivareth watched me for so long that I became conscious of every place her scales touched: the pressure under my knees, the broad warmth along my spine, the tip of her tail lying over my left boot as gently as a hand. Want lived plainly in her expression. Not appetite for flesh. Something lonelier and, in its way, no less dangerous.

“When you fell,” she said, “I caught your wrist. The lure had made you slick with sweat. You were sliding out of my hand. I wound around you because there was no ledge for my weight, and you said, ‘Don't let go. Whatever happens, don't let go.’”

A shred of memory returned: green eyes below me in the dark, a gold-brown arm stretched until it trembled, the terrible swing of my body over open air. My own voice tore out of me: *Don't let go.* Her answer came through clenched teeth: *I will not.* My hands burned because I had clung to her wrist.

“Then I woke,” Sivareth continued, “and for one astonishing moment a human wanted my strength instead of fearing it. You cannot expect me to discover that I was mistaken about the moment and enjoy the correction.”

“No,” I said. “But I expect you to make it.”

Her throat worked once. Then the Hushvault moved around me.

Coil after coil drew away. Air found my body in cold strips. I sat up, dizzy, while the immense lengths slid from the nest and gathered behind Sivareth's human torso. Nothing barred the way between me and the passage.

She reached beneath a folded fur, drew out my sheathed knife, and laid it across my open palm. My pack followed. “You are released, Kerric Alver.”

I strapped on the knife. “Thank you.”

“I do not enjoy the correction.”

“I noticed.”

“If you step onto the upper shelf, the net will take you. If you lead them deeper, I will kill any who approach the clutch chamber.”

There was no boast in it. That steadied me more than a claim of harmlessness would have.

I found the eastern passage where the mineral wall narrowed. Meltwater foamed ankle-deep along one side, carrying chips of volcanic glass that glittered in my lamplight. The main tunnel climbed toward a gray mouth fifty paces ahead. Beneath a low arch, the floor pinched into a throat scarcely wide enough for Sivareth's largest coils. Above it ran an old runoff gutter. Someone had stuffed the drainage notch with rolled canvas and tied it off to keep the hunters' ledge dry. Water trembled behind the plug.

Halfway to the mouth, I crouched behind a broken spur of stone. Glass-rain hissed beyond the overhang. I could have stepped outside and gone downslope alone. Fever tugged at my balance; the storm would have opened my face before I found the caravan tents.

A pebble clicked overhead.

“Hold,” Halvek whispered. His voice came through the rock as clearly as it had across a hundred campfires. “The gold one takes the bait first. Then drop both sides.”

Someone murmured, “What about Kerric?”

“If he can walk, he can duck.”

“And if he can't?”

Silence answered.

I pressed my hand against the cut thong at my neck. Another memory rose, whole enough to hurt: Halvek kneeling beside the weakened shelf before he sent me forward, hiding a small iron wedge inside his sleeve. His missing fingertip white against the stone. *Go farther in.*

One royal scale would pay a caravan's debts for a season. Halvek had spoken often of families waiting through winter. Apparently he had decided one scout was a fair price for all of them.

I backed down the passage.

Sivareth waited exactly where I had left her. She had put out the lamps near the cleft and gathered herself into a strike so compact it made the chamber seem larger. Her eyes dropped to the knife in my hand.

“They are there,” I said.

“Yes.”

“They used me.”

“Yes.”

I hated that she did not sound triumphant. It left me nothing easy to fight.

“The throat is flooding,” I said. “You cannot pass it quickly without exposing your back to the shelf. The net has barbs. But they've blocked the old drain to keep their footing. Cut the canvas and their ledge washes out.”

“My hands cannot reach the notch while I shield my spine.”

“Mine can.” I set my pack down and checked the knife's edge. “If you carry me.”

Sivareth's coils stirred, then stopped. “Ask clearly.”

“First, every part of me stays loose until we agree.”

She lowered her hands. “Agreed.”

“You may coil around me until we are back across the flooded throat. No crushing. Leave room for a full breath. My knife stays in my right hand. If I say stop, you let go immediately, even if you think I'm wrong.”

She repeated each condition, word for word. Formal precision stripped the warmth from her voice, but could not hide the hunger beneath it.

Then she asked, “What happens when you say stop?”

“You let go.”

“Even if I am afraid for you.”

“Especially then.”

Sivareth bowed her head. “Ask me.”

The old warnings crowded close. Never invite a serpentfolk to touch you. Never bargain inside her den. Never let one learn the shape of your fear. They had kept me alive on bad roads. They had not prepared me for this.

“Hold me,” I said. “On those terms.”

She moved slowly enough that I could have stepped away. The first coil passed behind my knees and lifted. Another curved around my hips, firm but not fixed, and a third rose over my left shoulder to shield my chest. I could draw a full breath. My right arm remained free, the knife angled away from both our bodies.

“How is this?” she asked.

My heart hammered against her scales. “Acceptable.”

“A stirring declaration.”

“Get us through alive and I may improve it.”

She flowed into the passage.

Speed changed everything. The body that had seemed too large for the Hushvault narrowed, lengthened, and found purchase on wet stone where my boots would have slipped. Her scales flexed under me in waves. At the throat she turned her back to the high shelf and raised two coils like a roof.

The barbed net fell.

It struck with a clang and a chorus of shouts. Hooks scraped gold scales, caught between them, and pulled tight. Sivareth hissed beside my ear. The sound vibrated through my bones. Her loop around my waist contracted, stopped before it stole my breath, then eased by a finger's width.

“Kerric!” Halvek shouted. “Down! Crawl out!”

I saw his boots on the shelf through a gap in the net. The canvas plug bulged above us, its retaining cord knotted around a stone tooth. Sivareth surged forward. An arrow cracked against the coil shielding my chest.

I leaned out and slashed once.

The cord parted. The canvas shot from the notch. A wall of black runoff burst over the hunters' ledge, full of glass grit and storm gravel. Men yelled and scrambled uphill. One side of the net went slack; Sivareth rolled, tore free of the other anchors, and drove through the throat with me held at the center of her motion.

We reached the far spur as a section of ledge collapsed into the channel. The hunters crowded onto a high tongue of rock beyond the break, hemmed against the outer wall. Bruised, drenched, alive. Halvek clung to an anchor spike, his red scarf pasted to his throat.

“Kerric!” he called. “Come up here. One scale, that's all. It feeds every family in the train through winter.”

“You loosened the shelf under me.”

His eyes flicked toward the others. “I knew she would catch the lure.”

Not me. The lure.

Sivareth lifted her head above the broken ledge. The hooked pupils of her eyes thinned. “If you cross into my lower halls again,” she told them, “your families may divide the bounty on your boots.”

No one mistook her meaning.

Halvek held out his hand to me. “You know what she is.”

I did. She had warned me more honestly than he had.

“Storm should drop by noon,” I said. “The eastern slope will be passable an hour after. Tell the caravan I found another road.”

Sivareth carried me back through the throat while the hunters argued behind us. Only when we entered the warm chamber did she lower my boots to the fur.

“Stop,” I said.

Her coils opened.

There was no pause, no plea, no clever claim that the danger remained. One instant I rested inside a living wall of warmth; the next I stood free, swaying in soaked boots with my knife still in my hand. Sivareth withdrew so quickly that the last loop struck the floor with a heavy rustle.

She turned her face toward the dark cleft. “The storm will weaken by noon. I will show you a western path when you wish to leave.”

I sheathed the knife.

On a shelf beyond the nest stood a clay pot, a bundle of dried river fish, and six carefully stoppered jars. Ordinary provisions, except that the jars had been arranged by someone with claws and the pot was large enough to bathe a child. My stomach cramped at the smell of smoke and salt.

“You said you weren't eating me,” I said. “You never said whether you would feed me.”

Sivareth glanced back. For an instant, the queen who had ruled seventy winters looked startled. “For how long?”

“One meal. One honest conversation. Then I decide what story goes down the mountain with me.”

“I will not flatter your species.”

“That would make two of us.”

She busied herself with the pot while I sat on the edge of the furs. The chamber felt larger now that I knew I could cross it. It also felt colder. Water squelched in my boots when I stretched my feet toward the nearest lamp.

Her gaze dropped to my boots.

The tip of her tail paused a short distance from my ankles. “May I?”

I looked at the open passage, my knife, and the queen waiting for an answer.

“One coil,” I said. “Around my feet.”

Her scales whispered over the stone, stopping just before they touched me.

“How tight?” she asked.

stories.title: Held Together
stories.prompt: a Married hero couple going through a rough patch get captured by a married villain couple and are surprised at how healthy their relationship is.
stories.body:
# Held Together

Aveline Ormont woke with Harlan Ives's spine braced against hers and his elbow trying to occupy the same narrow inch as her ribs.

"Don't move," they said together.

His laugh came out thin. "Good. Still communicating."

"You moved on two."

"You changed the plan after one."

The room returned to her by pieces: a white ceiling too low for a clean leap, walls faced in gray ceramic, a ventilation slot near the top, and four black bands fastening their wrists and ankles to a jointed metal frame. They sat on the floor back-to-back, knees bent in opposite directions. A harness crossed Aveline's sternum. Every breath pressed Harlan's shoulder blades into hers.

The half-masks were still strapped to their faces. On incident reports they were Tensile and Sideslip; the aliases kept witness accounts tidy, not their identities secret. After nine years of marriage, they almost never used them for each other.

Beyond the wall, the stolen phase-key sang on a rising, glassy note.

The prototype could uncouple bonded matter for seven seconds. Its designers meant it for jammed rescue machinery. The remote buyer had not paid the Dacres for humanitarian intentions.

That sound pulled the last seconds of the fight into order. A loading dock. The key suspended in its transport cage. Sana Dacre's gloved hand held inside one of Keaton Dacre's pale spatial offsets and passing through a sealed panel where no hand belonged. Keaton bending the distance between two support pillars until Harlan's charge carried him sideways. Harlan calling three. Aveline releasing on the count she had heard. The concrete floor twisting under her field, not when she commanded it but a sick beat later. Then the Dacres' damping net folding around them.

Six weeks ago, she and Harlan would have blamed bad acoustics and started solving the room. Tonight blame arrived first, already sharpened by practice.

"You said three after you went," she said.

"I went when you pulled."

"I hadn't pulled yet."

"Then the dock threw itself at me for personal reasons."

Aveline tested the band at her right wrist with a thread of tensile force. Her field caught the load between steel and bone. Usually she could stretch that invisible line, store the strain, and cast it somewhere useful.

The wall answered with a soft mechanical click. The band tightened.

Harlan jerked against her. A second click drew the harness snug enough to shorten her next breath.

"What did I just say?" he asked.

"You said don't move, then moved."

"Because my hand was being crushed."

"It's not crushed."

"Excellent. I feel better now that you've ruled on it."

The phase-key's whine climbed another fraction. Aveline counted three dark circular nodes in the nearest wall, then found two more reflected in the metal frame. A damping room: directed force went into the walls, came back as torsion, and wound their restraints tighter. Harlan's phasing would count as a change in force. The Dacres had built the cell for them, or for people enough like them that the distinction did not help.

Above, voices passed through the vent.

"Extraction is at forty-one," Sana said. Her tone was brisk, each word fitted like a tool into foam. "Buyer window closes in two hours. I need the narrow coupler."

"Left drawer," Keaton said.

"You moved it."

"I prevented you from throwing it through the wall."

"That was the broad coupler. It had forfeited indoor privileges."

A drawer rolled open. Metal rattled. The Dacres, Latchkey and Parallax in the case files, had spent eleven years turning theft into a specialty and pursuit into a marital hobby. Aveline had expected the private workshop, the redundant escape route, the capture without needless injury. She had not expected bickering about tool storage while two kidnapped heroes sat behind the wall.

"I'll finish the cradle," Sana said. "You take guard and eat something."

"You take guard. I can finish the cradle."

"You cut a seal with the polarity reversed last month."

"Once. The seal was designed by a sadist."

"Guard, Keaton. Food. In that order."

"Half a sandwich now, guard, other half during the transfer. You haven't eaten either."

A pause.

"That allocation is acceptable," Sana said.

Footsteps crossed overhead. A drawer closed. Someone wound an old kitchen timer, its spring ticking with absurd domestic patience.

Harlan shifted his head until it almost touched hers. "No one stages that much boring logistics for an audience they think is unconscious."

"They know we're awake."

"You think the sandwich is psychological warfare?"

"I think Parallax bent a twenty-meter dock into a cupboard and put us in it. Forgive me if I don't nominate him for husband of the year."

"I didn't nominate him. I said he remembered lunch."

"Unlike you, who remembers everything except the count."

His shoulders went still. She felt the stillness because nine years of marriage had taught her the difference between Harlan resting and Harlan withdrawing. Once, she had known better than to follow him into that quiet with a blade. Lately she seemed to keep one ready.

The timer ticked. The key whined. On the wall opposite, a pale outline of a hand appeared, measuring an empty span between two nodes. It repeated the gesture twice, fingers opening and closing, although no one stood there. One of Keaton's spatial projections had left an afterimage attached to the ceramic. Sana could steer those offsets well enough to put her hands through a lock, but reconciling the false angle with her own sight brought on the aura. The residues themselves lasted minutes and were harmless, useful mostly for making witnesses doubt where a body had been.

The ghost hand touched the third node. Aveline marked the sequence.

Above them, Sana said, "There. The aura's back."

The scrape of a stool stopped.

Keaton's voice lost its amusement. "How much?"

"Bright edge on the left. No occlusion."

"Then no more projections."

"I reported an aura. I did not hand you my decision."

"I think continuing is unsafe."

"You have now told me twice."

"Because you're about to put your hands through a compression fold while half-blind."

"Once is concern. Twice is you sliding into command."

Silence caught in the vent. Aveline waited for the explosion. Harlan's back had become attentive against hers.

Keaton said, "Blue mug."

No answer came. Footsteps moved apart, one set toward the workbench and one toward the far side of the room. The kitchen timer was lifted, turned, and set down again. A shorter interval began.

"Code phrase," Harlan murmured.

"Or theater."

For ninety seconds, only the timer and phase-key spoke. Then it rang.

Keaton returned first. "Do you want the transfer delayed, the physical extraction reassigned, or me to trust your assessment and stop hovering?"

"Reassign extraction," Sana said. "I keep the geometry calls. You can refuse any fold you can't hold. You cannot revise my calls without asking."

"Agreed."

"And I will eat the other half of your sandwich."

"That was not among the offered remedies."

"I am broadening the remedy."

The work resumed.

Aveline stared at the ghost hand until its fingers faded from the wall. "Convenient," she said.

"What is?"

"Their little demonstration. They pause, they negotiate, they steal the key."

"Yes," Harlan said. "Terrible people. Alarmingly functional meeting."

She pressed the back of her skull against his. "We have a window before the buyer arrives. Old release. I load the right band; you phase on three."

"We don't know how much torsion the room has stored."

"Then phase briefly."

"You just accused me of going early."

"I'm giving you a count."

She felt his breath leave. "Fine."

Aveline gathered the smallest useful line between her wrist and the frame. One. The field took tension, a tautness under her skin. Two. Harlan's body became strangely absent against her, pressure vanishing from one shoulder before the other.

The room boomed.

He snapped solid before three. The wrist bands spun half a turn, wrenching them both toward the frame. Aveline let her field go. Its delayed recoil struck after her command, shoving the load sideways. Pain flashed across her ribs. One wall node flared amber.

Harlan made a sound through his teeth.

"You came out early."

"Astute."

"Harlan."

His left arm lay across her hip where the twisted frame had thrown it. She caught his hand. His fingers stayed open.

"Squeeze," she said.

"I am."

He was not.

She dragged one fingernail across his palm. His hand did not twitch. When she pinched the web between thumb and forefinger, he guessed, "You're touching my wrist."

Fear entered her so quickly it found anger already waiting.

"How long?"

"It comes back."

"That wasn't the question."

"A minute, usually."

"How long has this been happening?"

His jaw moved against her hair. "A while."

"Days?"

"Aveline."

"Weeks? You took point through the barrier collapse on Tuesday. You phased the passenger deck on Friday. Were you numb then?"

"I could still move."

"Were you numb?"

"If I tell you yes, are you going to hear anything after it?"

"Try me."

"That's not an invitation. That's a deposition."

The harness dug into her sternum. "You hid a change in your power while we were working."

"And you haven't?"

Her field pulsed under her ribs, a late echo of the force she had already released. She said nothing.

"Right," he said. "Only one of us gets to be evidence."

Locks clacked. The door opened, and Sana Dacre stepped into the room carrying two foil water pouches. She was a compact woman in a black work suit, her mask pushed onto her forehead. A fading prismatic crescent shimmered at the edge of her left eye. She glanced at the amber node, then at the new angles of their restraints.

"I told Keaton you would test it before listening," she said.

"Do you two wager on kidnapping?" Aveline asked.

"Not money. It complicates taxes."

Sana crouched just outside kicking range and threaded a long straw toward Aveline's mouth. Aveline drank despite herself. The water was cool.

"Stop fighting the room and it will stop tightening," Sana said. "We don't intend to hurt either of you."

"Then release us and return the key."

"No. You may have water. You may not have the key."

She moved the straw to Harlan. Aveline watched her watch him struggle to close his left hand.

"Transient sensory loss?" Sana asked.

Harlan's tone brightened falsely. "I'm trying a new hobby."

"Poor choice of venue." She did not ask again. She set the pouches beyond reach, stood, and left them locked inside.

In the workshop, Keaton said, "The throat on this coupler is too narrow."

"Because you cut it against my measurement," Sana replied.

"Against an old measurement. The buyer changed the case."

"If you'd measured the case instead of admiring your own geometry—"

The sentence stopped.

When Sana resumed, her voice had lost its blade. "That was contempt. I'm sorry. You did measure it. My objection is that you changed the tolerance without telling me."

Keaton took a moment. "Apology accepted. I changed it because I thought the original throat would crack the key jacket. I should have told you before I cut. I still think the wider tolerance is safer."

"I still think it will slip under transport. Bring me the blue shims."

"Those I did not move."

Their disagreement continued, technical and unresolved.

Aveline had believed, without ever phrasing it, that decent conflict belonged to decent people, or at least to calm rooms. The Dacres had chained two people to a machine and were preparing to sell stolen hardware to someone worse. Their affection absolved none of it. It also did not vanish when the job went wrong.

The phase-key gave three sharp pulses. Somewhere above, a receiver chimed in answer.

"Buyer vehicle crossed the outer marker," Keaton said. "Forty minutes."

Harlan's fingers twitched in Aveline's hand.

"Six weeks," he said.

She looked down at his knuckles.

"It started as pins and needles after long phases. Then shorter ones. Last Friday my whole left side stayed numb for three minutes." He swallowed. "Tonight I have maybe twelve reliable seconds in total before it spreads. Less now. I didn't tell you because you would take me off patrol. Then you would watch every step I took. Then I'd be your responsibility instead of your partner."

Aveline wanted to refute the order of events. She could hear herself doing it: *Of course I'd take you off patrol. Of course I'd watch you. How could I not?* Each sentence would prove his fear while avoiding hers.

"My field recoils late," she said. The admission left her colder than the room. "Four to six seconds after I release a load. I don't control when. On the dock I released on your count, but the force landed after you'd moved."

He was quiet long enough for the key to pulse again.

"How long?" he asked.

"Three weeks."

"You let me think I mistimed it."

"You let me think you were fine."

She almost answered, *You first.* That would buy them ten more minutes of assigning fault and no way out of the room.

"I'm frightened," she said. The words felt less safe than any accusation. "Every symptom you hide sounds like you choosing patrol over coming home with me. I turn questions into verdicts because I want you to reassure me before I admit I need it."

His thumb made a weak pass across the side of her hand. "I'm frightened you'll love me into being useless."

"Then give me current facts. Exact ones. Tell me when sensation changes, how many seconds you have, and what you will stop for. I will not override a stop."

"And your recoil?"

"I name the load and count the delay out loud. If I don't know, I say I don't know. You get a stop too."

"That sounds suspiciously like a plan."

"It is a request. Don't make me repeat it elegantly."

"I accept the inelegant request."

They began with movements small enough to fail safely. Aveline drew a thread of tension into the right wrist band and let it fade before the wall could take it. Harlan phased the tip of one finger for less than a second. The nearest node dimmed, then brightened. They tried opposing directions. The restraint gave a grudging millimeter.

The room did not punish force itself. It punished an unanswered change, winding any imbalance forward. If Harlan removed a piece of the load while Aveline held its shape, the lattice searched for somewhere to put the difference. If she caught that difference and waited through her recoil, the next node briefly emptied.

The kitchen timer rang overhead. Keaton's steps moved from the workbench to the extraction cradle. Sana's moved away. Their task handoff pulled power from the cell nodes; the ghost hand on the wall thinned.

"That's the window," Aveline said. "On my two, phase the right locking pin. I hold the band. When the pin comes back, I take the release."

"I have eight seconds before I need a full recovery."

"Understood. One. Two."

The pin blurred inside its housing. Harlan's shoulder stayed solid against hers, but the band tried to jump toward the space the pin had left. Aveline caught the sudden torsion, held it in a narrow line, and felt the node begin to drain.

"Stop," Harlan said.

The buyer's signal pulsed. The open pin was almost clear. Every trained instinct told her to finish.

She released.

The pin snapped solid. Her field recoiled five seconds later, but because she had let the load die instead of casting it, the force only jarred her wrist. Harlan sagged against her.

"Numbness?"

"Left jaw. Early."

"Then we wait."

"Thirty-two minutes."

"We wait."

Sensation returned in increments he named without jokes: jaw, shoulder, first two fingers, palm. Above, the Dacres fitted the buyer case and argued about padding. When the timer was wound again, Aveline and Harlan adjusted their sequence.

At the ring, Harlan phased only the locking pin, not his arm. Three seconds. Aveline held the band in place until he returned, absorbed the released twist, and counted.

"One. Two. Three. Four—recoil."

The field kicked. She turned it into the seam of the right-hand wall node. Ceramic cracked. The restraint sprang open with a noise like a snapped cable.

Harlan rolled free as she tore loose the remaining bands. For a moment they knelt facing each other, masked, bruised, and newly embarrassed by having bodies their spouse could not safely guess at.

"Five good seconds," he said.

"Recoil window unknown after that load."

"Door?"

"Door."

The cracked node had released the cell latch. Beyond it lay the workshop: a long central bench, rolling tool cabinets, the humming extraction cradle, and an open buyer case lined with copper mesh. The phase-key hung above the case like a sliver of frozen lightning. At the rear wall, a steel hatch stood between stacked crates. Keaton's pale afterimages crossed the room in old routes—a shoulder turning beside the bench, a hand lifting beside an empty doorway, the outline of a quick kiss lingering near Sana's temple while the real couple worked six feet apart.

Sana saw the broken door first. "They're out."

Keaton swept one hand across the air. Distance lurched. The five paces between Aveline and the cradle folded into twelve, and a rolling cabinet seemed to jump into her path. She caught its momentum in her field, grounded the cabinet, let the load go, and called, "Cabinet. Recoil in five, maybe."

Harlan slipped through the false angle before it settled. "Four seconds. Left foot dull."

Sana snapped a ring of black latches from her belt. They clamped onto the bench and cast a wire loop across Harlan's route. He went translucent for half a heartbeat, but Keaton shifted the exit of the fold. Harlan emerged beside the buyer case instead of behind it.

"Two seconds," he said.

Aveline's recoil hit. The cabinet shot across the workshop. Sana ducked; Keaton pulled the distance in front of her sideways, and the cabinet crashed harmlessly through the projected space into a shelf.

The phase-key wobbled in its cradle. Its whine rose.

"Aura doubled," Sana said. "I can steer one precision reach."

"Then none for pursuit," Keaton replied.

"Mine to call."

"Understood."

They were still criminals. They were still very good. Keaton collapsed the space around Harlan while Sana turned toward the key, gloved fingers finding the cradle's hidden catches. If she seated it in the buyer case, its shielding would close.

"I can't reach the key," Harlan said. "One second, maybe."

Aveline saw the old solution: tell him to spend it, catch him if he fell, decide that the risk was necessary because she was better at necessity. She let the thought pass without turning it into an order.

"Can you reach the retaining pin?"

"Yes. Left side will go."

"Your call."

He looked at the open case. "Do it."

Aveline cast her field, not at the key but at the wire loop Sana had anchored to the bench. She pulled. Sana braced instinctively, feeding force through the latches. Aveline caught it and held.

"Now," Harlan said.

His fingers passed through the copper housing and touched the retaining pin. For one second, the pin ceased to hold anything.

Aveline released the wire. Sana stumbled back as the tension vanished. Four seconds later, the recoil arrived and snapped through the empty housing. The cradle opened. The phase-key dropped short of the buyer case.

Harlan, solid and falling, knocked the case lid away with his good hand. Aveline caught the key in a sling of tensile force and drew it into the broken cell, where the remaining damping nodes swallowed its motion and pinned it harmlessly against the floor.

Keaton reached Harlan first. He could have struck him. Instead he hooked Sana's arm and pulled her clear of the humming cradle.

"Job's gone," he said. "Rear hatch."

Sana's gaze fixed on the key. The prismatic crescent beside her eye had spread into a hard, bright arc. One projected reach might still cross the room. It might also leave her blind inside a collapsing fold.

Her hand closed on Keaton's sleeve. "Agreed."

He bent the distance to the hatch. Sana threw one last latch behind them, tangling the pursuit route without pretending it would hold forever. Then the Dacres were gone together, their fading outlines pacing the workshop after them.

Aveline made it two steps toward Harlan before her knees folded. He was already sitting, his left side slack, so she lowered herself with her back against his. The position kept them both upright, spared her ribs, and let them watch opposite doors.

"Inventory," she said.

"Left leg absent. Left hand mostly absent. Face coming back. Pride critically injured."

"Ribs bruised. Right wrist strained. Recoil after small loads still around five seconds. After large loads, unknown."

The phase-key buzzed against the floor. The buyer signal went on blinking inside its empty case.

"We cancel tomorrow's patrol," Harlan said.

"Yes. We tell the team we are medically unavailable. We tell the clinic and the field technician everything."

"Everything measurable."

"Everything we're embarrassed by too."

His head rested lightly against hers. "At home, if one of us says pause, it means pause. Not abandonment. Not surrender."

"And the person who asks for it says when they'll come back."

"Ten minutes?"

"Or an honest estimate. No invented precision."

"You wound me."

"Can you feel it?"

He considered. "Right side only."

Harlan's phone lay in the confiscated gear tray under the bench, just within reach of his right hand. Hers had been cracked on the dock.

"Who makes the call?" he asked.

"Your right hand works."

"Your voice sounds more authoritative."

"That has been identified as a hazard."

He laughed, and when it ended he did not add another joke. "I'll dial," he said. "You tell them where we are."

He dialed with his right thumb. When the dispatcher answered, Aveline gave their location, the key's condition, and, before habit could edit the sentence, both sets of injuries.
