stories.body:
# Not Friday

The apartment door clicked shut behind Yasmin, and Omar said, “Bro, just trust me. She likes you.”

Kian kept his attention on the bowl he was carrying to the kitchen. Three curled chips and a drift of salt moved across the bottom with each step. “You said that about the last four girls, and—”

“Shut up. I wasn’t wrong about the last four.” Omar intercepted the bowl, dumped its contents into the bin, and shoved it back into Kian’s hands as if returning a serve. “They didn’t leave because you misinterpreted signals. They left because you waited six-plus months to be a man. Now ask her out before she gets tired of you.”

In the living room, the game they had abandoned was still spread across the coffee table: bright cardboard territories, neat piles of wooden pieces, four glasses making wet rings among them. Yasmin’s chair sat angled away from the table. She had been the first to notice the time, the first to stand, and the only person who had put her glass in the sink.

“That is an incredibly stupid definition of being a man,” Kian said.

“Fine. Be a fern. Just be a fern who asks Yasmin to dinner.”

Kian took out his phone. No new message waited on the screen. He put it away. “She has a bus.”

“She has nine minutes before the bus.”

“Why do you know that?”

“Because she said, ‘I have nine minutes before the bus.’ You were busy pretending to study the board after she squeezed your shoulder.”

“She squeezes everyone’s shoulder.”

Omar looked toward his own shoulder, apparently reviewing the evidence available there. “No. Continue, though. I love watching a defense attorney ruin his career.”

Kian set the bowl in the sink. He had spent most of the evening noticing Yasmin without looking directly at her: the small crease between her eyebrows whenever Omar invented a rule, the ink smudge on the side of her hand, the way she laughed before she tried to hide it when Kian made a terrible move on purpose. Or mostly on purpose. Noticing was safe. Noticing asked nothing of anybody.

“The last four,” Omar said, ticking them off on his fingers. “The woman who invited you to a wedding and clarified twice that she had one hotel room. The woman who sent you apartment listings in her neighborhood.”

“Her rent was going up.”

“The one who held your hand through an entire bad movie.”

“She was scared.”

“It was a comedy. And the one who asked if you’d ever date someone exactly like her.”

Kian dried his hands on the dish towel, although they were not wet. “Exactly like her could mean a category.”

Omar’s mouth fell open. For once, no insult arrived. He dragged both palms down his face instead.

Those four women had not vanished in one dramatic migration. They had simply stopped offering chances for him to classify. One met someone. One moved. One became a friend who now sent him cheerful messages about the person she planned to marry. One had told him, with extraordinary kindness, that she had assumed he was not interested and had adjusted accordingly. Omar counted all four as victories for his own perception and defeats for Kian’s timing. Kian counted them as situations in which he had successfully avoided making a woman uncomfortable.

Lately, that count felt less honest.

“Nine minutes,” Omar said. “Probably eight now.”

Kian looked at the door. His stomach tightened so abruptly that it felt as if he had missed a stair.

Omar slapped the dish towel over his shoulder. “Go.”

“If this goes badly, you’re not allowed to say anything about it.”

“If this goes badly, I’ll bring food and say nothing for an entire evening.”

“You can’t do that.”

“I’ll bring enough food that it won’t matter.”

Kian listened for footsteps in the hall, though Yasmin was already several floors below. He could stay. He could send her a message tomorrow, after selecting each word for maximum reversibility. He could ask whether she wanted coffee, which they had done twice in the past month, or whether she wanted to visit the second half of the gallery they had not finished, or whether she needed company while buying the lamp she had mentioned. There were dozens of ways to spend time with Yasmin without admitting why he wanted it.

He put on his shoes.

“Okay,” he said. “I am going for it.”

“That sounded like a hostage statement.”

“Good night, Omar.”

The lift was on another floor. Kian took the stairs, moving fast enough to make confidence briefly indistinguishable from gravity.

On the first landing he tried, *I think we both know there’s something here.* It sounded assured, which was the quality Omar valued. It also assigned Yasmin a conclusion before she had spoken.

On the second landing: *Omar thinks we should go out.* That had the advantage of being true and the disadvantage of making Omar sound like the person requesting the date.

By the third, he had reached *Would you maybe want to do something sometime?* This one asked nothing they had not already done.

He pushed through the lobby door into the cool night. Across the road, past two parked cars and a bare-limbed street tree, Yasmin stood beneath the bus shelter’s flat roof. The illuminated panel at one end gave her coat a pale blue edge. She was looking down the road, not at her phone.

Kian waited for the signal, crossed, and had time to remember the coffee she had suggested after everyone else canceled. She had arrived with a book and never opened it. The lamp had taken twenty minutes to choose; afterward she had proposed dinner, and he had texted the group to see who wanted to join. At the gallery she had touched his sleeve and said, *We should come back, just us.* He had answered that quieter days were better for everybody.

Each memory had once seemed inconclusive alone. Together, they did not become consent, or a promise, or even proof. They became a history of questions he had answered as if she had asked different ones.

She saw him when he was a few paces away. Surprise lifted her face, followed by a smile that made hope flare so quickly he distrusted it.

“Did I leave something?” she asked.

“No. I just—” He glanced at the route display. Six minutes. “I thought I’d wait with you.”

“You didn’t bring a coat.”

“I did not think that part through.”

Yasmin shifted to make room beneath the shelter, though there was plenty. Kian stood beside her. The glass behind them carried faint scratches and a strip of old adhesive where a notice had been torn away. A paper cup rolled along the curb, stopped against a tire, then rolled back when the wind changed.

“Thanks,” she said. “For waiting.”

“Of course.”

She looked down the road again.

He had caught her. That had seemed like the difficult action in Omar’s kitchen. Now the silence presented the larger one.

“Do you want to hang out properly sometime?” he asked.

Yasmin turned to him. “Properly?”

“Yeah. You know. Deliberately.”

“Have I been spending time with you by accident?”

“No. I mean the two of us.”

“Coffee was the two of us.”

“Right.”

“The gallery was the two of us until you invited six people.”

“Only Omar came.”

“He came because you told him you had an extra ticket.”

Kian rubbed his thumb along the side of his phone. He had not taken it from his pocket, but his hand had found it anyway. “I mean something a little more... proper than that.”

Yasmin watched him work. Her expression was not cold or angry. That made it worse. She looked tired in a way he had not noticed upstairs, the skin beneath her eyes darkened by the blue-white panel.

“Kian,” she said, “what are you asking me?”

The simplest answer crowded against his teeth. Instead he said, “I like spending time with you. I thought maybe you felt the same.”

“I do.”

Relief arrived before understanding. “Great. So maybe we could do that more. Just see how it—”

“No.”

The relief collapsed so fast it left him light-headed.

Yasmin folded her arms, not tightly, and looked toward the road. “No more invitations that could mean a date if they go well and nothing if they don’t. I don’t want another one of those.”

“I wasn’t trying to—”

She waited.

Kian heard the unfinished lie and let it die. Of course he had been trying to. The escape hatch had not appeared by accident; he had built the sentence around it.

“Omar sent me,” he said.

Yasmin closed her eyes for a moment. “That is not better.”

“I know. It sounded more honest before I heard it out loud.”

“Did he give you a message to deliver?”

“No. Well, sort of. He said you liked me.”

“That is mine to say.”

“Yes.”

“Did he send you down here to inform me how I feel?”

“No. He sent me because he thinks I’ve been ignoring signals.” Kian heard the courtroom opening in his voice and hurried through it anyway. “The coffee, and the lamp, and when you said we should go back to the gallery—”

“I remember my own calendar.”

“Right.”

“And I know what I meant. Do you?”

His hand came out of his pocket. The phone stayed there. “I thought you might be interested.”

“I am interested.”

For the second time, relief made a foolish rush forward. This time he stopped it before it reached his mouth.

Yasmin saw something in his face. Her arms loosened. “I like you, Kian. I’ve liked you for months. But Omar doesn’t get to declare what I’ll say, and you don’t get to keep gathering evidence instead of asking me.”

“I wasn’t trying to make you wait,” he said.

“What did you think was happening?”

He searched for an answer that did not make him sound careless. “I thought we were becoming closer.”

“We were.”

“And I didn’t want to presume. I didn’t want to make every friendly thing you did into something else, or make you regret being kind to me.”

“That part is decent.” Her voice softened, but not enough to offer rescue. “I liked that part about you. For a while.”

The traffic signal changed. A delivery rider went through the intersection, bag rocking behind the seat, and the faint electric hum dwindled along the next block.

“What happened after a while?” Kian asked.

“After a while, it stopped feeling like you were protecting me from pressure. It felt like I was carrying all of yours.”

He looked at her.

“I had to invite you,” she continued, counting the facts against her fingers. “I had to make it obvious we could be alone. Then, when you added everybody else or called it an errand, I had to decide whether to push harder and risk cornering you. And if I backed off, I had to wonder if I’d imagined the whole thing. You got to be comfortable either way.”

The accusation was not perfectly fair. He had not been comfortable. He had examined messages until commas developed motives. He had lain awake after the gallery composing three versions of a question and sending none. He had felt sick each time she left, and grateful each time she came back.

But none of that discomfort had required Yasmin to know anything. It had been private, protected discomfort. He could not offer it as his share of the work.

“Tonight was the last time,” she said.

He must have reacted, because she added, “I’m not leaving the group. I’m not going to make game night strange. I just decided I wasn’t asking you anywhere alone again. If you wanted friendship, fine. If you wanted something else, you knew where I was.”

Before she got tired of you, Omar had said. He had made *tired* sound like a timer on Kian’s chance. Kian had missed the part that mattered: what Yasmin was tired of.

The route display changed from four minutes to three.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“Thank you.”

She did not say it was fine. Kian appreciated that, though it gave him nowhere easy to stand.

“Omar thinks asking is the brave part,” he said. “He thinks if I say something confident enough, the rest has already happened.”

“Omar treats ordering lunch like a championship final.”

Kian laughed once. Yasmin’s mouth bent, but she kept her gaze on him.

“I think I was doing the opposite,” he said. “Waiting until I knew the answer so well that I wouldn’t really be asking.”

“You can’t know it that well.”

“I know.”

He had said those words several times tonight, usually to hurry past something unpleasant. This time he waited after them. The wind pressed his shirt against his arms. A bus turned at the far intersection, too distant for him to read the number.

Yasmin looked at it, then back at him. She did not fill the silence.

Kian’s prepared lines were gone. He felt no sudden surge of the kind of courage Omar had tried to lend him. What remained was smaller and less impressive: one question, and Yasmin’s right to dislike it.

“Would you have dinner with me on Friday,” he said, “as a date?”

Yasmin’s expression changed, though he could not yet read how. “I can’t Friday.”

The answer struck with clean, familiar force. His mind opened every exit at once.

*That’s okay, I only meant if you were free.*

*No pressure. Forget I asked.*

*We can all do something another time.*

He could erase the date so thoroughly that by tomorrow both of them might doubt it had been offered. He had done versions of that before, smiling through the retreat so the other person would not have to soothe him. He had called it taking rejection well.

Yasmin waited. A bus passed on the opposite side of the road, interior lights revealing faces and then taking them away.

“Okay,” Kian said. The word came out thin. He swallowed. “Is that no to Friday, or no to going out with me?”

Yasmin stared at him for half a second. Then some of the weariness left her face. “Friday is my cousin’s birthday.”

“Ah.”

“I can do Sunday.”

The yes was so ordinary that he almost missed its arrival. There were no hidden conditions in it, nothing for him to decode. Sunday. Four days away.

“Sunday would be good,” he said.

“For a date,” she added.

“For a date.”

“Dinner, not an errand that develops food.”

“Dinner. I’ll even choose a restaurant before we meet.”

“That sounds dangerously decisive.”

“I may send you two options.”

“Acceptable.”

The approaching bus slowed at the intersection, and its route number came into view. Yasmin stepped toward the curb. Kian’s happiness was physical and embarrassing, a warmth rising into his face despite the cold. His mind tried to sprint ahead: which restaurant, what time, whether he should tell Omar, whether Yasmin’s smile meant she wanted him to kiss her now.

He stopped at the curb beside her.

“I could walk you home,” he said. “If you want.”

Yasmin glanced at him, then at his shirtsleeves. “No, thanks. I want the bus, and you’re going to freeze.”

The refusal landed beside the yes. His mind reached automatically for a connection between them, some hidden amendment in her tone.

There wasn’t one.

“Okay,” he said. “I’ll message you tomorrow about where?”

“After ten. I have an early meeting.”

“After ten.”

The bus sighed to the curb and opened its doors. Yasmin stepped aboard, then turned before tapping her fare.

“Good night, Kian.”

“Good night.”

She went down the aisle without looking back. The doors folded closed, and the bus carried her through the intersection.

Kian stood beneath the shelter roof for another moment. In his pocket, his phone began to vibrate. Omar, almost certainly, demanding a score before the teams had even been chosen.

Kian let it ring while he crossed the road. Sunday was a date. Tonight, Yasmin wanted the bus home alone. Both answers were clear enough to leave alone.

stories.title: By Wing and Welcome
stories.prompt: After your kid daughter nurses a bat back to health, a strange looking couple show up on your doorstep, asking to be her god parents, claiming said bat was their son
stories.body:
# By Wing and Welcome

The pear had dried inside the medicine dropper as a clear amber plug. I stood at the sink working it loose with a pin while Beatrix sat at the kitchen table and wrote one last line in her bat notebook.

“You don’t know it’s the last,” she said without looking up.

“He flew away a week ago.”

“That’s an observation. It’s not a conclusion.”

At sixteen, my daughter knew how to make a correction sound like testimony. Her notebook lay open beside the ventilated shoe box that had occupied our laundry room for three nights. It held the weights she had taken morning and evening, every water change, and the wing observations the wildlife-center volunteer had requested, followed by twice as many the volunteer had not. Inside the box were the old hand towel, a jam-jar lid, and several dark stains I had decided not to investigate closely. Beatrix had written the date of the bat’s departure on the last page and, below it, *Right wing level in flight. Circled porch light twice. Did not wobble.*

I rinsed the dropper. “The wildlife center said we can throw the box out.”

“They said they might.”

“The laundry counter wants its square foot back.”

That earned me the beginning of a smile. Seven nights earlier, we had watched the little brown bat climb the towel Beatrix had pinned inside the open box, hang for several minutes with his injured right wing folded tight, and then drop into the dusk. She had followed the volunteer’s instructions with maddening care: leather gloves, a closed door, daily photographs of the wound, no handling that could be avoided. The pear mash had been the volunteer’s reluctant improvisation after he refused every approved food and dragged himself toward the slice Beatrix was eating. He had skimmed the grass, lifted over the hedge, and vanished. Beatrix had clicked after him, two soft notes made with her tongue, the sound she had used to coax him to drink. Something above us had clicked back.

Beatrix maintained that this was evidence of a continuing relationship. I maintained that it was evidence of a bat.

Someone knocked on the front door.

Not the quick double tap of a neighbor, or the knuckle-and-bell assault of a delivery driver who had somewhere else to be. Three slow knocks sounded through the house. A pause. Then three more.

I put down the dropper. “Stay here.”

“I can see the door from the stairs.”

“That was not a counteroffer.”

The porch light showed me two people through the narrow pane beside the door. They stood shoulder to shoulder although there was plenty of room. Both wore dark coats buttoned to their throats despite the warm night. The taller one had a long, grave face and black hair combed flat behind ears that came to delicate, unnecessary points. The shorter one’s silver-brown hair was cut close to her head. Her eyes caught the porch light with a reddish shine, then went dark when she turned them away.

I checked the chain before I opened the door four inches.

“Can I help you?”

The tall visitor bowed. It was not deep enough to be theatrical, which somehow made it stranger.

“I am Raskel,” he said. “This is Vesper, my wife and balance. We have come by wing and welcome to the keeper of our son.”

Vesper closed her eyes for half a second.

“We’re Bram’s parents,” she said. “Your daughter saved him.”

Behind me, a floorboard gave a tiny complaint. Beatrix had not stayed in the kitchen.

“I don’t know anyone named Bram.”

“You knew him otherwise,” Raskel said. “He was injured. He came here in a lesser shape.”

“Smaller,” Vesper corrected. “Not lesser.”

Raskel inclined his head to her. “In a smaller shape. Brown-furred, narrow-faced, with a tear through the second joint of his right wing. He was sheltered in a box that smelled of oranges and soap. Your child fed him pear.”

There are sentences a person expects to hear at their front door, and there are sentences that make the chain feel as thin as thread.

I started to close it.

“We mean her no harm,” Vesper said quickly. Her hands remained visible at her sides. She had long fingers, bare of rings, the nails thick and dark as if bruised. “We came to thank her, not frighten you.”

“You came to my house after dark and said a bat was your son.”

“We did argue about the hour,” she said.

“The formal call is made at the rescued one’s hour of waking,” Raskel said.

“Raskel lost the argument and kept the hour.”

He looked genuinely wounded by this account of events. I would have found them funny anywhere but my porch.

“How do you know what was in the box?” I asked.

“Bram told us,” Vesper said.

“A bat told you about my laundry room.”

“Our son did.”

Raskel drew himself straighter. “He told us also that your daughter offered mealworms, which he refused past wisdom, and pear mash, which he accepted past dignity. That she replaced the water twice each night. That she made two notes before bringing the dropper near, so he would not startle and reopen his wing.”

Those were intimate facts. They were not proof. For three nights, the laundry-room window had been cracked to keep the room cool. Anyone willing to stand in the side yard could have watched us through the gap in the blind.

I thought of the stains in the box, of sickness, of teeth. I thought of Beatrix crouched on the floor in leather gloves, whispering, “I know you’re scared. I’m going to be boring now,” before she changed the towel. I had been proud of her steadiness. Now every small scene rearranged itself under the pressure of strangers who claimed to know it.

“What do you want?” I asked.

Raskel placed one hand over his chest. “When a child of our house receives the shelter that preserves him, his parents must come to the sheltering child. If she and her household accept, we become her godparents. We answer her call. We open our house. We stand between her and abandonment as your child stood between ours and death.”

The word *godparents* went through me more sharply than *bat* had.

“No.”

Vesper turned toward him. “I told you to begin with what it doesn’t mean.”

“A promise is diminished if first described by absence.”

“And an evening is lengthened if the door gets shut.”

“You are not becoming anything to my daughter,” I said. “You don’t get authority over her because she helped someone. You don’t get time alone with her. You don’t get to decide you’re family.”

Raskel’s pupils widened until almost no iris showed. Vesper touched two fingers to his sleeve, and he became still.

“We ask,” she said. “We do not decide.”

“He said *must*.”

“We must offer.”

“And if we refuse?”

Raskel answered before she could. “A welcome spurned is returned to the wing that bore it.”

“That sounds like a curse.”

“It means we go home,” Vesper said.

A faint scratching came from above the porch light.

I looked up through the gap. The light fixture was a square of frosted glass under the porch roof. Beyond it, the siding and soffit met in hard shadows. I could see nothing moving.

Vesper had looked up too.

“Who else is here?” I asked.

“No one who will cross your threshold uninvited,” Raskel said.

“That is not an answer.”

“Bram came with us,” Vesper said. “He’s above the door.”

I shut it hard enough to make the chain jump, then turned the deadbolt. Beatrix stood halfway down the stairs with her notebook folded against her chest.

“Back from the door.”

“Is he okay?”

“Beatrix.”

“They know about the mealworms.”

“Which means they know something. It doesn’t mean what they say it means.”

Through the door, Raskel said, “Our son’s wing is knit. His flight remains crooked when he tires, but he is in no danger.”

“He can hear us?” Beatrix asked.

“Apparently everybody can.”

She came down one step. “Ask them what side of the lid the water was on.”

“You are not going out there.”

“You don’t know the answer.”

I did not. I had supervised the gloves, made the calls, cut the air holes, and kept a folded towel under the door so our cat could not investigate. Beatrix had arranged the world inside the box.

I opened the door to the chain again. “Which side was the water on?”

Raskel glanced at Vesper.

“Left, near the corner,” Vesper said. “He knocked grit into it the first night. You moved it to the right on the second, and he knocked it over entirely.”

“Why wouldn’t he drink unless Beatrix clicked?”

“He could not see well in the room after striking his head,” Raskel said. “He knew the sound belonged to the child who did not seize him when he woke.”

From the stairs behind me came two quiet clicks.

The answer arrived above my head.

Two notes, the second higher than the first. Then a rustle no heavier than dry leaves.

Beatrix slipped past my arm before I could stop her. I barred the doorway with my forearm, and she stopped inside the chained door, close enough to see the visitors through the glass.

“Bram?” she called.

Another pair of clicks sounded from the porch roof.

Vesper’s face changed. Until then, she had been watching me with the patience of someone approaching a frightened animal. Now she looked up, and worry stripped the careful plainness from her voice.

“He didn’t tell us how you called him.”

“He came anyway,” Beatrix said.

Raskel lifted his chin toward the darkness. “Bram. Descend and present yourself to the household that preserved you.”

“Don’t order him,” Beatrix said.

At the same moment, I said, “Bring him down where I can see him.”

Beatrix twisted around and looked at me. “You too.”

“I need to know what’s outside my door.”

“He knows what’s inside.” She held up the notebook as if it were evidence in a trial. “You’re both making him prove things with his body. He doesn’t like being watched when he can’t fly right.”

Vesper looked at her husband. “She understood that from three days.”

Raskel lowered his gaze.

Beatrix turned and went quickly to the kitchen. She returned with the old towel from the shoe box. I nearly told her not to touch it with bare hands, then saw that she had already washed it. It smelled faintly of our detergent.

“I’m opening the door,” she said. “Not all the way.”

“Beatrix.”

“You can hold it.”

That was how she offered compromise: a practical job, already assigned.

I kept the chain on and opened the door as far as it allowed. Beatrix folded the towel into a thick strip and laid it on the inner sill.

“You can come to this side if you want,” she called. “Or you can stay up there. I won’t put you in the box.”

She clicked twice.

For several seconds, nothing happened. A car passed at the far end of the street, its tires whispering on pavement. Raskel and Vesper stood apart now, leaving the center of the porch empty.

A small shape dropped from the roof.

It opened its wings less than a foot above Raskel’s head and struck the doorframe with a soft, leathery slap. I caught the door before it bounced against Beatrix. The bat clung to the outside trim, trembling. His right wing sagged a fraction lower than the left, and a pale line crossed the dark membrane near the joint.

I remembered that line raw and red under the laundry-room light.

“Hi,” Beatrix whispered.

The bat crawled sideways onto the towel.

Vesper unbuttoned her coat. “May I come close enough to cover him? The change is private, and the light hurts.”

I wanted the door shut. I wanted Beatrix behind me. I wanted proof to be something clean that could be examined without granting anyone an inch.

“One step,” I said.

Vesper stepped up and spread her coat across the opening, making a dark tent between the door and the porch rail. Raskel turned his back. Under the coat came a rapid series of clicks, a shudder through the towel, and the muffled scrape of something gaining weight. Vesper reached inside her coat lining and passed a bundle beneath the screen.

The change took less than a minute. It did not sound easy.

When Vesper dropped the coat, a thin boy stood barefoot on the porch in gray shorts and a shirt too large for him. He looked eleven or twelve. His hair stuck up in soft brown points, and his face had the pinched, furious dignity of someone discovered after crying. He held his right arm close to his ribs. A healing scar ran from his wrist toward his elbow in the same curve I had seen on the wing.

He looked at Beatrix, then at the dropper still in my hand.

“I hate pear mash,” he said.

Beatrix’s mouth opened.

“I drank it because you wouldn’t stop,” he added. “And the worms were dead.”

“You’re a bat,” she said.

“Sometimes.”

“You could have told me.”

He stared at his bare toes. “I couldn’t change without tearing the wing again. And my mouth wasn’t right for words.”

I unhooked the chain.

“The kitchen,” I said. “All of you. The door stays unlocked, and nobody makes any promises until I understand the nouns.”

Raskel bowed again. “Your caution honors the threshold.”

“My caution is going to make tea.”

We went inward in stages. Beatrix and Bram crossed the entry together, with the towel around his shoulders. Vesper followed them. Raskel waited on the porch until I stepped aside for him, then entered last. I closed the front door but left the deadbolt unturned.

At the table, the visitors looked no more ordinary under the brighter light. Raskel’s ears were definitely pointed. Vesper’s eyes flashed whenever she turned too quickly. Bram seemed mostly like a tired boy until he clicked his tongue at the sink and flinched at the answer.

“Hard room,” he muttered.

The refrigerator compressor started. He clapped both hands over his ears.

“Does it always do that?”

“Several times an hour,” I said.

“Why?”

“It keeps food cold.”

He regarded the refrigerator as if this were an inadequate defense.

I set water to boil. Beatrix opened her notebook to a clean page but did not pick up her pencil.

“If I say no,” she asked, “does anything bad happen to Bram?”

Raskel placed his palms flat on the table. “The shelter already given cannot be ungiven.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

He glanced at Vesper, but she waited for him to try again.

“No,” he said. The word came out stiffly. “Nothing happens to him.”

“Do you get mad at me?”

“I would regret that our houses remained apart.”

“He’d be disappointed,” Vesper said. “I would too. We’d still be grateful. We’d leave you our number in case you changed your mind, unless you told us not to.”

I put five mugs on the counter, although I had not yet agreed they were staying long enough to drink.

“What does godparent mean to you?” I asked.

Raskel began, “By the old obligation of—”

“Tonight,” Vesper said. “In this kitchen.”

He considered the correction. “It means that if Beatrix calls to say she is unsafe or without shelter, we answer. If she needs what we can give, we do not pretend not to hear. We do not replace you. We acquire no custody. We ask before entering your home.”

“And no secret visits,” I said. “No taking her anywhere without asking me. No gifts with obligations attached. No deciding that your customs outrank my rules for my child.”

His mouth tightened at the last condition.

“If a rule endangered her?” he asked.

His objection was immediate and ordinary. My answer came more easily.

“Then you tell me,” I said. “If there’s no time and she’s in danger, you help her. Afterward, you tell me everything.”

Raskel nodded once. “That I can promise.”

“Is it magic?” Beatrix asked.

Vesper smiled. “No.”

“Not even a little?”

“No spell,” Vesper said. “We can break our word, and you can send us away. We would have to live with either.”

I poured the tea. “Beatrix, do you want them to be your godparents?”

She did not answer at once. She looked at Bram. He had lowered his hands from his ears but kept glancing suspiciously at the refrigerator.

“Does saying yes create anything between Bram and me?” she asked.

“No,” Bram said.

Raskel looked pained again, but Bram continued.

“I mean, I’d like to see you again. You’re bossy, but in a useful way. I don’t want you stuck with me because I got hurt.”

Beatrix nodded. “I don’t want your parents assigned to me because I fed you. That would be buying people backward.”

“It is not a purchase,” Raskel said.

“Good. Then I can pick.” She looked from him to Vesper. “If I say yes tonight, can I say no later?”

Raskel’s answer took a long time. Vesper did not rescue him.

“Yes,” he said at last. “A door that cannot close is not a welcome.”

Beatrix glanced up at me. However determined she was to choose for herself, she wanted to know whether I would stand beside her afterward or make the choice a fight between us.

I sat down. “My conditions stay.”

“Mine too,” she said. “And don’t come at night without calling. We have school.”

Vesper extended her hand across the table, palm up, stopping well short of Beatrix. “Agreed.”

Beatrix considered the hand and then touched two fingers to it. “Then yes. You can be my godparents the way we said it here.”

Raskel placed his hand over his chest. This time his bow was only a tilt of the head.

“By wing and welcome,” he said, “we will answer.”

The kettle ticked as it cooled, and the refrigerator started again. Bram groaned.

I put a bowl of fruit on the table. Bram chose a whole pear, which made Beatrix laugh so suddenly that tea slopped over the edge of her mug.

“You said you hated pear.”

“Mash,” he said. “It’s different when it has corners.”

“Pears don’t have corners.”

“This one does from sound.”

He clicked at it, then toward the dark pantry. His face brightened despite himself. “There are crackers in there. Top shelf, behind a metal tin.”

I checked. He was right, although he could not have seen inside the closed pantry.

“It lasts a few minutes after he changes,” Vesper said. “Very useful for finding things in the dark. Miserable in kitchens.”

Bram bit into the pear and winced when the sink rang under a dropped spoon. Beatrix moved the spoon onto a folded dishcloth. She did it without comment.

We arranged for them to come back on Saturday afternoon, after lunch, with a phone call first. Vesper wrote two numbers on a page from Beatrix’s notebook. Raskel added a third and said it reached a neighbor if both of them were flying. I decided not to ask whether that was a figure of speech. One impossible thing at a time seemed like a sound household policy.

When they left, I turned off the entry and porch lights, and Vesper screened Bram with her coat while he changed beside the front door. She carried him outside with the coat buttoned around him. A moment later, he slipped from the collar and went over the hedge on wings that still pulled slightly to the right. Raskel and Vesper walked away beneath him, their faces raised to follow sounds I could not hear.

I locked the door. Then I checked the porch roof, the windows, and both household phone numbers. Raskel answered the first. Vesper answered the second with, “You are correct to test them,” before hanging up.

In the kitchen, Beatrix had written *Saturday, two o’clock* on the calendar. The cleaned dropper lay beside her notebook.

“Can we keep the box until after they visit?” she asked.

I looked at the towel missing from it and the dark little stains in the corner. “Sunday morning. Then it goes.”

“That’s a conclusion,” she said.

I added pears to the grocery list.

stories.title: Roads Under Impossible Stars
stories.prompt: Two estranged best friends take a beat-up car into the desert for one last road trip before their lives go separate ways. Late one night, beneath a sky crowded with impossible stars, a meteor burns across the horizon—and the girl who wished things could go back to how they were discovers that, for a few minutes at a time, they can. But every time she rewinds the night, the desert changes: roads lead somewhere different, abandoned buildings appear where there was only sand, and her friend remembers pieces of conversations that technically never happened.
stories.body:
# Roads Under Impossible Stars

The question cards have gone soft at the corners, though I laminated them when we were sixteen. I hold one above the dashboard vent and read it in the solemn voice Paloma used to hate and secretly love.

“Would you rather know exactly where you’re going or never have to go alone?”

Paloma keeps her eyes on the road. “Did you stack the deck?”

“There is no deck. They’re in alphabetical order.”

“That is worse.”

It should be enough. Once, *that is worse* would have been the opening move in a ten-minute argument about whether alphabetical order counted as fate. Tonight it falls between us and stays there.

The hatchback’s loose fan belt shrieks whenever Paloma lets the speed drop below forty. Its air conditioner died before either of us learned to drive. We have the windows open, and the desert comes in hot and mineral-dry, fluttering the old paper itinerary on my knees. The route is marked in purple pen: fuel, lookout, campground, breakfast. We drew it the summer after sophomore year and followed it every August until last year.

This is the last trip. Paloma leaves Saturday for a year of trail repair, invasive-plant surveys, and living out of cabins with unreliable power. I start college three days later. Those facts sit in the car with their knees spread.

I tuck the card behind the sun visor. “Snack?”

“No.”

“You always want the sour ones after dark.”

“Then you have successfully documented a past version of me.”

The fan belt squeals. Paloma changes down, jaw tight, and the sound fades into the tires’ steady hiss.

I flatten the itinerary against my thighs. “The lookout should be twelve miles up.”

“If we’re still on the right road.”

“We are.”

“Romy, that map is four years old.”

“Roads don’t expire.”

She glances at me then, quick and incredulous. Beyond her profile, the last red seam of sunset has vanished. “Some do.”

I turn the map toward the window as if there might be enough light to prove something. There isn’t. “I thought we said we’d try to have a good trip.”

“I am trying.”

“You wouldn’t even answer one question.”

“Because the question is embarrassing.”

“They were all embarrassing. That was the point.”

“The point was that we were sixteen.” Paloma grips the wheel higher. “This trip can’t make that happen again.”

The words hit harder for being obvious. For months, I have been storing better versions of this conversation: calmer versions, funnier versions, versions where she admits the job is a mistake before I have to ask. None of them begins with me saying what I actually mean.

“You’re the one leaving,” I say.

“And you’re the one who disappeared.”

“I gave you space.”

“You read my message and didn’t answer for nine weeks.”

“What was I supposed to say? Congratulations on blowing up the plan?”

“There was no plan. There was a joke about renting an apartment together if neither of us could afford anything else.”

“It wasn’t a joke to me.”

“Then you could have told me.”

Her voice has gone thin and even. I know that voice. It is the railing at the edge of a drop.

The sky above the windshield is crowded with stars. Not bright, exactly. Numerous. They fill the dark between the familiar constellations until there is hardly any dark left, thousands of pale points like salt ground into black stone. Paloma sees them too. Her anger loosens just enough for wonder.

“Pull over,” I say.

“No shoulder.”

Then the meteor comes.

It burns from left to right across half the horizon, low and slow, its white head trailing a green seam that stays open behind it. The inside of the car flashes silver. I see every crack in the vinyl dash, every loose hair against Paloma’s cheek, the purple roads on my useless map.

“I wish we could go back,” I say. “Just go back to before we ruined this.”

The fan belt screams.

Paloma’s unfinished breath runs backward through her teeth. The radio spits a syllable, swallows it, spits it again. Gravel ticks up from beneath the car, strikes metal, then lifts away into the road.

The dashboard clock changes from 11:54 to 11:48.

Paloma says, “Did you stack the deck?”

My hand is above the vent. Between my fingers is the same question card.

For three seconds, I cannot feel the heat.

“Romy?”

I look at the odometer. I noticed the mileage when we passed the last fuel stop, because Paloma accused me of being the sort of person who would calculate the cost down to the cent. The number is nine miles higher than it should be. The fuel needle is still nudging empty. The temperature needle still trembles above the midpoint.

“No,” I say. “They’re in alphabetical order.”

“That is worse.”

This time I laugh, because I know the line is coming and because terror needs somewhere to go. Paloma gives me a suspicious look, but one corner of her mouth moves. That tiny success feels so good I almost miss the road changing.

Where the highway should bend around a black ridge, the pavement divides. One lane runs straight between reflective posts. The other narrows toward a wooden sign whose painted arrows have been scoured blank.

Paloma slows. The belt squeals again, later than it did before.

“Was this on the map?”

“No.” I search the purple line. There is no fork for another thirty miles. “Take the wider road.”

She does. The crowded stars seem close enough to snag in the windshield chips.

I could tell her. I mean to. But she has smiled at me, barely, and the last six minutes are clean again. I ask if the field crew has assigned her a cabin yet. I ask what kind of boots she bought. I make my voice interested instead of injured.

Paloma answers carefully. Yes, a shared cabin. No, she does not know her roommate. The boots are secondhand. Then she says, “You don’t have to pretend to be excited.”

“I’m not pretending.”

“You called it blowing up the plan.”

The car seems to narrow around us.

“I didn’t say that.”

Paloma blinks. “No. You didn’t.” She rubs two fingers against her breastbone. “I thought you did.”

Ahead, the green scar of the meteor still hangs above the horizon, already thinner.

“I wish we could go back,” I say.

The world catches.

Heat folds over me. The tires hammer the same patched strip twice. The clock drops by five minutes, not six, and the blank sign is gone.

Now a survey station stands in the sand.

It is a low concrete building on spindly metal legs, all its windows punched out. A wind gauge turns on the roof though the air inside the car has gone still. The hatchback passes it slowly enough for me to see a row of hooks beside the door and a coffee mug upright on the sill.

The radio crackles to life. Its antenna snapped off two summers ago, and it has received nothing but engine noise since. A man is reciting irrigation prices in a bored voice. He moves on to a school closure, then a warning that loose cattle have been reported along the north fence. He never names the county, the school, or the road.

Paloma reaches for the dial. “What station is that?”

Static answers her.

“Do you remember the fork?” I ask.

“What fork?”

“Nothing.”

She stares out at the survey station shrinking behind us. “I feel like I’ve already lost you.”

The sentence is so quiet I almost decide I imagined it.

“You haven’t.”

Her face twists. “That isn’t what I meant.”

“What did you mean?”

“I don’t know.” She presses her palm to her sternum now. “I’m sad about something you haven’t said.”

I set the cards on the floor. “Then let me say something different.”

I apologize for not answering her message. I tell her I panicked. I tell her I thought our lives would overlap longer than they are going to. Every sentence is true and arranged to conceal the ugliest truth behind it: I wanted my silence to hurt.

Paloma listens. For a while, the road stays straight.

“Thank you,” she says. “But I’m still going.”

My tongue is already shaping the wish. The meteor’s seam is fading, and I say the words faster than before.

The return is not even four minutes.

We are passing an empty motor court, six little stucco rooms bowed around a gravel lot. Their doors stand open. A dry swimming pool gleams under the impossible stars, its bottom tiled with blue fish. There was only sand here in every previous night.

Paloma grips the steering wheel. “We have passed this place.”

“We haven’t.”

“There was a mug in a window.”

“That was somewhere else.”

“There was somewhere else?”

The fuel needle dips as we watch. The temperature needle creeps higher.

I describe the clock retreating and the roads changing. I do not say how many times I have seen it happen, or that I knew before the second wish that the words would work.

“Pull over,” she says.

“We don’t know what’s out there.”

“Exactly.”

She turns into the motor court. Gravel knocks under the chassis. The engine fan rattles with the busy, brittle sound of a coin in a dryer. Paloma parks facing the road and leaves the motor running.

“Say it again,” she says.

“What?”

“The wish.”

“Why?”

“I want to hear what happens.”

“You won’t remember all of it.”

“Apparently I get pieces.” She looks at me, and I see fear underneath the anger. “How many times have you made me do this?”

“Three. The first was an accident.” I make that distinction do too much work.

“You told me I chose fences and dirt over you.”

My mouth goes dry. I said that after the second return, on a road that no longer exists.

Paloma continues, “Then you asked if I could promise we’d still be best friends when I came home. I said I couldn’t promise what a year would do. You looked at me like I’d failed a test.”

“Those conversations didn’t happen anymore.”

“They happened to you.”

“I changed them because I was getting them wrong.”

“You changed them because you didn’t like my answers.”

The engine ticks hot beneath the hood. In the rearview mirror, the motor court rooms are black squares full of stars.

I can still repair this. I hear myself think it and hate how reasonable it sounds.

“I wish we could go back.”

The courtyard jerks sideways.

The return is shorter now. We are on the road again, moving fast, the motor court nowhere behind us. Paloma has both hands on the wheel and the dazed look of someone waking from a fall.

“Slow down,” I say.

“Don’t.”

“What?”

“Don’t ask me the boots question again.” Her knuckles pale. “I’ve answered it enough.”

“Paloma, I’m trying to get us out.”

“You keep saying that after you put us somewhere worse.”

The radio breaks in with weather for a valley outside the windows, promising frost in the upper orchards. Sand streams silver beneath the stars. There are no trees in sight.

The road drops. Our headlights reach over the slope and find nothing on the other side.

Paloma hits the brakes. The rear of the hatchback sways. Below us, a flash-flood channel has torn the pavement away, leaving two ragged ends and fifteen feet of black air between them.

I grab the dash. “I wish we could go back.”

The fan belt shrieks before the words leave my mouth.

We snap backward less than a minute. This time Paloma is already braking, though the culvert is gone. The road runs level into the motor court’s courtyard, but the buildings have multiplied and closed behind us in a horseshoe. The dry pool blocks the center. She wrenches the wheel, misses the cracked curb by inches, and stops beside a dead ice machine.

Steam feathers from under the hood.

Paloma kills the engine. For a moment neither of us moves.

Then she unclips her seat belt. “Do not touch the radiator cap.”

“I know.”

“You once tried to put dish soap in the washer reservoir.”

“I was twelve.”

“Stay here.”

She takes the flashlight and gets out. Anger has not made her stupid or cruel; that would be easier. She props the hood, examines the hoses without putting her hands near them, and comes back sweating.

“We wait,” she says. “At least half an hour. Then we can put some drinking water in the reservoir. Maybe it holds long enough to find a real road.”

“If there is one.”

“There has to be one for us to look.”

She sits with the door open and her feet on the cracked pavement. The meteor’s scar is a green thread now. Around it, too many stars shine over the motor court roofs.

“That last one saved us,” I say.

“Yes.” Paloma wipes dust from her shin. “It did.”

“So it isn’t all—”

“Don’t turn almost killing us into evidence that you were right.”

I lean my head against the seat. The upholstery smells like hot pennies and the coconut spray we used three summers ago because the car had begun to smell like wet shoes. All the years of us are still here in stupid layers.

Paloma says, “I remember apologizing for leaving. More than once. I remember you accepting it once. I remember you telling me I always choose whatever makes me feel important. I remember promising to call every day, and I remember refusing to call at all.”

“You didn’t say all those things in the same version.”

“I know.” She looks at me. “That is not helping.”

The radio whispers through the dead engine, a woman announcing livestock notices from very far away.

“I was trying to find the honest conversation,” I say.

“You were trying to find the conversation where I said yes.”

I look at the meteor thread. If I speak quickly, there may be enough left. I could go back before the culvert, tell her at once, use the motor court as proof. I could omit the lie about the number of returns. I could begin with the right apology.

“I wish we could—”

Paloma shuts her eyes.

I stop.

The words remain unfinished in my mouth. Nothing lurches. The clock does not change. Somewhere in one of the rooms, metal taps metal at an irregular pace.

When Paloma opens her eyes, she does not thank me.

“Nine weeks,” I say. “I knew what to write after the first hour. I wanted to say I was hurt and I wanted you not to go. Instead I kept waiting because I thought if I stayed silent long enough, you’d get scared and come fix it. Then every day made it harder to admit that was what I was doing.”

She studies the gravel between her shoes.

“I wasn’t confused,” I say. “I was punishing you.”

The star-crowded dark gives her no privacy. I look down at my hands.

“I wanted you to ask me not to go,” she says at last. “I would still have gone. But I wanted to know it mattered.”

“It mattered.”

“You made me guess.”

“Yes.”

“And tonight you made me keep guessing which things I’d actually said.” Her voice shakes. “You don’t get to decide those versions were disposable just because you erased them.”

I want to explain that I remember every answer she gave me. The defense sounds ugly before I say it, and I close my mouth.

“I’m sorry,” I say. It is the first apology tonight I cannot test in advance. “What do you want now?”

She gives a tired, almost disbelieving laugh. “Right now? I want the engine not to crack. I want to get out of the haunted motel. I want to leave on Saturday without you treating it like a vote about whether I love you.”

“Okay.”

“It isn’t okay.”

“No. But I heard you.”

She rubs her face. “And after my first week, maybe we have one call.”

Hope rises so fast it hurts.

“Maybe,” she repeats. “You don’t get to turn that into a contract.”

“I won’t.”

“You already want to schedule it.”

“Very badly.”

This time her laugh is one breath long, unwilling and real. It does not restore anything. I let it end.

We wait. The meteor seam thins until I cannot tell it from the green ghost left by staring too long. One by one, the surplus stars go dark. No thunder follows, no final shudder. The desert simply regains its distances.

When the engine has cooled, Paloma wraps a shirt around her hand and eases open the reservoir cap. We sacrifice two bottles of drinking water. The hatchback starts on the third try.

The motor court’s exit leads to a service road neither the paper itinerary nor the car’s old navigation disc recognizes. We take it because it exists. Behind us, the broken sign hums in the headlights, though none of its letters are lit.

An hour before sunrise, the service road meets a divided highway. The lane paint is fresh. A sign promises fuel without naming a town. The odometer says we have driven thirty-seven miles more than the map can account for.

Paloma takes the wheel. I hold the flashlight on the temperature gauge whenever the dash light flickers out. The paper itinerary has slipped under my seat, and neither of us reaches for it.

After a long stretch of ordinary static, I ask, “When should I text?”

“Sunday after my first week.”

“If you don’t answer?”

“Then I didn’t answer.”

The hatchback rattles into its highest gear. I watch the needle settle and do not ask again.

stories.body:
# The Players Above

Anjali Bose had her miniature halfway through the painted archway when the voice said, *Not that square.*

It did not speak into the room. Malik kept narrating from behind his cardboard screen, rain worried the cabin roof, and Devika crunched a rice cracker with the concentration of someone disposing of evidence. The voice arrived in Anjali's thoughts without sound or direction, patient as a fingertip placed on a line of text.

*The flagstone ahead of you is hinged. Move to the left.*

The left square put her scout in the ideal position to search the archway. It was exactly the sort of useful suggestion the voice had been giving for three weeks: take the stairs before an elevator stalled, wait through a green light before a delivery bike shot across it, bring an umbrella under a stainless blue sky. Anjali had called those incidents instinct because the other explanation was that an invisible stranger had begun managing her life.

Now it was managing her weekend campaign.

She kept her hand on the miniature. “I appreciate your advice, formless voice, but what do you want with me?”

Malik stopped behind the screen. Devika stopped chewing.

The presence in Anjali's mind brightened, not quite laughter but pleased surprise. *Me and some friends are having a cosmic game. One of us has created a great peril, and the rest of us must guide you and your companions to both figure it out and then solve it.*

Anjali looked at the map, the bowls of cooling noodles, and Malik's collection of metal dice in its shallow steel case. “Like in a TTRPG?”

*Oh, you have those too?*

Every die in the case tipped onto an edge.

Not one fell. Twelve-sided, twenty-sided, the squat four-sided die that should not have been capable of balancing on anything but a face: all stood in a rigid silver garden. On the kitchenette counter, a serving spoon rose from the curry pot and settled upright on its bowl.

Something knocked against the outside wall.

The impact traveled from the kitchen cupboards to the floorboards beneath Anjali's boots. A second knock came from the front of the cabin, then a third from the wall facing the lake. They were too evenly spaced to be branches.

Malik folded his game screen flat. “Mine says get below the windows.”

Devika swallowed. “Yours what?”

“The voice I've been pretending is stress.” He lowered himself beside the table. “It says we have about twenty seconds.”

Devika was already sliding from her chair. “Mine says take the back door.”

For one absurd second, Anjali was offended. She had thought the voice chose her.

Then the window beside the kitchen went black.

It was not darkness on the other side of the glass. Darkness would have reflected the room. This swallowed the hanging lamp, the table, Anjali's own startled face. A narrow joint bent across the pane, too long for a leg, and dragged one pointed end down the glass with a sound like a wet finger on china.

They crawled toward the stone fireplace. Malik reached up just far enough to turn off the lamp. Rain and the banked fire gave the room a dim red pulse.

*That is the peril,* Anjali's voice said, its delight gone. *It has arrived sooner than we calculated.*

“Your calculations are having an ugly night.” She kept her own voice low. “What is it?”

*A seeking shape. Its maker placed an anchor near you. The shape will learn to reach farther each time it finds the path you intend to use. If it reaches the road after sunrise, there will be so many intentions to follow that we do not know how to contain it.*

The road lay uphill beyond the parked car. In the other direction, a narrow path descended to the dock and Malik's aluminum boat.

“Can it cross water?” Anjali asked.

The answer came at once. *Poorly. The dock is your safest route.*

That clean certainty loosened the knot under her ribs. She turned to the others. “Mine says the dock. Boat gets us across the lake before dawn.”

“Mine says stay low and watch its center,” Malik said.

Devika stared toward the back door. “Mine says moving is better than waiting.”

They took raincoats from hooks without standing upright. Malik went first with the long-handled fireplace poker because it was the nearest thing to a weapon. Anjali carried the cabin flashlight and the marked-up game map without knowing why she had grabbed the map. Devika pocketed their phones and Malik's car keys.

Outside, the rain had thinned to cold needles. The path to the dock ran between black spruce trunks, down twenty slick wooden steps, then over a strip of pebble beach. Anjali knew the geometry: eighty paces from back door to water, the boathouse on their right, no branch paths. A single line. A correct line.

They reached the twelfth step before the world below them folded.

The spruce shadows joined across the path. Something assembled itself from their absence: three jointed limbs braced between the trunks, then five, then more than Anjali could count as they crossed and recrossed. It had no skin and no face. Rain vanished into it. One reaching point struck the handrail where Devika's throat had been a moment before, showering them with splinters.

Malik dropped flat. Devika hauled Anjali backward by her hood as another limb swept over them.

The flashlight rolled down two steps and shone upward. For an instant its beam entered the shape through a seam at its center. Anjali saw a hard object turning there, no larger than her fist: a many-sided black stone whose edges stayed sharp while everything around it flexed.

“Anchor,” Malik said. “That's the center.”

The shape contracted. The flashlight went out.

They scrambled uphill. Anjali lost the map, recovered it, and reached the back door with wet knees and a bleeding palm she did not remember cutting. Malik slammed the bolt. The next impact dented the door inward, but the hinges held.

On the table, the dice remained balanced. Anjali swept the noodles aside and spread out the damp map. It showed ruined towers and underground rivers, nothing outside the cabin. Malik flipped it over. On the blank paper he drew the lake, road, cabin, dock, car, woodpile, and the old fire clearing north of the porch.

“Exact words,” Anjali said. “Not what we think they meant.”

Malik wrote as they spoke. Her voice had called the dock *safest*. His had said, *Stay low. Its anchor cannot hide from an eye beneath its reaching limbs.* Devika's had said, *Movement preserves more possibilities than shelter.*

“Three pieces of useful advice,” Anjali said. “And it was waiting on the dock path.”

*Because its maker anticipated water,* her voice said. *You should try the road while it is extended downhill.*

She almost repeated that. Instead, she asked Malik, “Did yours say anything just now?”

His expression tightened. “It says the car is covered.”

The cabin creaked. A pointed limb tapped once on the road-facing window.

Devika placed the phones on the map. Their batteries had all fallen below twenty percent although none had been low at dinner. “We test before we vote ourselves off the island.”

They agreed aloud to make another attempt at the dock. While saying it, they each committed to the woodpile: out the front, sharp right, shelter behind the stacked birch. Malik set a camping lantern in the road-facing window so they could see any movement. Anjali's voice protested that returning to the dock was unwise, then recommended the woodpile as soon as Anjali pictured the route clearly.

The lantern went black. A branch of the seeking shape unhooked itself from the cabin roof and descended toward the birch stack.

“It doesn't hear lies,” Malik said.

“Or it hears them and doesn't care.” Anjali marked an X over the woodpile.

The door latch clicked behind them.

Devika was gone.

Malik lunged for the bolt, but before he reached it the door opened again. Devika slipped inside carrying the fallen flashlight. Mud streaked one sleeve. She relocked the door and leaned against it, breathing through her nose.

“Are you trying to get killed?” Anjali demanded.

“I was trying to get our good flashlight.” Devika set it on the table. The lens was cracked, but its beam worked. “It was lying beside the steps. I saw it through the mudroom window, and I went before I could decide it was a plan.”

“The thing?”

“Still stretched toward the woodpile. One of its points passed over the steps after I was back inside.”

Malik looked from her to the map. “What did your voice say?”

Devika rubbed rain from her face. “Nothing until I picked up the light. Then it asked what I thought I was doing.”

Anjali drew a small circle beside the back steps. One route on the map did not end in an X.

“It didn't know,” she said.

“Mine doesn't know everything,” Devika replied. “It mostly knows how to give orders.”

There was something in the way she said it, an edge that had been waiting longer than the question. Malik heard it too.

“What order?” he asked.

Devika looked at neither of them. “Go north along the shore. Alone. Let the shape spend itself on the two people taking the obvious routes.”

The fire popped behind Anjali. Her neat drawing of the cabin suddenly resembled the little square rooms on the other side of Malik's screen, each waiting to disclose what it contained.

“How long has it been saying that?” she asked.

“Since the dock.”

“And you didn't tell us?”

“I did not leave.” Devika's voice sharpened. “You told us the dock was safe because yours sounded kind. Forgive me for taking ten minutes to work out whether mine being cruel meant it was wrong.”

Outside, the shape scraped across the roof toward the road. The woodpile route had taught it enough to reach both sides of the cabin.

*The road remains possible,* Anjali's voice urged. *If you go now, alone, it may follow you away from the others. You are the best at reading the field.*

The praise found the exact weak place in her. One correct path. One person willing to take it. Anjali picked up the car keys, and Malik caught her wrist.

“Mine says the car is certain death,” he said.

“Mine says it's the only move that keeps the thing from town.”

“And hers says sacrifice us,” Devika said. “Listen to the pattern, not your favorite narrator.”

Anjali looked down at the map. Dock, woodpile, car: each route had become more dangerous after one of the voices judged it. The advice had saved them from the immediate strike and sharpened the next one. Their guides did not need to betray them. They only needed to keep guessing.

She let the keys fall.

“You said the rest of you must guide us to solve it,” she told the formless voice. “What counts as solved?”

Silence lasted long enough that she knew the answer had been withheld, not unknown.

*If you expose the anchor,* it said, *one of us can open a return aperture. We cannot touch what our friend placed while the seeking shape encloses it. That is part of the game.*

“A rule.”

*Yes.*

“Does the shape read our minds?”

*No. It receives our forecasts. Each interception gives it more material reach.*

Malik gave a small, furious laugh. “You've been feeding it.”

*We have also kept you alive.*

Both things were true, which made the voice harder to dismiss and more dangerous to obey.

Anjali turned the map toward her friends. “Devika got past it because she chose after her guide had made a prediction. So we need a plan none of them can finish predicting.”

*I can help you construct—*

“No. Helping now means silence.”

The presence recoiled. Anjali had not known it could feel farther away while remaining inside her thoughts.

“All three of them,” she said to Malik and Devika. “Tell them. If one gives a hint, we stop.”

Devika's instruction took seconds. Malik had to argue with his voice, which apparently regarded silence as a category error. At last he nodded.

The cabin settled around them. Without the voices, the rain sounded larger.

They built their answer from ordinary game-night objects. Malik's steel dice case had a hinged lid and a stubborn latch. Devika tied the fireplace poker to orange utility cord, making a hook long enough to catch the anchor without putting her hand inside the shape. Anjali divided the approaches to the fire clearing into three routes and marked each with torn strips of dish towel. They carried the same useful supplies to every route: light, spare cord, and a cup of Malik's heavy metal dice.

The dice served another purpose. Close to the anchor, they balanced at impossible angles. A handful cast near the porch fell normally; near the north wall, two stopped on edges. Farther into the trees, pine needles hung in little bridges between roots without touching the mud. By comparing the useless, eerie balances along all three approaches, they located the anchor's current resting place near the center of the fire clearing.

They did not choose who would take which path. Instead they agreed on three arrangements, each equally workable. In the first, Devika would take the lake path, Malik the ridge, and Anjali the stony wash. The second moved Devika to the wash, Malik to the lake, and Anjali to the ridge. The third put Devika on the ridge, Malik in the wash, and Anjali by the lake. Devika would always carry the hook, Malik the case, Anjali the brightest lantern. Every route converged on the clearing from a different side.

“I hate plans with tables,” Devika whispered as they stood at the trail fork.

“It's three rows.”

“In the rain, while hunted by evil geometry.”

“Conditional geometry,” Malik said. “We don't know that it's evil.”

“I am comfortable being prejudiced against this one.”

He put a twenty-sided die beneath an enamel mug on a flat stump. One through six would repeat the first arrangement, seven through thirteen the second, fourteen through twenty the third. No one would know until the mug lifted.

Beyond the stump, the seeking shape had thinned itself through the forest. Anjali saw one narrow limb reach toward the lake path, another tremble above the wash, and a third comb the ridge. All three choices were sincere because they had committed to obeying the die. The forecasts, deprived of a favorite, had pulled the construct in three directions.

Malik shook the mug against the stump. The die rattled like a tiny machine trying every future in turn.

He lifted it.

Sixteen.

Devika ran for the ridge. Malik plunged into the wash. Anjali took the lake path, lantern swinging at her side.

The shape reacted a heartbeat too late. A limb snapped down behind Anjali and punched through the trail where her boot had been. She ducked under another, then raised the lantern high. Its light vanished into the reaching black, keeping that branch extended toward her while the rest of the construct tried to gather itself.

Across the clearing, Malik slid on wet stones and drove the open steel case beneath the shape's center. Devika came over the ridge above him. The orange cord uncoiled behind her.

The anchor was no longer hidden. Its stretched limbs had drawn the dark body thin as burned cloth, and the many-sided core turned in a web of tight black strands.

Devika swung the poker. The hook glanced off one edge with a bell-like crack that Anjali felt in her teeth. She pulled it back, planted both feet, and swung again. This time the bent iron caught around the anchor.

“Down!” she shouted.

Malik dropped over the case. Devika hauled. The anchor tore free, snapping the strands one after another, and struck the steel tray hard enough to buckle its bottom. Malik slammed the lid. A pointed limb wrapped around his ankle and dragged him half a meter through the mud before Anjali struck it with the lantern. The glass burst. The limb loosened, darkness streaming from it like ink in fast water.

Malik rolled onto the case and forced the latch closed beneath his weight.

The shape came apart overhead. Its pieces had no gravity of their own; they whipped toward the steel box from every direction, bending young trees and stripping wet needles from branches. The dented lid began to open under Malik's chest.

Anjali reached for the absent voice. “I need you now. Open the return aperture.”

*Where?*

“Under the case.”

The mud beside Malik split along a line too fine to be a crack. Gray light widened beneath the steel, no landscape beyond it, only depth without distance. The opening did not resemble any door Anjali had seen or imagined. Good. It belonged to its own rules.

Malik shoved the case sideways. The leading edge crossed the gray line and vanished. The pull on his ankle released so suddenly that he kicked free. He pushed again. The aperture took the case, the anchor, and the last hooked strand of the seeking shape.

Then it closed.

Rain struck mud. Needles fell from the shaken trees. Somewhere down by the water, a frog resumed an argument it had apparently been saving.

Devika sat on the ridge with the poker across her knees. Malik stared at the empty place where his dice case had been.

“That was my good tray,” he said.

“Call it an equipment cost,” Anjali said.

“I will call it evidence.”

“Of what? We sent it away.”

He held up his hands. The latch had scored a red line across one palm. “Of poor purchasing decisions.”

By the time they returned to the cabin, the spoon lay on its side in the curry and every die had fallen flat. Dawn diluted the windows. They changed into dry clothes, wrapped Malik's hand, and reheated noodles that had acquired the texture of packing material.

The voices returned only when invited.

Devika listened to hers first. Her mouth tightened. “It says preserving one participant was considered an acceptable victory condition.”

“Tell it there was no victory condition,” Malik said. “There were three people.”

She did. Whatever answered made her push her bowl away.

Malik's voice, by his report, apologized with a list of incorrect forecasts. That was apparently the only kind of apology it knew how to make.

Anjali's waited.

“You wanted something with me,” she said. “Was it only to win?”

*At first, I wanted to see what you would do. Then I wanted you to survive. I mistook permission to advise you for permission to place you inside our game.* The voice had lost its careful cheer. *We believed that because we opposed the maker, we stood on your side.*

“You were on our side. You were also above the table.”

*I understand the distinction now.*

“You understand that there is one. We'll see about the rest.”

She tore a blank sheet from the back of Malik's campaign notebook. Across the top she wrote SESSION ZERO. Beneath it, the three friends argued out terms. No created perils without the informed agreement of everyone exposed to them. No hidden victory conditions. Every participant could withdraw, including the people being guided. Information about danger belonged to all of them, not to whichever player hoped to claim the cleverest rescue.

The formless voice objected once, saying it could not promise what the maker would accept.

“Then you cannot promise another game,” Anjali said.

That ended the objection.

When the page was full, Malik and Devika added their names. Anjali left space beneath them.

*Does this mean we will play again?* the voice asked.

She slid the page to the empty place beyond the fallen dice. “It means you can take the rules to your friends. No one makes another move until everyone at both tables agrees.”

stories.body:
# A Very Good Dog

Pickle, alive and delighted inside the adult human body of the most feared villain in the Tri-City Area, galloped on hands and knees across the black-glass floor of Maledict’s skyscraper laboratory with the butler’s left shoe in his teeth. The butler caught him around the waist an instant before he charged headfirst through a rack of humming weapons. At the same time, on the other side of the paired silver circles, Maledict stared down at Pickle’s rough brown legs, one forepaw naturally white with fur from ankle to toes, and reminded himself that the indignity would last exactly fourteen hours.

“Sir,” said the butler, wrestling eighty gleeful kilograms of Maledict away from an armed security drone, “your body is trying to fetch the surveillance equipment.”

The human body barked. No sound came out but a hoarse, delighted *ha!* Pickle dropped the shoe, slapped both hands on the floor, and lunged after the drone.

Maledict attempted to say, *Then fly it higher.* His new mouth produced a rusty woof. His tail thumped the base of a machine that could remove a city block from history.

Fourteen hours. That was all.

The butler had the reversal instructions. At midnight, he would stand Pickle-in-Maledict inside the penthouse circle. Maledict would bite and hold the silver activation plate folded against the inside of Pickle’s collar. Both halves had to engage during the same thirty-second window. The butler could prepare the circle, restrain the dog-minded man, and send the signal, but he could not press Maledict’s plate for him.

Maledict had designed it so no subordinate could steal his body. At present, this seemed less like genius.

The butler recovered his damp shoe. “The pet shuttle is waiting, sir. I have placed the poison capsule and lock override in your collar. Press the counterseal to the override, and its live code will transmit here. Three hours to settle into the target’s home, eight for the household to quiet, one for the operation, and two in reserve. Then you activate the plate. Midnight precisely.”

Pickle bounded onto a steel console in Maledict’s body and began trying to catch his own reflection in the dark window. Forty-nine stories of glass-and-steel fortress glittered around him. Maledict lifted his white forepaw with as much dignity as it allowed.

Fourteen hours later, he would be human again. Brightguard would be dead. Her counterseal would be his. No one would ever laugh about the ultimate evil learning to sit. His tail struck the machine again.

The automated shuttle delivered him to Brightguard’s townhouse at ten thirty, exactly as it had delivered the real Pickle after every scheduled grooming appointment for six years. The front gate scanned his face, his collar, and the pad of his white forepaw. Green lights rippled along the path. Maledict walked straight into the home of his oldest enemy.

The townhouse was all clean concrete, warm timber, and broad windows facing the city. A rescue drone rested on a charging rail above the entry. Compact emergency shields hung among ordinary coats. On a bench lay Brightguard’s silver-and-blue field helmet, its visor still scrolling air-quality figures.

Brightguard herself came down the open stairs fastening the cuff of a contemporary rescue suit. She was older than Maledict by a decade and looked stronger for it: silver at both temples, laugh lines around alert eyes, and the relaxed balance of someone who had caught falling trains without needing to pose afterward.

“There you are,” she said.

Maledict braced for interrogation.

She planted her feet and patted her left thigh twice.

He had studied floor plans, thermal cycles, patrol routes, password changes, grocery deliveries, and the maintenance records of every drone in the building. He had not studied two pats on a thigh.

Brightguard waited. He chose a respectable compromise and sat.

“Pickle.” Her smile bent sideways. “Home means white paw, then red ball. You know that.”

She held out her hand. Something in his borrowed shoulder moved before he decided. His white forepaw landed in her palm. Motor memory: an irritating residue the exchange had carried along with balance, gait, and the location of an itch behind his left ear.

“There’s my boy.”

Maledict reclaimed his paw. The red ball lay in a basket beside the door. He picked it up, set it neatly at her feet, and looked up for confirmation.

Brightguard blinked. “You never hand it over. I have to chase you around the kitchen.”

First error, and he was not fully inside. He snatched the ball and bolted. Brightguard laughed and pursued him past the stairs. He hated the absurdity until she feinted left, he cut right, and the dog body executed a perfect skid beneath the dining table. The red ball squeaked between his teeth. Brightguard pointed at him from the other side, breathing hard and grinning.

“Cheat,” she said fondly.

He won in twelve seconds. He did not return the ball for four minutes.

Brightguard’s command wall filled the living room with maps and emergency feeds while she unfastened pieces of her rescue gear. Municipal crews searched a damaged transit tunnel. News panels carried the same urgent banner: **Maledict missing after unexplained energy event. Public advised to report unusual activity.** His organization had canceled its noon ultimatum. Hero channels, police networks, and three amateur tracking groups all admitted they could not locate him.

Maledict sat beneath the command wall and felt tremendously clever.

“Snack?” Brightguard asked.

She opened a cabinet bearing a small painted paw. Inside, clear containers stood in labeled ranks: liver buttons, salmon twists, dental braids, frozen pumpkin cubes, emergency cheese. This was not a random supply. It was an arsenal of indulgence.

Brightguard selected a liver button. “Your favorite.”

The smell struck Maledict like a warm fist. He turned his head away.

“You love liver.”

He kept his nose pointed at the ceiling.

Brightguard crouched and inspected his muzzle. “You once opened a latched picnic cooler for these.”

Her fingers moved beneath his jaw, gentle but methodical. She checked gums, eyes, ears. Maledict endured it until he saw a cucumber slice on her lunch plate. He had eaten cucumber at state dinners. Cucumber was civilized.

He stole it.

Brightguard froze with one hand inside his ear. “You spit cucumber behind the radiator.”

It was crisp, cold, and magnificent. He stole a second slice.

Her health app came out. A blue diagnostic fan swept from his nose to his tail. Maledict’s collar warned him with a silent vibration that deeper imaging would find the poison capsule and override key.

He seized the liver button from the floor and swallowed.

His dog tongue informed him that his human judgment had been catastrophically wrong. Salt, iron, fat, smoke: the button vanished in one blissful gulp. His ears lifted. His tail betrayed him with such force that it slapped Brightguard’s knee.

She lowered the scanner. “Okay. Appetite’s fine. Opinions are apparently under renovation.”

Maledict stared at the cabinet.

“One,” she said.

He sat without being asked.

“Shameless.” She gave him another.

Across the Tri-City Area, the butler removed a fist-sized black crystal from Maledict’s human mouth.

“No, sir,” he said. “That is a forbidden artifact. It is also sharp.”

Pickle crouched behind Maledict’s desk, grinning with all the villain’s teeth. He slapped one hand on the carpet, inviting pursuit.

The penthouse outside the laboratory had been designed to intimidate diplomats: long planes of black stone, a sunken audience chamber, and windows that made the city appear small enough to pocket. The dog in Maledict’s body had already overturned the throne, drunk from a decorative fountain, and discovered that the security drones fled when chased.

A command call flashed on the wall. The butler straightened Maledict’s collar, guided him into the throne, and arranged a desk high enough to hide his hands. Pickle immediately put his chin on it.

Six silhouettes appeared on the screen. “Our master remains in strategic seclusion,” the butler announced.

One silhouette asked for proof of life. Pickle’s borrowed fingers rose. For one promising second, human motor memory arranged them into Maledict’s dreaded gesture of dismissal. Then he spotted the butler’s recovered shoe and crawled under the desk after it.

The butler blanked the screen. “His displeasure is extreme.” He ended the call before Maledict’s body emerged with the shoe.

At the townhouse, Maledict followed Brightguard upstairs to locate the counterseal. She went into a tiled washroom. He followed, distracted by the open door and the chance to study the bedroom beyond.
