Under the metallic cloth, darkness smelled of wet dust, machine oil, and the rosemary soap Coru bought because she said unscented soap made every room smell faintly of clinics.

“I will count upward,” she said by my ear. “Nothing happens until you say ready.”

Beyond the shed, the pale scanning bar reached the far fence and began its return.

“Ready.”

“One,” Coru said, and stepped into the garden.

The sheet settled over us. “Two.” Her next step jarred my teeth. Under her shirt, heat climbed toward pain. “Three.”

I could see only a strip of ground: cabbages flattened by blast wind, black mud, the white stones I had laid between beds. Coru's gait dragged on the left. Each impact sent a clockwise shiver through rain caught in hoof-shaped depressions.

“Four. Five.”

The search machine's rotors changed pitch.

Coru stopped.

The scan found us as a milk-pale glow through the sheet. My body begged to tear free and run. The machine hovered somewhere above the pear trees, making tiny adjustments that sounded like an insect trapped against glass.

“Six,” Coru said softly.

The light travelled from my feet to my head. Her arms did not tighten. She left me room to make the signal.

I pressed one finger to the plate beneath her collarbone. One tap, not two. A touch with no agreed meaning except that I was still there.

“Seven,” she said.

The machine drifted nearer. Wind from it lifted an edge of the sheet. Beneath us, Coru's left knee gave a fraction. She corrected before our outline split.

“Eight.”

The light held. Against my ribs, her coolant pumps hammered faster than I had ever heard them at the workbench.

“Nine.”

The pale bar slid away.

The whine turned toward the house. Something clicked twice overhead, indifferent and final, and the machine moved on to inspect the roof tile embedded in our kitchen table.

“Ten,” Coru said. Then, “Moving.”

She crossed the remaining garden without waiting for speed to become grace. At the drainage ditch she lowered me onto my feet and pulled the sheet clear. Steam lifted from the vents along her back. Her left leg locked straight.

Behind us, the house stood with one green shutter open. Through the kitchen doorway I saw the floury table, the dead lamps, and a wedge of pale sky where the roof had been. It did not look like proof of anything. It looked like rooms in which we had lived, and might never live again.

“Grate,” Coru said, her voice roughened by heat. “Now.”

The culvert mouth lay beneath brambles at the base of the garden. Its iron grate had warped exactly as I remembered, the lower corner sunk deep in clay. I opened the pry bar, but Coru took it from me and studied the bars.

“Weak point here.” She wedged the flat end where the frame had twisted away from the stone. It was old breaching geometry stripped of explosives and applied to county drainage work. She levered once. Rust groaned. On the second push, something inside her hip cracked loud enough that both of us heard it.

The grate shifted.

I caught the bar as her hand slipped. Together we opened a gap wide enough to crawl through. Coru followed stiffly, dragging the grate back until brambles covered the entrance.

Inside, runoff reached my ankles. The culvert divided twenty paces in, one branch narrowing north beneath the road, the other dropping west through an older stone channel. Sound multiplied between them. Shells became doors slamming ahead and behind. Water struck the walls and returned from directions that had no relation to its source.

Coru stood at the fork, head turning. “I cannot resolve the ground activity.”

It was the first thing she had not known since she turned the pin.

I remembered clearing silt here three springs ago, before the county stopped sending crews. The north branch looked wider, but it climbed to a mesh screen under the road. The west channel kinked twice and opened past the alder ditch.

“Left,” I said. “It sounds wrong because of the bend. It stays below the fields.”

Coru aimed our lamp down the narrower dark. “Footing?”

“Bad for twelve metres. Better after.”

She stepped in first, pressed her weight against the submerged stones, and held out her hand. The old routines remained open behind the panel. Closing them here would have comforted me and endangered us.

I took her hand. Above us, the bombardment tightened around the road. Coru tested the next stone; I told her where the channel turned. At the twelfth step the footing rose, exactly as I remembered. Beyond the bend, my knowledge ended too. Coru angled her lamp across the black water and stepped. I followed before she had to count.

stories.title: Mother of Monsters
stories.prompt: The kingdom calls her the Mother of Monsters, a cursed woman who commands beasts, goblins, and things that should never have crawled from the dark—but when humanity finally marches into her ruined sanctuary to destroy her, they discover the monsters are not her servants; they are refugees, and she is the only thing protecting them from mankind.
stories.body:
# Mother of Monsters

Rennic counted six companies behind the broken arches.

The smallest kept low to the floor, which meant goblin skirmishers. The broad shadows with horns would be shock beasts. Something pale and jointed moved along a wall where no stair remained. Lookouts flashed hand signs from the upper galleries, and each rank withdrew before the next. It was the cleanest retreat Rennic had seen in twelve years of border fighting.

“She has them drilled,” said the bowman at his shoulder.

Rennic watched a horned silhouette lower its head and vanish into the Roofless House. “Then they know what happens when their commander dies.”

Across the slope, the army’s shield line shone in the last sun. The old sanctuary rose above it without roof or tower, a stack of blackened halls left open to weather. Trees grew from its upper floors. Rain had polished the faces off the stone saints. No one knew who had built it, only that things fled here and did not come out.

The ram had opened a knee-high wound in the eastern wall. Sappers were already fitting timber teeth into the crack so they could pry it wide enough for the main force. Through that wound, an advance man had crawled at noon and failed to return.

The general’s runner pointed with a red baton. “First file enters. Recover our man if he lives. Find the Mother. Kill her before the third horn.”

A finite order. Rennic liked orders that ended.

He lowered himself through the breach with four soldiers behind him. The stone scraped scales from his coat. Inside, he found a passage so low that even the goblins must have stooped. The file went on knees and elbows, shields shoved ahead. Behind them, sapper mallets struck in pairs. Dust jumped from the ceiling with every blow.

The passage opened into a long chamber. Rennic rose, sword ready, and saw that the enemy had abandoned its barracks.

Beds lay in rows, if beds they were: straw nests, a sand trough, blankets stretched between pegs, a stone basin padded with moss. Feeding bowls stood beside some of them. Leather slings hung from the walls. Bundles waited by the far door, tied for travel.

No weapons.

“Efficient,” Rennic said. “They carried the iron and left the weight.”

The spearwoman prodded a little coat with her boot. It had four sleeves, the lower pair patched at the elbows. “Captain.”

“Eyes on the door.”

He led them past a wicker screen. Behind it were clay toys: a cart with round stones for wheels, a bird with too many wings, three dolls made from knotted grass. The youngest soldier looked at them until Rennic snapped two fingers.

The room proved nothing. Raiders nested. Wolves played before they learned blood. Coordination meant command, and command meant the woman they had come to kill.

At the far door, the corridor dropped sharply. Rennic heard a wet, sawing breath below and raised his fist. The file froze.

Around the corner crouched a goblin in a stained apron. Its ears had been cut down to ragged nubs. Between its knees lay the missing advance man, white-faced and awake, one leg trapped in a frame of narrow sticks.

“Cage,” breathed the mace-bearer.

He lunged before Rennic could answer. The goblin flung itself across the wounded man, not at the attacker. Rennic caught the mace shaft on his sword guard and drove it aside. The iron head smashed plaster.

“Hold.”

“It has him.”

“I said hold.”

The advance man clawed at Rennic’s boot. “Don’t hit the little one.”

His leg was wrapped from ankle to thigh. Two straight slats held the shin; the supposed cage was a raised brace keeping the blankets from touching it. A dark stain had spread through the wrapping, but the knot above it was tight and properly placed.

The goblin showed small teeth. “Longbones kicked my splint.” Its voice was hoarse but perfectly clear. “Tell him stop kicking.”

“The wall came down,” the advance man said. “When the ram struck. It pulled me clear.”

“She ordered it?” Rennic asked.

The goblin blinked. “Who?”

Another paired blow sounded behind them. Grit sifted over the blankets. The goblin snatched up a wooden bowl and covered the wounded man’s face before the dust reached him.

Rennic sheathed his sword. “Make a litter.”

The spearwoman and the youngest soldier threaded two poles through a canvas sling. The goblin slapped their hands away twice, retied the support, then climbed beside the injured leg as they lifted. The healer carried a case of bone needles on a cord around their neck and a butcher’s cleaver at their belt. The cleaver made the mace-bearer stare.

“For bandage,” the goblin said. “For meat. Sometimes for men.”

No one laughed.

They could have sent the litter back. It would take two bearers, and the breach was narrowing under falling grit even as the sappers widened the outer face. Rennic pictured the file cut in half, his target moving deeper, the third horn sounding while he tried to save one man. He pointed forward.

“We find another way out.”

The wounded man shut his eyes. The goblin muttered something that sounded like a diagnosis of Rennic’s intelligence.

Beyond the infirmary, the ordered retreat broke apart.

Goblins came through one doorway carrying sacks between them and departed by three others. A squat creature with digging claws tested a low tunnel, recoiled at its smell, and planted itself in the path until those behind chose another route. Two furred beasts dragged a grain chest in opposite directions. A horned dam shouldered through the press with a mewling young one caught gently in her jaws, then turned back into the crowd for a second.

No officer corrected them. No signal united them. They argued, shoved, yielded, returned.

“They’re routing by kind,” the bowman said, but his voice lacked conviction.

At the center of the chamber stood an arch filled with solid masonry. Chisel marks showed where a door had once been sealed. An old woman with blue-scaled hands stumbled toward it carrying a basket of eggs. She glanced back at the soldiers.

Somewhere deeper in the ruin, a woman called, “Come through if you mean to flee them.”

The sealed arch darkened. The old woman stepped into stone and disappeared.

Rennic reached it three strides later. His sword point struck mortar. He pressed his palm against a wall that had become only a wall.

At his boots, a torn packet leaked salt. The grains had fused into one cloudy, translucent lump shaped like the spill. A goblin child darted in, scooped it up, and scolded the empty arch. “Now we need the hammer again.”

The child ran on with its salt.

“A gate,” said the youngest soldier.

“A trap,” said the mace-bearer.

Rennic studied the branching doors. He had seen the old woman look back. He had heard the condition in the unseen speaker’s words. Flee them.

“She is sorting who goes where,” he said. “The rest are theater. Move.”

He chose the corridor with the freshest claw marks. It brought them through a storehouse and robbed him of another explanation.

The kingdom’s grain marks showed on half the sacks. Spears and hunting bows lay stacked beside them, along with three helmets split by heavy blows. There was guilt enough in the room. But beside the trophies hung a row of iron collars, each cut through at the hinge. Branding irons lay in a bucket of rainwater. One bore a baron’s wheat-sheaf. Another Rennic knew from the pens along the southern road.

The youngest soldier touched a brand on the wall where someone had pressed it while hot. The plaster around the mark had gone brown.

“Don’t,” Rennic said.

The soldier snatched his fingers away.

On a shelf, arrowheads had been sorted by size and bound into bundles. Rennic recognized the triangular hunting points used in his own valley. One winter, something had torn open three sheepfolds there and killed his sister when she ran outside with a lamp. The prints had been confused by snow and blood. The steward’s proclamation had said the Mother’s beasts took livestock to feed her army. Rennic had carried that sentence for nine years because it put a will behind the night: one mind that wanted, ordered, and could be ended.

He picked up an arrowhead. Brown rust crusted the socket.

“Those came out of bodies,” the goblin healer said, watching him over the litter. “Most did.”

“And the grain?”

“Stolen.”

“The helmets?”

“Won.” The healer showed their teeth again. “Or stolen. I mend legs, not histories.”

The mace-bearer touched one split helmet with two fingers. “My boy wore this crest.”

The healer’s cut ears flattened. “Then ask whoever took it.”

“You hide them.”

“Yes.”

The healer checked the injured man’s foot, pinched a toe, and watched the response. Beside them, the helmet stayed split. The splint kept the broken leg straight.

Rennic put down the arrowhead.

The first horn sounded outside, its note rolling through the open courts. The sappers had set the main braces. Two signals remained.

They found Iskava in an inner hall under a strip of darkening sky.

The old throne stood against the far wall, carved from the same black stone as the sanctuary. A woman sat upon it in a torn white dress. Her dark hair hung loose around a narrow face; iron circled her head in a fan of spikes. Creatures crowded below her. Some knelt. Others waited under side arches, clutching packs, children, tools, cages of chirping insects.

Rennic felt the shape of the mission return. There was the seat, the supplicants, the woman at the center. The Mother of Monsters looked at him without surprise.

He drew his sword.

“Iskava.”

“That is mine.” Her mouth barely moved. “The other thing is yours.”

“Release them.”

A goblin near her barked a laugh. A feathered creature said, “Release yourself,” and chose the left-hand arch despite Iskava pointing weakly to the right.

No punishment followed. Iskava merely turned to a scaled youth carrying a sleeping bundle. “Not that way. The stair ends in the rain court.”

“My clutch is there.”

“Then go.”

The youth went. Another refugee seized its sleeve and pulled it toward a different arch. They shouted over each other until both disappeared into an ordinary passage.

Rennic advanced. The kneeling creatures drew back, and he saw that none knelt to Iskava. They knelt beneath the arch around her, waiting for their turn.

The throne was no throne. Its seat had cracked away. Iskava’s back was wedged against a carved slab that sagged from the arch above her. Both hands gripped grooves in the stone. Gray whiteness had crept from her fingertips to her wrists. She braced with her legs because her feet could no longer find the floor.

“Come through if you mean to flee them,” she said.

The arch behind her opened on darkness full of moving torchlight. The torchlight belonged to a different chamber. Three goblins carried a litter across. Then a black hound limped to the threshold and stopped.

“Go,” Iskava whispered.

The hound backed away, whining, and turned toward the side passage instead. Iskava did not force it. She could not even keep it from stepping on the hem of her dress.

Rennic tried the arch. Cold stone met his palm where torchlight and an open room appeared to be. The view remained, impossible and close.

“You welcomed me when I entered,” he said.

“No.” Iskava’s teeth clicked on the word. “You broke my wall.”

“You could send them beyond the army.”

“I can send no one. They cross while escaping pursuit, if I have given shelter and they choose the step. The House bends what I open.” She nodded toward the visible chamber. “It has no will. Nor enough doors.”

“If I kill you?”

“It closes.”

She did not bargain. She looked past his sword and counted those waiting. An insect-winged child had collapsed against a pillar. Its father picked it up, tried the threshold, and struck stone. The child’s head lolled against his shoulder.

“Awake,” Iskava told him. “I cannot carry a sleeper.”

The father shook the child, pleaded, bit its fingertip. Its eyes opened. The path opened too, and the pair staggered through. Iskava sagged lower against the slab.

The injured advance man raised himself on the litter. “Captain.”

“Quiet.”

“She never commanded that goblin. Little one found me alone.”

The healer slapped his chest. “Lie down before I command you dead.”

The second horn sounded.

Rennic knew its exact meaning. The eastern crack was wide enough for two abreast. The third signal would send the shield column through. Once the hall filled with soldiers, every figure before them would become a type again: fangs, horns, claws, target. No one in a packed breach could afford the time Rennic had spent being wrong.

The mace-bearer raised his weapon. “Finish it.”

Iskava turned her head toward the next refugee. It was the old woman with blue-scaled hands, back again without her egg basket. She carried a goblin child now.

“You crossed already,” Iskava said.

“Missed one.”

“Of course you did.”

The old woman stepped through.

Rennic saw how to end the mission. One stroke. The target could not lift a hand to stop him. His sister would remain dead. The split helmets would remain split. Tomorrow’s proclamation would call the surviving refugees a scattered enemy, and the next captain would count their flight as proof of organization.

He sheathed his sword.

“Back to the breach,” he ordered.

The file obeyed from habit. They carried the wounded man at a punishing pace while the goblin healer trotted beside the litter, swearing each time it jolted. Refugees pressed themselves against walls to let the soldiers pass. Some hissed. One threw a cup. The mace-bearer came last, saying nothing.

At the sleeping chamber, the eastern wound had grown tall enough to show helmets beyond it. Three sapper posts held the cracked lintel while an iron pin locked their crossbrace. When the pin came free, the sappers would replace the frame and pull away another course of stone.

Rennic set his hand on the pin.

The bowman understood first. “Captain, no.”

“Third horn is moments away. Anyone going out, go now.”

“What do I report?”

“What you saw.”

The bowman looked back through the rooms, then ducked into the breach.

The youngest soldier followed him as far as the opening, stopped, and returned to the litter. The spearwoman planted her shield over the wounded man against falling debris. She did not look at Rennic.

The mace-bearer caught Rennic’s wrist. “My boy is in that storehouse.”

“His helmet is.”

“You think that matters?”

“I think killing her kills everyone who hasn’t crossed.”

“They killed ours.”

“Some did.”

The mace-bearer’s grip tightened. He had understood every room. Understanding had changed nothing he was willing to do.

“Then go out,” Rennic said.

The man struck him in the mouth. Rennic tasted blood and drove his shoulder under the man’s chest. They hit the wall together. The iron pin shifted a finger’s width; the lintel groaned. Outside, sappers shouted.

The mace-bearer went still. Rennic released him.

For one breath, the man stood between the army and the ruined rooms. Then he shoved himself through the breach after the bowman.

Rennic looked at the two who remained. “I can’t order this.”

“Good,” said the spearwoman. “Pull.”

They dragged the litter clear. Rennic kicked the retaining hook loose and hauled on the pin with both hands. It came out hot from friction. The crossbrace snapped sideways.

The eastern wall folded inward.

Stone struck stone with a noise too large for the chamber. Dust swallowed the beds, the little coat, the clay bird with too many wings. Rennic curled over his head as blocks rolled past. A timber post clipped his shoulder and spun him to the floor.

When the thunder ended, the breach was a slope of broken masonry packed to the ceiling. A blade poked once through a gap, withdrew, and could not find it again.

The third horn sounded outside.

No column came.

They returned to the inner hall by torchlight. Rennic’s left arm hung numb. The spearwoman and the youngest soldier bore the litter. The goblin healer walked ahead, cleaver drawn now. “Wall-dropper coming,” the healer called. “Still armed. Give space.”

Only a few remained at Iskava’s arch. She could no longer speak. Each crossing left her shuddering. The gray pallor had reached her throat.

A six-legged beast went through carrying two sacks of grain and came back without them. It lowered its body beside an old goblin who could not walk. The goblin climbed on, and the beast carried them both to the arch.

The last was the horned dam. She arrived with one young in her jaws and another nudging her hind legs. At the threshold she set the first down, pushed both ahead, then hesitated. The distant chamber wavered.

Iskava’s fingers slipped in the stone grooves.

Rennic put his good shoulder against the sagging slab. It was only masonry. He could hold that much.

The dam gathered both young and crossed. The arch became solid. Iskava folded where she sat, the iron spikes sliding from her head and ringing across the floor.

The refugees already beyond the threshold moved on through the deep chambers, their torchlight thinning along several routes. Those left in the hall lifted Iskava away from the cracked seat. They would not let Rennic touch her.

The goblin healer knelt beside the wounded soldier and cut away the blood-soaked wrapping. “You,” the healer said to Rennic.

Three goblins turned at once.

“Big longbones with the bad face. Hold this.”

The healer gave him the end of a fresh bandage. Rennic sat below the wall he had dropped and drew the cloth taut while the healer bound his soldier’s leg. Around them, refugees shouldered bundles into the dark without waiting for Iskava to wake.

From somewhere beyond the buried breach came the scrape of shovels. Then, farther along the Roofless House, iron picks began testing another wall.

stories.title: Where Sleep Takes You
stories.prompt: You have the power of teleportation. However you also have narcolepsy and keep accidentally teleporting to random locations every time you fall asleep.
stories.body:
# Where Sleep Takes You

I put the emergency tag, shoes, and coat beside the bed while Talune watches from the doorway with the blue mug in both hands.

The mug is hers. We established this ten minutes ago. The discovery has not encouraged her to leave.

“Shoes need to be on you,” she says.

“Shoes do not make good pajamas.”

“That has never stopped you.”

I point at the soft-soled boots already on my feet. “I mean the spare shoes. The ones by the bed. Look at them being spare.”

Talune drinks the last of her tea and surveys what remains of our shared bedroom. Her side is a pale rectangle on the floorboards, four clean screw holes, and one forgotten loop of silver tinsel caught behind the radiator. The bed is mine because she bought the sofa; the sofa is hers because I once teleported away from it during a film and returned to find she had eaten my share of the dumplings. This was judged, by both of us, to establish ownership.

In the kitchen, half the cupboards stand open. We have divided the duplicates: two strainers, three wooden spoons, four years of takeaway containers without lids. Talune's boxes have gone three streets east to an apartment with yellow cabinets, a bathroom fan that screams, and a bedroom not occupied by me. She can walk back in six minutes.

I can come back in less than one.

“Live call,” she says. “Just for tonight.”

“Absolutely not.”

“You don't have to talk. Put the phone on the pillow and I'll hear if you go.”

“You will hear me breathing, which you hate.”

“I hate your whistle. Your breathing is otherwise acceptable.”

I kneel to check the kit attached snugly under my sleep shirt. The little pouch has cash, gauze, a foil blanket, a short pencil, and no zipper, magnets, or clever clasps. Two press studs hold it shut. The embossed steel tag gives my name and an emergency number in letters that cannot be wiped by a jump. I used to carry a bank card until teleporting combed its stripe blank for the third time. Talune used to keep a hotel key in her pocket until I borrowed the trousers and woke locked out of a room I had paid for.

Everything close and secured comes with me. Loose blankets do not. Pillows do not. Dignity varies.

“I will message you if I jump,” I say. “I wake, I come home, I message. Then you go to sleep.”

“In that order?”

“It's a strong order.”

She puts the blue mug on my windowsill, apparently undecided about its legal status. “What if you don't wake?”

“Then I don't mind where I am.”

The joke lands badly. Some nights a quiet destination lets me sleep for an hour. Some nights cold or noise returns me to myself at once. The part between is unavailable for review.

Talune looks at the bed instead of me. “What if you wake somewhere you shouldn't be?”

“I come back.”

“What if you're hurt?”

“I come back.”

“What if you can't get awake enough to picture here?”

“Talune.”

She picks up the mug. “Live call.”

“No.”

Her mouth tightens, not quite anger and not quite surrender. She has spent years developing expressions with no emergency value whatsoever. “Message after every one.”

“Immediately.”

“Even if it's three in the morning.”

“Especially then. You'll see I'm back, and we can both sleep.”

She gives me a long look. We both leave the arithmetic alone.

At the front door, Talune hugs me with the mug trapped between us. Then she carries it away, settling the final disputed object through theft.

“I intend to wake at home,” I tell her.

“Excellent,” she says. “Do that.”

Alone, I make the apartment exact.

I turn the rug so its worn edge meets my left heel when I stand beside the bed. I leave the lamp on low. The radiator knocks twice every few minutes, with the self-importance of someone at a door. Dust warms on the shade. The fitted sheet has a cold patch near the wall and a small rough place where an old spring presses up. I know this room awake, ill, laughing, furious, and half blind with fatigue. To return deliberately, I need to hold a place in my mind clearly enough that it becomes more present than wherever I am.

It is an easy room to remember.

I brush my teeth. I secure my phone to my wrist with the ridiculous running band. I lie down in boots, leggings, sleep shirt, and kit. The coat waits close enough to mock me but not close enough to travel.

I open a puzzle on my phone, because I am not yet tired and because refusing to monitor whether I am tired is the closest I come to relaxation. The clue is *Put into boxes, eight letters*. I type C-A-T-E-G—

My cheek is pressed against coarse plastic. A motor screams beyond a corrugated wall.

I sit up too fast. My phone strikes my eyebrow, held by its wrist strap, and something collapses beneath me with a dry, enveloping crunch. For half a second I understand nothing except cold air and the smell of rubber.

Then the place separates into things. Bundles of flattened packing sleeves support my weight. A corrugated roof, high and black between hanging lamps. Orange racks. A closed roller door shivering in its frame. The motor starts again, nearer or louder; I cannot tell which. White light flickers through wired glass.

My hands are already reaching for home.

Rug edge. Radiator. Warm dust. Rough spring. The room gathers around the memory, and the freight shed is gone.

I land beside the bed with my knees locked. My shoulder hits the wall. The lamp trembles on the crate that serves as a bedside table.

I type **back** before the room has settled.

Talune's reply arrives while I am still rubbing the mark above my eyebrow.

**Hurt?**

I look down. Both boots. No obvious blood. My left wrist is red from the phone band.

**No. Freight shed. Very glamorous.**

Three dots appear at once.

**What was moving?**

**Nothing near me.**

**You said motor.**

I have no memory of telling her that. I read my message again. I did not.

**Lucky guess. Go to sleep.**

**Was there an exit? Anyone there? Were you warm enough?**

I start to type three different answers and discover I possess none of them. The freight shed in my mind has already flattened into plastic, noise, and the decision to leave.

**Back means safe**, I send.

The reply takes longer.

**Back means back.**

I reset the rug. I straighten the lamp. The tooth mug is three centimeters left of where I put it, so I correct that too, though no part of teleportation has touched the bathroom. When my room is exact again, I lie down.

My phone says 12:41. I have slept eleven minutes.

The next gap is less violent.

I wake curled on something cool and yielding, with wet seeping through the knees of my leggings. Night presses close on every side. The air smells of soil and cut stalks. When I lift my head, low clouds hold the glow of a distant town, and a row of black trees leans along the horizon.

I am in a field. It is not raining. Nothing is approaching me. My right hand rests in clover, and a small beetle shines on the steel tag at my waist.

I check the time. 2:18.

For one astonished moment I am pleased. More than an hour of sleep, uninterrupted after arrival. My limbs feel heavy in the good way, as though they belong to gravity instead of vigilance.

Twenty paces away, a tin awning juts from a low agricultural building. The ground beneath it appears dry. I could go there. I could make sure it is empty, sit against the wall, and perhaps sleep again. If someone finds me, I can leave before they finish asking how I crossed the fence.

My phone is dark. Talune is waiting for **back**.

I do not quite choose. The apartment comes faster than the question: rug, radiator, dust, spring. Damp grass snaps out of existence.

This time I arrive crouching. Mud flakes from my boots onto the floorboards.

**Back**, I send.

Talune replies before I can unfasten the phone.

**Hurt?**

The pleasure of the long sleep drains away. **No. Field. Fine. You were supposed to sleep.**

**I was. Phone woke me.**

It is a lie with poor structural support. We both know her phone gives my messages a soft two-note chime, and we both know what Talune's sentences look like when she has just woken. Capitals disappear. Punctuation becomes theoretical. The message on my screen is fully dressed and standing at attention.

**Good night**, I type.

**Good night.**

I clean mud from the floor. The boots are damp inside, so I change socks and put them back on. I consider the coat. It is rainproof, warm, and miserable to sleep in. Saving it for somewhere worse feels sensible. Also, if I use everything on the first night alone, the first night has won.

At 2:46 I lie down again. My body is tired enough to ache. My mind starts making bright, stupid inventories: coastlines, rooftops, locked rooms, winter roads. Places are not summoned by fear. Fear has tried.

I turn the phone face down.

The mattress gives beneath me.

Rain needles my face.

I am on my back, staring up through a grid of yellow steel. A lamp beyond it scatters light in the water on my eyelashes. Something clangs hard enough to punch the sleep from me.

I roll to my side. My palm skids over wet concrete and catches on a jagged edge. Heat opens across the skin.

There is a painted line beside my shoulder. Beyond it, rain stripes a darkness cut by two parallel rails. Not a passenger platform: no signs, no benches, no tidy edge. A service walkway, narrow and slick, roofed in sections by cable trays. Red lamps burn at ground level. Farther down, an alarm begins a patient electronic pulse.

I get one boot under me. It slides. My hand slaps down again, and this time I see blood diluted pink around my fingers.

Home.

I seize the radiator knock and lose it beneath the alarm. Rug edge, lamp dust, rough spring. The walkway wobbles. A few steps away, a door stands under a shallow shelter, its green emergency bar bright in the rain.

Home, now.

The apartment takes me.

I arrive in the correct place and the wrong arrangement, pitched forward with my weight committed to a floor that is no longer wet. My knees hit first. I catch myself on the wounded hand and make a noise like a chair dragged over tile.

The lamp falls. Its shade rolls beneath the bed.

For several seconds I stay on all fours, watching blood bead on my palm. The radiator knocks twice.

I send **back**.

Talune calls.

I reject it.

She calls again. I reject that too and type **Fine. Small cut.**

The third call keeps vibrating against my wrist until I answer.

“What happened?” Talune says.

“I slipped.”

“Where?”

“Here.”

“Before here.”

“Some kind of rail service platform.” I sit back against the bed. The room tilts a fraction and rights itself. “Not a public one. I don't know. There was an alarm.”

“Are you bleeding?”

“A little.”

“Wash it.”

“I know how cuts work.”

“Then why are you still sitting on the floor?”

I look automatically toward the corner of the ceiling, where there has never been a camera. “Go to bed, Talune.”

“I was in bed.”

“You were staring at your phone.”

“Yes.”

She says it without even trying to protect my feelings.

I push myself upright, using my elbow on the mattress. “I am home. You can sleep.”

“Are you dizzy?”

“You are not listening.”

“Because you sound dizzy.”

“I said I'm home.”

“And I can hear the part you're using that word to cover.”

My hand throbs. In the bathroom, I run it under water and wedge the phone between my ear and shoulder. “You moved out so you wouldn't have to do this.”

“I moved out because the yellow cupboards made me happy and because I would like to invite people over without telling them that my roommate may disappear between the starter and dessert.”

“So invite them.”

“I intend to. That's not the same as wanting you dead in a drainage culvert.”

“I wasn't in a drainage culvert.”

“Congratulations.”

“Stop monitoring me.”

There is a pause. Water ticks against the basin. When Talune speaks again, her voice is quieter.

“All right.”

The answer catches where resistance would have been easier. I tear open the gauze packet with my teeth. “All right what?”

“I will stop.”

“You can't just turn your phone off.”

“You told me to.”

“I told you to sleep. If I call because I need you, that's different.”

“Then call because you need me.”

“How am I supposed to know if I need you?”

“Carys.” Her patience tears. “You want me unconscious but also available to confirm that every decision you made while I was unconscious was safe.”

“I want you to be my friend.”

“I am your friend. I cannot be the little green light that comes on when you get back.”

I press gauze to my palm. It stings sharply enough to clear the last fog. “You always wanted the messages.”

“I wanted to know you were alive.”

“Same thing.”

“No. It isn't.” A cupboard opens on her end of the call, followed by the soft knock of glass on wood. She is in her yellow kitchen, probably filling the blue mug again. “What was beside you on the platform?”

“Tracks.”

“On the other side.”

I close my eyes. Rain. Cable trays. Red ground lamps. A green bar. “A door.”

“Locked?”

“I don't know.”

“Cover?”

“Some.”

“Could you have got out of the rain?”

“I don't know.”

“In the field?”

I say nothing.

“You came back because I was waiting,” Talune says.

“I came back because that is what I do.”

“Those are the same answer.”

The bathroom light is too white. On the floor by my boot, a blade of clover worked loose from the tread has survived the cleaning cloth. I crouch, pick it up, and drop it in the bin.

“The shed could have had a forklift coming through,” I say. “The field could have had a bull. The platform had rails. Home is safer.”

“Usually.”

“Reliably.”

“You just arrived reliably on your knees.”

That is unfair, chiefly because it is exact.

Talune exhales near the receiver. “I don't want you to stay somewhere dangerous to prove you can. I want you to look before you spend the one useful thing you know.”

I know home. That is what she means. The room is not a rope attached to my waist; it is a sensory fact I can hold when I am properly awake. Tonight I have been grabbing it like a handle before I know whether I can stand.

“Three questions,” Talune says. “Not to me. You answer them there.”

“I hate questionnaires.”

“Awake?”

I wait.

“Hurt?” she continues. “Safer here or known place?”

“That third one has too many words.”

“You can afford the metal.”

I turn the tag over. The back is blank except for scratches left by years of keys I no longer carry. “And then?”

“If you need help, you call me. Once. If I don't answer, you use the emergency number. If you don't need help, send a message when you can, and I do not have to answer.”

“How will I know you got it?”

“You won't.”

The word opens a small, cold place in me that has nothing to do with weather.

“I'm three streets away,” she says. “I'm still going to worry. I am just not going to stay awake as evidence that worrying works.”

My palm has stopped bleeding through the gauze. “What if the next place is worse?”

“Then it is worse whether I'm watching my phone or not.”

Her voice shakes at the edge of the sentence. She covers it by drinking from the mug.

I take the pencil from my kit. On a strip of waterproof tape from the bathroom drawer, I print the questions in letters that grow smaller toward the end: **AWAKE? HURT? SAFER HERE OR KNOWN PLACE?** I wrap the tape around the back of the tag.

“Done,” I say.

“Good.”

Neither of us hangs up.

Finally Talune says, “I'm putting my phone on sleep mode. Your calls will ring. Messages won't.”

“Good.”

“Good night, Carys.”

“Good night.”

The line goes quiet.

I finish cleaning the cut and bandage it without making the dressing so thick I cannot close my hand. In the bedroom, I put the lamp back together. I remove the damp socks, dry my feet, and dress again. This time I add the thin weatherproof layer and zip it to my throat. It whispers whenever I move. I have been saving it for a hypothetical worse place, as if fabric could be used up by being worn.

Cash. Gauze. Foil blanket. Pencil. Tag. Phone. Boots.

I do not reset the rug.

At 3:37, I lie down. The jacket is unpleasant against the sheet. My palm pulses. Talune's contact shows a crescent beside it. Her phone is quiet; the icon tells me nothing about her.

I put the phone face down and let my eyes close before I feel ready.

The hum comes first.

It is soft and steady, threaded with an occasional plastic tick. My hip rests on coarse carpet. My face is warm, but cold has found the gap above my collar.

I open my eyes.

Metal shelving rises on two sides, stacked with boxes of envelopes, toner cartridges, and paper cups. An amber light glows on a power strip beneath a desk. There is no window. Above me, a vent breathes refrigerated air into the cramped room.

I do not move yet.

Awake?

Enough to read the labels twice. The clock on my phone says 5:52.

Hurt?

The bandaged palm is dry. My head is clear. My feet are warm. The carpet has pressed a grid into my cheek, but this does not qualify.

Safer here or known place?

Here is cold, private, and probably trespassing. Home is known. Home is also three seconds away once I can summon it without panic, and nothing in this room requires three seconds.

I sit up slowly. The storeroom door has no interior lock. A narrow pane of wired glass shows a dark office beyond: blank monitors, wheeled chairs, the green glow of an exit sign. No voices. No machinery. Beside the door hangs a laminated fire plan. I find the storeroom square, trace the short corridor to a stairwell, and listen.

Silence, except for the vent and the blood moving in my ears.

I type one message.

**awake, unhurt, staying five minutes**

It shows as delivered. No reply appears. No reply is required.

I turn the phone face down on the carpet and study the office through the glass: the sightlines between desks, the stairwell door, the shadow where a cleaner's cart might be parked. If the corridor remains empty, I can walk out. If it changes, I can come home.

Four minutes remain. I use them to learn the door.

stories.title: All the Ways They Knew Her
stories.prompt: Every summer, the city closes the old park road for a sprawling street festival, and every summer she spends the day weaving through the crowds on rollerblades. This year, halfway down the avenue, she realizes something strange: everyone she passes seems to recognize her.
stories.body:
# All the Ways They Knew Her

At the northern barricade, Maris Calder set all eight wheels on the old park road and made herself the same promise she made every summer: no foot on the pavement until the southern gate.

The promise had been harder when she was younger and believed difficulty required witnesses. Now it was private, which made it better. She bent her knees, pushed twice, and entered the festival between a rack of paper parasols and a man walking backward with three lemonades.

The road was smooth where bus tires polished it all year and gorgeous when there were no buses. For one afternoon it belonged to strollers, dancers, wandering eaters, children with painted faces, dogs alarmed by drums, and Maris. She knew how each of them moved. Small children launched sideways without warning. Couples joined at the hand had the turning radius of gates. A person carrying food would protect the food before protecting any other part of the body. Dogs telegraphed; teenagers did not.

She did not need people to notice her. She needed them to continue being themselves for the half second it took her to pass.

A trumpet opened a bright hole in the noise. Smoke from the grills made the sunlight visible. Maris coasted behind a wagon, counted the sway of two shopping bags, and slipped through just before they knocked together. Her left skate hissed over a paper napkin. Her right missed a dropped fork by the width of a wheel.

This was the pleasure she returned for. Not solitude exactly. Solitude was available on the paths before breakfast, with beetles ticking in the weeds and nobody selling anything fried. Here she could be among thousands of people without any one encounter having to hold. Every body offered a problem with an immediate, courteous solution. She read the gap, passed through, and left no debt behind.

“There she is,” a woman called from a drink stall.

Maris lifted two fingers without looking over. The woman could have meant anybody. There were hundreds of people to be there.

“Happy festival!” the woman added, more distinctly.

Maris answered, “You too,” because the words fit through a smaller gap than a conversation.

She crossed the first block with the lazy confidence of someone on a familiar floor. The stall positions changed each year, but the crowd kept its old tides: outward along the curbs, inward toward music, sudden dams wherever free samples appeared. She took the middle until a cluster of toddlers forced her toward the shade. Two teenagers there saw her and struck identical poses, one arm extended as if presenting a prize.

“It’s you,” one said.

The other waved both hands.

Maris glanced behind her. A dancer in silver streamers was coming up the road on stilts, tall enough to deserve anyone’s excitement. Maris pointed a thumb that way.

The teenagers laughed. One held up a folded blue booklet, but Maris was already past, listening to the clicks behind her as people raised their phones for the dancer.

At the dumpling stand, a man carrying a paper tray stepped left before Maris signaled. She went right to avoid him. He went right too, smiling in apology, then planted himself against the counter and swept one arm toward the open road.

“After you,” he said.

She carved past. That could still be ordinary. A good skater was visible in a crowd. The knee pads and wrist guards might suggest competence even if the scuffed boots did not. People sometimes gave her too much room. She preferred that to too little.

Then a woman with a sunhat tucked her elbow in before Maris had chosen a side. A family closed around its wagon. Two men carrying a rolled rug stopped across from each other and waited. Ahead of Maris, space opened in little sections, not quite a lane but the rumor of one.

Faces began to turn.

Maris slowed without letting either skate stop. Her body disliked the change before her mind found a reason for it. Slow crowds were harder than fast streets. At speed, decisions expired behind her. At walking pace, every glance remained available for inspection.

A man near the puppet booth said, “That’s the skater from the program.”

“Where?” someone asked.

Maris pushed hard. A string of festival flags flickered overhead. The drums behind her lost a contest with a fiddle ahead. On both sides, people carried the same blue booklet: folded into back pockets, curled around cups, used as fans. She had seen them at the barricade in volunteers’ hands and nowhere else because she had not been looking. Now they seemed to flash on every block.

She considered turning onto the grass, taking the wide path behind the stalls, and recovering the road farther down. It would keep her moving. It would also be cheating. The route was the road, northern barricade to southern gate. Fourteen summers. She had made it through a thunderstorm, a loose frame bolt, and one parade so dense she spent ten minutes rolling in place behind a papier-mâché fish.

Whatever this was, it would have to make room.

She ducked under a balloon string. A food courier wheeled a bicycle across her line; she tapped one brake, pivoted, and missed the rear tire. Someone cheered. More people joined in, a scattered clap that traveled ten yards and died of embarrassment.

Maris’s face went hot.

“What program?” she called, but the courier thought she was angry with him and shouted an apology. By the time she looked back, the people who had clapped were studying their food.

At the next crossing, a little girl stood in front of her with a blue booklet open against her chest.

The girl’s father caught her by the shoulders. “Don’t block the road.”

“But look.” The girl raised the booklet beside Maris as if checking the color of paint against a wall. “It is her.”

Maris swerved onto the crosswalk, circled the white painted figure there, and came back without putting a brake down. The father had drawn the girl to the curb. He looked mortified. The girl looked exactingly pleased.

“May I see that?” Maris asked.

The booklet had been folded backward. Before the girl could turn it over, three women in matching aprons called to the father from a stall. He answered them; the girl answered him; a stroller filled the space between Maris and all of them. Maris caught a glimpse of dark wheels printed against blue and then the crowd moved the booklet away.

“The photo exhibit,” the father said over his shoulder. “Halfway down.”

She was already three body-lengths past him.

Halfway down was where the road widened around an old traffic island. Maris knew it by the rough patch that tugged at her left skate and by the five seconds of shade cast by the trees. This year a canvas awning occupied the curbside lane. Blue arrows pointed toward it. COMMUNITY PHOTOS, they said, the only words she managed to read before momentum carried her beyond the entrance.

She could continue. She could reach the southern gate, take off her skates, then walk back and ask a complete question like a person with shoes on. The promise had rules. The promise did not say she had to be ignorant.

Behind her, somebody said, “She never stops.”

Maris made a wide turn around a planter and skated against the current.

It was her first circle back in fourteen years.

She approached the awning at a crawl. Interlocking mats covered the sidewalk beneath it, their edges curled by heat. She braked on the road and caught the center pole with one hand.

Her face, nearly three feet high, looked back from the first display panel.

It was an excellent photograph. Last summer’s sun had found the damp at her temples and a loose dark curl behind her ear. Her head was turned toward the route ahead; her mouth held the beginning of a grin. The photographer had caught both feet off the ground in the brief lightness between strides. Behind the portrait, reduced to pale overlapping squares, were other versions of Maris: red helmet, no helmet, short hair, long braid, old gray skates, current black ones. A dozen partial bodies crossed through one another while the large face stayed sharp.

The same design filled the program cover stacked at the entrance.

Across the panel, white type read: THE RIDER WHO NEVER STOPS.

Someone behind a table said, “Oh.”

Maris turned. The speaker wore a volunteer badge, reading glasses on a cord, and the expression of someone who had just seen weather arrive through an open window.

“Is that you?” the volunteer asked.

“You printed my face on a few thousand things,” Maris said. “You tell me.”

The volunteer set down a roll of removable tape. “Yes. You’re right. Sorry. I knew that was a foolish question.”

Outside the awning, people passed with the programs. Most looked from the cover to Maris and tried to disguise the second look as interest in the display. A boy pointed openly until the adult with him lowered his hand.

Maris held the pole harder. The metal was warm and slightly sticky. Her wheels wanted to roll backward on the road’s crown.

“Who took it?” she asked.

“The large one? A person watching the dance demonstration last year. You crossed behind the last row. We can pull the submission form.”

“And the others?”

“Many people.”

The volunteer came around the table but stopped several feet away. Maris noticed the stopped distance and resented being grateful for it.

“The exhibit is about recurring details,” the volunteer said. “Things that turn up in photographs over the years. That striped umbrella has been here since the first festival. There’s a terrier in seven different families’ pictures. We found you in fourteen summers.”

“You found me.”

“In the pictures. We didn’t know who you were.”

“That distinction feels important to you.”

The volunteer’s mouth tightened. “It did yesterday.”

That answer was inconveniently better than an argument.

Maris looked again at the panel. Fourteen summers was correct. She had first skated the road because a friend had canceled and she had refused to waste a day of perfect pavement. The next year she came alone on purpose. She had thought the repetition belonged wholly to her, a line laid down and erased each time by traffic the following morning.

“How long have you been collecting these?”

“Submissions opened in winter. Once we noticed the pattern, we put requests online and in the neighborhood bulletin. We asked skate groups. Nobody gave us a name.”

Maris had never joined a skate group. Her accounts were private and mostly abandoned. She spent the rest of the year moving through different streets in shoes.

“So you couldn’t ask me.”

“We tried to reach you,” the volunteer said.

“You tried to learn who I was. That isn’t the same task.”

The volunteer looked toward the large photograph, then down at the programs. “No. It isn’t.”

A pair of visitors entered the awning and halted when they saw Maris. One whispered, “Oh, wow,” with the delight of finding an actor still standing beside the costume. The volunteer moved between them and the display.

“We’re closing this section for an adjustment,” the volunteer said. “The other wall is still open.”

They went, reluctantly, to photographs of handmade boats and family picnics. One looked back twice.

“I want to see what you used,” Maris said.

The volunteer slid a plastic portfolio from beneath the table. “Would you rather sit?”

“No.”

Standing still on skates was more work than moving. Maris shifted her weight in tiny increments while the volunteer opened the portfolio to contact sheets. The first page held photographs from four households. Not one had been taken of her.

In one, two children chased soap bubbles beside a fountain; the edge of Maris’s red helmet appeared above a woman’s shoulder. In another, an elderly couple toasted paper cups at a picnic table. Maris was a blur behind them, recognizable only by the old gray skates and the orange laces she had forgotten owning. A third showed a tower of sugared pastries, a fourth a dog staring with grave suspicion at a brass band. Maris crossed the farthest corner of each.

The volunteer turned the page.

Different cameras, different years, different reasons to press the button. A baby held up toward a puppet. Three friends showing their painted cheeks. A marriage proposal that Maris remembered because the answer had been shouted so loudly she nearly hit a trash bin. She appeared in a sleeve, a bent knee, a dark comma of hair. Then, as phones improved, she sharpened. She grew older by degrees the pictures had no reason to care about.

Anger had been easier when she imagined one patient stranger waiting every summer with a lens. There would have been a person to tell off, a simple shape to the wrong. The contact sheets offered families, accidents, celebrations, and no gaze that followed her farther than a fraction of a second.

“They weren’t watching me,” she said.

“No.”

“You were.”

The volunteer rested one hand on the portfolio. “Once we saw the pattern, yes.”

On the display, the repeated fragments had been cropped, brightened, and arranged to move in the same direction. Whole afternoons had become evidence for a single sentence. Maris examined the caption cards tucked into the portfolio sleeves. The anonymous skater crosses the festival without stopping, one said. Through weather, changing crowds, and passing years, she remains in motion.

“Where did this part come from?” Maris tapped the sleeve. “Without stopping.”

“The photographs seemed to show it.”

“Photographs seem to show whatever happened for a hundredth of a second.”

She turned the next page herself.

There she was sitting on a curb, eating something from a paper tray with both skates stretched into the gutter. She remembered the burned roof of her mouth, though not what she had eaten. Another photograph caught her crouched over a wheel with a hex key. She remembered that exactly: the soft grind that warned of a loose axle, the fear that the bolt had stripped, the relief when it tightened.

In a wide family picture, everyone faced the camera except a small boy on the road and Maris several yards away. The boy had fallen. Maris was stopped with her palms out, waiting to see whether he would cry or spring up furious. She could not remember his face. The picture had preserved only the back of his green shirt.

“This one was cropped here,” she said.

The volunteer followed her finger. In the exhibit version, the boy was gone. Maris leaned forward, weight pitched into apparent speed.

“We were trying to keep the sequence clean,” the volunteer said. The words emerged automatically, then seemed to sour in the air. “I hear it.”

The next image showed Maris laughing on one skate while the other rested on a bench. She studied the hand of somebody outside the frame, holding her front wheel. No face, no clue. She did not remember the repair or the joke. For several seconds she wanted the missing memory with an intensity that embarrassed her.

“Can I have copies?” she asked.

“We need to ask the contributors.”

“Of photographs of me.”

“Of their photographs,” the volunteer said, quiet but not apologetic. “Some include their children. I can give you contact information where they agreed to share it, and I can ask the rest. I won’t promise for them.”

Maris looked down at the children in the photographs. She disliked the answer and believed it.

A gust bellied the awning. The big panel flexed, making her printed smile buckle and return.

“All right,” Maris said. “Here is what you can do now. Stop handing out that cover. Cover these panels. Give me the source list and the captions, with no form saying I approve any of this.”

The volunteer nodded after each item. “We have plain schedules at the information tent. I can have those brought over. The programs already distributed—”

“I know you can’t pull paper out of people’s hands.”

“And the family photographs can stay if we cover your portions?”

Maris looked at the soap-bubble children, the suspicious dog, the proposal. “Today. Until you have asked me about anything that makes me the subject.”

The volunteer did not call it a compromise or thank her for understanding. She picked up a radio and said, “Stop distributing the blue covers. Use the schedule inserts only. Bring the blank rolls from storage, please.” Then she took the tape she had set down earlier and began measuring brown packing paper across the large portrait.

The first sheet sagged. Maris caught the lower corner before it stuck to the display.

“Higher,” she said. “The tape will peel when the canvas heats up.”

The volunteer glanced at her wrist guards. “You have experience mounting exhibits?”

“No. I have experience falling because someone thought tape could do more than tape can.”

For the first time, the volunteer smiled. It was brief and tired. She found clips under the table.

They worked from the outside inward. On the family photographs, the volunteer folded paper masks only over Maris, leaving the actual subjects visible. The result was strange: brown slivers at the margins, rectangles hovering in open road, one neat patch where a helmet had been. It did not erase her so much as announce where she had been removed.

People kept approaching. Some accepted the explanation that the section had closed. One complained that it was the reason she had come to the exhibit. Another asked Maris if she would pose beside the cover before it disappeared. Maris said no. A man studied the packing paper, shrugged, and went to look at the terrier series.

Outside, people kept eating, playing, pointing, and moving south.

When the last large panel was covered, Maris checked the road. She could still glide to the southern gate without putting a foot on pavement, but the uninterrupted run was gone. She had held the center pole. She had circled back. Finishing now would mean only that she had obeyed the narrowest wording of the rule. She was suddenly uninterested in winning against herself on a technicality.

Behind the table, the mats were too soft and uneven for skates. She sat in the volunteer’s folding chair and loosened her laces. Her socks were damp. The air against her ankles felt indecently cool.

The volunteer returned with a thin stack of schedules, contact permissions, and a release form clipped on top. “The standard packet,” she said. “You don’t have to sign it.”

Maris read the first paragraph. It granted permission for her likeness to be displayed in future festival materials. She took the volunteer’s pen, crossed out the paragraph, and drew a line through the signature box. In the margin she wrote her name, Maris Calder, and beneath it the one place the archive could contact her.

Then she pulled the first caption sheet closer.

Outside, someone passing the awning said, “Wasn’t that the skater?” Someone else answered that they thought so. Maris turned to the photograph of the fallen boy in the green shirt and wrote beside its caption: Stopped here. Ask the family what happened next.

stories.title: Witch Cold
stories.prompt: Your best friend, a cute magical girl has a witch cold. Every time she sneezes, she casts a random spell, and she has absolutely no control over it.
stories.body:
# Witch Cold

The warning on Mallow Fenn's door had three stars drawn in the corners and one damp blot through the middle.

WITCH COLD, it said. DO NOT KNOCK. LEAVE THINGS. GO HOME.

I shifted the soup bag onto my hip and knocked.

"You left out the part where you open the door for your best friend."

"Go home," Mallow called. Even through two inches of painted wood, she sounded as if she had swallowed a dish sponge.

"I brought ginger soup, electrolyte drinks, fever tablets, the tissues you like, and the tissues you pretend you don't like because the box has cartoon lambs."

"Put them down. Then run."

I was deciding whether that counted as fever drama when she sneezed.

The sound began with a tiny, helpless hitch and finished like a firecracker inside a pillow. The grocery bag in my left hand turned inside out without tearing. Its bottom passed somehow through the cartons and bottles; the contents dropped around my shoes while the bag floated down after them, perfectly intact and now covered in printed warnings meant to face inward. At the same instant, every key on my ring hummed a different soft note. Heat bit my palm. I dropped them onto the doormat.

There was a silence behind the door.

"That crossed the wall," I said.

"I wrote *run*."

The humming keys made a nervous little chord between us. I gathered the fever tablets before one slid under the hall radiator, stacked the drinks, and checked the soup container for cracks.

"What's your temperature?"

"Fine."

"A number, Mallow."

"Thirty-eight point nine."

"When did you last drink anything?"

She answered too slowly. "Recently."

I sat down among the lamb tissues. "All right. I'm staying here. If you don't open the door, I'll spend the evening asking medical questions at conversational volume. Your neighbors already think I'm strange."

"They think you're loud."

"They can think two things."

The lock clicked. Mallow opened the door six inches and glared through the gap with one watery eye.

On ordinary days, she could make pink look dangerous. Tonight her rose-colored hair was tied in a knot that had lost its argument with gravity. Two star-bright clips still held her bangs back, though one was upside down. She had wrapped the frilled mantle from her transformation clothes over flannel pajamas and thick socks. Its pearly ribbons trailed into a drift of used tissues.

"One minute," she said. "Put everything inside and go."

"You're shivering."

"I'm magical."

"You're wearing three socks."

She looked down. One foot did, indeed, have an extra sock. "That isn't relevant."

I put my shoe in the gap before she could close it.

Her face changed. Irritation stayed, but fear moved underneath it. "I can't pick the spell. I can't aim it. I can't make it small because you're close. It isn't that kind of magic."

"I understand."

"You brought oven mitts."

"The keys got hot."

"You understand nothing."

Then she swayed against the doorframe. I caught the edge of the door rather than her, because I had listened to at least one thing.

"One minute," I agreed. "Starting after you've had water."

Mallow knew me well enough to hear the fraud in that, but she was too tired to defend the threshold. She stepped back.

Glittering boots stood beside a bucket half full of crumpled tissues. A silver wand lay disassembled in a ceramic baking dish on the coffee table. Star charms, spare ribbons, and a thermometer crowded the end table. The cute parts of Mallow's life had never seemed childish to me. They were equipment she cleaned, stitched, charged, and sometimes fell asleep wearing. The pink just made the maintenance easier to find under a sofa.

I cleared a route from the couch to the bathroom, put her phone within reach, and poured an electrolyte drink into a plastic tumbler. No metal. No glass. I set the soup in a saucepan, reconsidered the saucepan, and emptied it into a ceramic bowl.

"See?" I said. "We can reduce the obvious risks."

Mallow sat at the kitchen table with the mantle tucked under her chin. "The spells don't care what's obvious."

"Last one affected a container and metal. So we keep containers flexible and metal away from our hands."

"That is one sneeze, not a sample."

"It's more of a sample than we had ten minutes ago."

Her nose wrinkled.

I froze with the soup bowl between us. Mallow snatched two tissues, pressed them to her face, and sneezed.

The drink rose out of her tumbler in a shining blue-green globe. Soup lifted from its bowl in one ginger-scented mass. Three drops under the leaky tap trembled upward. Even the dampness in the sponge pulled itself free in a wobbling bead.

Mallow ducked. I did the opposite. I clapped a lid over the tumbler and managed to trap half the floating drink; the rest burst against my wrist and hung there like a bracelet. The soup drifted toward the ceiling. I lunged with the bowl, caught one edge of it, and sent the other edge spreading in a golden sheet above the cabinets.

All around us, metal began to sing. The sink gave a low note. Two spoons in the drying rack answered in close harmony, and the cabinet handles trembled with a pitch that made my teeth itch. Heat rose from them in waves.

"Don't touch the tap," Mallow said.

"I know."

"You were reaching for it."

"I changed my mind."

The spell released the liquids without warning. Soup slapped onto the cabinets and floor. The damp sponge rained on Mallow's head. My bracelet became a wet sleeve.

For one startled second we stared at each other. Then Mallow began to laugh. It came out as a sick little wheeze, but it was still her laugh, the one that always made her cover her mouth as if joy were something she had spilled.

"One minute," she said.

"Paused for cleanup."

I fed her the portion of soup I rescued from the bowl, seated her on the couch, and improved the apartment. Towels went over sharp corners. Hot utensils went onto ceramic plates. I marked a clear square around the couch with pink ribbon from her sewing basket, set a lidded drink in the center, and placed nested pillows against the wall.

Mallow watched with the exhausted patience of someone witnessing a squirrel design a bridge.

"The first spell reached into the hall," she said.

"But only a few feet."

"You don't know that."

"The liquid spell stayed in the kitchen."

"You don't know that either. Check your water bottle."

The bottle in my bag was empty. I found its water hanging under the hallway ceiling like a clear, quivering light fixture.

"Fine," I said. "Wide radius. But categories. Matter, then liquid. If we keep you away from breakable things and track each effect—"

She sneezed into the lamb tissues.

Nothing moved.

We waited. The screws in a bookshelf warmed and hummed a descending scale. Mallow pointed at the floor.

The floor lamp's shadow now belonged to the wastebasket. It was tall and narrow, with the lamp's crooked neck, though the basket itself was round. My shadow wore the branching silhouette of the fern on the windowsill. Across the room, Mallow's small dark outline clung to a cushion, curled like a sleeping cat.

I lifted an arm. The fern-shadow stayed still. One of its leaves waved when I did.

"Matter, liquid, shadows," Mallow said. "Excellent categories. You should publish."

"Harmless."

"Probably."

I looked at my borrowed leaves. "You are very negative when you're feverish."

"I'm negative when I'm right."

The jokes thinned after that. Mallow drank when I handed her the cup, but only because arguing cost more energy. I moved the lamp, carried the wand in its baking dish, unplugged appliances, and took every loose object I distrusted into the bedroom. Each trip made the apartment look safer and gave me something to do besides consider the water under the ceiling.

On my fourth pass, I noticed Mallow's peculiar stillness.

Her eyes had squeezed shut. Her nostrils flared, then flattened under two pinching fingers. Her chest hitched once. She swallowed hard and sat frozen until the impulse passed. When she opened her eyes, tears had gathered at the corners.

"How many times have you done that?"

"Done what?"

"Held one back."

"I'm fine."

"That phrase has expired."

She reached for her drink. The cup rattled against her teeth. "Since before you got here. It buys time."

"It makes you dizzy."

"Being sick makes me dizzy."

"Mallow."

"It doesn't get rid of the spell, okay? The sneeze comes later. But later might be after you leave."

I wanted to shake sense into her, which was unfair when she was already shivering. "So you've been sitting here alone, not drinking because you might sneeze near the tap, trying not to breathe?"

"I was doing fairly well until someone knocked under a sign that said not to."

"You could fall. You could choke."

"I could turn you into steam."

Soup dripped from the ceiling into a towel. Our incorrect shadows lay across one another on the rug.

Mallow's voice went rough. "I don't want the last normal thing I see tonight to be you deciding I was just panicking."

I sat on the coffee table, outside my ribbon square. The fern-shadow folded itself under me. "I don't think you're panicking."

"You think you can out-organize it."

"I think your fever is still going up."

She needed someone close enough to bring water if her hands shook, and I was one of the things closeness could ruin.

The bathroom was my next idea. I presented it more humbly than the others, which meant I only called it sensible twice. Tile, anchored fixtures, no windows, and a tub she could lie down in. We cleared out razors, bottles, hairpins, and a cheerful metal shelf that hummed when I carried it away. I brought towels, the phone, water in a capped plastic bottle, and a wide ceramic cup. Mallow shuffled behind me, wrapped in her mantle, stopping twice to lean against the wall.

"A bare room is still a room," she said.

"I heard you."

"Did you?"

"No claims of safety. Fewer things to hit us. That's all."

She considered, then nodded. It was the first part of my plan she had agreed to, and the agreement felt more useful than all the padding.

Mallow sat on the closed toilet lid. I climbed onto the broad sink counter to move the ceramic soap dish away from the edge. We had nearly finished when her breath snagged.

"Stay there," she warned.

I stayed. She lifted a tissue. Her face crumpled, helpless and apologetic.

The sneeze struck.

The sink expanded beneath my hands. The faucet shot upward into a silver tower. Grout lines thickened into white roads, and Mallow grew so quickly that my mind refused the sight. My shoes slipped on a counter that had become a ledge. The edge took me at the knees.

I fell.

Mallow lunged from the toilet and caught me in both hands.

For a moment there was only the heat of her palms, the hard beat under one of my feet, and her face hanging above me as large as the moon. My clothes had shrunk with me. The rest of the bathroom had not.

"Don't move," she whispered.

"Wasn't planning to."

My voice came out absurdly small. Mallow made a sound between a laugh and a sob, then lowered me into the soap dish on the counter. I stood up with both hands on its slick rim. Six inches tall, approximately. My useful estimate did nothing to improve the fact.

Mallow turned away sharply. Her shoulders jerked. One finger pressed beneath her nose.

"Put me in the medicine cabinet," I said. "No, the hinges are metal. The tub. Wrap me in a towel and put the cup over—"

She shook her head, unable to answer. Her chest pulled in another broken sip of air.

"You need to sit. Put the stopper over the drain. Move the phone where I can—"

Her eyes were squeezed shut. Tears ran down her flushed cheeks. She wasn't following my instructions because every part of her was occupied with not sneezing on me again.

I stopped.

The metal faucet began to cool under my hand. Somewhere in the apartment, a spoon gave its last fading note.

"Mallow," I said. "What do you need?"

She drew three careful breaths before trusting herself to speak. "I need to put you down somewhere I can see you. I need you not to run at me if I fall. And I need to sneeze."

"All right."

"The phone on the floor. Screen unlocked."

"All right."

"No counting down. It makes me nervous."

I had been about to suggest a countdown. "No countdown."

She set the ceramic cup on its side beneath the sink's overhang and padded it with a folded washcloth. Its mouth faced the toilet. The low shelter kept me in her sight without leaving me exposed on the counter. She laid the phone flat on the bath mat, close enough that I could walk across the screen if I had to call for help.

"If you start to fall," I said, "tell me. I won't come out until the sneeze is over."

Mallow lowered herself to the floor with her back against the tub. The tissue trembled in her hands. "I can't promise what happens."

"I know."

This time, I did.

She let the sneeze come.

The shower curtain vanished with a sound like a hundred soap bubbles popping. In its place floated a flock of smaller bubbles, each no bigger than my thumb. They bounced off the tub, the ceiling, and Mallow's hair. Whenever one touched something, it emitted the same bright, mechanical question: "What time is it?"

The pipes warmed and hummed. The tap contributed a high, bashful note.

"What time is it?" asked a bubble against Mallow's knee.

"Eleven forty-three," she told it hoarsely.

"What time is it?" asked another, colliding with her ear.

"Still eleven forty-three."

A bubble drifted into the cup. "What time is it?"

"Summer," I said.

Mallow laughed until she coughed. I laughed too, leaning against a hill of washcloth inside my ridiculous ceramic cave. We still had to wait for the tap to cool before she could refill the bottle, and the bubbles kept asking long after the question had become unbearable.

But Mallow drank. She breathed without trapping each breath behind her teeth.

We handled the rest of the night one sneeze at a time.

The next one rounded every right angle in the bathroom. The phone slid off the suddenly curved tile, and Mallow caught it against her slipper without diving for me. We waited until corners returned before moving anything. Another sneeze made anything blue leak clean water: the stars on her mantle, the shampoo bottle outside the door, even the painted stripe on a towel. The apartment became damp for no reason we could remedy. Near dawn, the bath mat sprouted ankle-deep clover that smelled strongly of toast. It swallowed the phone, so Mallow uncovered it only after the pipes had finished their warm chord.

None of the spells resembled the one before. Some faded in minutes. The wrong shadows remained. So did my size.

Between sneezes, Mallow lay in the dry tub with a rolled towel under her neck. She warned me when she felt the tickle building. I tucked myself into the cup; she waited for my answer; then neither of us pretended the arrangement made us safe. It only told us what to do with the parts we could choose.

Sometime after the last humming note dwindled in the pipes, she slept. I watched long enough to see her breathing settle, then curled into the washcloth with the phone glowing faintly beyond the cup.

Morning found the bathroom full of clover, soap bubbles, and gray light.

Mallow woke with one arm over her eyes. She checked her temperature, drank, and sat still for a while. The fever had broken. Her nose was pink but quiet.

"How long since the last sneeze?" she asked.

I checked the phone. "Two hours and twelve minutes."

She rubbed beneath her nose experimentally.

"Don't you dare force one."

"I wasn't going to."

"You were considering it."

"Only for scientific purposes."

"You told me not to let you turn me into steam."

"A persuasive review. Testing denied."

She looked into the cup. With the fever gone, her eyes were steadier. Her hair was still a catastrophe, and one star clip now cast the shadow of a fern.

"I'm sorry," she said.

"No."

"You're six inches tall."

"Yes. Very observant. We'll add it to your chart."

"You came in after I told you not to."

"Also true."

"I'm still sorry."

I let that stand. She let my answer stand beside it.

Mallow changed into dry pajamas, moving slowly and narrating where she was so I wouldn't imagine her collapsing out of sight. She refused to promise a reversal. She did promise breakfast and a call to an aftercare service that handled stubborn magical effects.

In the kitchen, most of the soup still decorated the ceiling. Mallow opened a fresh carton, heated it in a ceramic bowl, and waited until it cooled. She poured a tiny serving into a clean bottle cap and set it beside me on the table. Then she lowered her phone, already open to the number she meant to call, until I could reach it.

"Food, phone, clear route," she said. "Anything I'm forgetting?"

"The lamb tissues."

She placed the box on its side to make me a shelter. The cartoon lambs were now larger than horses.

Mallow settled into the chair across from me, wrapped both hands around her own soup, and surveyed the water-stained walls, the switched shadows, and the best friend who could have stood comfortably in her teacup.

"Which problem first?" she asked.

I lifted the bottle cap with both hands.

"Breakfast."

stories.title: Every Flower She Knew
stories.prompt: She ventures alone into a wild valley where beautiful flowers can heal the sick, restore strength, sharpen memory, or bring peaceful sleep—and others can kill with a touch. She knows every dangerous bloom and carefully avoids them, returning to her village with baskets of wondrous flowers that have helped her people for years.
stories.body:
# Every Flower She Knew

At the valley boundary, Ressa ties four requests to the handles of her empty baskets.

The red cord has three knots: a child, a fever, the third day. The yellow cord asks strength for the thatcher whose winter roof is still open to the sky. The gray belongs to an old woman who has misplaced, somewhere in her own memory, the hillside where she buried her best bean seed. The blue cord is for the fevered child's mother, who has not slept longer than an hour since the sickness began.

Ressa tests each knot with her thumb. She checks the reed ribs of both baskets, the waxed skin covers rolled beneath their rims, and the four fitted compartments inside. Her crescent knife is sharp. Her wooden tongs close cleanly. Flint and char wait in a lidded horn. Nothing has been forgotten.

Last, she turns her hands over. No cut, no split nail, no place where sap might enter. The inspection is habit, like the rule that has governed every harvest she has carried home: a flower tied to a request is not hers to use.

Behind her, in the dark, someone coughs. The child's mother has walked as far as the boundary and no farther. Nobody follows Ressa into the valley.

“Before moonrise?” the woman asks.

“If the weather keeps its manners.”

It is not comfort, but the woman knows better than to ask for that. She touches the blue cord once and returns toward the roofs below.

Ressa waits until the first gray light shows the path, then crosses between the two boundary stones.

The valley opens beneath her in folds of wet green. Mist lies low along the stream, leaving the slopes clear. Flowers stripe the ground: yellow shelves on the sunward rock, blue pockets under thorn, white drifts in every shaded hollow. A stranger might see abundance. Ressa sees distances.

Three handspans between the copper bells and the path. Six paces around a thorn-star root, because its buried runners sting as fiercely as the purple points above ground.
