Never step downhill of a nodding cup when rain sits inside it; the water carries a rash that blinds for half a day. She knows where sweetness means medicine, where it means bait, where the stems can be touched safely but the pollen cannot.

At the first turn, widow's lace trails from beneath a black rock.

Most of it is furled in the morning, each white flower twisted to the width of a finger. Three blossoms in the deepest shade have already opened. Their petals overlap like fine cloth, and drops of clear nectar jewel the curled edges. Beautiful enough to draw an unknowing hand.

Ressa gives the patch the whole width of the path. Years ago, a goat had leaned through a fence and brushed one open blossom with its nose. It took three steps before its front legs folded. There was no poultice for widow's lace, no useful dose hidden inside the poison, no safer part of the plant. Skin against petal, sap, root, or pollen meant death.

She plants her staff beyond the last trailing leaf and steps onto a pale stone. Above her, the slope rises in broken ledges: another pale stone, a pine root curved like a hook, a shelf of dark rock hidden under moss. The upper traverse is longer and meaner than the low path, but she checks its first handholds whenever she passes. Valleys change. Good paths do not become faithful because one has used them for years.

The healing patch grows near the valley floor, where the stream divides around a warm stone. Red mercy holds its petals upright as if offering a cup. Ressa crouches outside the patch and studies it before she cuts. Young blossoms are orange at the throat and good only for stomach cramps. Mature ones show a dark line down each petal. Of those, she takes six, clipping above the lowest paired leaves so the plants will branch again. She leaves nine mature flowers open to insects and seed.

The stems bead milky sap. She wraps each one in dock leaf and binds it with thread before laying it in the red-cord compartment. Red mercy has broken dozens of village fevers. It had cleared the shaking sickness from the potter's household last spring and eased an infected cut in the shepherd's palm. It could not knit a crushed chest or call breath back once it had gone. Ressa knows that boundary too.

She closes the compartment. Six should be enough for the child, with two doses to spare if the fever climbs again.

Lion's breath grows farther up the sunny shoulder, thick-stemmed and gold. It smells of pepper when she cuts it. Three petals chewed slowly will lend a tired body the force to work for an hour, sometimes two. They do not heal what the work has worn down. A person who borrows enough strength to lift on an injured back may finish the lifting and lose the use of the back afterward.

Ressa takes four flowers. The patch is small this year, and the thatcher's roof can wait through one more dry day if it must. She pinches spent heads over the bare earth, scattering seed, then wraps the flowers in waxed cloth. A breeze travels through the patch after she rises, bowing every gold head over the seed.

Silver ledger hides its usefulness. The plant is low and gray, with four dull petals no wider than a thumbnail. Goats eat around it. Children complain of its chalky taste. Yet half a flower held beneath the tongue can bring back an observed detail that fatigue or age has buried: a face glimpsed at a market, the order of words in a message, which hillside received morning sun in the year the bean harvest was best. It supplies nothing a person never knew. When the cooper took it to discover who had stolen his adze, he remembered only that he himself had carried the tool outside and set it down. Ressa found it under nettles.

She harvests three silver flowers from separate plants. The gray cord brushes her wrist as she packs them.

Moon hush comes last, because its blue petals bruise if carried beneath heavier stems. It grows under hazel where afternoon arrives early. Steeped in hot water, one petal gives a child a quiet hour; a whole flower can carry a sleepless adult through a night without dreams. Too much leaves the limbs loose and the mind slow after waking. It brings rest, not recovery. Ressa has seen people wake grateful and still ill.

She selects two open blooms. The child's mother will need only half of one if the fever turns.

To seal the last stem wrapping, Ressa sets a coal glowing inside the cup of her hooded lamp and warms a bead of pine gum on her knife. As the gum softens, the coal's orange edge turns blue. The little flame leans toward the baskets.

It leans toward all of them. Red mercy or widow's lace, healing cup or killing petal, every freshly cut valley flower draws fire and colors it blue. The pull reveals nothing useful except that a basket should never be left beside an open hearth. Ressa keeps the lamp between her knees, shielding the coal while she seals the cloth. Even so, the blue tongue lengthens toward the nearest compartment.

“Greedy nuisance,” she tells it, and caps the lamp.

The first rain strikes the hazel leaves.

Ressa looks up. A gray wall has swallowed the upper rim of the valley. The morning wind should have carried weather east, but down here the air has gone still. Cold drops begin to rattle through the canopy.

She pulls the skin covers over both baskets and knots them beneath the cords. There is another patch of red mercy beyond the hazel, and on a clear day she would inspect it before turning home. Today she leaves it untouched. She straps one basket to her back, takes the other on her left hip, and begins the climb.

Rain reaches the valley floor before she does. The stream darkens and swells around its warm stone. On the sunny shoulder, lion's breath bends under the drops, gold heads striking the earth. Ressa slows enough to keep mud from shaking the baskets, but no more. Fog pours down the slopes and eats the distance between one landmark and the next.

By the time she reaches the black rock, her sleeves are soaked and her right thigh has begun to tremble.

She stops well above the turn.

Widow's lace has opened across the low path.

Cold rain has made dusk at midday. Hundreds of white blooms spread from the rock to the streamward drop, lifting on runners Ressa stepped past that morning. The safe strip of mud is gone. Petals tremble under the rain and shed clear drops onto the stones below.

The fog makes the mass seem endless, but Ressa does not need to see its end to understand it. She lowers the hip basket onto a dry hump of stone. Then she backs up four paces before taking off the other. Nothing from the patch has touched her. Nothing will.

She eats a heel of oat bread and inventories the valley.

The direct path is closed. No boot or glove in the village can be trusted against widow's lace sap. Cutting the flowers would bring them nearer. Fire would pull toward the cut blooms, scatter heated sap, and leave the roots alive. The patch will furl after dawn if the rain passes.

By dawn, the fever may have gone beyond the work red mercy can do.

The upper traverse remains. It climbs above the patch, crosses two steep gutters, then rejoins the home path just inside the boundary stones. She has walked it three times in twenty years, never with full baskets, never in fog. The first section is marked by the pale stones and hooked roots she inspected on her descent. After that, the route relies on narrow footing and the shape of the rock beneath the hand.

Ressa looks at her trembling thigh. Harvesting requires long crouches, careful cuts, no wasted motion. Careful work still spends the body. She has enough strength for the ordinary low path. She does not have enough for the upper one.

She considers dividing the flowers. Take only the red mercy and leave the rest wrapped under the stone. The back basket alone would be lighter. But the climb would still exceed what is left in her legs, and abandoned moon hush would drink rain through its wrapping by morning. She considers waiting. The child has survived three days. Some survive four.

That is not the counsel she would give beside a bed. She would name the danger, name the remedy, and use what offered the better chance.

Rain ticks against the basket skins. Beneath the covers lie four lion's-breath flowers, because a man needs strength to close a roof. Beside them lie three silver ledgers, because an old woman wants to find a hill inside her own life. Both needs are real. Neither request requires every flower she has cut.

Ressa has always thought her rule kept the harvest honest. It has. Yet if the thatcher came to her with a shaking thigh and a child depending on what he carried, she would not send him up a wet cliff to protect a flower.

Basket handles split. She mends those before loading them again.

She opens the yellow compartment.

Lion's breath burns like pepper and green wood. She chews one flower, petal by petal, and swallows the fibrous heart. Warmth spreads from her tongue to her jaw, then down her throat. Her pulse kicks harder. The ache remains in her legs, but force gathers beneath it, clean and dangerous as a loaded sling.

From the gray compartment she takes half a silver ledger, hesitates, then takes the whole flower. The upper traverse will punish a blurred sequence. Chalk coats her mouth. For several breaths, nothing changes.

Then she remembers the morning.

Not as a vision. The fog stays thick, the rain cold. But details she had let pass return to their places: the first pale stone canted inward; the second shone because water ran across it; the pine root hooked left, while the dead root below it hooked right and would tear free under weight. Beyond the dark shelf, a seam split the rock at the height of her shoulder. She had seen red beetle shells in it.

Ressa reties both request cords. On each she adds a small cross-knot, the village mark for a dose spent on the road. No one will have to ask what became of it.

She repacks the weight. Red mercy and moon hush ride against her back, protected from jolts. Strength and memory go on her hip. She raises her staff and starts upward.

The first pale stone holds. The second is slick, as remembered. She tests it twice, shifts her hip basket ahead, and steps with her weight low. At the pine roots she grips the living hook and avoids the dead one. A white petal floats through the fog below her and catches against the rock. She waits until rain washes it down before crossing.

The lent force urges her to hurry. She refuses it.

At the first gutter she sets both baskets on a ledge, climbs three body lengths, and hauls them separately with cord. Mud slides beneath her left boot. Her knee strikes stone. The lion's breath lets the leg hold, but pain flashes sharp enough to warn her what the flower has not repaired.

The silver ledger keeps offering details. Dark shelf. Shoulder-high seam. Beetle shells. A notch shaped like a bite, good for the right foot but too shallow for the left. She uses each memory only after the staff confirms rock beneath the fog.

Other memories arrive with the useful ones. Silver ledger does not know kindness.

She remembers the miller's first wife gripping her wrist while red mercy cooled a fever but could not stop the blood leaving her body. She remembers the winter when moon hush gave a burned boy six peaceful hours and his last breath came before waking. She remembers every face she carried into the valley as a cord and carried out again as an untied string.

At the second gutter, she nearly puts her hand into a curtain of rain-heavy leaves. Their sawed edges come clear a finger's width from her skin: glass nettle, not fatal, but its sting would close her hand for hours. She steps back. The sharpened memory supplies the safe hold lower down, a knob of stone she noticed because a snail shell gleamed on it. She probes until her fingers find the knob.

Halfway across the high slope, daylight thins toward evening. Ressa lights the hooded lamp. Its flame rises blue at once and pulls toward the cut flowers on her back. She holds it high and away, exposing only a narrow slit. Fog shines around her in a small blue chamber. Beyond it, the world is rain and steepness.

The lion's breath begins to ebb at the dark shelf.

It goes first from her shoulders. The back basket doubles in weight. Then her thighs start to shake again, not gently now. Every strain the flower allowed her to overrule waits in the muscles. She sits against the rock before the weakness can choose the place for her.

The village is close. She knows because the stone beneath her palm bears three shallow grooves cut by generations of basket rims. Past this shelf, the traverse narrows, turns around a shoulder of rock, and meets the ordinary path above the widow's lace.

Her lamp flame stretches sideways until it licks the metal hood. The flowers are pulling harder as the distance between lamp and back basket shortens. Heat touches her knuckles.

Ressa caps the lamp. Darkness and fog close together.

She rests until her pulse stops hammering, then moves by contact with stone. Staff forward. Left palm in the long seam. Right foot to the bite-shaped notch. Slide the hip basket. Bring the left foot beside the right. The silver ledger holds the morning's rock under the evening's rain, but she tests every placement. Once, her staff finds empty air where she remembers a shelf. She stops, feels lower, and discovers that runoff has covered it with a thin sheet of moving mud. She scrapes the mud aside before trusting her boot.

Around the rock shoulder, a faint white blur hangs at knee height. Widow's lace has climbed higher here than it had in the morning. Ressa backs away until stone presses her spine. She remembers a root above her head, reaches only after the staff finds its trunk, and edges around the bloom with her face turned into the rock. One wet petal brushes the outside of her basket cover.

She keeps her weight on the rear foot and does not turn the basket.

The skin cover is whole. The petal has touched no part of her body, but clear moisture gleams on the wax. She cannot carry that surface against herself. Gripping the clean underside with her wooden tongs, she folds the contaminated corner outward and pins it away from her with the point of her knife. The knife goes blade-first into the mud, not its sheath. She leaves it there and moves on.

The boundary stones emerge from the fog as darker columns in the dark. Ressa crosses between them with both baskets. Only then does she call.

Feet answer on the path below. The child's mother arrives first, carrying a shuttered lantern and a blanket. Two neighbors follow. Ressa makes them stop while she explains the folded basket cover. One neighbor takes the clean hip basket. The other cuts the back straps with a sickle, careful never to touch the marked corner. Together they lower the basket onto a door plank and carry it level.

Ressa walks behind them. Without the baskets, she should feel light. Instead, every step finds the bottom of her strength.

In the child's house, the hearth has been banked under flat stones. This is how the village prepares valley flowers: no bare flame, no hanging lamp near the table. Steam lifts from a pot over the covered coals.

The child lies beneath one thin sheet, face bright with fever, breath quick and dry. Ressa washes her hands, checks the whites of the eyes, the color beneath the nails, the stiffness of the neck. Common fever still. Dangerous, but still within the red flower's reach.

She unwraps one mature mercy bloom and tears its petals into a glazed cup. Hot water darkens them from red to brown. She waits until the surface stops steaming, then feeds the child three spoonfuls, pauses, and gives three more.

Nothing happens quickly enough for the mother. She kneels with her hands locked between her knees. Twice she asks whether the dose was strong. Twice Ressa answers, “Strong enough.” A stronger dose would not make the flower faster.

The child's breath eases first. Sweat beads along the hairline. After a while, one small foot pushes free of the sheet. Ressa touches the ankle. The heat is leaving.

The mother makes a sound that is almost a laugh and almost the beginning of weeping. She reaches for the child.

“Let the sweat come,” Ressa says. “You can hold a hand.”

The woman takes the child's hand and bows her head over it.

Ressa prepares half a moon-hush flower in a second cup. The mother refuses it until the neighbor with the lantern settles beside the bed and promises to watch the child's breathing. Then she drinks, grimacing at the bitter water, and lies down on a mat without releasing the small hand. Her eyes close before the cup cools.

The two baskets remain near the door, their compartments not yet sorted. The thatcher has heard Ressa returned. He stands outside, rainwater running from his hair, and asks through the doorway whether she can prepare the remaining lion's breath tonight. Behind him, the old woman with the gray cord waits under a shawl.

Ressa's legs have begun to shake so hard the cups rattle when she stacks them.

“Morning,” she says.

The thatcher looks at the sleeping mother, the damp child, and Ressa's bloodied knee. “Morning,” he agrees.

Ressa lowers herself to the floor before her legs give way.

stories.title: The Morning Her Hand Moved
stories.prompt: For a thousand years, an entire civilization has lived in the temples, streets, and gardens carved into the body of a colossal stone goddess they believe died before history began—until one morning, her outstretched hand moves.
stories.body:
# The Morning Her Hand Moved

“Not there,” Neshra said. “In the old hollow.”

Odal lowered the water jar anyway. Its round base touched the paving with a damp clay knock.

“The old hollow catches grit.”

“The old hollow catches the jar when someone kicks it.” Neshra hooked two fingers through the handle and dragged it half a handspan toward the shallow depression worn beside the garden stair. “Water has spilled this way since my grandmother’s grandmother. It knows where to go.”

Odal looked across the waking palm. Dawn had laid copper along the four raised fingers, turning the houses cut into their joints into rows of bright chips. Farther downslope, where the thumb joined the hand, shutters opened over the market street. A bell sounded under the wrist, then another from the temple built into the head of the lifeline. Between them lay gardens, cistern mouths, stairs recut so many times that the stone dipped like soap beneath generations of feet.

“Water doesn’t know anything,” Odal said.

“Which is why it can be trusted.”

They said nothing more while they lifted the fig’s root mat from its bed. It was the oldest tree in Neshra’s terrace, old enough that three retaining walls had been built around it and two had cracked. Its roots were fine as hair at the edges and thick as wrists near the trunk. Neshra teased away the salt-burned strands. Odal followed with fresh soil, packing it with the heel of one hand. They had always worked well in the gaps between what they said.

Below them, early traffic threaded the lifeline: flour porters leaning into straps, children running messages, a pair of white-robed keepers sweeping yesterday’s flower offerings into baskets. No one looked up at the stone face miles beyond the wrist. A thousand years of records began with Ammara already dead; the oldest prayers placed her death before counting, before writing, before the first stair. Her hand had remained open beneath the sky long enough for the people upon it to forget that open was a position.

Neshra passed Odal a pruning hook. “When we reset the western wall after harvest, we’ll make this bed deeper.”

“You’ll make it deeper.”

“And you’ll complain that I set the spillway too high, then set it exactly where I mark.”

Odal cut a dead root with more force than it required. “I came for the thinning.”

“You came because you know the work.”

“Those are different sentences.”

Neshra reached for the next root and pretended the distinction was too small to hold.

* * *

Pressure.

It is the first thing that returns, though it has never wholly left. A patient weight lies against her. Within that weight are prickles, threads, islands of warmth. Above it, heat touches one side of her and cold the other.

Something in her hand remains unfinished.

She means to bend her fingers.

* * *

The water climbed out of its groove.

Neshra watched a bright tongue ease over the channel’s uphill lip, hesitate on flat stone, and begin to crawl toward the fig. Odal saw it at the same moment. They both turned toward the jar.

It had not fallen. It stood in the old hollow, trembling hard enough that rings disturbed the reflection at its mouth.

“Under us,” Odal said.

A deep knock traveled through Neshra’s knees. Soil lifted in little jumps. Along the terrace, trellis leaves shivered though the air was still. The lower temple bell struck once, not pulled by any keeper, and held its note until another sound swallowed it: stone grinding against stone somewhere too large to locate.

Neshra put a palm to the paving. The familiar warmth was there, gathered from yesterday’s sun, but beneath it came a slow vibration like a millstone beginning to turn.

“A settling,” she said. “The finger ridges do it after cold nights.”

Odal pointed east.

The sun had cleared the little finger a moment ago. Now the black edge of stone rose across it. Chimneys and roof gardens tilted into silhouette. The horizon itself seemed to lift, carrying half the district with it.

The jar slid from the hollow.

Odal caught it before it reached the stair. Neshra caught Odal’s belt. For a breath they formed one astonished chain, water slapping, sandals scraping, while the garden found a new direction for down.

Then everyone in Ammara's Palm began to scream.

Neshra hauled the jar against the fig’s retaining wall. “Rope. The waxed coil.”

“We need the cut.” Odal pointed to the irrigation trench running along the terrace’s upper boundary. It was knee-deep, wide enough for a body if they cleared the leaf screens. “If this keeps turning—”

“The jars first.”

“Mother.”

“Without water, what do you intend to survive on?”

That reached the part of Odal that knew the garden. They seized the rope.

They worked while the slope steepened grain by grain. Neshra threaded the coil through the jar handles and around the fig trunk, then took a second rope to the melon trellis. Odal kicked open the trench screens and scraped out leaf mold with the pruning hook. Beyond the terrace, tiles spun down a street that had become a chute. A loaded handcart rolled through a shrine rail and vanished toward the hollow of the palm. People clung to doorframes. Others crawled toward whatever had once been uphill, choosing routes by a memory the stone no longer honored.

The bells kept striking. Their ropes and clappers had acquired directions of their own.

“Leave the trellis,” Odal said.

“It will tear out the whole bed if it swings.”

“Then cut it loose.”

Neshra lashed it shorter. The vines were heavy with unripe melons. Months of water hung there, green and useless and precious.

Another knock rose through the palm. The four fingers moved against the sky.

Not a settling. Not any word Neshra had.

* * *

The movement is wrong only because it is slow.

Intention has gone ahead without her. It waits at the end of the gesture while the path toward it stretches, crowded with resistance. She sends herself into the fingers. Stone answers stone. Each joint yields by a measure smaller than pain and larger than mountains.

Something spills across her palm.

She remembers no weight there, but when she reaches for memory, it comes apart. First there were scratches. Later, perhaps the same instant, the scratches crossed one another and deepened. Warmth collected in patches. Hair-fine intrusions entered places where her outer self had no pain to give.

Now, as she curls her fingers, the pressure breaks into motion. Much of it slides without choosing. Some of it does not.

She cannot yet tell the difference.

* * *

By the time the paving became too steep to stand on, the courtyard wall had become a floor.

Neshra and Odal straddled its tiled cap, backs pressed to the terrace they had crossed horizontally all their lives. The water jars hung from the fig in their rope cradle. Above, beds bulged behind their retaining stones. Below, the rest of Ammara's Palm dropped toward the palm’s center in a clutter of roofs, dust, and torn vegetation. The nearest finger continued its dreadful ascent, its ridge streets turning toward them like the face of a tower.

Odal sawed through the rope holding the two smallest jars.

“No.” Neshra grabbed their wrist.

“The wall is cracking.”

“Then pass them down one at a time.”

“Down where?”

There was no courtyard below them anymore, only air and a slope of paving sharp enough to skin anything that touched it. A seed jar broke loose from the shed, bounced once, and burst. Bean seed sprayed across the palm like thrown gravel.

Neshra released Odal’s wrist.

They cut. The small jars fell together, striking the paving at different pitches before they smashed out of sight. Relieved of their weight, the fig’s upper branches sprang and thrashed. The largest jar remained tied close to the trunk.

“The packs next,” Odal said.

Neshra had filled them with cuttings and seed envelopes after the first tilt. One year could be starved and replanted. Seed was the argument against panic.

“They weigh less than a jar.”

“Everything weighs more now.”

Neshra looped the pack straps through the trellis rope instead. Odal’s mouth flattened.

From the joint below the terrace came a wet crack.

At first Neshra thought a cistern had split. Then warm liquid welled from a hairline seam in Ammara’s stone, clear where it emerged, blue at the edges. It ran across the courtyard wall and soaked their sleeves. The smell was mineral and bitter, like lime burned in a kiln.

Odal dragged their hand from it. “I can’t feel my fingers.”

Neshra’s own fingertips had gone thick and distant. She tore strips from the tail of her work shirt, wrapped their hands, then hers. The liquid found the irrigation cut and poured into it, carrying leaf mold toward the drain.

Their shelter began to fill.

They crawled along the wall cap, clinging to chisel marks. Odal jammed the pruning hook into the drain mouth. A plug of wet leaves came free. Brine rushed through, leaving brittle blue scales wherever it met the cooler stone. More scales formed as Neshra watched, layered like fish skin over the grate.

“Scraper,” she said.

“In your pack.”

The pack hung above them from the trellis line. Neshra climbed for it.

Her knee, bad since the southern wall had fallen twelve years before, failed on the second step. Odal caught the back of her belt and shoved her against the bed. Loose soil pattered around them. Neshra reached the pack, found the flat bronze scraper, and slid down on her hip.

Odal took the tool without comment and attacked the blue crust.

The hand stopped moving.

Dust continued to fall. Bells slowed and struck themselves quiet. Across the tilted district, cries separated into single voices. Neshra felt the stillness the way she felt a missing tooth, by testing the place with everything around it.

Odal scraped until the drain ran clear. “We go now.”

“Where?”

“Toward the wrist. The service channel is cut deeper than the street.”

“If it hasn’t split.”

“We test it.”

“And if the hand moves while we’re exposed?”

“If it moves while we’re tied under a tree?”

The fig creaked above them. Half its root mat had drawn from the soil, pale fibers stretched in the sun. Neshra looked past it to the terrace: the narrow beds she had brought back after blight; the vine descended from a cutting her mother had stolen from a temple wall; the shed Odal had roofed at sixteen and cursed every rainy season since. Broken things, but not gone. Not yet.

“You take the jar and go,” she said. “I’ll free the root mat and follow.”

Odal laughed once, without humor. “You want to inherit me the way you inherited that tree.”

“I want you away from here.”

“Then come.”

“Someone has to keep enough alive for us to come back to.”

Blue crust whispered as it formed over the drain. Odal scraped it away with short, furious strokes.

“This is what you do,” they said. “The roof sags, you add a brace. The soil slips, you build another wall. Father leaves, you double the beds. I say I don’t want the terrace and you plan a deeper one for me.”

Neshra gripped the wall until grit entered her wrappings. “Work stays where you put it.”

“No, it doesn’t.” Odal struck the grate clean. “That’s the entire morning.”

The paving beneath them gave a small shudder. Both looked up.

Nothing moved. A gull crossed the enormous gap between thumb and finger, veered at the altered wind, and disappeared.

Neshra said, “I don’t know another way to lose things.”

Odal scraped twice more, though the grate was clear. Then they crawled to the rope cradle, tested every knot, and shifted the surviving jar lower against the wall.

“We keep the water,” they said. “We cut the melons, the upper trellis, and both packs. If that takes the fig, it takes it. Then we test the channel together.”

Neshra looked at the roots. “Give me one turn of the rope to take the load off them.”

“One.”

They worked side by side, Odal cutting vines while Neshra shifted the main lashing to a lower anchor. Melons dropped and split, their sweet smell rising strangely through the bitter brine. Juice and blue water ran together over the stone. Neshra could not stop herself from tucking one seed-heavy piece into a crack beside the jar.

Odal saw. They said nothing.

* * *

Pain returns as shape.

She has four fingers in motion and one turned across them. She has a palm exposed to heat. She has a wrist that will not accept the demand made of it. Her name arrives from deeper within, less like a sound than a boundary remembered.

Ammara.

She is Ammara, and she has been waking long enough for pressure to acquire rhythms.

Along the creases of her palm, liquids run in repeated courses. Hardnesses accumulate beside them, break, and are restored. Rootlets drink from the thin debris gathered in her hollows. The living crust irritates her. It also changes with a regularity that stonefall does not.

She tries once more to close her hand.

* * *

The last movement came without warning.

The courtyard wall rolled under Neshra. The terrace rose toward vertical. Her rope turn tightened with a crack, and every load she had connected answered at once.

The fig tore another span of roots free. Its trunk wrenched sideways, driving the trellis against the rope that held the packs. The packs swung, struck Odal, and pulled them from the wall cap.

Their safety line snapped taut.

Neshra’s lower anchor shifted. Stone dust burst from its socket. She saw the arrangement in one clean instant: tree, trellis, packs, Odal, herself. Every careful knot had made one body of them. When the fig went, it would carry the wall’s cracked cap and the full water jar too.

She reached for the pruning hook. It spun past her. Odal hung below, one boot braced against a seam, both wrapped hands clutching the line at their chest.

“The knife,” Neshra said.

Odal could not free a hand.

Neshra drew her belt knife. The slope changed another fraction, crushing her shoulder into stone. Above her, the root mat peeled with the soft, intimate sound of cloth tearing.

She cut the first pack strap. Seeds streamed out, hundreds of pale flecks whipping into the gulf. The trellis shifted; Odal dropped the length of a forearm and slammed against the wall.

Neshra cut the second strap.

For one foolish beat she reached toward it, recognizing the waxed envelopes inside. Then it fell. The trellis groaned as the load redistributed through the vine ropes to the fig.

“Tree,” Odal managed.

Neshra put the blade against the main lashing.

She had grafted that fig in the third year after her mother died. She knew the twist of every limb. She knew which hollow kept winter water longest and where Odal, as a child, had carved three crooked lines in the bark to prove a knife was sharp.

The root mat lifted again, carrying half the terrace bed with it.

Neshra sawed through the rope.

The garden left them.

Fig, trellis, soil, tools, seed, and shattered paving slid as one dark mass. The trunk struck the courtyard lip and split. For a moment its roots combed the wall. Then it rolled away across the impossible palm, breaking smaller with each impact until dust hid it.

Freed from the pull, Neshra’s anchor held. She hauled Odal upward. Odal found the irrigation cut with one knee, then an elbow, and dragged them both inside. They lay wedged shoulder to shoulder in the bare channel while the stone continued to turn.

The surviving jar swung on its short line. Neshra caught it between her ankles. Odal hooked a foot around hers and steadied all three of them.

There was nothing left to cut.

* * *

Across Ammara’s hand, loose things fall. They bounce, fracture, disperse. Others move before the slope takes them and after it stops. They fasten themselves to hardness. They unfasten. They gather around smaller warmths. When one slips, another changes course.

Not one pattern. Thousands.

Her attention travels slowly, but the patterns repeat faster than she can lose them. Along a finger ridge, a cluster pours from a broken hollow, then divides around a fallen shape to recover the warmth trapped behind it. At the base of her thumb, moving points brace a line across a gap while others cross. In the crease of her palm, two warmths remain together after the rooted growth beside them tears away.

Weather does not protect itself from weather. Debris does not choose what to release.

The word returns without scale: lives. They are lives whether she can feel each one or only their multitude, whether they have wounded her surface or mistaken it for ground. She has already harmed them by waking. To finish the small gesture would press her fingertips into the center of her palm and grind their patterns between living stone.

Her joints plead for completion. The unfinished curl burns through wrist and forearm. She holds it.

Motion dwindles through her hand. One finger settles by the breadth of a house, and Ammara stops that too.

Then she attends to the minute, organized warmth upon her, not knowing how to tell it that she knows.

* * *

The world became still in portions.

First the jar ceased swinging. Then grit stopped traveling past Neshra’s cheek. Last came the fig’s remains, far below: a final branch turning end over end until it lodged against a roof.

Neshra waited for the next increment. Her muscles trembled in expectation of it.

Odal’s foot remained locked over hers. “Is it done?”

Neshra looked up at the nearest finger. It stood curved over the palm, an inhabited cliff where streets crossed sideways and buildings clung at angles no builder had planned. Beyond it, two more fingers had bent inward. Ammara's Palm was open no longer, but it had not closed.

“It stopped,” she said.

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“It’s what I know.”

They began with injuries. Odal could move every finger once the numbness eased, though two had swollen. Neshra’s bad knee bore no weight, and her shoulder burned where the last turn had pinned it. Neither was bleeding badly. The jar had lost a third of its water. Its rope held.

The terrace above them was a ragged face of soil. Their home still stood at its far edge, but the door now opened over empty air. The wristward service channel appeared intact for twenty paces before dust and the new angle hid it. Distant voices called names. Somewhere nearer the thumb, people were striking a steady sequence on a bell: three, pause, three. Whether it meant shelter, injury, or prayer, Neshra could not tell.

Warm brine continued to seep from the opened seam. Blue scale flowered across the drain grate.

Odal picked up the scraper.

“Wait,” Neshra said. She tore another strip of cloth and wound it over their thinning hand wraps. “Now.”

Odal cleared the grate. Neshra held the jar between her feet and watched the stone for movement. When Odal’s wrist tired, they exchanged tasks. The scale broke with a sound like thin ice and gathered in blue curls against Neshra’s palm.

“When the strain quiets,” Odal said, “we test the channel.”

“Together.”

“Yes.”

Far beneath them, under the tilted streets and cisterns, a tension passed through the wrist. It was too deep to be a collapse and too controlled to be settling. Neshra felt it through her hip and the soles of her feet. Odal froze with the scraper against the grate.

The hand did not move.

After a while, the drain began to clog again. Neshra took the scraper, and Odal braced the jar.

stories.title: A Crown for the Endless Fire
stories.prompt: Deep beneath the mountains, you find a woman crowned in antlers and burning candles standing on a bridge above an endless fire.
stories.body:
# A Crown for the Endless Fire

Nine candles wait below the place where your map ends.

You find them after the mountain closes behind you. The sounding charge gives one flat blow, softer than it should be, and the passage folds in. Stone strikes stone with a force you feel through your teeth. Your lamp goes out. By the time you spark it alive again, the return tunnel is a wall of fresh rock leaking dust.

Three men began the shift, counting you. One stayed above to mind the cable drum. One went back when the air soured. You continued because the blue line on your waxed map needed only another finger's length to meet the cold shaft the old borings promised. You are alone now, with half a skin of water, a survey hammer, sixty paces of rope, and the map in its iron case.

The charge has opened a crack at the base of the collapse. Red light pulses through it.

You follow the light because every other direction is stone.

The crack widens into a descending throat, then gives you to a cavern so vast that your lamp cannot find its roof. A bridge crosses the emptiness. It is a single black course of stone, one person wide, without curb or rail. Beyond it, cut into the opposite wall, a stair turns upward. A cold draft touches the sweat on your face. It is the route your instruments promised.

Under the bridge burns a fire with no bottom.

Flames rise out of depth in red terraces. Each blazing shelf reveals another beneath it, and another, until the eye loses scale and keeps falling. Nothing feeds the fire that you can see. Nothing is consumed. The roar is not loud so much as complete; it enters your chest and leaves no room there for another sound.

Someone stands at the bridge's center.

The nine candles burn above the figure's head. They sit in soot-black clay cups fixed along the branches of an antler crown, four to one side, five to the other. The antlers spread across the whole width of the span. Their lowest tines rest near holes cut into the bridge, as if the crown has roots in the stone. Firelight shows a long garment, bare hands, and a face that is sometimes brown flesh and sometimes a hollow made by shadow.

You raise your lamp. The figure has no shadow behind it. The fire has taken all the darkness for itself.

Your boot touches the bridge.

"Put it back."

The voice is a woman's, roughened by heat. It reaches you cleanly through the roar.

You keep your boot where it is. "The tunnel collapsed."

"I heard it."

"The stair behind you draws air. It has to reach an upper working."

"It reaches what it reaches." The crowned head inclines. Candle flames pull sideways, though the cold draft comes straight toward you. "Put your foot back on your ledge, Temba."

Hearing your name from the cavern stops you more surely than the command. You search the ledges, the black openings, the underside of the bridge. Nothing moves but fire.

"Who told you my name?"

"You did."

"I said nothing."

"Your case says it whenever the fire leans close."

The iron tube at your hip has begun to tick. Clear growth feathers over its latch, delicate as ice. You slap it away with your glove. The glass cracks, but new threads creep from the hinge.

You look up. The woman's face is lost behind the crown. Melted candle grease runs from its leather brow band down both temples. Perhaps the pale streaks are old wax. Perhaps they are bone. You cannot tell whether the antlers are strapped to her head or enter it.

"I am crossing," you say.

She lifts one hand from the crown.

All nine candles lean toward you.

The fire below narrows. A red blade rises beside the bridge and stands for one breath higher than your head. It is too straight to be a natural flare. Heat strikes your face. You recoil, boot scraping off the span, and the blade collapses into the gulf.

The woman's hand returns to the antler grip.

"You are staying there," she says.

You tell her about the collapse. You tell her your lamp has less than an hour and the water scarcely more. You tell her the upper crew will not know which branch took you because the blast stripped your chalk arrows from the wall. These are facts, ordered as you would enter them in a failure report. You keep your voice level. A frightened man may be ignored; a surveyor presenting conditions expects an answer.

The crowned woman gives you one.

"Behind me are air chambers. Sleeping rooms. A cistern. People who have never seen the sun and people who remember it badly. My daughter breathes through the shaft you feel on your face. You will not bring that fire to them."

"The fire is under us."

"Part of it is."

"I am not burning."

"Not yet."

You pull the map case from your belt. Glass has sealed half its circumference. "This is ash melted onto cool iron. I have seen bloom after furnace bursts. It isn't alive."

"I did not say it was."

"Then it cannot follow anyone."

The woman turns her head slightly. Candle three wavers. Candle seven burns low and blue. The other flames remain bent toward the case in your hand.

"Throw the tube behind you," she says.

You set it on the ledge instead. Every measured turn, every slope, every marked seam between the surface and this cavern lies inside it. The map is the one thing that can tell the upper crew where the missing men went. It is also five months of your life reduced to blue wax and black figures.

"Now my hands are empty."

"The bridge is still closed."

"You said the case carried fire."

"I said it speaks your name."

You hate riddles most when time is short. "What are you?"

At that, she shifts her feet. One candle gutters, and a bead of wax falls onto her knuckle. She flinches. The movement is small and involuntary. Whatever the crown may be, pain reaches the woman beneath it.

"I am the reason the far side is still breathing," she says.

The crown moves with her as she kneels. A long outer tine settles into one of the holes in the bridge. Its tip fits exactly. Flame gathers beneath the span, following the antler's shadow upward. You cannot see whether the stone contains a vent, whether the antler opens something, or whether the fire simply knows her.

You uncoil your rope.

The bridge crosses no more than fifty paces of open gulf. At the center, separate slabs overlap around a thick locking stone. You could loop the bridge, hang beneath its edge, pass under the crowned woman, and climb on the far half. The stone has survived heat that would soften iron. Your rope is braided cave fiber, not hemp, and you have trusted it over longer drops.

"Do not put weight under this bridge," she says.

"Then stand aside."

"No."

You work a loop over the near end. The rope's hook is plated in thin glass, but its gate still closes after you strike it twice with your hammer. You test the line with your full weight on the ledge.

"The last man carried a hook like that," the woman says.

"Did you stop him?"

"I let him explain."

"And?"

"I listened until I mistook an explanation for safety."

Her far side remains hidden behind the crown, but the hand gripping its left branch changes. The thumb presses a scar that circles her wrist like a white cord.

"He crossed," she says. "By dawn, glass had flowered through the cold shaft. It sealed two chambers before we broke it. The fire took the moving air and climbed inside it. I heard my sister striking the other side of a clear wall until she had no breath to strike again."

The words carry no ceremony. She might be reciting the dimensions of a grave.

"One accident does not establish a rule."

"It established mine."

You lock the rope around your harness.

The woman lifts candle seven from its clay cup. It continues to burn between her fingers, though grease runs over them. She lowers it near the antler tine seated in the bridge.

"If you go over the edge, Temba, the rope burns."

"You would murder me for a theory."

"I would keep you from murdering people for a route."

The charge behind you has not finished with the mountain. A grinding shock passes through the cavern. Pebbles leap on your ledge. The bridge bows, too little for the eye but enough for the rope to twitch against your palm. Far below, whole curtains of flame tilt toward the cold stair.

For an instant the woman is perfectly visible.

She is not a skull or a shape made of ash. She is a woman perhaps ten years older than you, with cropped hair plastered to her forehead and soot caught deep beside her mouth. The crown's leather band has rubbed the skin above her ears raw. Her eyes are dark, intent, and afraid.

Then the flare rises, and shadow takes her again.

"The mountain will bring the roof down," you call. "If that happens while we argue, your bridge dies with me."

"It was built to die before what is below can cross."

The meaning reaches you as she turns the antler in its socket. A crack opens across the black locking stone at her feet.

The crown is not only a warning. It is a key.

You clip the rope and lower yourself over the ledge.

Heat hits the soles of your boots. The endless fire has no smell of wood or pitch, only hot minerals and a sweetness from the candles above. You swing beneath the bridge, catch its rough underside, and move hand over hand. Fine ash rises around you. Wherever it touches the iron parts of your harness, it hardens into clear barbs.

"Climb back," the woman says.

You keep moving.

The first antler tine enters a second socket.

The nine flames bow. A thin tongue of fire slips upward, not beside the bridge now but along its underside. It finds the rope ahead of your hands. The fiber darkens.

You swing hard, reach past the burning place, and seize a stone lip. The rope parts behind your shoulder. Your legs drop into red light. For one terrible count you hang by your left hand while the severed line whips away into the gulf.

Your right hand catches the bridge.

You drag yourself back to the near ledge with two fingers blistered and the iron rings on your harness crusted shut. The crowned woman has not moved from the center.

"I warned you," she says.

"You burned it."

"Yes."

No apology. No triumph.

The candles shorten. Wax that had been running down the cups now crawls upward along the wicks. The fire's roar deepens until the bridge hums.

The woman's head snaps toward candle one.

"How long?" you ask.

She does not pretend not to understand. "Until the white rise? Less than you need."

"Can your crown shield this ledge?"

"For a little while."

"Can it shield me?"

"If I come to you."

"Then come."

"The bridge opens behind me, and you run for the stair."

You say nothing.

"There it is," she says. "The honest part."

Your right hand will no longer close fully. You cut the damaged rope away and flex the remaining buckles to break their glass. The map case waits on the ledge, ticking faster. You think of the crew above lowering another man into the cleared shaft tomorrow, then a drill cage next month. You think of pipes laid through this cavern to draw heat. On paper it had been an elegant project: endless power under a mountain already full of old cuttings. No fuel roads. No smoke.

The woman knows the thought by the direction of your eyes.

"Why did you sound the wall?" she asks.

"To find the shaft."

"Why?"

"To measure the heat."

"For whom?"

"People who freeze."

"People always arrive shivering. They leave carrying fire."

"Heat can be contained."

She looks at the glass on your harness. You have no answer that does not sound like the ones before.

Candle one turns white at the base.

The crowned woman takes the long tine from its socket and stands. "Go into the passage behind you. Lie flat when the rise comes. If the collapse holds, you may have an hour after."

"An hour for what?"

"Whatever a man does with his last hour."

"And you?"

"I close the bridge."

She plants both hands on the crown. Antler tips sink into sockets on either side of the locking stone. The rack now lies across the span like a gate. Each candle burns at the height of her face.

Your lamp dies.

The only way left is through her.

You sling the map case across your body. Then you take up the survey hammer.

Her gaze drops to it. "You have measured badly all night."

"Move."

"No."

You step onto the bridge.

The stone is hot through your boots. Three candles lean toward you and six toward the fire; you remember the pattern that came before the straight flare. You advance when the flames flatten, stop when they lift. The woman waits at the center, hands wide on the antlers.

When twenty paces remain, she twists the crown. Fire climbs the right edge of the bridge. You throw yourself left, one boot half over emptiness, and keep moving.

At twelve paces she lowers her head. The antlers turn every gap into a point. There is no space beside her, none beneath her, and no room for you to swing the hammer without giving the fire your balance.

"You can drop the bridge," you say. "But you're standing on it."

"My stone stays."

You look past the candle glare. The locking stone is cut in two layers. Her feet are on the far slab. Yours are on a chain of near slabs held by the black wedge between them.

She has told you the truth.

"Give me your name," you say.

The request surprises her.

"If you kill me, I want a woman's name, not a crown."

Wax strikes her cheek. She does not wipe it away.

"Maelka."

Now that you have it, she seems more dangerous, not less.

"Maelka, I am not going back."

"Then you have chosen the fire."

You rush her.

She turns the crown.

The locking stone drops.

The bridge comes apart under your feet, slab after slab tipping into the gulf. You run on falling ground. One step exists long enough to take your weight; the next rolls as you leave it. Fire opens between the joints in white columns.

Maelka's antlers fill your sight.

You swing the hammer at the lowest tine. She jerks the crown aside. Iron grazes bone, throwing a spark. A clay cup breaks. Burning wax spills across her shoulder, and she cries out, a human sound torn thin by the roar.

The last near slab falls.

You jump.

Your chest strikes the far edge. The hammer leaves your hand. Your legs swing over the endless fire, and the iron map case slams against the stone below Maelka's feet. One of her hands closes around your wrist. The other braces the crown, which has twisted sideways on her brow.

Only now are you close enough to see the cords working in her neck. Blood runs from a cut beneath the leather band. Her breath smells of smoke and bitter leaves. She is a woman. You are still not certain she is only that.

Below you, the map case shines.

Glass branches race over it, join the plated rings of your harness, and climb. They do not climb toward your body. They reach past you, thin clear fingers stretching toward Maelka and the cold stair behind her. Fire moves inside them, red as blood behind skin.

All the crown's remaining candles lean toward your chest.

Maelka could release you. Her grip tightens instead.

"Empty yourself," she says.

You claw at the harness buckle. Glass has locked it. Your burned fingers slip.

"The knife," she says. "Left boot."

You drag out your black-glass survey knife and saw through the shoulder strap. The case and harness hang from the waist belt. Fire enters the clear branches one joint at a time. Heat presses through your clothes.

"Faster."

"The belt is iron-tongued."

"Then cut yourself out of it."

You slice leather. The harness falls away, but the map case remains slung across your throat.

You drag its strap over your head. For a moment the case hangs from your free hand. Inside it are the blue route, the figures, the proof that you were right about the cold shaft. There is enough there for another crew to find a different descent. Your fingers close around the strap.

Maelka sees.

"I cannot hold both the man and his road."

The glass reaches for her wrist.

You let go.

The iron case falls without turning. The fire receives it far below, a black fleck vanishing into brightness. The clear branches snap. Six candles on Maelka's crown stand upright. Two pull weakly toward your boots.

She pulls.

You kick against the broken edge and come over it on your stomach. Maelka drags you until your boots are on sound stone, then lets you lie there while the white rise fills the gulf.

The remaining bridge vanishes in light. Ash strikes the crown and melts into its wax, plating the antlers in a translucent skin. Maelka kneels over you with her head bowed against the weight. Each candle burns within a small clear hollow. Her arms shake. Whatever power you imagined in her has a woman's muscles beneath it, and those muscles are near their end.

The flare subsides. Where the bridge stood, there is only open fire.

You have crossed.

Maelka sits back. One branch of the crown is cracked where your hammer struck it. The empty clay socket leaks wax down her shoulder. She touches the cut at her brow, examines the blood on her fingers, and looks at you.

"I told you no."

"You pulled me up."

"The road fell first."

Behind her, the cold stair waits. It is close enough to touch. You have no map, no hammer, no rope, no lamp, and no iron except two boot nails you begin prying out with the black-glass knife.

"Will the fire follow those?" you ask.

"The candles will tell me."

"And if they lean?"

"You have seen the answer."

You remove the nails and set them at the broken edge. They tumble soundlessly into the light.

The last two flames rise straight.

Maelka takes a candle stub from a waxed pocket and lights it from a wick protected inside the crown. She fixes the stub into the cracked cup with wax from her own cheek. The act is practiced, almost ordinary. This, more than the fire, convinces you that she has stood here before and expected to stand here again.

"What happens to me now?" you ask.

"You walk ahead. You keep your empty hands where I can see them. You tell my daughter why part of the mountain fell."

There is no welcome in it. There is passage.

You enter the stair. Maelka follows close enough that the antler points throw nine narrow shadows past you onto the wall. One shadow moves when none of the candles do. You decide not to look back a second time.

Below, deep beneath the mountains, the endless fire burns against an empty gulf. It has lost your map. Maelka has not lowered her crown.

stories.title: The Name the Water Took
stories.prompt: You emerge from a hidden jungle pool only to discover the water has washed away more than your clothes—it has taken your name, your past, you have no memory of who you are or how you got there.
stories.body:
# The Name the Water Took

My hands find mud, a root smooth as bone, three startled pebbles, and no clothes.

I have been searching the bottom long enough for my lungs to hurt. I surface into green light and a commotion of wings. Warm water streams from my hair. The pool is small, no wider than a room, sunk among trees whose roots grip its rim. Rain dimples the surface, but nothing floats there. No dress. No sandals. No torn scrap to prove I wore anything into the water.

I cannot remember what I wore.

That absence opens beneath the first. I know what clothes are. I know rain by the cold touch of it and the metallic smell rising from leaves. I know that the orange bars between the trunks mean evening and that a jungle path will soon become difficult to read. I know how to tread water without splashing.

I do not know where I learned.

I reach for my name and find the same soft bottom, the same blind roots.

On the bank, a woman says, “Don’t go under again.”

She stands beneath a broad-leafed tree, rain silvering her gray hair. She is perhaps sixty, lean and weather-browned, in trousers tucked into mud-dark boots. A folded cloth rests over one forearm. Her other hand is visible and empty.

I back away until my heels strike the drop at the pool’s center. My body does it quickly. Too quickly. There is strength waiting everywhere: in my thighs, my belly, the pull of my shoulders. I feel no ache except the clean sting in my lungs.

“Who are you?” I ask.

The woman’s mouth tightens. Not surprise. Preparation.

“Eswen,” she says. “I know the name you used. I have a wrap for you. May I come close enough to set it down?”

Used. Not use.

“Set it there.” I point to a flat stone. My hand is brown, unwrinkled, the nails pale crescents. No ring. No mark where one has been.

Eswen approaches the stone and crouches slowly. The cloth is plain and clean. She puts it down, retreats five steps, and turns her back.

I climb out.

The bank should be slippery. My feet choose holds before I can think about them, toes locking around stone, arms taking my weight. I come over the rim in one smooth motion and nearly laugh. The pleasure is sudden, animal, outrageous. My heart drives hard and evenly. I could run. I could climb one of the immense trees and look down through the rain.

Then I see Eswen’s shoulders shaking once beneath her wet shirt.

I snatch up the wrap. It clings for an instant, then loosens. Water beads on my skin in round, bright drops. More rain strikes me and skitters off without wetting me at all.

“What happened to me?”

“Cover yourself first,” Eswen says. “Then come with me. It isn’t safe to take the trail in the dark.”

“You knew I would be here.”

“Yes.”

“Did you put me in that water?”

She turns. Her eyes catch on my face, then force themselves down. “No. You walked in.”

“Why?”

“I brought answers. You arranged them.” She takes one careful breath. “I promised I would wait until dawn. I can do that much.”

She gives *much* the force of a limit.

The shelter is fifty paces uphill, a leaf roof pitched over four poles and a raised plank floor. I count without deciding to count. A low table stands inside. Two bedrolls occupy opposite corners. There are water jars, a shaded lantern, a canvas pack, a metal cup, and three thick paper packets sealed with black wax.

BODY. PEOPLE. WHY.

The labels are written in the same severe hand.

“Sit,” Eswen says. “Drink half that cup.”

“Whose handwriting?”

“Yours.”

The answer strikes nothing in me. I lift the cup. The water tastes faintly of boiled leaves. My hands do not shake.

Rain rattles harder on the roof. The wrap is damp, but my skin beneath it stays dry. Heat gathers under the cloth as if I am standing too near a stove.

Eswen unfolds a fan made from woven reeds and begins moving air across my face.

“Stop hovering over me,” I say.

“Then take the fan.”

I do. The sharpness of the answer steadies me more than kindness would have. “Why am I not wet?”

“The film lasts a few hours. Nothing settles on it. Water, sweat, mosquitoes. That means you can overheat without noticing soon enough. Drink.”

Two mosquitoes circle my knee and veer away. I hold a hand beneath the roof’s runoff. A clear dome forms over my palm and spills from the edges. No oil gleams on my skin; no scent rises from it.

Eswen watches me test it. She has expected testing.

“Have you seen this before?”

“Open a packet.”

“Are you a physician?”

“No.”

“A relative?”

Her face changes, so slightly I might have missed it if I were not studying her. “Open a packet, or don’t. You chose that arrangement because you knew you would ask faster than anyone could answer.”

I lay my fingers on WHY. The wax is already scored, easy to break. I move instead to BODY.

Eswen gives a short, humorless sound. “Yes. You would.”

Inside is a single sheet protected by waxed paper. The first line says: **The name I have used for sixty-three years is Amaya.**

I read it twice.

Amaya.

It is a serviceable name. Three syllables, open at both ends. It produces no face, no room, no sense of being called from far away. If it belongs to me, it belongs the way the wrap does: because someone left it where I would need it.

Below the name is an inventory dated yesterday. Age, eighty-four. Heart enlarged and failing. Breathlessness after twenty steps. A scar across the left knee, another beneath the right breast, two missing back teeth, a finger broken and badly set at thirty-one. The last paragraph predicts what the pool will do, though its caution is blunt: *If it behaves as it did before, the body that emerges will appear between twenty and twenty-five, with no acquired scars and no known illness. Do not mistake physical evidence for an answer to any larger question.*

I press two fingers to my neck and count. I squat, stand, squat again. My heart accelerates neatly. My left knee is smooth. My right little finger is straight. I explore my teeth with my tongue and find them all.

Eswen sets a polished steel mirror on the table.

The face inside it is perhaps twenty-two. Wide dark eyes. Black hair hacked short enough that it barely brushes the jaw. A strong nose, rain-dark brows, an angry red mark on one cheek from some leaf or insect before the film formed. I recognize anger. I recognize the habit of bringing my face close to glass when I want detail.

I do not recognize the woman.

“Amaya,” Eswen says, trying the word softly.

Nothing answers except my attention.

“Use it tonight,” I say. “It will be less confusing.”

She nods, but relief does not come. She pours more water and points to it.

The heat thickens. Every few minutes I fan my neck and drink. It is absurd to need cooling while rain blows through the shelter. The slick saves me from the insects whining beyond the lantern, and I am grateful for that small, ridiculous mercy.

I open PEOPLE.

There are twelve photographs, a family chronology, and three pages of names and addresses. The first photograph shows Eswen as a newborn in the arms of a woman who looks a few years older than I do now. The woman has my eyes, my nose, my strong square hands.

The next photographs proceed without magic. Eswen at six beside a dark-haired mother in her late twenties. At fourteen, nearly as tall as her. At thirty, laughing beside a woman gone gray at the temples. The last was taken recently. Eswen stands straight, though her face has softened with age. Beside her is a small, bent woman with one hand pressed to her chest.

I look from the picture to Eswen. The bones around her eyes are the infant’s bones. The shape of one ear persists through every image. Her chronology says she is sixty-one.

“You’re my daughter.”

“I am Amaya’s daughter.”

“That is a careful answer.”

“I have been practicing careful answers for two months.”

The photograph of six-year-old Eswen has a note on the back in the same severe handwriting: *My little minnow, furious at the river for moving faster than she could.*

“Minnow,” I say, looking up.

Eswen goes rigid. “Don’t.”

“It’s written here.”

“For you to know. Not for you to use.”

“If I wrote it—”

“She knew which river. She knew why I was furious. She knew I lost a shoe and lied about it for a week. You read one line.” Eswen takes the photograph from my hand, then seems to think better of keeping it and places it face down between us. “That name belonged inside all that.”

My first feeling is humiliation, hot and childish. The second is suspicion. She has chosen the facts, the pace, the shelter. She can put any life around me and call it mine.

“Show me your hands,” I say.

“What?”

“Your hands.”

She lays them on the table. The knuckles are swollen with age. A pale burn crosses the heel of the left palm. The chronology mentions the burn at seventeen. The shape matches the photograph taken afterward.

“You could be the woman in these pictures,” I say.

“I am.”

“That doesn’t make their account true.”

“No.”

“Who else knows I came here?”

“No one who knows where the pool is.”

“Where is home? How much money do I have? Did I have a spouse? Other children? Enemies? Did I commit crimes? Are people waiting for me?”

“Those are in the notebooks.” Eswen taps the canvas pack. “You get those at dawn.”

“Why dawn?”

“Because I won’t lead the trail in darkness, and because I promised one night.”

“Promised whom?”

“My mother.”

“Me.”

“No.” The word lands flat and hard. “Not yet. Maybe not ever. I don’t know.”

Rainwater runs from the roof in ropes. I want to reject the photographs, but they have weight and wear. One bears a thumbprint beneath the glaze. Another has cracked exactly where it was folded years ago. Ordinary objects are good at surviving the people who give them meaning.

I slide WHY toward me, then stop. “Tell me without the letter. Did you lead her here?”

Eswen lowers herself onto the other stool. Weariness makes her look older than sixty-one. “I led Amaya from the road. She couldn’t have made the walk alone.”

“Knowing this would happen.”

“Knowing what she believed would happen.”

“You had seen the proof.”

“I had seen records.”

The distinction sounds like mine. That makes me dislike her for using it.

“You could have refused.”

“I did. She hired a guide. She planned to leave before I arrived. Her heart was failing, and she thought dying in the jungle was better than dying in her bed while I stopped her.” Eswen’s fingers close around the edge of the table. “So I came. I carried food. I made her rest. I waited while she took off her boots and then put them back on because she was afraid. I did not push her into the pool.”

“You helped.”

“Yes.”

The answer offers me no soft place to strike.

“Did she know she would forget you?”

“She believed facts could rebuild what memory lost.”

“Do you believe that?”

“Open the packet.”

I break the black wax.

The letter inside begins, *To the woman with my face: I am sorry for the fear. I chose this with a clear mind.*

The hand is controlled, its pressure deep where the pen begins each line.

*I am eighty-four. My heart will not carry me through another season. I have had sixty-three years I was never promised, and I want more. Wanting more is not wisdom, but it is honest.*

The words make something in me lift—not recognition, but appetite. I look at my smooth hands and imagine decades multiplying ahead: mountains I could climb, trades I could learn, the simple luxury of waking without pain. Whoever wrote the letter knew the seduction. She had felt this strength before.

*Eswen will tell you what matters. Trust the packets first, then trust the consistency of her account. Go home with her. Read my journals. In time, the shape of the life may become yours even if its images do not return. It happened once. It can happen again.*

I glance up. Eswen is looking past me at the rain.

“She ordered you to reconstruct her.”

“She asked.”

“The letter doesn’t sound like a request.”

“No.”

Beneath it are older papers, copied and recopied where damp has eaten the originals. A dated clinic examination describes an unknown young woman found feverish and naked near a jungle track sixty-three years ago. She had no autobiographical memory, no identifying marks, and the manner of someone educated in observation. A later deposition, signed **Amaya**, gives the location of this pool and describes the same impossible film on the skin. There is a photograph of the young woman in a borrowed dress. Her hair is longer than mine. The face is mine.

Another page explains the name. The unknown woman chose it when a clerk refused to leave an official line blank. No revelation, no recovered syllable. A sound she could bear answering to.

The earliest pages refer to damaged belongings recovered from a camp downstream: an empty food tin, a rotten satchel, notes rendered illegible by water. No name survives. No witness. No proof of who entered the pool before Amaya came out.

I arrange the papers by date, then reverse the order. Sixty-three years. A renewed young woman becomes Amaya, makes a life, raises Eswen, grows old, and returns to the same water. Now I sit in her place, borrowing her chosen name and examining her daughter as if grief were a discrepancy in a report.

“You knew,” I say.

“Yes.”

“You helped her destroy me.”

Eswen’s gaze comes back from the rain. “I helped my mother reach the thing she wanted. I don’t know whether she destroyed herself. I don’t know whether you are her, or the next part of her, or someone the pool left holding her consequences.” Her voice roughens; care gives way. “I know she expected me to do the joining. As if I could tell you sixty-one years in the right order and get my mother back. As if those years weighed nothing in my mouth.”

“You’re withholding evidence because you resent her.”

“I am withholding my life because it is mine.”

The rain eases. Drips tick against the broad leaves outside. Somewhere near the pool, a frog makes a sound like a finger drawn over a comb.

I want to ask which foods Amaya liked, whom she loved, what frightened her before sleep. I want Eswen to speak until every blank in me is filled. The questions line up cleanly: earliest memory, happiest day, worst mistake, habits, loyalties, private promises. I know how to test an account by returning to one detail from three directions. The skill survived because it is not, by itself, a memory.

I hear the interrogation before I begin it.

Eswen has placed her hands in her lap, away from the table. The burned one cups the other. She has spent the night answering only what she promised, and I have treated every boundary as another packet to force open.

I turn the childhood photograph face up. I do not read the note again.

“What do you want?” I ask.

Eswen frowns, suspicious now in her turn. “Tonight?”

“After dawn. From me.”

For a long time she says nothing. The jungle fills the space without helping either of us. Water falls from leaf to leaf. A night insect starts its rasp, pauses, and starts again.

“I want you to take the notebooks,” she says at last. “There are medical facts you need, accounts, a house address. Read them yourself. I’ll show you the road. After that, I want to decide when I’m ready to hear from you.”

“How would I contact you?”

“The address is written down.”

“Do you want me to use Amaya?”

Her eyes go to my face, then away. “I don’t care what name you use.” A pause. “That’s not true. I care. I just don’t get to choose it.”

“I’ll keep it for now.”

She nods once.

“And you don’t have to call me anything you don’t mean.”

“Good.”

It is not forgiveness. It is enough instruction for one morning.

Eswen lies down in her corner with her back to me. Sleep does not come to her quickly. I hear every change in her breathing until I make myself stop listening for messages inside it.

I read.

The notebooks are dense, impatient, sometimes funny. They contain household repairs, heart symptoms, debts owed and collected, people I may need to notify, and complaints about a neighbor’s fruit dropping over a wall. Amaya records the pool more often as death approaches. She is afraid. On one page she writes that fear has made every hour taste expensive. On another, she insists Eswen will understand eventually, then scratches out *understand* so violently the paper tears.

Nothing returns to me. Not the house described room by room. Not the names of the dead. Not the daughter sleeping ten feet away.

Near midnight, the film on my skin begins to fail. Sweat gathers first at my scalp. I touch the dampness and grin before I can stop myself. By then my stomach is a hollow animal. I eat cold rice and sour fruit from a tin, then eat the portion Eswen left untouched after she wordlessly pushes it across the floor. Hunger is almost joyful in this body. My jaw works without pain. My fingers are quick with the spoon.

The night does not restore me. It merely passes.

At dawn, pale light finds the mist above the pool. My shoulders ache from hunching over the table, and my legs are sore from the climb to the shelter. These small pains delight me. They were earned by muscles with years left in them.

Eswen rolls the bed mat, ties back her gray hair, and checks the trail with a stick. I pack the photographs, letters, and notebooks in the canvas bag. It is heavy. I adjust the straps until the weight rides close to my spine, apparently another thing my body knows how to do.

At the pool, I pause.

The water is green and warm-looking, untroubled by the rain. There is no sign it has ever held a person. No clothes wait beneath the surface. No name rises when I search for one.

Eswen does not tell me to hurry.

I turn away first.

At the mouth of the trail she says, “Ten paces behind me. Close enough that you don’t miss a turn. Far enough that I don’t feel watched.”

“All right.”

She starts downhill. I let her reach ten paces, then follow.

The young body wants to close the distance. I could do it in seconds. Instead I keep Eswen where she asked to be, ahead of me with only the trail stick, while Amaya’s written life travels on my own back.

stories.title: The Apes Above
stories.prompt: Humans abandoned Earth many years ago for space stations; below the Dino Council is meeting to discuss what to do about those pesky apes in orbit throwing rocks at them.
stories.body:
# The Apes Above

The pebble came down a rain gutter during the first attendance count, clicked twice against the stone, and rolled toward the floor drain.

Ketta stopped it beneath one foreclaw.

It was black, thumb-sized, and blistered on one side. A thread of silver insulation clung to it like shed skin. Nothing in the hills above the Stone Choir made stone like that. Nothing on Earth had put that particular scorch on it, either, until one of the human stations had thrown it down.

She set it on her motion tablet. The tablet already carried the larger figures: three nursery roofs broken in Fern Basin, one irrigation trench blocked, six eggs moved because the ground beneath their warming beds had cracked. No deaths. The line mattered. So did the word *yet* that she had not written after it.

Above the council benches, a blue point crawled across the noon opening in the roof. One of the stations. Humans had left the surface so many generations ago that their stairways to the sky had become cliffs furred with vines, but they had not gone far enough to become stars. On clear nights their habitats crossed the dark in tidy rows. Lately, the lowest one had begun dropping untidy pieces of itself.

The long-necked chair finished counting those present, those present by proxy, and one marsh delegation whose three heads claimed to constitute either one vote or three depending on the motion. He lowered his chin to the speaking height.

“The councillor for Fern Basin has the floor.”

Ketta rose. Ankylosaurs did not rise impressively from council benches designed by hadrosaurs, but her tail club struck the aisle with a satisfying report.

“I move that the Upthrower’s next window be used against the lowest human station.” She nudged the pebble into the light. “The apes above have thrown seven loads in forty-one days. The intervals are shortening. Fern Basin’s hatching migration begins in nine days. We will stop the throwing before then.”

From the defense benches, Othrik said, “Seconded.”

The ceratopsian marshal’s frill bore a map of old repairs, each pale patch a season in which something with teeth or weather had tested it. He did not tap the bench or make speeches when one word would hold.

The chair blinked with grave patience. “Before debate, the sponsor will define *against*.”

“The station.”

“A spatial definition. I require an operational one.”

The chamber began offering help. Strike its rock chute. Break its engines. Frighten it. Blind it. Tug it higher. Tug it lower. One small raptor moved to insert *without precipitating an extinction event*, and a sauropod objected that every motion should contain that phrase as a matter of good housekeeping. A duck-bill from the floodplain moved to describe the apes as *pesky*, which the clerk ruled descriptive but not operational, then asked the Council to authorize immediate ducking. The armored delegations rejected public funds for ducking on the grounds that they had already funded armor.

“Order,” said the chair, while councillors with horns attempted to determine whether they could fit under their desks without disqualifying themselves from speaking.

Ketta waited them out. The Stone Choir had been cut around natural ribs of basalt. Every footstep entered the walls and returned as a low, dignified hum, which was why the builders had chosen it for government. They had not anticipated three hundred representatives testing furniture with their foreheads.

“Cripple the station’s ability to release further mass,” Ketta said. “The Upthrower can place a penetrator through the ballast works.”

“Can,” called Pellik from the skywatchers’ gallery, “is doing unusually heavy labor in that sentence.”

She sprang down the gallery steps, feathered arms crowded with slates. She was narrow enough to pass between two arguing horned councillors without either noticing. The clock attendant at the chamber door turned the outer ring of the impact dial. Eighty-three minutes remained before the next predicted entry.

Ketta looked at the chair. “Is the gallery now permitted to amend verbs?”

“The skywatcher has been summoned as an expert.”

“I was summoned for the third agenda item,” Pellik said. “But the third agenda item may arrive before the first one finishes.” She laid her slates across the clerk’s table, covering a proposed subsidy for communal basking stones. “This is the low station over the last forty-one days.”

Each slate showed Earth as a circle and the station’s path as a loop drawn in wax. The earliest loop nearly touched the upper breath of the atmosphere. After each ejection, the next loop stood a little farther away.

Pellik used the black pebble as a pointer. “The released loads travel backward relative to the station. The station moves forward. Throw mass one way and the thrower is pushed the other. Every release buys it height.”

“How much?” Ketta asked.

“Not enough.”

“That is not a number.”

“Between twelve and nineteen days before the atmosphere takes the height back, depending on the mass of the load and whether the station can still correct its own attitude.”

“Can it?”

“Unknown.”

Ketta preferred unknowns that sat still in their own columns. Pellik’s moved around and borrowed one another’s hats.

Othrik came down from the defense bench. “Whatever pushes the station, the rocks fall on us.”

“Yes,” Pellik said. She pulled out a surface map stippled with impact marks. The old drops scattered over forest, salt waste, sea, and once the eastern edge of Fern Basin. The recent marks crowded toward one blank bowl in the southern highlands. “But the main masses have been moving here.”

“Quiet Caldera,” the clerk read.

No nests, no farms, no council districts, and not enough water to tempt anyone but mineral lickers. Even the caldera’s name had survived several attempts by musicians to improve it.

Ketta pressed one claw to the mark in Fern Basin. “This one missed your empty bowl by four hundred and twelve lengths.”

“Its largest piece did. The basin damage came from fragments after breakup.”
