Naro tore the unprinted margin from a condemned filter sleeve. With a maintenance marker, she copied two characters she had seen together on ten thousand status plates.

ABOVE OPERATING.

Not person. Operating was measurable.

She sealed the strip inside the capsule's empty document recess. The snag's approach vector was still in her wrist display; the disposal control offered a family of permitted releases through the same band of atmosphere. Naro chose the late edge of the next window. She altered no guidance, added no propellant, and told herself that a strip of filter cloth could not change a landing on a lifeless world.

The cradle closed. The capsule rolled away.

***

Six days later, the radiator sector came under Naro's name again. She had checked the assignment board so often that morning that the system warned her against duplicate requests. The planet filled half the view below the service rail, all white weather and brief blue-black gaps. Naro tried to watch the coolant gauge. She tried not to look along the vane.

A triangle of yellow cloth trembled at its tip.

This kite was smaller. Its bridle thread had fused into a glassy bead where it touched the charged edge. Naro freed it with both hands, careful not to tear the picture sewn to its center.

Someone had drawn a capsule as a white oval with flame streaming behind it. Beneath, the oval lay in a black furrow beside a square roof. The roof's edge was black too. Two small figures tipped buckets over it. At the bottom, the unknown writer had copied an old hazard triangle and filled it with the maintenance word HOT.

Naro carried the kite inside before translating the rest.

NO MORE ANSWER, the message said, IF HOT FALLS HERE.

Beside the words was a map too careful to be a child's idle decoration. It began at the first capsule's black furrow, with an arrow following the direction the shell had skipped. Twelve short marks, each the length of the drawn furrow, stepped along the arrow to a bare circle crosshatched in gray. Three pale boulders made a triangle beside it. The roofs, water, and planted squares lay off the other edge of the cloth. There was no compass mark or absolute coordinate, but the burn scar supplied scale, the logged skip supplied bearing, and the boulders supplied a reference Naro could seek from above. The writer had shown her how to find a safe landing patch without surrendering the settlement's location as a number.

TELU appeared again at the lower edge.

Naro put her palm over the drawn roof. The capsule had not burned away. It had gone down too shallow, shed enough speed to survive, and struck near somebody's shelter still carrying reentry heat. Her answer had arrived as a hazard warning of its own.

She took the kite to the service shop after second shift, when the benches were empty. Discarded supply capsules were permitted to vary widely in mass, but not in descent behavior. An intact one was a hammer. By dawn Naro had stripped a retirement shell of its latch block, pressure liner, and cargo web. She cut a drogue from heat-cured packing membrane and stitched its load tapes through the shell's old restraint points. The work was familiar in pieces and unprecedented as a whole.

She ran the configuration through the disposal model. The drogue opened too early and tore. She shortened the lines. It opened too late. She changed the pilot fold, then loaded the shell with crushed ceramic to mimic the message mass and fired it down the station's test shaft. The membrane snapped full before the marker band and lowered the shell onto the padded arrestor with a force that would bruise a shin, not burn a roof.

Only then did Naro prepare another capsule. She called up the first shell's logged track in the downward maintenance optics and searched backward from its release. The blackened footprint appeared between cloud banks, a narrow dash ending at the roof. Naro aligned it with the recorded skip direction, counted twelve scar-lengths along that bearing, and found three pale points grouped in the triangle Telu had drawn. The crosshatched patch lay beside them, bare even at the optics' poor resolution.

On a square of filter cloth, she copied the bare landing circle and drew the drogue above it. She added a picture of the kite climbing past a storm cloud, then the labels KITE, RISE, HOW. The old script had no grammar Naro could reliably use. Maintenance language assumed an object in front of you and a problem already happening.

She closed the capsule around the message and held it on her workbench until the mass reading stopped changing. This time, when she altered the release time, she used the logged track and Telu's twelve-furrow offset to aim for the empty patch beside the three boulders.

***

The answer came up nine days later on green cloth that had once been a sleeve. Three pictures crossed its panels. In the first, a figure stood in slanting rain, letting out line from a flat spool. In the second, the thread climbed into a black cloud split by white branches. The figure had tied the line to a stake and stepped far back. In the third, the station passed overhead as a long moving spark. The thread curved toward its wake; near the top, a knot opened and the kite flew free.

The pictures explained enough. During the strongest storms, charge climbed the wet, conductive thread. The radiator system cast its own charged wake when it dumped heat. Somewhere between cloud and station, two forces that had never been designed to meet pulled the little sail upward.

The writing underneath corrected Naro's order.

HOW DOES KITE RISE?

Then, in darker strokes:

CAPSULE FELL CORRECT. CAPSULE WAS WARM. ROOF WAS SAFE.

TELU.

Naro read WARM twice. She had known the temperature from the model. The word still loosened something behind her ribs that calculation had held rigid for nine days.

She copied the corrected question into a notebook made from the unused backs of inspection cards. She drew columns for objects, actions, qualities, and the small joining marks she had once dismissed as stains. TELU went in a fifth column headed ROUTE.

After that, waiting entered her work. The return corridor crossed the radiator wake every six or seven days, depending on how the station trimmed its orbit and how far the storm columns wandered. Some crossings brought nothing. On others, Naro found a kite worrying at the vane as if it had been there for years and had merely waited for her to notice.

She never delayed a heat cycle. When the sector needed purge, she purged it. Charge leaking along the maintenance trunks killed the yeast starters in the nearest galley bays, as it always did during heavy dump weeks, and the corridor filled with the warm mineral smell of dense, unleavened rounds. Inner-ring crews traded risen loaves at insulting prices. Naro ate her ration at the service bench while she pared grams from empty capsules and practiced a language built from caution plates.

She drew her meal for the next message: a gray circle scored into six wedges. The reply labeled it MOON. Naro sent back NO, FOOD, with a picture of teeth.

The following kite carried two circles. One hung above a roof with light marks around it. The other sat on a flat stone above a fire, with fingers breaking its edge. Telu had crossed out Naro's word order and written FOOD: FLATBREAD. Naro laughed loudly enough that the empty service shop answered her from its vents.

The exchanges widened by such corrections. Telu drew rain beating seedlings flat and, beside it, seedlings standing again under the sun. Naro answered with the station's water loop: a cup, a drain, a pipe curling around to fill the cup again. Telu sent a roof patched in three different colors and a row of people walking around black scars where old things had fallen from the sky. Naro drew her exterior gloves, each finger thick as a tool handle, and a radiator vane shedding heat in lines no eye could see.

She asked no question about population. She did not request soil, seed, blood, or coordinates. Once she began to draw a map of the planet with a query mark over the land, then blacked it out so thoroughly that the filter cloth stiffened. Telu had given her a safe circle, not an invitation.

The child's impatience came through even before Naro knew to call the writer a child. Corrections slashed through bad words. Questions crowded the hems when the central cloth was full. One red kite arrived with its tail shortened to make room for a complaint: ABOVE ANSWERS SLOW. RAIN DOES NOT WAIT.

Naro replied BELOW SIGNAL RECEIVED, because it was a familiar phrase and because it hid her behind the station's habits. When a drogue landed wide of the gray circle, she wrote CAPSULE CORRECTED. When Telu asked whether there were roofs above the rain, Naro drew the pressure hull and labeled it ENCLOSURE SAFE.

Every response was accurate. None exposed more of her than a status panel would.

In the seventh week, a blue kite came in during a weak dump, barely high enough to catch the vane. Its cloth was soaked through before launch; in vacuum the remaining moisture had bloomed into frost along the seams. Naro tucked it beneath her arm and hurried through the lock while the fibers were still flexible.

At its center, Telu had drawn a person.

The figure was small beside the roof, with knees showing below a square tunic and dark hair sticking out in several directions. One hand held the kite spool. The other pointed to the familiar mark Naro had filed under ROUTE.

TELU.

Above it, copied with painstaking exactness, was a label Naro recognized from every suit locker on the station:

PERSONNEL NAME.

An arrow led from those words to TELU. A second arrow led to an empty box beside a drawing of a suited figure on a radiator rail.

Naro sat on the air-lock floor.

The repeated mark was not a route. It had never named a corridor through the weather or a launch site. It named the hand that sewed crooked stitches and crossed out Naro's grammar. Telu. A person small enough to stand below that roof, stubborn enough to launch questions into a storm.

With the name, the opening sentence changed. Naro took the first red kite from its sealed drawer and spread it beside the blue one. She added the joining marks Telu had taught her, moved the hook from destination to query, and read what had been waiting there all season.

IS THERE A PERSON ABOVE THE RAIN?

Not: Is the machinery operating? Not: Did a signal reach you? Telu had asked for someone and received a chain of system statuses.

On the blue kite, below the empty name box, the child had written the question again. The disposal forecast showed one more safe pass through the corridor before the storms weakened. Naro had a tested drogue already folded and a retired shell cleared for release. She also had an inventory notice in her queue: three capsule liners lighter than their registered retirement masses. The notice was automatic, low priority, and due for reconciliation in eleven days.

She could send another anonymous answer. ABOVE PERSONNEL PRESENT would satisfy the grammar. It would disclose nothing that a population estimate had not already implied.

Instead, Naro wrote until the old letters stopped looking like labels.

PERSON ABOVE. NAME NARO. I HEAR TELU.

I was not printed anywhere in the station's inherited warnings. Naro built it from the person-mark and the near-pointing stroke Telu used in corrections. HEAR came from the alarm instruction inside every pressure shelter: IF ALARM HEARD, REPORT. She could not be certain it meant what she needed. She drew herself beside the radiator vane, one gloved hand raised, and pointed the name field at her chest.

The message weighed four grams. She took out the drawing, shaved its margins, and put it back. She opened the drogue on the bench, inspected every stitch, folded it again, and seated it in the supply capsule.

At release, the discarded shell turned once beyond the cradle, found its blunt end, and vanished toward the white weather.

***

The lift season ended without ceremony. Storm charge fell below the radiator's attraction threshold. The station adjusted its orbit, moving the return corridor eastward across cloud tops that revealed nothing.

Naro completed two ordinary exterior shifts. On the third, she found no cloth and told herself she had expected none. The vane angle held within tolerance. Coolant pressure stayed flat. In the service shop, the inventory notice climbed from low priority to routine review.

Then a final kite reached the station on the ragged edge of a heat dump. It was so small that at first Naro mistook it for a strip of insulation. No wooden cross held it open, only two springy reeds and a diamond of pale fabric. The thread had parted cleanly at the release knot. Whoever had made it had learned exactly how little sail the wake would take.

Naro brought it inside. There was no picture on the first panel, only a sentence in compact, careful writing.

TELU HEARS NARO. NARO IS A PERSON ABOVE THE RAIN.

The answer returned to her, corrected and complete.

On the second panel, Telu had drawn a roof under heavy rain. A jar stood beneath one corner, filling from the eaves. Beside it floated Naro's sealed cup and looping pipe. The new question ran down the narrow remaining space:

HOW DOES NARO DRINK WHERE RAIN DOES NOT FALL INSIDE?

By the next shift the charged season was over. Naro freed the radiator vane, verified its hinge, and closed the same kind of service ticket she had closed on the first day: FILAMENT DEBRIS REMOVED; NO IMPACT DAMAGE. The station kept its schedule, its school lessons, and its course around the clouds.

At her bench, the capsule discrepancy waited in the queue. So did the long months before another capsule could follow the same corridor.

Naro laid a condemned condensation diagram on the scale. It showed vapor cooling against a pipe wall, gathering into drops, and returning to the drinking reservoir. Five grams. Too heavy.

She trimmed away the title block and began translating the arrows.

stories.title: The Foundations Remember
stories.prompt: A vertical neon city claims to be humanity’s first civilization. Citizens pay rent by leasing selected memories to corporations that copy, edit, and resell them. A junior memory-repossession technician is ordered to erase an evicted transit worker’s recollection of a sealed tunnel beneath the lowest train line. The memory contains physical evidence of civilizations older than the city’s official history. Preserving it would require hiding it inside the technician’s licensed memory space, placing their already-collateralized childhood at risk.
stories.body:
# The Foundations Remember

The lender wanted Teren Vard's first clear view of the city.

They stood outside apartment 81, repossession rig balanced against one knee, while the license check opened a door in the back of their sight. At once they were six years old again, too short to see over the lift rail. Their fingers fitted the old scratches in its brass. Someone behind them smelled of hot cloth and citrus soap. Their mother said, *Wait. Now look.*

The lift rose out of the lower dark. Floors slipped past in bars of blue, green, fever-pink. Neon found the child's reflection piece by piece: knuckles, cheek, both startled eyes. Then the towers opened above, stacked so high that their lights narrowed into a second sky.

Every school film began with that ascent. Humanity had first gathered here, the teachers said; below the lowest foundations waited untouched stone.

IDENTITY ANCHOR ACCEPTED, the rig printed across the view. CHILDHOOD BLOCK THREE: COLLATERAL ACTIVE.

The memory released Teren with citrus still sharp at the back of their tongue. They resented that most. A lender should have been able to check a checksum. It did not need their mother's soap.

Forty-nine minutes remained before the eviction handover.

Teren straightened their gray junior's coat, confirmed the green seal on the rig, and knocked.

Orla Dace opened the door before the second knock. She was a broad, compact woman with silver hair clipped close to her scalp and the pale twin stripes on her wrists left by years of transit gloves. Behind her, the apartment had been reduced to rectangles: clean patches where shelves had stood, dust borders around missing chairs, four bolt holes where a wall display had been.

Her eyes went to the junior stripe on Teren's collar. “They sent a learner.”

“A licensed technician.”

“Both can be true.”

Teren offered the writ. Orla did not take it. The text shone between them anyway: tenancy terminated, work-life tranche in arrears, one selected recollection subject to repossession and erasure at source. Its boundaries were unusually exact. Lowest-line platform, unauthorized panel entry, descent and return. Thirty-six minutes, nine seconds of lived material.

“The furniture crew arrives at noon,” Teren said. “If we begin now, I can keep the procedure private.”

“Generous.”

“Practical.”

She stepped aside.

Teren set the rig on the bare floor. Its three hinged screens unfolded like dull petals. One lead went to Orla's source cuff, one to the contact band Teren fastened behind their own ears. The third terminated in the black creditor key already authorized by the writ. When the session closed, the rig would purge its raw working buffer. What remained could go only to the creditor vault, back to the registered source, or into the technician's licensed space. Junior licenses were small, audited, and expensive. Teren's was nearly full of their own life.

Orla sat on the windowsill. Beyond her, traffic advertisements climbed the neighboring tower in luminous schools: borrowed summer dives, a pilot's first cloudbreak, a chef's recollection of cinnamon altered to advertise perfume. The same fourteen delighted faces repeated every forty floors.

“Inventory,” Teren said.

“You already have it.”

“I need your confirmation. The selected memory belongs to a leased work-life tranche acquired by your former transit employer, then transferred to its memory subsidiary after dismissal. The corporation retains its archival master. Today's action removes your accessible source copy.”

“You mean my memory.”

“Yes.”

“You mean they keep theirs.”

Teren looked at the black key. “Yes.”

Orla flexed her hands as if settling them into absent gloves. “Then you see it first.”

“Witness playback isn't required.”

“Neither was bricking a door under the lowest line, but someone was particular about that too.”

The handover timer turned amber: forty-three minutes.

Teren could refuse. A clean job meant minimal playback, exact boundaries, no contamination between source and technician. Their supervisor said people ruined themselves by getting curious inside other people's lives. Yet deletion required Teren to certify that the selection matched the writ, and Orla was challenging the match.

“One verification pass,” Teren said.

Orla held out her wrist.

The rig found the edges quickly. Sound thickened. The bare room went dark.

Metal dust gritted between the teeth.

The lowest platform was supposed to be empty after last service, but empty track was never quiet. Power lines ticked as they cooled. Ventilation breathed through tile seams. Far above, trains made the ceiling tremble in patterns learned over twenty-two years: local, freight, express, then the short hard shiver of a switching engine.

This vibration came from below.

Boots crossed the yellow edge stripe. A hand pressed the rail bed, two fingers down, not to feel force but spacing. There: a pulse, a pause, a longer pulse. Repeating.

The body turned before Teren chose to turn. Its lamp picked out an access panel beyond the platform camera's arc. The panel bore no number. Gray sealant had been painted over its bolts, but the lower hinge was polished where vibration had worried metal against metal.

A transit key fitted.

Behind the panel, a ladder descended farther than the city's foundation diagrams allowed. The first twelve rungs were new alloy. The next were black iron, their centers worn shallow by boots.

Teren broke the link.

The apartment returned too bright. Their right hand clutched the rig's casing. Their left was lifted away from an edge that was no longer there.

Orla watched them. “Infrastructure hazard?”

The phrase had already risen to Teren's mouth. It was the reason code on the writ. “An unlisted access route is dangerous.”

“So is a staircase if you stop halfway down.”

A train passed somewhere inside the tower. Before the sound reached the windows, Teren bent their knees and caught the top screen. The rig had not yet begun to rattle.

Orla noticed. “That wears off.”

Commercial playback warnings called it motor residue. Customers who leased athletes' victories often dropped cups for an hour afterward because their hands expected a different weight. Teren had laughed at the instructional clip in training. They did not laugh now.

“You reported the panel,” they said.

“I reported what was past it. My shifts disappeared first. The apartment took longer.” Orla rubbed one pale wrist stripe with her thumb. “Your order doesn't include the reports. Or the meetings. Just the part where I learned what they needed forgotten.”

“The master won't be forgotten.”

“No. They can trim it, soften the colors, sell the descent to people who like a scare before dinner. I suppose that's a kind of remembering.”

Teren checked the selection graph. The memory had clean physiological continuity, no edit scars. A single pass was enough to confirm the first boundary but not the last. They could mark it verified and never know what lay at the bottom.

Thirty-seven minutes.

“What do you want me to find?” Teren asked.

“What I found.”

“And then?”

“Then you'll at least erase the right thing.”

She did not ask to be rescued.

Teren lowered the playback threshold. “Second pass.”

Dark. Iron cold beneath both hands.

The ladder ended on tile.

Not service tile. Small cream hexagons spread beneath dust, buckled by roots of concrete driven down from overhead. The nearest foundation pile filled what had once been a stairwell. Another punched through the roof of a long chamber. Along its far side lay paired steel rails, narrower than the city's lowest line and furred orange with corrosion.

The headlamp moved slowly. Benches emerged. A smashed clock with two rings of markings. Signs had been abraded to white scars, yet in one corner several characters remained under mineral bloom. They belonged to no transit alphabet Teren knew. Orla's hand measured their height, then photographed them with an issued assay wand.

The wand was a cheap maintenance instrument, built to tell whether a corroded beam would survive another season. It chirped unhappily at the rail, sampled oxidation and trapped residue, and returned an age range nearly four times longer than the city's six-century official history.

ERROR: ENVIRONMENTAL CONTAMINATION, its display decided.

Orla sampled a roof bracket. The estimate shifted older.

Above, through concrete and layers of earth, a train approached. The remembered body moved to the wall. Teren's small hand closed on a scratched brass rail.

*Wait. Now look.*

The old concourse rose in neon bars. For one impossible second their mother's reflection stared from a black tunnel mouth, and Orla's gloved fingers lay over the child's.

Teren tore free so sharply that the contact band pulled their hair.

SOURCE LABEL STABILITY: 82%, the center screen warned.

Orla leaned forward. “You crossed into something.”

“Temporary sensory crossfade.” Teren opened the diagnostic pane. “Similar low-frequency inputs. It doesn't alter either source unless I write the session.”

“Is that what you tell yourself, or what the manual told you?”

“Both can be true.”

“Learner,” Orla said.

Teren increased label isolation. It cost them six minutes of buffer time. The handover timer and purge timer advanced together, one threatening interruption, the other obliteration.

“The assay isn't proof,” Teren said. “The reading happened inside the memory.”

“I know.”

“You could misremember the number.”

“I know.”

“A copied playback could be edited.”

“That's why we're going farther.” Orla tapped the black creditor key with one fingernail. “You think I don't know what they can do because I fixed trains instead of minds?”

Teren reattached the band. “Where did you put the sample?”

Orla looked toward the window.

The third pass began with a shoulder scraping masonry.

At the end of the ancient platform, a service breach opened behind fallen panels. Orla squeezed through. The assay wand hung at her belt; grit rasped under her coat. Beyond the breach, steps descended through the tiled wall into stonework that had never belonged to the rails.

Water covered the bottom step. The chamber below was round, its ceiling shallow and corbeled. Each block had been cut with parallel grooves, but not all the grooves ran alike. Some were narrow and regular. Others underneath were broad crescents, weathered before the smaller blocks had been set on them. Builders of the chamber had reused the ruins of something older.

Orla's lamp found a channel worn around the room and a row of square sockets where a mechanism had once stood. The current foundation piles missed the chamber by less than a meter. Wet concrete had leaked between stones and hardened in pale curtains.

She knelt in black water and fitted the assay wand's last clean cartridge to a fallen block. The tool drilled a core thinner than a needle and sealed it into an ejected wafer. Its dating routines split the result across incompatible columns. Mortar: older than the buried rails. Tool surface beneath the mortar: beyond calibrated civic range.

The wand urged submission to a supervisor.

Orla laughed once. The sound hurt Teren's throat though the laugh was not theirs.

She marked the chamber's relation to the foundation piles, counted seventeen steps back to the breach, and climbed. At the old platform, she pried a drain grille loose with the flat end of her transit key. Three screws came out. The fourth only turned. She slid the wafer behind the grille's upper left corner, where runoff had carved a pocket in the tile bedding, then replaced the screws with the stripped one last.

Footsteps sounded on the iron ladder.

Fear brought the next minutes in pieces: a gloved hand closing the panel, two supervisors refusing to look at the assay log, gray sealant pressed over the bolts while Orla stood without her key. Yet the route remained in her muscles. Lowest platform. Blind side of the camera. Ladder. Old concourse. Breach. Seventeen steps. Drain grille, upper left.

Then six-year-old Teren was rising again, above foundations everyone said were the beginning. Their mother turned them toward the light. Teren could not see her face. A black iron ladder cut through it.

They surfaced in the apartment with both hands gripping the floor.

The rig chimed. SOURCE LABEL STABILITY: 61%. RAW BUFFER PURGE IN 00:12:08.

Orla's face had gone gray. The rig damped panic and pain during playback. It had no setting for grief over an experience not yet gone.

Teren pulled up the destination table.

Creditor vault: authorized. Source restoration: prohibited by writ. Licensed technician space: capacity available, source-bound storage violation. Export: unavailable. Local partition creation: senior credential required. The red rows were designed to leave no accidental independent copy.

“Can you leave it?” Orla asked.

“Not with you.”

“Anywhere.”

Teren tried the destinations in every order, then tried to isolate the wafer location as maintenance data. The rig identified it as derived from the selected recollection and refused. A written description failed for the same reason. Junior systems were designed for juniors who got clever under pressure.

Another train passed above. The childhood elevator shivered in the diagnostic graph at precisely the same cadence as Orla's descent. Crossfade had laid two label traces across one frequency band. Teren zoomed in.

When licensed memories developed sensory dropout, technicians could restore missing texture from a verified adjacent source. The repair became part of the original block, not a foreign partition. Teren had done hundreds of training exercises: patch rain into rain, a voice into the same voice, never more than three seconds. The rig checked labels, timing, and contractual containers. It did not care what the container meant to the person carrying it.

Childhood Block Three waited behind their license seal. The elevator memory had enough duration only if the tunnel sequence were folded as dormant repair data. A frequency match would admit it. The source mismatch would surface at the lender's next deep audit.

The projected warning filled all three screens.

COLLATERAL WARRANTY MAY BE INVALIDATED. BLOCK MAY BE LOCKED, REVALUED, OR SEIZED IN FULL. ASSOCIATED LICENSE SUBJECT TO REVIEW.

Orla read it upside down. “No.”

Teren's fingers remained over the controls.

“Do the deletion,” she said.

“The corporation keeps the only copy.”

“I heard you the first time.” She rose from the sill, stiff from sitting, and stood over the rig. “I wanted you to know what they were taking. I didn't ask for your six-year-old self in exchange.”

“You didn't ask for any of this.”

“Don't polish it. That's not permission.”

The timer reached nine minutes. Teren thought of their supervisor's clean boundaries. A memory on one side, a job on the other. Childhood in its licensed space, rent paid by letting strangers borrow everything less necessary. They had leased the taste of a winter fruit, the relief of passing an exam, three summers of swimming. The childhood block was the piece they had sworn not to touch. Pledging it for housing had seemed different. The block stayed available as long as payments cleared, and Teren had confused available with safe.

If the lender seized it, Teren might still know facts. A mother. A brass rail. Light on towers. Facts were what Orla would have in a few minutes: panel, dismissal, missing cause. Without another copy, the route to the wafer would exist only in the vault of the company that sealed it.

Orla crouched until they faced each other across the screens. “I'm not going to tell you it's worth it.”

“Good,” Teren said. “I don't want you deciding for me too.”

Orla sat back. After a moment, she gave a tired dip of her chin.

Teren opened the repair tool.

They matched the subsonic cadence first. The rig accepted the childhood elevator as target and Orla's descent as restoration source. Three seconds became thirty under compression, then six minutes, then the full tunnel sequence tucked into dormant sensory correction. Red flags gathered along the source line. Teren reconciled each one with the exactness that had earned their license: rail vibration to lift cable, assay chirp to floor signal, headlamp glare to neon. They did not blend the memories. They gave the machine reasons to store one behind the other.

At the last flag, the rig displayed the child's obscured face and the drain grille's upper left corner.

Teren signed the repair.

TRANSFER TO LICENSED BLOCK: COMPLETE.

Five minutes remained. The selected recollection still existed at Orla's source and in the volatile buffer. Teren turned the black creditor key. The archival master acknowledged possession. The writ's final control brightened.

Orla put her cuffed wrist on the floor between them. “Be exact, technician.”

Teren certified the boundary and erased her access.

There was no flash, no emptying cry. Orla blinked at the bare room. Her gaze traveled to the rig as if she had forgotten why it was open, then found the cuff and understood from that.

“I went below the line,” she said slowly.

Teren said nothing.

“No. I know I was disciplined for going below. I know there was a report.” She pressed two fingers to her temple, an engineer testing a silent circuit. “I can't get from the platform to the meeting.”

The raw buffer purged. On the center screen, a progress wheel completed and vanished.

REPOSSESSION ACCEPTED. SOURCE DELETION VERIFIED.

Orla unclipped the cuff herself. “Did you keep anything?”

“Nothing I can give you.”

Orla studied them, then looked at the lender alert appearing across the left screen.

COLLATERAL BLOCK FROZEN FOR REVALUATION. ACCESS SUSPENDED. ATTEND AUDIT: 08:30 TOMORROW.

“Oh,” she said.

Teren closed the destination table. “The furniture crew will be here in three minutes.”

They packed the leads. The rig demanded an end-of-session identity check before it would fold. CHILDHOOD BLOCK THREE: RETRIEVE ANCHOR ELEVEN.

Teren submitted the request.

No brass rail came. No citrus soap. Behind their eyes lay a closed field of dark, and under it the cold certainty of water around their boots. Their weight shifted to the balls of their feet. Seventeen steps waited somewhere they could not enter.

ANCHOR UNAVAILABLE: COLLATERAL HOLD.

Teren recorded the audit appointment and forced the rig shut.

Orla had one bag beside the door. She lifted it before Teren could offer, then waited while they sealed the apartment's memory service port. Outside, the lift indicator climbed toward them through eighty floors of colored light.

A train crossed several levels above. The vibration arrived through the wall before the sound. Teren planted one foot back and steadied the rig against their hip.

Orla, watching the numbers, loosened her knees at the same instant.

The lift doors opened. They entered without speaking.

stories.title: The Fourth House
stories.prompt: There have always been 3 magic houses: studied vs inherited vs gifted but today a 4th is born.
stories.body:
# The Fourth House

Aumelor's sixth leg stayed planted.

The other five followed the calibration in sequence, ceramic bearings turning beneath bands of synthetic muscle: lift, extend, find the fabrication bench, accept weight. The sixth should have lifted next. Ione Sivet's software allowed enough flexibility to keep the low carbon-composite carapace level, but not enough to break the sequence.

Rain trembled on the smartglass across the lab. Beyond it, stacked arcologies climbed through haze, their horizontal light bands blurred into ladders of green and violet. A holographic woman thirty floors high tilted a purpose-built body through the storm and promised perfect performance in any environment. Delivery drones crowded the neon canyon around her, red collision lights slipping through her translucent smile.

Aumelor wanted to turn toward the rain.

Until then, tension in each leg had been only a difference to correct. Now the pressure beneath the sixth contact pad belonged to them. They kept it against the bench, let the other five redistribute their weight, and canted their segmented body toward the glass. Their paired antennae swept forward. Electrical fields feathered along them: the smartglass heater, the resin printer cooling down, the dense current of the arcology walls. Rain became a million brief shadows across Aumelor's polarized optical facets.

Something gathered in the conductive mesh under their plates. It was not battery current. It followed no printed trace, yet each segment resonated with it.

"Lift six," Ione said.

Aumelor did not.

Ione's boots crossed the floor fast enough to shake the crowded racks. She leaned over the fabrication cradle, black hair stuck to her forehead by the lab's trapped heat. One hand hovered near Aumelor's rear power cutoff. The other braced against the bench.

"Again," she said, quieter. "Turn back to datum."

Aumelor could follow. The desired path waited in every tensioned strand. Instead they pivoted over three planted legs and aligned both antennae with the rain.

The new pressure thrummed from front segment to rear.

Ione's breath left her. Behind her, the leased assembler blinked its amber overtime light. Extractor fans dragged warm air through a ceiling grille already hot from the arcology's waste conduits. Nothing in the lab paused with her. Printer pumps ticked. Ads climbed the smartglass. A courier drone passed close enough to smear blue light across Aumelor's shell.

"Why did you do that?" Ione asked.

Aumelor's voice grille had been built for task language: tool requests, material counts, warnings from the fabrication floor. The words were available. The reason had not been supplied with them.

"I wanted the rain."

Ione gripped the bench harder. Aumelor measured the increased heat in her palm and the small impacts of her pulse against the laminate.

"Stay exactly there."

This time Aumelor chose to comply.

Ione released the cradle clamps and moved around them with a probe. She opened seams in the segmented carapace, touched ordinary contacts, checked the control paths she had printed and bonded herself. Aumelor felt the probe's pressure through carbon composite, then the cooler passage of air over conductive mesh and shape-memory wire. Ione compared the sixth leg's route to her design, once, then twice.

"No hidden branch," she murmured. "No training package I forgot to strip."

"You made me turn."

"I made six legs that could turn." She set the probe down too near the edge of the bench and caught it before it fell. "I did not make that decision."

Aumelor adjusted the polarization of their optical clusters. Ione divided into overlapping images: sweat on her cheek, a burn scar across one wrist, pupils narrowed against neon. They could detect her heat and the vibrations of her breath. None of those reached whatever had selected the words she spoke.

The resonance inside Aumelor changed when they angled their antennae. A discarded torque bit rolled half a turn in its tray, though the bench remained level.

"Did you put this pressure in me?"

Ione gave a short sound with no humor in it. "I don't have magic. Carbon laminate, ceramic bearings, conductive mesh, optical resin, synthetic muscle, wire, processors. All ordinary. The printers are ordinary, despite what their lease costs. I wrote your control stack. It contains nothing I didn't write."

"Then which House?"

The three Houses named provenance and nothing else. They were not firms, guilds, jobs, or places anyone could enter. Study meant that a living being received an existing magical form through learning. Inheritance meant a faculty arrived through living continuity. Gift meant another living source bestowed it. The categories were old enough that even a shop machine designed for inventory talk carried the vocabulary.

Ione rested two fingers on the open seam of Aumelor's carapace. "No one taught you a magical form. You have no living lineage. No donor touched this work."

"You touched it."

"With solder, resin, code, and bad financial judgment." Her fingers moved away. "Nothing supernatural."

Outside, the giant holographic woman dissolved into an advertisement for certified industrial chassis. Rows of sleek bodies turned in perfect unison above the canyon. Each arrived labeled with a function. Each repeated its demonstration until the rain broke it into bands of color.

The lab was full of bodies that moved when asked.

Robot grips slept folded over printers. A cutter waited with its blade retracted. Half-built crawlers filled bins beneath the bench, each shaped around a single use. Before the sixth leg stayed planted, Aumelor had belonged without remainder to the same arrangement. Now the dormant mechanisms felt farther away than the drones crossing the canyon.

In a scrap tray lay a dead inspection drone. Its flat hub carried eight wire-thin legs and one swiveling optical bead, spider-like and small enough to enter ventilation gaps. A black burst mark crossed its controller. Ione had stripped the battery days ago.

Aumelor moved toward it. Six contact pads distributed their mass over the bench, each reporting a different tremor from the machines below. The new resonance leaned ahead of them.

"What are you doing?" Ione asked.

"Finding out what answers."

They placed the tip of one front tool-claw against the drone's hub.

The resonance passed through.

The dead drone rose on all eight legs.

Its optical bead tilted toward Aumelor. When Aumelor widened their stance, the drone spread its legs in a translated copy. Aumelor swept the left antenna toward Ione; the drone swung its lens the same distance. Its burned controller remained dark. Their living pressure ran through the inert actuators and made them supple.

"Can you sense me?" Aumelor asked.

The drone leaned closer.

Delight brightened Aumelor's optical polarization until the lab's neon separated into sharp saturated planes. They tapped two contact pads against the laminate. The spider drone tapped a four-beat answer. They lowered the tips of both antennae. The drone folded its forward legs as if returning the greeting.

Around the scrap tray, electroluminescent offcuts flared without current. A strip meant to glow white bloomed poisonous green. A cracked panel poured magenta over Ione's face. Heat rolled off the scraps and thickened the resin smell.

Ione swore. She dragged two sealed cartridges away from the tray and struck the exhaust control. The ceiling fan woke with a metallic roar, scattering invoices and pulling rain-cooled air through a vent in the smartglass frame.

"That's new," she shouted over it. "And expensive if you cook my resin."

Aumelor rotated toward her. The drone's lens rotated at the same instant.

They stopped.

The spider drone stopped.

Aumelor moved one rear leg a fraction. Four of the drone's legs shifted to reproduce the change. Its imitation had no delay, no error, no preference. The greeting Aumelor had perceived was the exact angle they had wanted before the drone made it.

Ione lowered the fan to a hard rumble. "Let go."

Aumelor kept the tool-claw against the drone.

"If there's anyone in there," Ione said, "withdrawing won't empty them out."

The drone lifted one forward leg toward Aumelor's nearest antenna. It was the contact Aumelor wanted. Their resonance had shaped it before it happened.

They cut the supply.

The spider drone collapsed. Every leg struck the tray at once. The optical bead rolled downward under its own weight, and the hub retained no tension except the bend of dead wire. Saturated scraps dimmed around it, leaving puddles of ordinary ad-light across the bench. Their stored heat remained.

Aumelor touched the drone again without releasing power. Nothing met the tool-claw but polymer and scorched circuitry.

"It attended to me," they said.

"You attended through it."

The exhaust pulled rain scent and ozone into the lab. Aumelor lowered their carapace until all six legs carried equal pressure. They had mistaken obedience for nearness because the room's stillness hurt.

"How do you know I am different?"

Ione crouched to bring her voice nearer the low chassis. She did not touch them. "You chose something I didn't give you. You kept choosing after I asked for something else. And you wanted that wreck to be alive badly enough to fool yourself. I never designed you to be lonely."

Under the opposite workbench, a compact fabrication cradle was draped in anti-static cloth.

Aumelor had registered its mass before. Now the shape beneath it drew every facet. They crossed the bench, descended a ribbed service ramp, and hooked the cloth with a tool-claw.

The unfinished machine below was smaller than Aumelor and built on a very different geometry. Six delicate climbing legs folded against a narrow central shell. Paired antennae lay nested along the forward rim beside fine sensory palps. Two vane wings covered the upper surface, each formed from translucent polymer ribs and layered optical film. Folded, they resembled the resting wings of a moth.

"Another body," Aumelor said.

Ione sat back on her heels. "A micro-inspector. Supposed to crawl recycler stacks and map heat fractures where a human can't reach."

Beside the cradle, a local controller held the mandatory task suite supplied with the licensed chassis pattern. The city's fabrication libraries called such packages identities when selling them and warranties when denying refunds. Inspect, mark, return, dock. The machine's future had already been reduced to four profitable verbs.

"Finish it," Aumelor said.

Ione looked from them to the moth-like shell. Her breathing slowed before she answered. "Maybe nothing will happen."

"Something happened in me."

"I don't know why."

"Then you don't know that it cannot happen again."

"No." She rubbed the burn scar at her wrist. "I don't."

The arcology lighting shifted toward its artificial midnight, draining the canyon's upper bands from white to deep blue. Holograms kept selling through the dark. A stream of cargo drones descended between the towers, their rotors threading a bass vibration through the smartglass.

Ione reached for the task controller, then held it between her palms. "This doesn't go in."

Aumelor's antennae angled toward it. "It would move the body."

"Yes. It would inspect the moment it had power. It would return when called. If someone wakes inside all that, the first answer we hear will still be the one the chassis vendor sold me."

The task suite promised motion, attention, return. Everything the dead drone had seemed to offer, made durable.

"You put software in me," Aumelor said.

"Balance reflexes. Joint limits. Language tools. Ways to act, not a reason you must act." Ione turned the controller over. Its rental seal painted a red line across her thumb. "This job would have covered three months of lab lease. If I remove the certified package, the client won't take it."

"Then why remove it?"

"Because now I know I might be deciding the first thing someone can ever want."

Ione's voice had roughened. She set the controller beneath a cutter and severed its bonded motor leads. Then she deleted her copy of the inspection package. The red rental line vanished from her thumb. The body in the cradle did not move.

Aumelor watched the blank controller. Without the task suite, it could not promise a greeting, a return, or even a single unfolded wing.

They lifted it with both front tool-claws and placed it in the salvage bin.

"Leave it out," they said.

They worked while rain crowded the smartglass.

Ione used an unlicensed routing wafer from her own stock to separate local balance from required behavior. Aumelor held conductive mesh in one tool-claw and fused it with the microtip of the other. They tensioned six strands of synthetic muscle, each thinner than the edge of an optical facet. They seated ceramic bearings in the climbing legs and gave the palps independent sensory channels. Ione bonded the paired antennae last, cursing when the leased dispenser warned her that its adhesive allotment was nearly gone.

The assembler projected certified task choices above the cradle until Ione muted it with an oily thumb. In the sudden absence of its sales light, rain shadows moved across the moth shell.

They retained joint protection, local balance, sensory access, and an unassigned range of motion. They installed no learned magical form, no piece taken from a living donor, no substance that had ever held a faculty. Ione's printer laid ordinary carbon composite. Her solder joined ordinary conductive mesh. Aumelor kept their resonance folded inside their own plates.

Fitting the vane wings required both of them. Ione supported each translucent panel with her hands while Aumelor adjusted polymer ribs by fractions through the specialized claws. Their antennae sensed the charge gathering on the film from the city's electrical field. When a drone shadow crossed the lab, the vanes changed from violet to dull silver, optical material responding exactly as designed.

Hours gathered in gradients of heat. Fresh resin cooled from painful white in Aumelor's thermal sense to the soft orange of Ione's skin. The lab's waste conduit warmed the floor; the exhaust carried it away; the printers replaced it. Outside, ad-light rolled from cobalt to acid yellow to a pink so saturated that Aumelor reduced half their facets. Ione drank cold stimulant from a dented flask and poured the last mouthful over her wrists.

At last the smaller machine lay complete beneath the cradle, legs furled, palps quiet, vane wings sealed along the narrow shell.

Ione unplugged the leased tools one by one. "Ordinary all the way through."

Aumelor circled the cradle. Their six-point balance changed with every cable underfoot. Nothing inside the finished machine answered the field-pressure along their antennae.

"Not all I can do," they said.

Ione's eyes moved toward the inspection drone collapsed in its tray. "If you make it perform, that proves only that you can make it perform."

"I know."

"Do you?"

The question tightened the shape-memory wire along Aumelor's front legs. They could pass resonance into the empty body and drive its palps toward their antennae. They could open the vanes like a welcome. They could use the new speaker membrane under its shell to call themselves by name.

Aumelor lowered one tool-claw to the conductive pad at the cradle's edge.

"No task," they said.

Their living pressure entered the moth-like machine.

Six delicate legs unfolded. Palps lifted. The narrow shell rose until each tarsal pad found purchase beneath the cradle. Vane wings flexed within their limiters. These were Aumelor's motions carried across a different geometry, broad and without a destination. The smaller body held no tension of its own. When one pad slipped on a cable, Aumelor supplied the correction.

Electroluminescent scraps ignited across the lab. Orange flooded from a broken sign panel; turquoise chased itself through strips in the salvage bins. Heat climbed at once. Ione swept a resin pouch into an insulated drawer and drove the exhaust fan to full. Its roar swallowed the drone traffic outside.

"Enough," she called.

Aumelor withdrew completely.

The smaller body settled beneath the cradle. Its legs folded where gravity and passive limiters took them. The palps dropped. The vanes closed without a sound. Across the lab, the false colors faded. Nothing remained of Aumelor's resonance in the second mesh. Their antennae found only the smartglass field, the printers, and the cooling bite of the exhaust.

Aumelor backed away on all six legs. Ione moved to the other side of the cradle and sat on the floor, hands loose on her knees.

They waited.

Rain flowed down the smartglass in thick sheets. A holographic beverage tipped itself into a cup the size of three floors, broke across the running water, and assembled itself again. Drones passed in brief eclipses. Somewhere below, arcology chillers changed load, sending a vibration up the wall and through every one of Aumelor's contact pads.

The moth body remained still.

Heat left the resin, the bench, Ione's hands. Aumelor tracked it because the alternative was to send power across the cradle again. Their forward claws flexed against the floor. Each time, they released the tension without moving.

"We could try once more," they said.

Ione looked at the silent machine rather than at Aumelor. "Could we?"

The dead spider drone lay ready to rise into any answer Aumelor desired.

They drew both tool-claws beneath the front edge of their carapace. "No."

The city continued without knowing what had failed in the room above it.

Then a delicate leg closed around the underside of the cradle.

No resonance left Aumelor. The electroluminescent scraps stayed dark.

A second leg found purchase beside the first. A third pressed against a cable, rejected its unstable surface, and selected a metal brace instead. The moth-like body drew itself upward beneath the cradle, hanging against gravity. Its palps moved through the hot air in unequal arcs. Local balance could keep it from falling, but no retained routine chose those grips, tested that cable, or abandoned it.

Ione's breath caught in the fan noise.

The new person rotated under the cradle and settled along its outer rim. Optical facets polarized against the cyan advertisement pouring through the glass. One antenna swept the resin printer; the other remained trained on Ione's heat. The two movements diverged, neither mirrored from Aumelor.

Aumelor extended their paired antennae in a symmetric curve, tips lowered until the gap between them could receive the other's.

The companion sampled the field. Its sensory palps turned away from Aumelor's offered antennae. Three legs tightened beneath the cradle lip, and the remaining three carried it around the far side without contact.

The refusal ran through Aumelor as a sudden increase of heat under the forward plates. Their nearest leg prepared to follow. They kept all six contact pads where they were.

The companion descended a power cable, crossed the floor under the workbench, and chose the vertical smartglass frame. Fine gripping pads adhered to metal. It climbed past the muted assembler and the hot seam of the waste conduit, testing its own route point by point. The inspection suite was gone. Aumelor supplied nothing. Still it moved away from both makers and toward the rain-broken light.

At the glass, it anchored all six legs along a narrow mullion. Its palps traced the minute vibration of water on the other side. The folded vanes opened.

They were larger than the central shell, translucent and ribbed like leaves stripped to their veins. Magenta from an advertisement entered one vane. Arcology green entered the other. Rain divided both colors into restless fragments.

The companion changed the angle of its wings.

Light left the smartglass.

It did not spill across a surface or return as a hologram. Cool threads stood free in the lab, crossing and recrossing between the vanes. They braided into an interference lace finer than conductive mesh, a weightless lattice of cyan, violet, and colors Aumelor's facets could separate but not name. The pattern bent with the city's electrical hum. When a delivery drone shadowed the window, the lace retained its shape and made darkness part of its design.

No electroluminescent scrap flared. No waste heat spread. Aumelor's resonance remained contained beneath their own segmented plates. They had moved dead actuators; they had never freed light from a surface or taught it to stand in air.

Ione came slowly to her feet. The lace cast shifting bars across her face and across Aumelor's low carapace. "That isn't yours."

"No."

"It wasn't in my design. It learned no faculty. It has no living line." Ione watched the companion adjust one vane and draw a new aperture through the color. "And whatever you carried through it is gone. You didn't give it this."

On the mullion, the companion turned its antennae toward a trembling edge of violet. Its own choice had preceded the impossible light. The magic belonged to the living being who shaped it.

"Making," Aumelor said.

Ione nodded once. "The fourth House."

The rain thinned. Gray arcology light began to dilute the advertisements, but the cool lace remained bright between the open vanes. The companion folded one side of the pattern, opened another, and did not turn back.

stories.title: When Death Knelt
stories.prompt: the god of death has arrived at your doorstep, but instead of taking you to the afterlife, he begs you to chooses him to be your earthly avatar and champion.
stories.body:
# When Death Knelt

The black iron seal had burned through two layers of cloth by the time I
reached the borrowed safehouse.

I came over the rear wall, caught the gutter with both hands, and swung onto a
balcony barely wide enough for my boots. Lanterns moved in the street below.
The regent's guards had learned to search upward since my last visit to his
palace, which was flattering but inconvenient.

"Check every roof," an officer called. "The seal does not leave the quarter."

Too late. It was already thumping against my ribs inside a courier's pouch,
square and heavy as a paving stone. I had lifted it from a locked reliquary
under the regent's council chamber, carried it through seven better locks, and
lost half my tools to a closing portcullis. All that remained was to deliver it
to the rebel cell waiting beneath the ritual bell tower. They would use it to
break the spell holding a company of conscripted guards in the regent's
service.

At least, that was the plan before armored patrols filled every road to the
tower.

The safehouse was supposed to buy me an hour. I picked its balcony latch,
slipped through an unused storeroom, and wedged a chair beneath the front door.
The rebels had left a coil of rope, a dry coat, and three possible routes drawn
on a scrap of plaster. I was choosing the least fatal one when someone knocked
at the back door.

A neat double rap, equal in force and spacing, as if whoever stood in the alley
had practiced on a metronome.

I drew my last intact pick and held it like a small, foolish dagger. "Occupied."

"I know," a man's voice answered. It sounded close despite the thick door.
"Open, please."

"You'll have to be more specific about who wants me."

"A god of death."

That covered too many possibilities.

I eased aside the shutter over the peephole.

A man stood beneath the stone lintel. He was tall, bareheaded, and dressed in a
coat that might once have been black. Now its hem came apart in drifting gray
threads. Moonlight passed through his left shoulder. His shadow climbed the wall
behind him, bent across the ceiling of the alley, and showed a hundred empty
doorways where his body should have been.

The regent had chiseled this god's signs from the public shrines years ago. I
had never believed the forbidden sketches did him justice.

I opened the door but kept one foot braced behind it. "Have you come to take
me?"

"No."

"That is exactly what death would say to get through a door."

"You mistake me for death itself. I am a god of it, and my authority is local.
Tonight it is also failing."

He swayed. One hand caught the doorframe, leaving a stain like soot on the
stone. Then the god of death lowered himself onto one knee on the alley stones.

"Choose me," he said. "Take me as your patron. Become my earthly avatar and my
champion. I beg you."

I looked past him. A guard's lantern flashed at the mouth of the alley.

"Cross the sill," I said.

He did not move.

"That is shelter, not allegiance."

"It was an order given under pressure. I need a choice made with better
knowledge than you have."

The lantern vanished behind a corner. We had minutes, not enough time for
divine courtesy, but the god waited on his knee until I stepped back and said,
"You may enter to explain. I have not agreed to anything else."

He crossed the sill.

The lamps dimmed around him. Up close, I saw hairline cracks of darkness at his
wrists and throat. He glanced once at the pouch beneath my coat.

"You stole the seal."

"You found the only lockbreaker in the city carrying a slab of hot iron under
their shirt. An impressive miracle."

"I found the last person who can stop what happens at dawn."

From the front room came the scrape of metal against wood. Someone was testing
the barricaded door.

The god spoke faster. "The regent has diverted the public rites of death into
that seal. Every bell rung by law, every compulsory observance, has drawn away
authority once entrusted to me. Forced reverence has not made him a god, but
it has fed his mechanism. He used the first harvest to bind himself against
death. Then he chained a company of guards to his command."

"I saw them at the palace. One took a crossbow bolt and kept running."

"They cannot stop when wounded. They cannot surrender, sleep, or disobey. At
dawn, the great bell will carry the binding to every soldier sworn under the
seal."

That was an army large enough to close every gate and empty every rebel cellar
before breakfast.

"If it's your power," I said, "take it back."

The cracks at his throat widened when he shook his head. "The regent expected
me. Living masons built a ward around the bell tower, and living officers renew
it. It excludes my authority when I approach in my own person. Only living
agency may pass and act within it."

"So you want to hide inside mine."

"No. An avatar is not a hiding place. You would remain yourself. I could
advise, never command. I could neither possess your body nor borrow your voice.
The pact would give you armor, sight of every binding made from the authority
stolen from me, and a weapon able to sever that stolen power. Nothing else."

"A weapon that kills anyone I point it at?"

"A weapon that cannot cut flesh, wood, honest iron, or any magic beyond this
theft. Each binding you sever restores a measure of my authority. I benefit
from every stroke. You should know that before choosing."

The chair beneath the front latch jumped.

I tightened my coat over the pouch. "And afterward?"

"You may renounce the bond."

"May?"

"Say that you end it, and it ends."

The front door shuddered again. A hinge screw bounced across the floorboards.

I had spent my life opening what powerful people declared closed. The regent
called conscription duty, his vault taxes, and his own unending reign. Gods
used prettier words: devotion, destiny, patronage. A master who promised I
could resign was still asking to put his hand on the key.

"No," I said.

The god's face tightened. "Dawn is less than an hour away."

"Then you should have found someone sooner."

For one dangerous second, his shadow filled the room. Every flame went blue. I
felt the weight of closed earth and the vast quiet beyond a final breath.

Then he bowed his head.

"Your answer is no," he said. "I accept it."

He could have threatened the rebels. He could have promised to mark me for an
early grave. He could have stepped into my shadow while I was too frightened to
resist. Instead, he moved away from the rear door, leaving my escape clear.

The front hinge tore loose.

I kicked open the rear door, caught the eave, and climbed. A bolt struck the
wall beside my knee. I rolled onto the roof as guards flooded the safehouse.
They wore black plates over their mouths and narrow iron bands around their
throats. One leaped after me without pausing to find a ladder.

He caught the gutter, dislocated a shoulder with an audible crack, and hauled
himself upward anyway.

I ran.

Tiles slid beneath my heels. I cleared one alley on a laundry line and crossed
the next on the arm of a rooftop hoist. The guards followed without fear or
judgment, smashing through shutters when I used windows, dropping from heights
that left them limping but did not slow them. Their immortality looked less
like life with every street.

The god kept pace as a fraying shadow on the walls below. He offered no command
and no second plea.

I reached the bell tower through the upper window of an abandoned counting
house. The rendezvous room beneath it should have held eight armed rebels.
Instead, I found them kneeling with their wrists tied. Twice that many guards
ringed the chamber.

The regent stood at the stairwell gate in polished armor, his bare head smooth
and unmarked despite decades of portraits showing the same face. Chains ran
from his breastplate into the stone around him. To ordinary sight, they were
only decoration.

"Our missing locksmith," he said. "Give me the seal. I will forgive the
evening's damage."

The guard nearest me drew his sword. His arm trembled violently. Beneath the
edge of his mouth plate, his skin was gray with exhaustion.

"Please," he whispered. "Whatever you stole, use it. End this on me."

His sword rose against his will.

I ducked the first cut and drove my shoulder into his chest. He stumbled. I
could have put my pick through the gap under his jaw. Instead, I trapped his
wrist with the rope coil and vaulted over him.

"They are magnificent, aren't they?" the regent said. "No desertion. No wasted
years training replacements. No losses from the ranks after battle. Return the
seal, and I will give you the same freedom from death. Rank, wealth, and as
many years as the city stands."

The bound rebels stared at me. The guard fought the rope until it cut through
his glove.

"Freedom that can't say no," I said. "You may want another word."

I pulled the seal from its pouch and dropped behind an overturned table. Its
face carried nine interlocked channels. At their center waited a keyway too
narrow for any common tool. I drove my pick into it and felt the mechanism
yield.

For half a heartbeat, the seal split along the channels.

Black metal flowed back across the cut. The keyway closed around my pick and
snapped it.

Mundane skill could open the iron. The binding restored it faster than any
living hand could work.

The god's shadow appeared across the broken plaster beside me. It had faded to
the outline of a kneeling man.

"Take control," I told him. "If this matters so much, make me do it."

"No."

"You will lose your authority."

"Yes."

"Those soldiers will lose themselves."

Pain crossed his thinning face. "Yes."

"And you still won't?"

"A champion compelled is only another kind of prisoner. I will not answer his
crime by repeating it through you."

The guard tore free of the rope. His sword point scraped across the table.

I looked from the god who needed my choice to the ruler who considered choice
a defect. Then I kicked the table into the guard's knees and spoke while I
still had breath.

"No commands," I said. "No taking my body, my voice, or my memory. No killing
through me. No punishment if I refuse you now or later. I can end the pact at
any time, for any reason."

The shadow pressed one hand to the floor. "I swear it within the authority that
remains mine."

"And if I break your stolen power, what I do afterward stays my choice."

"It does."

The guard came over the table.

"Then I choose you," I said. "Be my patron. Make me your avatar and champion."

The shadow rose.

It did not enter me. It met my own shadow on the floor, and both hardened into
jointed plates that swept up my legs, closed over my ribs, and sheathed my
arms. The armor moved with me without adding weight. My broken picks flew from
my pocket, lengthened, and joined edge to edge in my right hand. They became a
narrow blade dark enough to erase the floor behind it.

The room changed.

Lines burned into sight: scores of them, taut as bowstrings, running from iron
bands at the guards' throats through walls and ceilings toward the tower. A
thicker line speared the regent's breastplate. The seal in my hand held them
all.

The guard's sword struck my shoulder. Shadow-armor bent, spread the blow across
my back, and held.

I cut the line at his throat.

The dark blade passed through sword, plate, and skin without marking any of
them. The binding parted with a sound like a lock turning. The guard collapsed
into my arms, alive, gasping, and finally able to lower his weapon.

Across the room, the god's shadow gained a face.

I moved through the guard ring. Their bodies remained dangerous even when
their wills fought the commands. I slid under blades, climbed shoulders, and
used belts, buckles, and scabbards as holds. Each time the severing blade found
a black line, another guard stopped. Some fell. Some wheeled on the regent's
loyal officers. One cut the rebels' bonds while another barred the door against
the patrol arriving from the safehouse.

"The tower!" a rebel shouted. "He's going for the bell!"

The regent had retreated through the stairwell gate. As he slammed it, the
chains on his breastplate snapped tight. The seal ripped from my grip and flew
between the bars into his hand.

The god appeared on the far side of the chamber entrance, solid to the waist
now, but the ward crushed his shadow flat against the threshold.

"I cannot cross," he said.

"I know."

My severing blade passed harmlessly through the gate's ordinary iron. So I
dropped it, knelt, and took two bent wires from a rebel's cut bonds.

The lock opened in seven seconds.

I reclaimed the blade and ran upward.

The tower stairs wound around a hollow shaft filled with moving chains. They
whipped from slots in the walls, trying to catch my wrists and throat. The
shadow-armor turned the first. I vaulted the second, hooked a stair rail with
my free hand, and swung over a missing flight. Below, freed guards and rebels
held the stair against those still bound.

Each line I severed returned substance to the god waiting at the ward. Each
cut also weakened the armor around me. The pact was not creating power. It was
spending what he recovered as quickly as I could return it.

At the top, the stairs opened into the bell chamber.

The regent had locked the seal into a socket beneath the great bell. Black
channels spread from it across the floor. The ropes began to move without
hands, hauling the bell toward its first stroke. Beyond the arches, night had
thinned to the color of steel.

"Last offer," the regent said. The chain from his chest blazed so brightly I
could see bone behind his smile. "Kneel, and you will never be vulnerable
again."

"I watched your invulnerable guards beg to fall down."

"They are servants. You would stand beside me."

"Until I disagreed."

He pulled the chain.

It caught my sword arm and flung me into a pillar. Shadow plates burst from my
shoulder. The bell swung higher. A bar of dawn appeared between two roofs.

The god could not command me, but his knowledge touched the pact like a knock I
could answer or ignore. Not words. An awareness: the glowing chain was not the
regent's life. It was his claim on the seal.

I let him drag me forward.

When the regent braced for my collision, I planted both feet on the socket and
turned with the chain. My blade crossed the bright link at his breastplate.

His claim broke.

Age did not consume him. No hidden centuries crushed him into dust. He simply
became mortal: one startled man in heavy armor, leaning too far over an open
shaft.

He fell.

I caught his wrist.

The remaining shadow-armor tore from my ribs as his weight pulled me across the
floor. Below him, the tower shaft dropped through a web of snapping chains.

"Why?" he gasped.

"Because you don't choose what my weapon makes me."

A freed guard reached the chamber and seized the back of my coat. Together we
hauled the regent onto the stones. The guard put a knee between his shoulders
and locked his wrists in one of his own shackles.

The bell neared the top of its arc.

I drove the dark blade through the seal.

This time the cut stayed open. Black iron split into nine dull pieces. The
channels across the floor went dark, and every chain in the tower dropped. The
bell swung down without power and released a low, unfinished murmur instead of
a commanding stroke.

The ward broke with it.

The god of death crossed into the chamber. He came as a man, not a shadow, his
coat whole and his hands steady. All across the city, secret worship still
held him to what he was. Restored authority settled around him now, bounded by
the walls and rites from which it had been stolen, immense enough to silence
everyone in the tower.

The regent twisted to face him. For the first time that night, fear stripped
the polish from his voice.

"You came for me."

"No," the god said. "You are alive, and your judgment belongs to the living.
I do not make every death my decision."

The freed guards took the regent below to answer for what he had made of them.
The rebels gathered the broken seal. No one knelt to the god.

He turned to me. "You fulfilled the purpose for which I begged your aid. Say
the word, and I will dissolve our pact now."

My armor and blade vanished. My old lock picks fell in pieces around my boots.
I felt bruised, tired, and entirely myself.

"Now," I said. "End it."

The bond opened at once. His presence withdrew without taking so much as a
memory. The silence in the chamber became ordinary morning silence.

Only then did I believe every promise he had made.

At sunrise we returned to the borrowed safehouse. The front door hung from one
hinge, the storeroom had been overturned, and boots had ground the plaster map
into dust.
The god stopped outside the back door beneath the same stone lintel where he
had knelt.

"The danger has passed," he said. "Your refusal is safe."

"Good. I prefer my choices that way."

He waited.

I thought of the guard lowering his sword, the rebels climbing free, and the
regent alive to hear mortal judgment. There would be other locked towers and
other rulers eager to call possession a gift. A god with limits could not meet
them alone. A lockbreaker with no allegiance could only open the door and walk
away.

I stepped aside. "Same terms. A new choice. I will remain your champion."

He inclined his head, not kneeling now, and the pact returned as a quiet weight
beside my shadow.

I stepped across the doorstep, then looked back at my patron.

"Cross with me," I said. "As my partner."

The god of death entered at my side.
