stories.body:
# The Ninety-Year Barrier

You land on your back with a mouthful of leaves and the clipped end of a blackberry cane still clenched in your fist.

For one hopeful moment, the worst thing in the world is the pain between your shoulders.

Then a woman leans over you.

Her hair hangs in ropes the color of woodsmoke. Burrs cling to her sleeves. Her eyes are green around pupils so wide and black that they seem to be drinking you in. She looks at your muddy knees, your bleeding thumb, the cane in your hand, and finally your face with the terrible attention of a starving person watching bread rise in an oven.

“It took me ninety-three years to cast this barrier,” says the Witch of the Dark Forest. “It was strong enough to withstand a dragon. Would you kindly inform me how a village youngin managed to break it? Before you start screaming, I am not mad at you.”

You scream.

The witch waits. When you have spent your breath, she offers you a hand.

You scramble backward instead and strike something that is not quite a wall. Pale threads flare in empty air. There are dozens of them, one behind another, each following the same upright curve. Where your shoulder touches, the threads tremble and shed flecks of cold light.

To either side, the barrier stretches through the trees as a faint green shimmer. Directly behind you is a hole shaped almost exactly like a falling child. Its edges peel inward in thin, luminous layers.

Beyond the hole lies the sunny bramble bank where you were kneeling a moment ago. Your basket has overturned there. Blackberries freckle the grass. A short cane rises from the bank, tied to a split hazel peg, its leaves bright and innocent.

Home is less than a mile beyond it.

The witch crouches. You tuck your scratched hand under your other arm.

“If you are not mad,” you say, “why are you looking at me like that?”

“Like what?”

“Like the butcher looks at a pie.”

She considers this with worrying seriousness. “I have not spoken to another person in some time.”

“That does not answer me.”

“No.” Her gaze drops to the cane. “Hold very still.”

A slow thump passes overhead, too deep to be thunder. The leaves turn their pale undersides to the sky. You feel the next beat through the soil.

The witch’s hungry expression vanishes. What replaces it is worse: fear, quickly mastered.

She stands and looks up through the canopy. “We have less time than I hoped.”

You rise too. The peeling threads have reached the height of your head. Each ends at the same blackberry cane, then lashes loose like a snapped harp string. Farther along the barrier, black scars stripe the trunks. One oak bears four grooves deep enough to hide your arm. Stones below it have melted into smooth, dark puddles.

“Was that the dragon?” you ask.

“Its claws. The glass is from its breath.” The witch steps to the hole, but not through it. “It tests the barrier every few years. When you opened this seam, the release rang along every layer. It will have heard.”

“Close it, then.”

“An admirable proposal. How?”

You glance toward the village side. The opening is close enough to jump. You bend your knees.

The witch snaps her fingers. Roots hump beneath the leaf mould between you and the gap. They do not grab you. They rise into a waist-high tangle and stop.

“You said you weren’t mad!”

“I am not. I am urgently unwilling to let you flee with the only explanation.” She closes her eyes for half a breath. When she opens them, she sounds less like a witch from a warning tale and more like a tired adult trying not to frighten a bolting pony. “I will not hurt you. I will not eat you. I need the truth in the order it happened.”

“Let me out first.”

“If I open the damaged layers wider, they may run apart faster.”

“Then move the roots.”

She does. At once. The tangle sinks back into the ground, leaving only cracked leaves.

That small obedience settles you more than the promises did.

Another wingbeat rolls across the forest.

The witch points at the clipped cane in your hand. “Begin with that.”

“I cut it.”

“With what spell?”

“My knife.”

“Show me.”

You pull the little pruning blade from your pocket. Its wooden handle is sticky with berry juice. The witch studies it without touching.

“Iron?”

“Steel, I think.”

“Runes?”

“There’s a mark from where I dropped it on the hearthstone.”

“Blessed by anyone?”

“My gran said I could use it if I wiped it afterward.”

The witch’s lips tighten. “No secret ancestry? No pact made beneath a red moon? No habit of waking with objects floating over your bed?”

“No.”

“Good. Spectacular explanations waste time. Tell me the ordinary ones.”

So you tell her about the blackberries.

The best berries grow on the forest side of the shimmer: large as the top joint of your thumb, black even in their deepest beads, with a sweetness that stays after the seeds are gone. Everyone in the village knows better than to cross the witch’s boundary for them. Everyone also knows that a bramble does not care about a boundary if sunlight lies beyond it.

Three weeks ago, you found a runner long enough to bow across the shimmer.

“It crossed?” the witch interrupts.

“I pushed it through.”

“And the barrier did nothing?”

“It tickled.”

Her stare sharpens until you wonder if she might chew the answer out of the air between you.

You explain what you did. You bent the green runner low without snapping it. On the village side, you scraped a shallow hollow in the damp soil. You pinned the middle of the runner into it with a forked hazel peg, leaving the leafy tip in the sun. Then you covered the joint and watered it whenever you passed.

“Why?”

“To make another plant.”

“You buried a branch.”

“A cane. And not all of it.”

“For three weeks.”

“It takes time to root.”

She turns to the low bramble mass inside the forest. A long green arc reaches from a parent cane, through the torn place, to the pegged shoot outside. Or it used to. You hold the missing length.

The witch kneels beside the inner stump. A bead of clear sap swells at its cut. She does not touch it at first. Two fingers hover above the wound, trembling.

“This morning,” she says, “the buried joint had grown roots of its own.”

“Yes. I tugged it. Gently,” you add, because adults often accuse you of tugging things wrongly. “It held fast, so I cut between the old plant and the new one. That is how you separate them. Except the light flashed, and the air made a noise, and I fell.”

“What sort of noise?”

“Like a sheet tearing underwater.”

She looks from the inner cut to the outer plant. Her eyes track a path you cannot see. Slowly, hunger returns to her face.

You lift the pruning knife. “You promised.”

“I am thinking.”

“You look hungrier when you think.”

“Then pray I remain famished.” She rises and presses her palm against the intact barrier beside the hole.

Light kindles under her skin. It runs into the air in branching veins, every pulse driven by the beat at her wrist. One pale curtain becomes five, then twenty, then more than you can count. The nearest is smooth and bright. The farthest is dim, ambered with age.

“The first year,” she says, “I fixed the ward to the oldest roots along the forest’s edge. Oak, thorn, ash, bramble. Living anchors do not crack when the ground freezes or wash away in floods. They grow, and the boundary adjusts with them. Every year I laid another course over the first. Ninety-three circuits. Ninety-three layers sharing force.”

She moves her hand. The bright sheets flex together.

“When the dragon strikes one place, its weight does not remain there. The ward carries the blow around the whole forest and tightens. Fire feeds pressure into the circuit. Claws pull the weave closed. The greater the attack, the more of the barrier answers it.”

“But I did not attack it.”

The witch turns, and her expression makes you wish you had said something less interesting.

“No,” she whispers. “You gardened.”

She drops beside the tear again, sweeping dead leaves from the soil. Fine roots thread the dark earth. Some shine with the same cold light as the barrier.

“The ward knows its edge through living continuities,” she says. “Not because it thinks. It has no mind. I taught my magic a pattern and tied that pattern to what grew here. Your runner remained part of this bramble while you carried it across, so every layer counted the whole cane as inward. When it rooted beyond the boundary, the ward acquired an anchor on both sides without recognizing a break.”

You picture the buried bend, quietly making its white roots while you hauled water from the stream.

“Then I cut it.”

“You made two plants where the ward still expected one.” The witch pinches the cuff of her sleeve and pulls a single loose thread. The cloth gathers toward her fingers. “The older root held one side of the pattern. The new roots held the other. When you severed the living bridge, all ninety-three layers tried to keep both anchors inside. They slid sideways through the crossing point.”

“Like dropping a stitch?”

She looks at you.

“My gran knits.”

“Like dropping ninety-three stitches through the same hole,” the witch says. “A dragon could batter this wall for a century and never manage what you did with a peg, a cup of water, and patience.”

The wingbeat comes again, nearer. Something vast cries above the clouds. The sound is thin at first, then opens into a scraping roar that shakes berries from the canes.

The witch stares at you as if you are the only lit window in winter.

You step back. “Stop that.”

“Stop what?”

“Looking as if you want to crack my skull and lick the clever part.”

She recoils. For the first time, she seems startled by you rather than the reverse.

“I do not,” she says. “I have spent ninety-three years answering my own questions. You are the first person in all that time to show me a question I did not know existed.” Her glance darts to the torn ward. “I am hungry for the answer. Not for you.”

“You already have the answer.”

“I have the failure. An answer lets us repair it.”

“Us?”

Heat touches your cheek. High above, clouds redden from within.

“I need the hands that made the mistake,” she says. “They understand it better than mine.”

You think of every grown person who has taken a hoe from you after asking for help, then complained that you never learn. You think of your basket in the grass, the path home, and a dragon following the torn seam toward roofs that can burn.

“I have conditions,” you say.

The witch’s eyebrows rise.

“You do not trap me afterward. You do not punish the village. You do not pull up my new blackberry plant.”

“The plant caused this.”

“I caused this. The plant did exactly what plants do.”

The witch glances at the little shoot beyond the shimmer. “That distinction has just become painfully clear.”

“Promise.”

She lays her glowing hand flat against her own chest. “I promise to let you leave when the barrier holds. I will neither harm nor confine you, nor harm your village for your deed. Your blackberry plant will remain rooted unless keeping it there directly endangers others. If it must be moved, you will choose where.”

“And no eating.”

“And no eating.”

“All right.” You close the pruning knife. “What do we do?”

The witch almost smiles. It is not reassuring, but it is less hungry.

First, you crawl through the hole.

The edges brush your clothes with a cold fizz. On the village side, you kneel by the new plant and loosen the soil with your fingers. Its roots are fine and white, no longer than your smallest nail, but there are dozens. The witch remains just inside, one palm braced against the ward. Sweat darkens the ropes of hair at her temples.

“Do not pull it free,” you tell her.

“I heard your condition.”

“I am telling the roots.”

You press the soil firm and set the spilled berries aside. Then you take the severed cane back through the gap and lay it beside its parent.

“This one is dead now,” you say.

“Dying,” says the witch. “There is a little current left.”

“Not enough to grow roots before the dragon comes.”

“I can lend it what I have.”

“Can you make it grow anywhere?”

“No. I can urge these cells to do quickly what they are already trying to do. I will pay for the haste.”

You look at the gray strain around her mouth. “How much?”

“Less than the dragon will charge.”

That is not a proper answer, but the sky is turning orange.

You choose a young runner still attached to the inner thicket. Instead of bending it across the boundary, you guide it along the forest side, following the shimmer. At either end of the tear, you scrape two hollows. The witch asks before taking your knife. When you nod, she trims away leaves that would rot underground and nicks the underside of each joint, copying your instructions exactly.

You pin both joints down with hazel forks. Her fingers sink into the soil beside yours.

Warmth spreads through the earth.

The runner shivers. White root tips nose from its green skin and curl downward. The witch gasps as if each one has drawn a thread from her. Her cheeks hollow. The light in the barrier dims, then steadies.

“Enough,” you say.

“Not yet.”

“They have taken. Look.”

You tug the runner gently. Both pegged joints hold.

The witch lifts her hands. They shake. “Now the outside plant.”

She kneels across from it with the ragged opening between you. Rather than touching the shoot, she asks you to place two fingers against its stem. You feel sap moving inside, or imagine you do: a faint coolness rising from root to leaf.

“Tell me when it changes,” she says.

With one hand on the living runner beside the ward and the other near the outer plant, the witch draws her magic out of the misplaced anchor. Light unwinds from those new white roots hair by hair. The shoot droops.

“Stop.”

She stops.

You pour the last water from your flask around it. After a breath, the leaves lift again.

“It is itself now,” the witch says. “No part of my pattern remains in it.”

The loose layers still flap from the tear. She gathers them against the runner you pegged parallel to the boundary. The oldest strand comes first, dull gold and stiff with ninety-three winters. She bends it around the first rooted joint, carries it along the cane, and loops it around the second. One by one the newer strands follow.

They do not close into a seamless wall. They overlap.

“You are leaving a gap,” you say.

“A gate.” The witch points to the two rooted joints. “Two known ends, each inside. The path between them is visible. I can loosen the overlap without asking a living thing to be both within and without.”

“Can another runner cross somewhere else?”

Her face goes still.

“I will have to walk all the way around,” she says.

“Often.”

“Yes.” She speaks the word as if it tastes medicinal. “Often.”

A shadow covers the forest.

The witch is only halfway through the layers.

The dragon descends beyond the treetops, unseen except in pieces: a hooked wing black against the burning clouds, a tail passing over an opening in the canopy, the brief copper gleam of scales. Its wings drive hot wind through the gap. Branches bow. Your basket tumbles across the grass outside.

“Go,” says the witch.

“You promised not to trap me.”

“I am releasing you early.”

“And if it breaks before I get home?”

She looks toward the village.

You see the answer before she gives it.

You snatch up the next loose strand. It passes through your fingers like cold water, but you cannot make it loop.

“Tell me what to do.”

The witch grips your wrist, then releases it so quickly her fingers barely close. “May I?”

You hold your hand out again.

She lays two fingers over your pulse. Warmth runs along your arm, not power you can command, only a path for hers. Together you guide the layer around the first joint, along the rooted cane, and around the second. The motion is the same as laying a runner into a trench: bend, do not break; pin, do not crush; make sure the living part lies where it can hold.

The witch takes the next three while you settle the one beneath them. Then six. Then twelve. The barrier brightens layer by layer.

The dragon strikes.

Fire pours through the trees in a white-gold sheet. The smell of hot stone and bitter sap fills your throat. Where the flames meet the intact barrier, light races away in two directions around the forest. The ward curves inward, but it does not open.

At the gate, the unfinished layers whip toward the rooted cane.

“Hold the peg!” the witch shouts.

You throw your weight onto the first hazel fork. The earth jumps beneath your knees. Roots strain in the soil. The witch braces the second joint with both palms, feeding the last loose strands around it while dragon fire turns the world beyond the shimmer featureless and bright.

The runner bends.

It does not break.

The overlapping layers draw tight across the gate. Force streams along the new path, around the entire boundary, and returns diminished to the old scorch marks. Trunks groan. Leaves tear free and spin in green clouds. The witch cries out, whether in effort or pain you cannot tell.

Then the fire ceases.

The barrier springs back. Its ninety-three layers settle into one cool shimmer, except at the gate, where two pale edges overlap like folded cloth.

Above, the dragon beats its wings once, twice. A claw scrapes the ward somewhere to your left. The sound travels around the circuit and fades. The vast shadow climbs.

It does not strike again.

For a while you and the witch remain kneeling with your hands in the dirt.

“Did it hold?” you ask.

She laughs once, breathlessly. “Youngin, it held because you told it where the edge was.”

“You told it.”

“You noticed.”

The gate opens when she presses the two rooted joints in turn. The overlapping light draws aside, leaving a narrow, clean passage. No ripping noise. No loose threads.

The witch goes through first. That surprises you. She stands on the village side and waits, giving you the whole opening and making no move to hurry you into it.

You cross.

She retrieves your basket. Most of the berries are squashed or scattered, so she opens her cloak and fills it from the forest brambles. She does not cross the boundary to do it; the gate remains open at her shoulder. When the basket is mounded purple-black, she hands it over.

“Payment?” you ask.

“An apology.”

“For the roots?”

“For telling you not to scream while looking, apparently, like a butcher contemplating pastry.”

You accept the basket. “You still look a little like that.”

“I am trying to improve.”

Behind her, the controlled seam glows between two small hazel pegs. Beside your boot, the new blackberry plant lifts its watered leaves toward the afternoon light.

The witch studies it, then makes herself study the barrier instead.

“There are things I could teach you,” she says carefully. “About roots, boundaries, and how to discover what a spell believes without being caught inside it.”

“Believes?”

“A figure of speech. You are correct; precision matters.” She tries again. “How to discover what pattern a spell has been given.”

You wait.

The hungry attention gathers in her eyes, but this time she notices it. She looks away toward the trees.

“Only if you wish,” she says. “Only if the person who cares for you agrees. Lessons at the gate, which remains open. No bargains concealed in gifts. No ninety-three-year obligations.”

“And I can stop coming?”

“Whenever you choose.”

You consider the shining barrier, the scorched stones, and the runner holding fast in its two neat hollows. You consider the walk home and what your gran will say about the knife, the berries, the dragon, and the witch. The knife will be the difficult part.

“Ask me again when my gran is here,” you say.

The Witch of the Dark Forest inclines her head. “I will.”

You point two fingers at your own eyes, then at hers. “And practice your face first.”

She presses her lips together, attempting something mild. It is a dreadful smile, but no longer a ravenous one.

You pick up your basket and start home, leaving the new plant rooted where you put it and the witch at the gate, practicing how to look curious without looking hungry.

stories.title: Tea for the First Guest
stories.prompt: "you know I didn't think when I accidentally entered a 2000 year old wizards tower I would get fresh tea." Said the young man "well you don't exactly live to be 2000 by trying to kill the first guest you have in centuries and I'm also starving for conversation." Said the wizard pouring his own.
stories.body:
# Tea for the First Guest

The path disappeared six steps after the rain began.

One moment it lay under the young man's boots, a pale strip winding between black pines. The next, water sheeted down the slope and every hollow became a stream. Wind drove the rain sideways. He bent over the parcel beneath his coat, though the flour inside was already turning to paste, and tried to remember whether the path had passed the split boulder before or after the stand of silver-barked trees.

Lightning answered by showing him neither.

It showed him a tower.

For the length of the flash, a round wall stood on the ridge above him, broken at the crown and webbed with ivy. He had walked these woods since he was old enough to be trusted with a gathering basket. There was no tower on that ridge. There was hardly a ridge.

Thunder struck close enough to jar his teeth.

He scrambled toward shelter.

The climb took longer than it ought to have. Wet stones rolled under his heels. Branches caught his sleeves. Twice he saw the tower between the trees, and twice it seemed farther to his left than before. By the time his hands found cold masonry, he was shivering so hard he could not close his fingers properly.

The ruin looked less promising up close. Ivy covered everything but a narrow arch, and the door inside it had swollen crooked in its frame. No light showed through the cracks. He shoved once, twice, then struck it with his shoulder.

The door gave way without resistance.

He fell across a polished floor into warmth, lamplight, and the smell of steeping leaves.

Behind him, the door shut with a soft click.

For several heartbeats he stayed on his hands and knees, dripping onto a blue-and-gold carpet. The room surrounding him was round, high-ceilinged, and entirely intact. Shelves climbed the walls. A fire burned beneath a copper kettle. Hundreds of little glass panes enclosed a stairwell spiraling upward through green leaves and white flowers.

At a table laid for two, an old man in a faded red robe poured tea.

The young man rose too quickly and nearly slipped. He caught the back of a chair. The parcel under his coat sagged against his ribs.

The old man gestured toward the other cup. His hair and beard were white, but his hands were steady, his eyes dark and alert.

"You know, I didn't think when I accidentally entered a two-thousand-year-old wizard's tower I would get fresh tea," the young man said.

It was not the wisest thing he had ever said. Cold, fear, and the absurd neatness of the sugar bowl had joined forces against him.

The wizard lifted the kettle over his own cup. "Well, you don't exactly live to be two thousand by trying to kill the first guest you have in centuries, and I'm also starving for conversation."

He poured.

The young man looked at the door. It had vanished. Where it should have been stood a walnut cabinet full of jars.

"I would prefer," he said carefully, "that those be separate matters."

The wizard blinked. Then he laughed, a rusty sound that surprised him as much as it did his guest. "Quite right. Tea first. Murder never. Conversation if agreeable. Sit down before your knees decide for you."

They nearly had. The young man sat.

Steam carried a scent both green and smoky. He wrapped his hands around the cup but did not drink.

"Fresh," he said. "Truly?"

The wizard pointed upward.

Behind the glass, narrow beds followed the rising stair. Tea shrubs filled the lowest tier. Higher up grew herbs, beans, small fruit trees, and one determined vine hung with pale gourds. Drops of condensation ran down the inner panes. Little copper mirrors turned near the ceiling, directing lamplight into the leaves.

"Plucked this morning," the wizard said. "The second leaves from the new growth. I tried preserving the spring flavor for seventy-three years, but every spell left an aftertaste of copper. Some problems yield more readily to gardening."

The young man took a cautious sip. It was hot, bitter at first and then sweet in the back of his mouth. Nothing stung, burned, or transformed him.

His host leaned forward. "What year is it?"

"The year?"

"Whose face is stamped on the silver coin? Does the eastern road still flood? Are sleeves narrow or broad? Did they ever rebuild the bridge with six arches? What do people call that dance where everyone kicks at once? Is salt still taxed?"

The questions came so quickly that the young man held up a hand.

"Which one do you want answered?"

"All of them. Eventually." The wizard sat back with visible effort. "The year first."

The young man told him. The wizard repeated the number under his breath and stared into his cup.

"Then I have been here two thousand and eleven years," he said. "Approximately. The calendar has altered twice that I know of, and once in a manner no sensible person could defend."

"You said two thousand."

"Conversation suffers when one begins it with arithmetic."

The young man's shivering had eased. Hunger rushed in to replace it. His glance strayed to a loaf on the sideboard.

The wizard caught the look. "Forgive me."

He crossed to the sideboard, cut the loaf, and spread two slices with herb butter. He did not wave his hands and conjure a feast. He used a bread knife, frowned at the uneven pieces, and gave the thicker one to his guest.

"Starter is nearly three hundred years old," he said. "The flour is newer."

The young man looked down at the sodden parcel beneath his coat.

"Not that flour," the wizard added.

The bread was dense, warm near its center, and so good that caution lost an argument with his stomach. He ate half the slice in three bites.

"What brings you through the wood?" the wizard asked.

"An errand."

"For whom?"

"My family."

"Large?"

"Large enough."

"What work do they do? How far is your home? Are houses roofed in slate now? Do people still dry apples above the stove?"

The young man swallowed. "My mother will be waiting for the flour. My sister will say I stopped somewhere to avoid helping mend the roof. My father will go looking when it gets dark."

The wizard smiled as though each ordinary fact were a jewel set before him. "A roof. Excellent. Tile, thatch, slate, split wood?"

"Thatch. When can I leave?"

For the first time, the wizard looked toward the walnut cabinet.

Rain hammered somewhere beyond the walls, though the sound seemed impossibly distant. "When the storm passes. The slope is treacherous. I can show you a safe way down."

"And the door?"

"Where it has always been."

The cabinet remained a cabinet.

The wizard refilled the cups. "Tell me, are there still wizards attached to courts, or has that fashion ended?"

The young man answered because the tea was warm, because the bread was good, and because leaving in that rain would have been foolish even if he could find the door. He told the wizard what little he knew. There were wizards who served councils, wizards who kept shops, wizards who traveled and repaired small household workings. The wizard interrupted to ask what a council meant in this case, what shops charged for weather-charms, whether household wizards were permitted to marry, and why anyone would pay to warm a bath by magic when firewood existed.

Then he asked about wars.

The young man knew only the one his grandfather remembered. The wizard wanted troop numbers, banners, border changes, and the names of rulers. He could not provide them.

"Songs, then," the wizard said. "What are people singing?"

The young man recited the first verse of a tavern song about a boastful cooper. Before he reached the turn, the wizard cried out in delight.

"Still? They still sing that?"

"You know it?"

"A version. The cooper was a potter, and the goat was a magistrate."

"There isn't a goat."

"Then what knocks over the cart?"

"A magistrate."

The wizard laughed again, less rustily this time. He demanded the rest, then stopped the young man every few lines to compare words. Soon the song lay dissected between them like a machine taken apart by someone more interested in its history than in hearing it run.

The young man put down his cup.

"You asked what people sing," he said. "You haven't let me sing it."

The wizard's smile faded a little. "No. I suppose I haven't."

"And you asked about my family, but you don't know how many of us there are."

"Large enough, you said."

"Six."

The wizard glanced at the loaf, the tea, the green stair. "Six," he repeated, this time without a second question ready.

The room fell silent. Under the rain, the young man heard a faint ticking from the copper mirrors as they turned.

"You are cold," the wizard said at last. "And hungry. I have been a poor host."

"You've fed me."

"Bread is an apology for forgetting supper."

He moved quickly around the room, gathering onions, carrots, mushrooms, and a handful of herbs from the beds behind the glass. A little flame sprang between his fingers to light the stove, but after that he chopped and stirred like anyone else. His knife work was fast and exact. He asked no questions while he cooked.

The young man watched the place where the door had been.

"My father will start looking soon," he said.

"The storm will finish first."

"You can't know that."

"I can." The wizard touched two fingers to the wall. The rain's murmur sharpened, and for an instant a faint pattern of pale lines spread from his hand through the stone. "Less than two hours. The stew requires one."

"Then I'll go after the stew."

"And another pot of tea. There are so many things you've not told me. The western cities, for example. And whether anyone remembers the astronomer who proved the moons tug the sea. Or the tower-builders. Or me."

The last two words were quiet. The young man almost missed them.

"I don't know who you are," he said.

The wizard's fingers tightened against the wall.

"I see."

"That doesn't mean no one does. You haven't told me your name."

"Names acquire complications. Titles are safer."

"I didn't ask for either. You asked whether I remember you."

The wizard returned to the stove. "The stew will be ready shortly."

The young man stood.

His damp clothes clung unpleasantly to his back. The warmth that had seemed merciful now pressed too close. He crossed to the walnut cabinet and pulled one door open. Jars of dried beans stood three deep inside it. He shoved at the cabinet's side. It did not move.

"Please don't," the wizard said.

"Show me the door."

"The slope is unsafe."

"That is my choice."

"Your choice to break your neck? Your family would hardly thank me."

"They'll thank you even less if you keep me here."

The wizard set down the spoon. His expression had gone still, but the fire beneath the pot flared hard enough to lick its iron sides.

"I have offered shelter, food, and guidance."

"And decided when I may leave. That isn't hospitality. A guest has to be free to go."

The flame sank.

For a long moment neither spoke.

Then the wizard came around the table. The young man braced himself, ashamed of his fear and unable to dismiss it. The wizard stopped an arm's length from the cabinet and pressed his palm against its center.

It blurred. Shelves and jars thinned like mist. The door appeared behind them, plain wood in a stone arch, exactly where it had been.

"It was never locked," the wizard said.

The young man reached for the latch. It lifted. When he pulled the door inward, wind threw rain across the carpet and nearly tore it from his hand.

Outside, the ruined ridge dropped into darkness. Water leaped white over the stones. Pines bent until their crowns swept the ground.

The wizard did not move to stop him.

The young man shut the door.

"Concealment," the wizard said. "Not confinement. Though I understand that may feel like a narrow distinction from your side of it."

"Why conceal the door from the inside?"

"Efficiency. The same working covers both faces."

"Why cover either face?"

"To prevent intrusion."

"From the guest you've been waiting centuries to meet?"

The wizard turned away. "I was not waiting."

"You knew how long it had been."

"I keep records."

"And you want to know whether anyone remembers you."

"A matter of historical interest."

The young man looked at the two cups, the cut loaf, the chair placed opposite the wizard's own. Nothing else in the room was arranged for two.

"Why haven't you gone outside and asked?"

The wizard picked up the spoon and stirred the stew, though nothing in the pot needed stirring. "I have crossed battlefields under burning skies. I have bargained with kings who chained the messengers who brought them bad news. I have stood at sea in winter and diverted a wave taller than this tower."

"That isn't an answer."

"It supplies context."

"It supplies hiding places."

The wizard looked up sharply.

The young man's heart hammered. The openable door stood behind him. Remembering that helped.

"One honest answer," he said, "for one honest answer. You ask me something, then I ask you. Neither of us interrupts. If either refuses, the other may refuse too."

"A formal exchange?"

"A conversation."

The wizard's mouth tightened. "You are impertinent."

"My sister says so. That's one answer."

To the young man's surprise, the wizard laughed. Only once, but genuinely.

"Very well," he said. "Why have you truly been watching the door since you arrived?"

The young man considered offering something easy. The wizard had not.

"Because when I was small, I wandered from home during a fair. A kind woman found me and gave me a honey cake while people searched. I remember the cake. I also remember that she held my wrist whenever I tried to look outside. She meant well. I was still terrified."

The wizard waited.

"Why haven't you left the tower?" the young man asked.

The spoon stopped against the pot.

"I did leave, at first," the wizard said. "Frequently. Then less often. I survived my teachers, my rivals, my friends. I survived people I had once thought unbearably young, and their children, and theirs. Each time I returned outside, the world had shed another layer of what I knew. Roads moved. Words altered. Houses vanished."

He set the spoon down.

"Once, I went looking for a library that held my earliest work. A market stood in its place. No one there knew the library had existed. A bookseller sold me a little volume of legends in which a fool bearing one of my old titles was eaten by crows. I corrected him. He laughed."

The wizard's gaze traveled up the green stair.

"I came home angry. I told myself I would wait until the world grew wise enough to value what it had lost. Later I told myself I was protecting dangerous knowledge. Later still, that solitude was necessary for a great labor. All had some truth. None was the reason."

"What was?"

"That if I went out and nobody remembered me, I would have to live in a world that had no place prepared for me. Here I could believe the invitation had merely been delayed."

The young man did not interrupt. The wizard noticed.

"My turn," he said. "What do you believe your family will do if you are late?"

"My father will take a lantern into the storm. My mother will tell him not to, then walk to the gate and wait where the rain can reach her. My older brother will blame me. My younger brother will defend me and make everything worse. My sister will say she knew I was avoiding the roof, but she'll keep water hot in case I come back cold."

The wizard looked toward the stove. "Six."

"Six. Did you ever finish the great labor?"

"Which one?" The wizard smiled ruefully. "I began nine. I finished three. Two were useless. One was dangerous, so I dismantled it. The others became excuses with excellent diagrams."

The young man sat again. The wizard ladled stew into two bowls.

They ate under the rule.

The wizard asked what work the young man did. He repaired roofs with his father and brother, though he preferred carving pegs and fitting the wooden frames. He asked whether he meant to do that forever. The young man admitted he did not know, and that not knowing frightened him more than the work itself.

In return, he asked which daily task had kept the wizard sane. The wizard said pruning. Spells encouraged plants to grow, but they did not decide what growth ought to remain. His tea shrubs needed judgment, patience, and the willingness to cut off living branches for the health of the whole.

The wizard asked whether people were crueler now. The young man said he had not lived in any other time and refused to flatter the past for him. The young man asked whether two thousand years had made the wizard wise. The wizard said no, but it had given him an impressive collection of corrected mistakes.

They disagreed about the stew. The wizard claimed it lacked salt. The young man insisted the herbs were the problem. Together they discovered the wizard had used a sweet leaf where he meant to use a savory one. The wizard blamed a three-century-old labeling system. The young man blamed the person who had spent three centuries refusing to replace it.

After supper, the wizard made a second pot of tea.

This time he asked whether the young man wanted it.

The storm softened while they spoke. Rain ceased striking the tower and began to patter. The pale lines in the wall dimmed. Cold crept into the room as the fire burned low, and the wizard let it. He did not feed the flames or propose dessert or discover another urgent question.

At last the young man glanced at the door.

"I should go."

The wizard nodded. "Yes."

He packed the remaining bread and a stoppered jar of stew into a dry cloth. The ruined flour he accepted with grave ceremony and set beside his own bin, promising it might still thicken something. Then he touched the door, and the concealment over it vanished completely. The walnut cabinet did not return.

Outside, the storm had moved beyond the hills. Cloud still covered the sky, but the rain was fine and silver. The slope below shone with runoff.

The wizard took a lantern from a hook. With his other hand, he lifted the second teapot from the table.

"You'll spill that," the young man said.

"I once carried a basin of volatile moonfire down four hundred steps while pursued by assassins."

"Did you spill it?"

"Extensively."

The young man held out his hand. The wizard gave him the lantern.

They crossed the threshold.

The safe path was invisible until the wizard walked it. He tested each patch of ground with the end of a plain wooden staff, avoiding loose stone and sudden channels. He used no spell to flatten the hill or stop the rain. When the young man slipped, the wizard caught his elbow; when the wizard misjudged a muddy root, the young man steadied the teapot.

At the foot of the ridge, the trees opened. Beyond them, the familiar path lay pale beneath the clouds. Far off, where it reached the inhabited road, a tiny light moved between the trunks.

"My father's lantern," the young man said.

He raised the one he carried and waved it. After a moment, the distant light waved back.

The wizard stood just within the shadow of the trees. Behind them, the tower no longer looked ruined. Warm windows climbed its round wall, and green leaves pressed against the glass near the top.

"The road is that way," the young man said. "You can walk with me as far as it. If you want."

The wizard looked at the answering lantern, then at the tower. Rain ticked softly on the teapot lid.

"Will they remember me?" he asked.

"No," the young man said. "You'll have to meet them."

The wizard considered this, adjusted his grip on the fresh tea, and took the first step out of hiding.

"She literally makes everyone smile when she walks in a room." "To be fair she does have an amazing personality that's why we're married."
stories.body:
# She Literally Has Wings

Twenty-three minutes before our first-anniversary party, my wife came through the apartment door carrying six folding chairs under one arm and our elderly neighbor under the other.

The neighbor was not injured. She had simply decided that the elevator was taking too long, and my wife had found her resting halfway up the stairs with a lemon cake balanced on her knees.

“I can walk,” the neighbor protested, although she made no attempt to get down.

“Of course you can,” my wife said. “You can also arrive with enough breath left to complain about the music.”

The neighbor smiled. People did that around my wife.

I hurried over to rescue the cake. My wife turned sideways so her wings would clear the doorframe, ducked the hanging paper garland, and set our neighbor gently on the couch. Six chairs hit the floor with a metallic clatter. Not one of the pearl-white feathers sweeping behind her so much as brushed the frosting.

“Show-off,” I said.

She kissed my cheek. “You married me for my upper-body strength.”

“I married you because you own a drill.”

“Romance.”

My best friend watched this exchange from the kitchen doorway with the blank, fixed stare of a man who had just discovered that gravity was optional in our home.

I had invited him early to help. So far, he had inflated four balloons, eaten three stuffed mushrooms, and asked why we owned a feather rake. I had explained that a feather rake was for grooming feathers. He had stared at me then too.

My wife opened her wings just enough to shake out the tips. In our small living room, they seemed to occupy every available gap without touching anything. The longest feathers caught the amber light from the windows. For an instant, their edges shone as if the sunset had followed her inside.

The apartment felt warmer.

It always did when she was happy.

I handed her the repaired paper garland. “Can you put this back up?”

She looked at me over one shoulder. “You want me to use the stepladder, don’t you?”

“Absolutely.”

“Because using my wings indoors would be unsafe.”

“And because the last time you did, we had to explain a ceiling-fan-shaped bald patch.”

“It grew back.”

“The security deposit won’t.”

The neighbor laughed so hard she had to hold the cake box level with both hands. My wife climbed the ladder, muttering about tyrannical landlords and husbands with no sense of adventure.

Our guests arrived in a happy trickle. My wife welcomed each one as if their presence had solved a problem she had been worrying over all day. She remembered whose new job had started badly and whose cat had stopped eating. She placed the shyest guest beside our neighbor, who could draw conversation out of a brick wall, and intercepted a bottle from a nervous coworker before it slipped from his damp hands.

Every time she crossed the room, shoulders loosened. Voices lifted. Smiles appeared.

I took credit for the snacks.

Ten minutes into the party, someone knocked from the hall. My wife tilted her head. A faint scratching came through the door, followed by a small and indignant bark.

“The dog got loose again,” she said.

“I’ll go.”

“You’re holding hot cheese.” She tucked her wings close and slipped out. “I’m fireproof. You’re not bite-proof.”

“That is a terrible division of labor.”

The door shut behind her.

My best friend seized my elbow and dragged me three steps toward the kitchen.

“Bro,” he said, keeping his voice low, “how did you not know your wife is an angel? She literally has wings.”

I looked toward the door. “Well, to be honest, I thought she was some bird demi-human or hybrid or something.”

His mouth opened. Closed. Opened again.

“Some bird?”

“Not some bird. Some bird demi-human. Or hybrid. The distinction seemed personal, so I didn’t pry.”

He pointed at the closed door with both hands. “She literally makes everyone smile when she walks in a room.”

“To be fair, she does have an amazing personality. That’s why we’re married.”

He stared at me so intensely that I checked my shirt for spilled sauce.

“You thought the light was her personality?”

“People use that expression all the time.”

“The physical light.”

“Some feathers are reflective.”

“She found my missing wallet from three streets away.”

“You always lose it.”

“That does not explain how she knew where it was.”

“You always lose it near food.”

He rubbed both hands over his face. “On your wedding day, she walked down the aisle and every flower in the room turned toward her.”

“The florist said those were very responsive flowers.”

“The florist was crying.”

“Weddings are emotional.”

He stepped closer. “Her feathers don’t match any bird. Strangers tell her their darkest secrets in grocery-store lines. She refuses to promise miracles in exactly those words. Did none of this add up?”

“It added up to her being unusual.” I heard my own voice sharpen. “Most people are, once you know them.”

“Sure. My unusual trait is that I can wiggle one ear. Your wife glows when she’s moved.”

“What did you want me to do, ask for a certificate?”

“I wanted you to ask your wife a question.”

That landed harder than the jokes deserved. I knew what he meant, but what I heard was that our marriage was a ridiculous accident. I heard him saying I had been fooled by the woman who had sat on the bathroom floor with me through food poisoning, rebuilt our cabinets when the top shelf collapsed, and learned to sleep with one wing hanging off the bed because I sprawled.

“I know her,” I said. “I know she hates olives and loves terrible detective shows. I know she counts under her breath when she’s angry because it stops her saying things she can’t take back. I know she keeps bandages in every coat and reads the last page of a novel first. Whatever category you think matters, I married a person.”

Behind me, the apartment door clicked shut.

My friend’s face changed.

I turned.

My wife stood with one hand still on the lock. A small red feather clung to her sleeve, probably from the dog’s ridiculous collar. Her wings were folded so tightly that their joints rose above her shoulders like white walls.

“A bird demi-human,” she said.

Her voice was quiet. Her smile was gone.

“Or hybrid,” my friend offered weakly.

She looked at him.

“I’m going to check the mushrooms,” he said, and fled.

My wife nodded toward the kitchen. “Can we talk?”

The kitchen had no door. Privacy required standing beside the refrigerator and trusting the party music to do its work. She faced the counter. I faced her back, where the smaller feathers lay in careful overlapping rows.

“I’m an angel,” she said.

“Right.”

She glanced over her shoulder. “That was not a quiz.”

“No. I know. I mean, I know now.”

“Did you ever wonder?”

“Of course I wondered. I just didn’t think it changed anything.”

She turned around. “You wondered enough to settle on an answer.”

“A loose answer.”

“You guessed what I was. You never asked what I am.”

“Because it doesn’t change how I love you.”

The words sounded good while they were leaving me. Then I saw her expression.

I had answered a question she had not asked. Worse, I had answered the version that made me noble: I had overlooked the wings because my love was too pure for labels. In the version on her face, I had overlooked part of her because I had decided it was none of my concern.

“That’s my intention,” I said slowly. “Not your hurt.”

Some tension left her shoulders, though her wings stayed closed.

“No,” she said. “It isn’t.”

The refrigerator hummed between bursts of laughter from the living room.

“Why didn’t you tell me?” I asked.

She traced one finger through a patch of flour on the counter. “The first time we had coffee, the server asked whether I could bless her pregnancy. Before I could answer, you told her I was off duty and asked me which pastry I wanted.”

“She was holding up the line.”

“I know. It was wonderful.” Her mouth almost curved. “Then you asked if the chair was comfortable with my wings. You didn’t ask whether I could heal anyone. You didn’t confess to me. You didn’t tell me I must be good, or pure, or wise. You wanted to know if I preferred custard or jam.”

“Custard.”

“You remembered.”

“That one was important.”

This time the curve came, but it faded quickly.

“When people hear the word, I become whatever they need an angel to be,” she said. “A sign. A judge. A messenger. A cure. Sometimes proof that something they lost is safe. Sometimes proof that they themselves are. They ask me for things I cannot give and resent me for having limits. Or they watch me, waiting for perfection.”

“I never wanted that from you.”

“I know. That was the problem.” She looked down. “I liked being only myself with you so much that every time I could have corrected you, I chose not to. At first it was relief. Then it was fear. Then enough time passed that telling you became an admission that I had let you marry me without saying it.”

I wanted to tell her that I would have married her anyway. It was true, but it would not make the choice retroactively mine.

“You should have told me,” I said.

“Yes.” She met my eyes. “I should have.”

“And I should have asked.”

“Yes.”

There was no neat division that made one of us innocent. Her silence had protected her from a fear I had not caused, then carried that protection into vows I had made without understanding it. My incuriosity had begun as courtesy and hardened into certainty because certainty was easier.

“I’m sorry,” I said. “Not because my guess was stupid, although it was very stupid. I’m sorry I mistook not judging you for knowing you.”

Her eyes brightened. Not with light. Just tears.

From the living room, someone called, “Wait, did you say angel?”

We both froze.

My best friend appeared at the kitchen entrance, holding the mushroom tray like a shield. “For the record, I told no one.”

Behind him, half the party was trying not to look interested and failing. The other half had given up pretending.

Our nervous coworker spoke first. “Can you really bless things?”

“Is that why the apartment feels so nice?” someone else asked.

The neighbor hugged the cake to her chest. “I knew those stairs felt shorter.”

The questions were smiling questions at first. Could she improve job interviews? Weddings? Lottery tickets? Could she do something about a football team’s defense? Someone asked whether a blessed houseplant still needed watering.

My wife answered the first two with a strained patience I recognized. Her wings tightened until the tips crossed at her ankles. The warmth in the apartment thinned. Nobody stopped smiling, but the smiles became the embarrassed kind people wore when they realized they had been laughing too loudly.

Then a guest near the window pushed forward. He had been quiet all evening. Now his hands shook.

“My brother is sick,” he said. “They’ve tried everything. If you could just touch him, or say something, anything...”

The room went still.

My wife’s face changed in a way I had never seen. It was not coldness. It was the look of someone standing at the foot of a familiar, impossible hill.

Every eye turned to her.

Mine did too.

For one ugly second, I waited for the miracle.

Then I saw what all those eyes were doing to her.

I moved beside her, close enough that our shoulders touched, and kept my mouth shut.

Her right wing loosened by a fraction.

“I’m sorry about your brother,” she said. “I can sit with him, if he wants company. I can listen to you. I cannot heal him.”

The guest’s face crumpled. “But you’re an angel.”

“I am.” She drew a breath. “I am not all-powerful. I am not a wish-granter, and I am not evidence that grief can be avoided if you ask correctly. What you feel around me is warmth, not happiness. It can make a hard thing easier to carry for a moment. It cannot make the hard thing untrue.”

She had said it without apology. The room did not know what to do with that.

I looked at her. She gave the smallest nod.

“All right,” I said to our guests. “No more requests. She came to her anniversary party as my wife, not as public emergency equipment.”

Several people lowered their eyes. My best friend began collecting abandoned plates with sudden dedication.

I turned to the man whose brother was ill. “You said they’ve tried everything. Does that include getting dinner into you this week?”

He blinked. “What?”

“You look exhausted. Does your brother need rides? Does someone need to sit with him while you sleep?”

The neighbor immediately put the lemon cake on the table. “I can make soup.”

The nervous coworker raised one hand. “I have a car.”

Someone by the window said they could cover an evening. Another guest found a pen. Within two minutes, the back of a paper napkin had become a schedule. It was not a miracle. It was six people arguing about soup containers, and it was something.

My wife’s wing brushed my wrist.

When I looked at her, the warmth had returned to the room. Softer this time. Nobody mistook it for a promise.

Later, I stood beside our crooked anniversary cake with a glass in my hand and abandoned the toast I had prepared. The original had three jokes about married life and a story about a smoke alarm. None of it belonged to the evening anymore.

“A year ago,” I said, “I promised to love my wife for everything she was. It turns out I had not done the sensible research needed to support that claim.”

My best friend coughed the word “wings” into his drink.

“Thank you,” I said. “We’ll address your contribution separately.”

My wife stood across from me. Her wings were no longer pinned closed, but her expression remained careful.

“I did know some things,” I continued. “I knew she was funny, generous, stubborn, brave, and capable of repairing plumbing while insulting it creatively. I knew she could make a room feel kinder just by entering it. I thought loving those things meant the rest did not matter.”

I set the glass down.

“It matters because it’s hers. I’m sorry I mistook being unafraid of a question for not needing to ask it. I married her for her amazing personality, and I would like to spend the rest of our marriage learning everything else she chooses to tell me.”

No one clapped right away. I was grateful. Apologies made poor performances.

My wife regarded me for a long moment. Then she came around the table.

“That is a direction,” she said, “not a pardon.”

“Understood.”

“After everyone leaves, you may begin with one real question.”

“Only one?”

“You have a year of homework to make up.”

The room laughed. More importantly, she did too.

Her light rose around her in a pale gold wash. It did not seize anyone’s mouth and bend it toward joy. The man with the sick brother was still grieving. The neighbor’s knees still hurt. My best friend was still an idiot. But grief shared space with soup, pain with cake, and idiocy with loyalty. One by one, people smiled because she had given them permission to remain imperfect in front of her.

I smiled because she had offered me another chance.

We stayed up after midnight cleaning. She washed plates while I dried, since wet feathers were a nuisance and my wings remained entirely theoretical. We spoke about ordinary things: the neighbor’s cake, the forgotten balloons, whether our friend should be banned from future anniversaries.

At last, only two glasses remained.

My wife leaned against the counter. “One question.”

I had hundreds. Where had she come from? Were there others? Did she have duties she had never mentioned? Had she lived before she met me in ways I had failed to imagine?

They could wait until she invited them.

“When you wrap your wings around me,” I asked, “what does it mean to you?”

She looked surprised. Then the final guarded line between her brows eased.

“It means I trust you enough to stop watching the door.”

She opened one wing and folded it around my back. The feathers settled over my shoulder, warm and heavier than they looked.

From the hallway came the scrape of a key against wood, followed by my best friend’s voice.

“I forgot my coat. Also, finally.”

My wife closed her eyes.

“May I ban him from our second anniversary?” I asked.

“That is an excellent second question.”

Her smile broke free, bright and completely her own. Mine answered before the room had time to.

stories.body:
# The Anatomy of a God

The bolt struck Avarrax beneath the ribs.

It should have killed a man. It punched through the white silk at his side, spun him half around on the temple steps, and drove a gasp from the hundreds packed into the court. Then Avarrax straightened.

Sun-colored light moved beneath his skin.

Edras saw it because he was a field medic, because he had spent half his life noticing what bodies tried to hide, and because he had watched that exact ripple before. It gathered in a hard knot below Avarrax's breastbone, divided toward his right shoulder and left hip, then returned to the wound. The bolt slid out as flesh closed behind it. Avarrax caught the bloody shaft without looking and snapped it between his fingers.

The crowd recoiled as one body.

On the execution platform, seven bound villagers watched the blood vanish from their conqueror's robe. One of them, a gray-haired potter with a split lip, had been struggling against her ropes. Now she went still.

Avarrax lifted the broken bolt. He was taller than any of his guards, broad beneath a mantle sewn with hammered gold. Light rimmed his shaved head and shone from his eyes. Whether the radiance came from his body or from some trick hidden in the temple roof, Edras could not tell. He could tell that the blood on Avarrax's fingers was real.

"One among you mistakes concealment for courage," Avarrax said. His voice filled the court without effort. "Therefore, all will learn the price of striking at a god. Begin with the prisoners."

The guards beside the platform lowered their hooked spears.

Edras pulled against the hand clamped on his shoulder. The guard behind him tightened his grip and forced him down until one knee hit the paving stones. Edras's medical satchel lay open nearby, its contents scattered for inspection: linen rolls, two wooden splints, three thin brace plates, a coil of waxed strap, needle, thread. They had taken his knives and medicines. They had laughed at the rest.

"This one first?" the guard asked.

Avarrax looked down at Edras. "The foreign physician has been offered mercy twice. He treated rebels who rejected my peace, then refused to name those who sheltered them." He descended one step. "Kneel willingly now, healer, or share their sentence."

Edras looked past him at the prisoners. The youngest was trembling so hard the platform rope quivered. The potter met Edras's eyes and gave one small shake of her head. Don't bargain for us, it seemed to say. Or perhaps only: Don't give him what he wants.

Behind Avarrax, the last trace of the healing ripple faded at his hip.

Edras remembered Miora on a narrow operating table, her fingers crushing his while her own body fought the surgeons.

She had been nineteen. A fall had broken her leg badly, but before the bone could be set, her gift had sealed it crooked. Every attempt to correct it provoked another burst of repair. Miora had listened to three surgeons tell her how dangerous the next attempt would be. Then she had looked at Edras and said, "If I change my mind, you stop them. Until then, you help them finish."

They had fitted dull plates over the three places where her healing gathered, not to damage them but to make each pulse circle harmlessly while the surgeons worked. Edras had counted the timing aloud. Miora had sworn at him for counting too slowly and made him begin again.

He remembered the sequence. He remembered something more important: the choice had been hers.

The guard shoved between Edras's shoulder blades. "Answer him."

Edras let his gaze travel over Avarrax as though assessing a patient. "Your wound is going to reopen."

Silence reached the far edge of the court in widening rings.

Avarrax touched his unmarked side. "Is that your final prayer?"

"Professional opinion. The lower return dragged. Either you're tired, or the trick is failing."

The light in Avarrax's eyes sharpened. His guard struck Edras across the mouth.

Pain flared. Edras tasted blood, but he had seen what he needed. At the impact, Avarrax's body had answered a threat that never touched him: the knot below his ribs brightened, the shoulder flickered, then the hip. Too fast to count by numbers. Not too fast to count by heartbeats.

Miora's pattern.

Not proof that they were the same kind of being. Not proof of anything beyond the path his flesh had just taken. But flesh was enough for the next few minutes.

Avarrax raised one hand, stopping the guard from striking again. "Explain my death to me, physician."

"I didn't say death. I said you're not invulnerable."

A murmur stirred under the colonnade. Avarrax heard it. That was the danger of ruling by spectacle: every boast required an encore.

"You saw an assassin's weapon fail," he said. "You saw my body cast it out."

"I've seen tavern performers swallow fire. I don't worship them either."

The guard's fingers dug into Edras's shoulder, awaiting permission.

Edras nodded toward the heavy execution frame behind the prisoners. Two upright posts supported a crossbeam, with ropes running through iron rings to a stone counterweight. The condemned were meant to be hauled into view one at a time. "Give me one attempt. No guards holding my arms. No priest whispering about miracles. Let me use that frame and what remains in my kit. If I fail, I'll fasten the prisoners to it myself. Then I'll kneel."

The potter's stare turned furious. Good. Fury meant she had not surrendered.

One of Avarrax's officers leaned close. "Radiant One, there is no need."

"There is every need." Avarrax smiled at the watching crowd. "Faith untested is only fear wearing ceremonial clothes."

Edras almost laughed. Avarrax had named his own reign and mistaken it for wisdom.

"Release him," Avarrax ordered. "Leave him his sticks and string."

The guard stepped back.

Edras rose slowly, gathered his splints, plates, and straps, and carried them to the frame. He did not look at the prisoners again. If his plan showed in his face, he wanted Avarrax watching the wrong face.

"Stand against the post," he said.

Several people in the crowd made small, disbelieving sounds.

Avarrax spread his arms. "Do you command your gods so casually where you come from?"

"Only the ones who volunteer as patients."

Avarrax stepped onto the platform and set his back against the right post. The wood was thick enough to survive a struggling body and old enough to have drunk years of rain. Edras looped the first strap around Avarrax's chest, threading one brace plate beneath it. He placed it over the fading knot of warmth he had seen below the ribs.

Avarrax watched his hands. "Your pulse is unsteady."

"I've had a long morning."

"You are afraid."

"That's what an unsteady pulse generally means."

The second plate went against the shoulder path, held between a short splint and the frame. The third lay along the return near the hip. Ordinary wood. Ordinary metal. Ordinary straps. With Miora, their purpose had been to hold a body in an exact posture while its own repair drove against the interruption and folded back on itself. The surgeons had adjusted them with calm hands in a clean room.

Edras had a stained execution frame and an audience waiting to see someone die.

He ran the free ends of all three straps through separate rings. The first he tied to the main line above Avarrax's head. The second he hooked to the platform rail. The third he wound around the counterweight's release peg.

"Is this your attack?" Avarrax flexed. The chest strap creaked. "A harness?"

"I haven't started."

Edras took the remaining splint in both hands and drove its end toward Avarrax's throat.

Avarrax caught it. Wood cracked in his fist. He backhanded Edras hard enough to throw him across the platform.

Edras landed on one shoulder and rolled. Around the court, the murmur broke into frightened laughter. Avarrax tore through the chest strap and stepped away from the post, dragging the other two loose.

For one sick instant Edras thought he had misjudged the strength of the waxed weave.

Then he saw the torn chest strap still looped through the upper ring, exactly where he needed it. The break had given him slack enough to tie its end to the counterweight line.

He crawled toward his satchel.

Avarrax followed at a leisurely pace. "This is the science your country sets against divinity?"

"Mostly we use it for sprained ankles."

Edras snatched the coil, rose, and rushed him. Avarrax seized the front of his coat. Edras wrapped the loose strap around Avarrax's forearm and let himself be lifted. His boots left the boards. He kicked the rail, swung sideways, and dropped the strap over the second iron ring.

Avarrax flung him down. This time Edras's head struck wood. The world flashed white.

He heard the youngest prisoner cry out. He heard the scrape of a spear as a guard shifted closer. Then Avarrax hauled him upright by the collar.

"Enough," Avarrax said.

Edras blinked until the frame stopped doubling. The three plates had slipped but not fallen. The straps crossed the repair paths. Above them, lines ran from ring to rail to counterweight in a crude triangle.

He needed the pulse.

"You're right," Edras said. "No one will believe sticks beat a god. Give them another miracle first."

Avarrax's smile vanished.

"The bolt wound happened too quickly," Edras continued. "Half the court didn't see it. Cut your palm. Let them watch you heal. Then kill me."

The officer below the platform said, "Radiant One, end this."

But Avarrax was looking at the crowd. Hundreds of faces had lifted toward him. Edras could almost feel the question move among them. Why refuse?

Avarrax released Edras. From his belt he drew a thin ceremonial blade the guards had not considered a weapon because it belonged to him. He drew its edge across his palm. A bright line opened.

"Witness," he said.

Light gathered below his ribs.

Edras pulled the upper line.

The first plate tightened. The healing glow struck it and divided. Edras stamped the hooked line off the rail. The second strap snapped taut across the shoulder path. Avarrax jerked, surprise breaking his composure for the first time.

One heartbeat.

Edras kicked the release peg free.

The stone counterweight dropped. The third strap cinched, catching the returning ripple. Golden light raced beneath Avarrax's skin, reached the first plate again, and circled.

His cut palm remained open.

Some of the radiance around him guttered. Not all. Edras could not tell whether the dimming came from the stalled repair, shock, or rage, and he had no time to decide.

Avarrax stared at his hand. "You actually managed to counteract my regeneration?"

Edras braced both hands on the line. "I don't know what your deal is, but where I am from guys like you aren't rare, hell, my stepsister is one of you. We know how to deal with your anatomy."

"What are you talking about!? I am a GOD!"

"You have the ego of one, that's for sure."

Avarrax roared and lunged.

The frame shuddered. One upright split near its base. Edras hauled on the line, but the counterweight bounced against the paving below, giving Avarrax half a stride of slack. That was enough. He caught Edras by the throat and lifted him.

His strength had not vanished with his healing. Neither had the light in his eyes.

Edras clawed at Avarrax's wrist. The court darkened at the edges. He had proved a limit and mistaken proof for victory.

"Guards," Avarrax said, his voice ragged but still vast. "Kill the condemned. Kill anyone who moves."

No spear fell.

The officers looked at one another. A young guard lowered his weapon first. Another backed away from the platform.

The potter moved.

She threw herself sideways, caught the counterweight rope in her bound hands, and pulled. The other prisoners understood before the crowd did. Three of them seized the line with her. Their combined weight dragged the stone clear of the ground.

The straps snapped tight.

Avarrax staggered backward. His grip opened. Edras fell, coughing, and rolled beneath the rail.

The youngest prisoner hooked one ankle around the cracked upright and dragged it toward the socket. The potter shouted, "Pull!"

People rushed from the edge of the court.

Not everyone. Many fled. Some crouched behind pillars. But a dozen villagers reached the platform and laid hands on the line. A mason looped it around the sound post. A woman with flour on her sleeves climbed up and cut the prisoners' bonds on the ceremonial blade Avarrax had dropped. Two guards turned their spears crosswise and used the shafts to brace the splitting frame.

Avarrax fought them. Wood groaned. His shoulder tore free of one strap, and the plate clattered across the boards. Golden light surged toward the gap, but the other two paths held it circling. He reached for Edras.

The potter caught the loose chest strap and flung it to him.

Edras wound it around the broken upright, passed it through the upper ring, and pulled until the first plate seated again. Avarrax's radiance flared, throwing hard shadows across the temple wall.

"I gave you peace!" he shouted.

"You gave us graves," the potter said.

With the frame stabilized, the crowd forced Avarrax back against the post. They bound his wrists with execution rope, added chains from the platform, and locked the counterweight line around a pillar base. The conqueror strained against them, but each struggle only drew more hands.

At last he stopped.

The cut on his palm still had not closed. A single bead of blood slid to his wrist.

The potter picked up a fallen spear.

Edras saw the grip she took, both hands low on the shaft. He stepped between her and Avarrax.

"Move," she said.

"No."

"He was going to hang my son."

The youngest prisoner stood behind her, rubbing his freed wrists. So that was her son. He looked from the spear to Avarrax and said nothing.

"I know what he meant to do," Edras said. "But the suspension is temporary. If you run that through him, I don't know what his body will do while the repair is caught. He may die. He may tear himself apart trying not to."

"And if we let him heal?"

"Then you judge him with clear heads and enough chains. Not in the same breath you escaped him."

The spear point did not lower.

Edras kept his hands at his sides. "He called fear faith. Don't let rage become justice because it also wants a better name."

The potter looked at her son. He reached past her and pushed the spearhead toward the floor.

After a long moment, she let it drop.

The court began to change shape. Guards removed their gold sashes. Villagers freed the remaining prisoners and closed the outer gates. Someone found heavier chains in the temple storehouse. The officer who had advised Avarrax to end the contest tried to slip away, but his own soldiers stopped him and took his sword.

Edras knelt beside the frame to inspect the straps.

"Careful," he told the four people who had gathered to learn. He pointed to each plate without naming a place on the body. "These marks show the order for him. Him alone. Keep the tension even. If his hand begins to close or the light gathers in one place, increase the counterweight by a little, not a lot. When you release him for water, washing, or judgment, loosen the plates in reverse, one at a time. Then let the repair finish before you suspend it again."

The flour-sleeved woman frowned. "You said people like him weren't rare where you came from."

"People who heal strangely aren't rare. That doesn't mean they heal the same way." Edras looked up at Avarrax. "I used this because I watched his body and recognized one pattern. Try it on someone else and you could kill them."

"Your stepsister," the young guard said. "Is she dangerous?"

Edras thought of Miora relearning stairs, rejecting every offered arm until the day she chose to take his. He thought of her laughing when he admitted that her swearing had ruined his count.

"She runs a bakery," he said. "Her greatest crime is charging too much for winter pears."

The guard flushed.

Edras removed a page from his field ledger. He drew the frame, the three straps, the counterweight, and the release order. He did not draw a body. Beside each plate he copied the tiny notch pattern he had cut into the metal, enough to keep Avarrax safely confined and no more.

"Who rules now?" someone asked.

No one answered immediately. The potter glanced at her son, then at the guards without sashes and the villagers coiling unused rope.

"No one alone," she said. "Not tonight. Tomorrow we choose a council. We collect testimony. We find every cell he kept. Then we decide how a man answers for calling himself our god."

Avarrax lifted his head. Even bound, even dimmed, he made the old court seem too small for him.

"I am not a man," he said.

Edras closed his satchel. "Maybe not. Your anatomy doesn't decide what you deserve. Neither does your title."

By sunset, the prisoners had become jailers and the worshipers had become witnesses. They carried the wounded out first. Edras checked each one at the foot of the platform, binding a burned hand, setting two fingers, cleaning the potter's split lip. No one asked him to heal Avarrax, and Avarrax asked for nothing.

When the court was nearly empty, Edras sat on the lowest temple step with his ledger balanced on his knee. He began a letter.

*Miora,* he wrote, *today the thing that once kept you safe helped me keep seven strangers alive.*

Behind him, chains shifted.

"Kneel," Avarrax commanded.

The potter walked past carrying a lantern. The young guard followed with a bucket of water. Villagers crossed the court in twos and threes, speaking of locks, witnesses, food, and morning.

No one knelt.

Edras bent over the page and kept writing.

stories.title: Friends of the Night
stories.prompt: While your predecessors were busy hunting the beasts that hid in the shadows, you decided to befriend them. And when war came to your lands, your enemies found their armies shrinking in the night.
stories.body:
# Friends of the Night

On my first night as warden, the alarm bell sent me beneath a row of dead faces.

They watched from the beams of the watch-house: long muzzles stuffed with straw, black ears stiffened by varnish, glass eyes fixed on the iron traps below. Each brass plate gave a year and a warden's tally. Seven beasts. Eleven. Nineteen, during the winter when the river froze hard enough for carts.

My own tally board hung blank beside them.

Outside, someone struck the bell again. I took a lantern from its hook, passed the old boar spear by the door, and went out with empty hands.

A ewe lay dead beside the grazing wall. Two shepherds stood over her, and the older one had already found the dark hairs caught in the thorn hedge.

"Hushbeast," he said. "Fresh."

The younger shepherd lifted his lamp toward the hillside. Every bush threw a hard little shadow. "We can drive it to the stone cut if we start now."

I crouched beside the ewe. Her wool was soaked at the throat, but the bites were small and paired. I had cleaned enough trophies as an apprentice to know a hushbeast's jaws. These wounds belonged to common hill dogs.

At the wall, a trench of crushed grass led away from one of my predecessors' iron jaws. The trap had sprung, but there was no foot in it. Blood shone on the teeth. Beyond it, the drag marks continued uphill, and the black hairs clinging to the hedge were wet at their roots.

"It came for the carcass," I said. "After the dogs. Then it found our trap."

The older shepherd looked at my bare belt. "And what will you put on your board?"

"The truth, if it fits."

It did not satisfy him. Truth rarely does when someone has lost an animal and needs the loss to have a face.

Before dawn I pulled every jaw trap between the grazing wall and the stone cut. The old hunters had pegged them beneath fern, buried them in stream mud, and wired them to trees where a struggling creature could spend hours tightening the teeth. I carried the traps back one by one and laid them under the trophies.

Then I dragged the ewe's carcass uphill.

The stone cut was a wound in the hill where earlier generations had quarried blocks for the grazing wall. Nothing grew in its deepest cleft. At sunset, the cleft filled with darkness before the rest of the slope, and that darkness joined the shadows beneath the gorse.

I set the carcass beyond the last patch of grass. Beside it I left a bowl of clean water and a rag spread with wound salve. Then I sat where the failing light could show both my hands.

The first hushbeast appeared only as a mistake in the shadows. A patch beneath the gorse thickened. Two low eyes opened in it, reflecting no light. A foreleg took shape and vanished again. The creature could have been the size of a hound or a pony; its edges changed whenever one shadow touched another.

It smelled the iron on my coat.

I removed the warden's chain and badge and laid them in the grass. The beast did not move.

So I backed away from the water. One pace. Then three. At ten, its wounded foot emerged from the cleft.

It drank without lowering its eyes.

When it had gone, the salve rag was gone too.

That was how our friendship began: not with a hand laid on a tame head, but with distance correctly judged.

For many nights I saw nothing. I kept taking up traps. I hauled the empty iron into the watch-house until it lay in rusting heaps beneath the preserved heads. The old hunters came to drink by my stove and told stories loud enough to make their trophies seem alive.

"They'll learn you have no teeth," one said.

"They learned yours were made of iron," I answered.

"Fine words won't bring back sheep."

"No. A sound wall and dogs that aren't starving might."

That lost me the warmth of the room. It also got the shepherds' dogs fed from the council stores, once I showed the council how many dead sheep bore their bites.

The hushbeasts kept to the far side of the wall after that. I knew because I walked the boundary every morning. Their tracks ended where the wall's shadow ended, as if paws had reached the stones and reconsidered.

When summer dried the gorse, three shepherds went uphill with oil and torches. They meant to burn the old den before the wind turned. I stood in the narrow path and told them the fire would race down through their own pasture.

"Then help us cut a firebreak," the oldest said.

So we did. By noon their anger had become sweat. By dusk we had cleared a broad strip around the stone cut, and there was nothing left for a torch to catch. The shepherds went home swearing that I had tricked them into useful labor.

That night, three hushbeasts waited on the other side of the grazing wall. The wounded one stood in front. The fur on its foreleg had grown back silver rather than black.

I raised one open hand. It lowered its head. Neither of us crossed.

In autumn, the younger shepherd's daughter wandered from the berry pickers before rain. The whole village searched until the clouds swallowed the moon. Her father came to the watch-house with mud to his knees and begged me to loose the hunting dogs.

I took no dogs. I carried one hooded lamp uphill and opened it at the grazing wall. Then I covered it, opened it again, and covered it, the signal I had used when leaving food near the stone cut. It meant only that I was present. I had no signal for a missing child.

The night remained ordinary for a long while.

Then darkness folded over the wall.
