The girl stepped out of the shadow of an ash tree less than twenty paces from us. She was wet, scratched, and furious because something kept nudging her whenever she tried to sit down. She said she had followed two silver eyes from a hollow tree to a boulder, then from the boulder to the wall. She could not explain the space between. Each time, she had taken the offered dark because the rain behind her sounded worse.

Her father gathered her up. Beyond the wall, several pairs of eyes closed one after another.

After that, no one tried to burn the den.

The old hunters called the rescue luck. The council called it evidence that my methods had value. Neither called it friendship. Perhaps I did too readily. The hushbeasts never came when summoned. They accepted meat when they were hungry and left it to rot when they were not. Once, when I walked into the stone cut without stopping at the edge, the wounded one knocked me flat and held one heavy paw on my chest until I understood that welcome was not ownership.

I liked them better for that lesson.

War reached us in the mouths of refugees.

They came over the southern track with burned sleeves, blistered feet, and nothing that could not be tied to their backs. They said an army followed: cavalry gathered from the invaders' own estates, officers in bright mail, and thousands of foot soldiers levied from farms and conquered villages. Those who marched too slowly were whipped. Those who ran were hanged beside the road.

We had a timber gate, a low grazing wall, and enough trained fighters to fill half the watch-house. The council sent riders asking for aid, but the larger garrisons had their own roads to hold.

Enemy outriders arrived before any answer. They burned the hedges bordering the southern track. At night they planted lanterns on tall stakes, each pool of light overlapping the next, until their camp stood inside a glowing fence. Wherever the light fell, the shadows broke apart.

The council met beneath the trophies in the watch-house. Five councilors sat at the table. The old hunters stood behind them with the satisfied faces of men whose worst warnings had finally become useful.

"You have fed the beasts for three years," the eldest councilor said. "Now feed them something that can hold a sword."

"They aren't mine to loose."

"Call them, then. Lead them into the camp."

An old hunter tapped the butt of his spear on the floor. "Open a gap in the lantern line and let hunger command them."

I looked at the black muzzles overhead. Generations of wardens had mistaken death for proof of service. Now the council wanted a larger tally.

"No," I said.

The eldest councilor's fingers tightened around the storehouse key. "You refuse to defend us?"

"I refuse to spend lives that weren't offered to me."

"They are beasts."

"Then why do you expect them to understand which uniforms to eat?"

The old hunter smiled without humor. "Give me your badge. I'll show you how the office was done before."

I kept the badge. The council kept the key. By sunset I no longer had access to the grain, lamp oil, medicines, or signal arrows stored for the watch.

That night I crawled close enough to the enemy camp to hear a homesick soldier singing under his breath. He stopped when an officer struck him.

The army was not one thing. At its bright center, officers ate at tables and pointed to maps. Near the lantern fence, men and women in patched coats slept sitting up. Some had boots; some had rags bound around their feet. When a dozen conscripts stumbled out of formation carrying cook pots, mounted guards drove them back with the flats of their blades.

Numbers held the camp together. Fear held the numbers.

I returned to the stone cut before dawn. The hushbeasts gathered gradually, occupying every joined shadow until the quarry seemed deeper than the hill could contain. The silver-footed one watched from a ledge.

I laid my knife on the ground. Beside it I placed a soldier's leather wrist guard, lost near the camp. Then I opened my empty hands.

"I won't ask you to hunt them," I said. "Some came to burn us. Many were dragged here. If any lay down their weapons and choose to leave, will you show them the dark road?"

The silver-footed beast's ears flattened.

"Only those who choose. Hurt no captive. If the lights make it too dangerous, stay away. If you simply do not wish to do this, stay away."

It stepped down and smelled the wrist guard. Then it took my knife in its teeth.

One by one, the eyes in the quarry closed. The shadows thinned. When morning came, both knife and wrist guard were gone.

I did not know whether I had been answered or dismissed.

The first three soldiers arrived the following night.

They came out of the shadow beneath a hay cart just inside the grazing wall and collapsed in the stubble. None carried weapons. One still wore an iron cooking chain wrapped around her waist. Another clutched my knife.

The villagers who had agreed to wait with me raised clubs and sickles.

"Put those down," I told them.

"You said deserters," the miller replied. "You didn't say we'd invite enemy soldiers to our fires."

"If surrender looks like a beating, no one else will risk it."

The woman with the cooking chain stood despite the others' attempts to hold her. "Prisoners?" she asked.

"Guests until daylight," I said. "After that, you may stay without weapons, or take food and use the western road. No one will send you back."

She studied us, searching for the hook inside the offer. At last she unwrapped the chain and let it fall.

The villagers found plain clothes. I found food by asking from door to door, since the council still held the stores. The miller complained the whole time and gave twice as much bread as anyone.

Before the three left by the western road, the woman told me how the darkness had reached them. A lantern near the latrine had tipped face-first into wet earth. Beyond it, two eyes opened under a wagon. Another soldier whispered from the dark that anyone who set down steel could follow. The three had passed the message onward before stepping beneath the wagon themselves.

The next night, fourteen came. Then thirty-seven. The night after that, the lantern by the horse lines went out, and more than a hundred vanished between one count and the next.

The army's commander moved the conscripts away from the perimeter. Bonfires replaced lanterns. Patrols carried braziers between the tents, showering sparks whenever they turned. The commander announced that ten soldiers would be punished for every deserter and ordered each file to watch its own.

Still the message passed: set down your weapon, cover the light, choose the dark.

By the fifth evening, the enemy had built a cage in the camp's center.

I saw the captive through a spyglass. It was a young hushbeast, small enough that the iron bars forced its body to hold one shape. Lanterns surrounded the cage on every side. Whenever it tried to flatten itself into the bars' shadows, a guard raised a mirrored plate and threw light between them.

The cage was bait. The commander wanted the others to cross the bonfire ring.

The council wanted the same thing.

"Now they'll attack," the eldest councilor said when I brought the news. "Be ready to follow."

"They may not come at all. I told them they could refuse."

"Then all your kindness bought us nothing."

I thought of the girl stepping from the ash tree, and of the soldier who had returned my knife. "It was never a purchase."

I left my badge on the council table.

After sunset, the silver-footed beast waited outside the watch-house. Its eyes shifted toward the southern hill, then back to me. I followed it to the last hedge shadow before the enemy's light. There the path ended. The bonfires had burned a ragged moat through the night.

"You brought them out," I whispered. "I'll go in."

The beast caught my sleeve in its teeth. Not hard. A warning, or a refusal, or merely fear. I put my hand beside its muzzle without touching.

"You may leave."

Its jaws opened. I crossed the light alone.

I wore the patched coat one deserter had discarded and carried a water bucket to hide my empty hands. The guards looked toward the hills, waiting for monsters. They did not look closely at another tired laborer. I passed the outer fires, then the cook tents, then rows of conscripts packed so tightly that turning in sleep would wake a neighbor.

At the central cage, the young hushbeast panted without sound. A guard held the cage key. Two more tended the ring of lanterns. Beyond them, under a striped canopy, the commander had placed archers facing outward.

I could not defeat them. That was the old wardens' answer to every danger, and all it had left me was a room full of heads.

So I set down the bucket and shouted.

"The hidden road is real!"

Faces lifted across the camp.

The key guard seized me. "Quiet."

"They cannot carry anyone who does not choose," I called. "They cannot cross while you keep the fires bright. If you want the road, make the night yourselves."

The guard struck me in the mouth. Around us, officers began yelling for ranks to form.

For one breath, nothing changed. I tasted blood and wondered if fear had finally found a shape too large to break.

Then a conscript near the cook tents dropped his spear.

The sound was small. Another spear struck the ground. A sword followed. Then hundreds of weapons fell through the camp in a clatter that drowned the officers' commands.

Someone kicked dirt over a lantern. Two women dragged a wet blanket across a fire. A cook overturned a cauldron, and steam swallowed a row of flames. Conscripts pulled down the tall lantern stakes while the guards swung at them. They did not fight back. They held the guards' arms, covered the lights, and kept shouting the message.

Set down steel. Choose the dark.

The key guard turned toward the commander. The young hushbeast pressed itself against the cage floor, as far from the lanterns as the bars allowed.

"You heard me," I told the guard. "Prisoner or road. You choose too."

His hand closed around the key. For a moment I thought he would throw it into the fire.

He unlocked the cage.

We smothered the nearest lantern beneath my borrowed coat. Darkness touched the cage, the commander's canopy, and the long shadow cast by an overturned wagon.

The young beast spilled through the open door like water released from a jar.

Its cry was too low to hear in my ears. I felt it in my teeth.

All across the camp, eyes opened in the newly joined dark.

The hushbeasts did not charge the officers. They did not tear at the archers or leap upon the commander. They moved among the people who had dropped their weapons. A shoulder brushed a waiting hand. A muzzle pointed toward the shadow of a tent. Each conscript had a final moment to step forward or draw back.

Those who stepped forward vanished.

The archers loosed into the dark. Several conscripts raised shields, not to attack, but to roof a corridor between the cage and the wagon. Others tore down bright canvas and threw it over the last lanterns. The shadows widened. The beasts returned again and again, carrying willing people through distances the eye could not follow.

The silver-footed one appeared beside me. Behind us, the commander shouted that every deserter would be hunted home.

The woman with the cooking chain had known the answer to that threat. There were homes no longer safe to return to, and others worth the risk. Refuge was not one place. It was the right to decide the next step.

I put one hand into the silver-footed beast's shadow.

The darkness felt like cold fur and deep water. It waited.

I chose.

We emerged beneath the ash tree by the grazing wall. Around us, deserters stumbled into the village fields in twos and tens, then in streams. Villagers guided them toward barns, kitchens, and the western road. No gate was locked behind them.

At dawn the enemy camp held empty bedrolls, abandoned armor, and cookfires cooling under mud. The commander still had cavalry, officers, and soldiers who had chosen to remain. He no longer had enough bodies to surround our grazing wall. By midday, his army was retreating along the road it had burned.

The council returned my badge in the watch-house. Beneath the trophy row, the eldest councilor raised a cup.

"To our warden," she said, "and the secret weapon under the hill."

I did not take the cup.

"They were not a weapon," I said. "And they were never secret. We were simply too busy hunting them to learn what they would choose."

That afternoon I took down the preserved heads. The old hunters watched in silence as I carried each one outside. No beast came to see. Friendship did not require an audience.

When the wall was bare, I burned the tally boards and hung a new one in their place. On it I wrote the first rule for whoever kept the night after me:

**A friend may answer, refuse, or leave.**

Beyond the open door, the watch-house shadow joined the shadow of the ash tree. Two silver eyes regarded me from the threshold. Then they closed, and the darkness moved uphill, free of every chain.

stories.title: The Throne Neither of Us Wanted
stories.prompt: You and your older sibling were very anxious if confused when a prophecy was made that one of you would kill your kind father for a throne neither of you particularly wanted. Even stranger, father was entirely unbothered.
stories.body:
# The Throne Neither of Us Wanted

The prophet interrupted a dispute about drainage.

That was the part I kept remembering afterward: not thunder, not a darkening sky, but a potter holding up a cracked clay pipe while my father leaned over the arm of the throne to inspect it. Rainwater had drowned three kilns in the lower quarter. The master of works blamed old foundations. The potter blamed the master of works. My father, who had spent the morning settling six duller quarrels with unfailing patience, asked whether either man had thought to widen the western culvert.

Then the woman among the petitioners dropped her basket.

Apples rolled across the floor. She stood rigid, her eyes fixed somewhere beyond the painted rafters, and spoke in a voice that seemed too large for her narrow chest.

“Before the next moonrise, one of the king’s two children shall kill their kind father and take the throne neither desires.”

The last apple circled on its side and fell still.

My elder sibling was beside me on the lower step of the dais. Their hand found mine so hard our knuckles ground together. I could not breathe. Across the hall, every guard looked first at us and then at Father.

He looked only at the prophet.

“Kind,” he said thoughtfully.

It was an absurd word to choose. I had already imagined steel, poison, my sibling’s face across a locked room, my own hands made monstrous by some mistake not yet committed. Father merely sat back, brow furrowed as if the woman had quoted a law he almost remembered.

“Listen to me, both of you,” he said. “There is an older—”

The protection bell drowned him.

Three iron strokes shook the hall. The captain of the guard went pale, then carried out the command that had been written for an assassin’s hour and could not be countermanded by the person it protected. Guards closed around the throne. Others seized my sibling and me, not cruelly but with a terrifying courtesy.

Father rose. “Suspend the protocol.”

“The protocol suspends royal authority until the threat is contained, Majesty.” The first minister had appeared at the foot of the dais. Even then, before I understood anything, I noticed how steady his voice was. “For your life, you must not communicate with either possible assailant.”

“They are my children.”

“Today, that is precisely the danger.”

My sibling shouted Father’s childhood pet name for us, a ridiculous little whistle he used when he wanted us to look up together. The guards dragged us through one door and him through another. He answered with the whistle before the doors slammed between us.

That sound frightened me more than the prophecy had. Father had sounded neither betrayed nor afraid.

He had sounded annoyed.


They confined us in the old schoolroom, which contained no blades, no balcony, and almost nothing we had not once broken. The painted map on the wall still bore the blue handprint my sibling had left at twelve while demonstrating a naval invasion with wet pigment. A guard removed the poker from the cold hearth. Another counted the spoons on our supper tray twice.

As soon as the lock turned, my sibling said, “I’ll confess to intending it.”

“No.”

“They will imprison me. Possibly exile me. You’ll stay clear of the succession, and Father will live.”

They had always done this: stepped between me and the kicked horse, the furious tutor, the consequences of my own ingenious failures. When we were children, I had loved them for it without qualification. As an adult, I had begun to understand the cost. They were forever building cages around themselves and calling the bars shelter for me.

I pulled a folded sheet from inside my coat.

Their expression changed as they read the first line. “You renounced your claim?”

“This morning, before the audience. I meant to give it to Father after we heard the petitions.”

“Why?”

“Because the council has been whispering that you’ll refuse the throne, and that makes me their convenient alternative. I thought if I removed myself, they would stop pressing you.”

“You did this without telling me.”

“You just offered to spend your life in a cell without telling me.”

We stood on opposite sides of the little table, each furious at the other for the same offense.

My sibling read the renunciation again. “This may look like preparation. You discard a claim before killing the king, then accept from necessity.”

“Your confession may look like a confession.”

“It would be one.”

“A false one.”

“False things still have uses.”

“Not if their use is destroying you.”

They put both hands flat on the table. Their voice, when it came, had lost its command. “I heard that woman, and for one moment I wondered whether it meant you.”

The admission hurt less than I expected. Perhaps because I had wondered the same about them.

“Did the moment pass?” I asked.

“Yes.”

“Mine too.” I set the renunciation between us. “Then we make one rule. Neither of us sacrifices anything else for the other without permission.”

“That sounds unworkable.”

“Only because you dislike asking.”

They almost smiled. “And you dislike waiting for an answer.”

We tore the renunciation together, once down the middle and again through my signature.


The first minister questioned us separately before dusk.

He sat across from me at the schoolroom table while a clerk recorded every word. He expressed sorrow, loyalty, and concern in that order. Then he asked which of us had more reason to resent Father.

“Neither.”

“Your sibling has been trained since childhood for a duty they openly despise.”

“Father did not invent the succession law.”

“No, but he has enforced it.”

That was true enough to make the question uglier.

He slid my torn renunciation across the table. Someone had taken the pieces from the hearth before they could burn. “You, meanwhile, sought release from your legal obligations.”

“I sought release for both of us.”

“Did the elder know?”

I said nothing.

The minister leaned closer. “If you name them as the danger, I can place you under separate protection and prevent a tragedy.”

“You have already separated us from Father. Is he safe?”

“For the moment.”

“Then why are you more interested in blame than safety?”

His careful sympathy disappeared. “Because government cannot wait upon family feeling. If the king remains unable to rule when the moon rises, the council must declare an incapacity. Your sibling will be crowned at once.”

“They can refuse.”

“The realm cannot.”

There it was: not murder prevented, but succession achieved.

When he left, my sibling returned from their interview with the same realization. The guard allowed us to sit together but not whisper, so we used the game of taps Father had taught us during long ceremonies. One finger meant yes, two meant no. Knuckles counted letters poorly. By the time we had tapped out HE WANTS CROWN, the guard had begun to suspect we were insulting him.

Father’s reaction, I tapped.

My sibling frowned. WORDING?

“Kind,” I said aloud.

The guard shifted. “No conversation about the prophecy.”

“I was complimenting you,” I told him.

He was young enough to be pleased despite himself.

My sibling’s gaze moved to the blue handprint on the wall. Below it, half hidden by a bookcase, was the little service door through which servants had once supplied our lessons. We had used it years ago to smuggle in a puppy. The puppy had grown too broad to smuggle out.

“I’m going to request permission,” my sibling said carefully, “to make a very poor decision with you.”

I tapped once.


The service passage was narrower than memory and richer in dust. We crawled until it joined a linen stair, stole two plain cloaks, and descended into the part of the palace that respectable people preferred to forget existed.

The old legal archive occupied three rooms behind the disused council chamber. Its newer records had been moved upstairs years ago. What remained smelled of mouse nests, damp leather, and the mineral chill of stone. Shelves sagged under boxes whose labels had faded to ghosts.

“What are we seeking?” my sibling asked.

“Something old enough to make Father pedantic in the face of death.”

“That describes most laws.”

We began with succession.

The windows had gone dark before we found the failed abdication bill. It was recent, written in a clerk’s clean hand, but the lower corner had been stained and gnawed away. Father’s corrections crowded the margins.

*Voluntary surrender remains impossible under the coronation oath,* he had written. *Find the prior remedy. No child of mine should inherit solely because I wish to leave.*

Beneath that, in darker ink: *They say the throne cannot be emptied except by death. Whose definition?*

My sibling traced the words without touching them. “He knew.”

“He was looking.”

We found the answer in a coronation record old enough that its pages had gone soft at the edges. The script changed halfway through, from dry accounts of taxes and robes to a witness’s description of uproar.

The sovereign’s adult daughter had entered the hall during a winter famine and invoked what the record called crown-death. Before the court, she named the granaries he had withheld and the petitions he had refused. Witnesses confirmed her charges. The sovereign answered each one, yielded the office, and was led from the throne alive.

The daughter sat in his place before sunset.

In the margin, a later scholar had explained the word that had sent guards rushing between us and our father.

*To kill the king is, in the elder law, to end the sovereign person while sparing the mortal bearer. Blood may challenge blood, that inherited power be answerable where ordinary petition fails. The challenger must speak true harms before witnesses, the sovereign must freely yield, and the challenger must bear the crown thereafter. Thus the crown is not escaped cheaply by either side.*

My sibling sat down hard on the floor.

“One of us kills him,” they said.

“As king.”

“And takes the throne.”

“Which neither of us wants.”

Relief made me laugh once, breathlessly. It died when I saw their face.

“The prophecy still isn’t a command,” I said.

“No. But the council is about to declare him incapable and crown me without any challenge at all.” They turned back to the failed bill. “He could not abdicate. Once they crown me by incapacity, I may not be able to either.”

A slip of paper protruded from the coronation record. It bore Father’s handwriting and a list of witnesses whose support he meant to seek for restoring the rite. At the bottom he had written: *Then open succession. Service must be chosen, not bred.*

Folded beside his note was a requisition slip dated three weeks earlier. The purpose line read *crown-death precedent*. Beneath it was the first minister’s angular countersignature and the square red seal of his office.

Footsteps sounded in the outer room.

We took the record and ran.


By the time we reached the throne room, the council had assembled in nightclothes beneath ceremonial mantles. The haste would have been comical if Father had not been standing below his own throne between two guards.

The first minister was reading the declaration of incapacity.

“Stop,” my sibling said.

Every head turned. My heart hammered from the run, but the guards hesitated. It was difficult to arrest the person they expected to crown within the hour.

Father saw the book under my arm and closed his eyes briefly. Not in fear. In recognition.

The minister recovered first. “The possible assailants have breached confinement. Remove them.”

“You knew what the prophecy might mean,” I said, holding up the requisition slip. “You had searched the same record.”

“An obsolete ceremony does not supersede the safety of the realm.”

“But an emergency coronation controlled by your council does?”

Murmurs moved among the witnesses. The minister raised his voice. “Their presence endangers the king.”

“My children do not endanger me,” Father said.

“Majesty, the protocol—”

“Is my shame, even if it is presently your authority.” He looked at us. Weariness had found him at last, but fear still had not. “I did not summon the prophecy. I don’t know why that poor woman spoke or whether she will ever speak so again. I was calm because I knew the old usage, and because neither of you has ever wanted power badly enough to spill blood for it.”

“You might have mentioned the other sort of killing,” I said.

“I tried.”

The protection bell had answered him. So had all the machinery he had left standing.

Father looked at the locked doors, the guards, the council already dressed for transfer of power. “I thought I had time to dismantle this safely. I told myself secrecy would keep you free of the struggle until I had solved it. Instead, secrecy left you helpless inside rules made in my name. I am sorry.”

The first minister snapped the incapacity document shut. “This family conference is irrelevant. The crown cannot be governed by affection.”

“Agreed,” my sibling said.

I knew their decision before they looked at me. Their whole life, they had stepped forward alone. This time they waited.

The question in their face was not whether I would let them save me. It was whether I would stand with them while we did something neither of us could undo.

I nodded.

They climbed the dais, stopped one step below Father, and laid a hand on the old record.

“Before these witnesses,” they said, “I invoke crown-death.”

The room seemed to draw breath through a single mouth.

The minister ordered the guards forward. None moved. Old law, once spoken aloud in the proper place, had its own momentum.

My sibling faced Father. Their voice shook on the first sentence and steadied on the second.

“I charge the king with preserving a custom that made imprisonment the answer to fear. I charge him with allowing a succession no heir may refuse. I charge him with hiding his remedies from those who would pay the price if he failed. His intent was kind. The harm was real.”

It hurt to hear because it was true.

The rite required corroboration. I stepped beside them.

“I witnessed guards take his children at the first sound of danger, by his law and against his will,” I said. “I witnessed ministers prepare a crown before establishing any crime. I witnessed my sibling and myself plan to surrender our freedom because the law gave us no safer tool. The charges are true.”

Father stood very still.

For the first time that day, he looked troubled. Not by death, but by judgment. He glanced toward the throne he had occupied for most of our lives, then toward the petitioners’ empty benches. Somewhere beyond the walls, three flooded kilns were still waiting for a culvert.

“I answer that I mistook good intentions for sufficient protection,” he said. “I believed I could repair unjust power while continuing to hold it. I was wrong.”

He removed the narrow circlet from his head.

“I yield the sovereign person. Let the king be dead.”

He placed the circlet in my sibling’s hands.

Then he stepped down, alive, and embraced us both.


The prophecy was fulfilled twenty minutes before moonrise.

My sibling sat on the throne long enough to stop the incapacity proceedings, suspend the protection protocol, and place the first minister under open inquiry. He protested that everything he had done was lawful.

“That,” my sibling told him, “is what the inquiry must examine.”

Their next order summoned petitioners, guild delegates, village speakers, judges, servants, and soldiers to choose a temporary assembly. Within one year, that assembly would propose a way to select future sovereigns from beyond our family. Within two, my sibling would submit their own office to whatever lawful choice followed.

The council objected to every word. It was the liveliest I had ever seen my sibling look at a meeting.

When they asked me to serve beside them, I said, “I still refuse the crown.”

“I didn’t offer it.”

“Then I accept.”

That night, long after the prophet had been found bewildered but unharmed and the council had exhausted itself, we ate in the old schoolroom. There were only two chairs, so Father sat on the table. Without a circlet, he looked smaller and older. He also looked, for the first time in my memory, like a man whose next morning belonged to him.

My sibling divided a cold pie into three unequal pieces and gave Father the largest.

“Favoritism,” I said.

“Compensation for killing him.”

Father considered his slice. “I expected death to ruin my appetite.”

We laughed too loudly. Relief was not clean. My sibling had inherited months or years of work they had never wanted. Father had lost an office he had tried, imperfectly, to use with kindness. I could still hear the protection bell in every sudden noise.

But we were together, and no one had chosen for anyone else.

Down the corridor, beyond guarded doors now propped open, the throne stood empty while the three of us finished our late meal.

stories.title: The Name I Kept
stories.prompt: You, the member of a superhero family, are talking with your older sibling, who was disowned for killing a supervillain, (had no choice). Shunned by heroes and family, you are the only one they can talk to. Also you are sick and tired of your parents calling them a failure and disgrace.
stories.body:
# The Name I Kept

At one seventeen in the morning, your mother calls your older sibling a failure for the third time on television.

The laundromat television has no sound. It hangs in a cage over the change machine, captions crawling beneath Crownfire's composed face. Her gold collar catches the studio lights. Your father sits beside her in the dark uniform he wears when he wants to look less like Palisade and more like a grieving parent.

WE LOVE OUR ELDEST CHILD, the captions say. LOVE DOES NOT REQUIRE US TO EXCUSE DISGRACE.

You set the blue laundry sack on a folding table hard enough to rattle its wire legs.

"Careful," Veyra says behind you. "There's a mug in the side pocket."

You turn. They stand just inside the glass door with rain on the shoulders of their gray coat. The laundromat's white light makes them look tired in a way daylight usually forgives. Their hair needs cutting. Their left hand is wrapped around a roll of quarters, and their right stays buried in their pocket.

You pull out the mug. It is chipped at the handle, not broken. "Why do you put a mug in with your clothes?"

"Because you keep forgetting to bring one when you visit." Veyra takes it from you. "And because it irritates you. I have few luxuries now."

They say it lightly. That is the first test.

You used to answer their lightness with your own. A joke could cover anything in your family: a missed birthday, a cracked rib, a camera waiting outside the emergency entrance. Tonight the joke catches against the words still moving across the screen.

"You saw it," you say.

Veyra looks up at your mother, then at the dryers turning in a row. "Hard to miss. She has excellent posture."

"She called you a disgrace."

"That part is easier to miss after a while. Sounds like weather."

They take the laundry sack to the machines at the back, where the television is hidden by a square pillar. You follow. The bag holds the clothes you washed for them last week when half the machines here were out of order: dark shirts, work trousers, two towels, one fitted sheet you folded badly. Veyra tips everything onto a table.

"Shirts together," they say. "Trousers flat. And stop crushing the collars."

"They're clean."

"Clean things can still be mistreated."

That is the second test. Practical correction means they are willing to let you stay.

You sort the shirts the way they taught you when you were small enough to believe Rampart could hold up anything forever. Seams matched, sleeves crossed, fold in thirds. Veyra turns the fitted sheet into a neat rectangle without looking at it.

Your right wrist gives when you lift the towels.

Their hand closes around your forearm before the towels hit the floor. They push your sleeve back. The skin above your glove line is swollen and yellowing.

"Training?"

"A rescue."

"Did you have it scanned?"

"It's fine."

Veyra bends your hand gently toward your thumb. Pain flickers up to your elbow. You pull away.

"That's not fine."

"Mother said swelling photographs badly. If I brace it, they'll ask questions tomorrow."

Veyra's mouth goes still. "What happens tomorrow?"

You should have begun there. Instead you straighten the towels and feel the hot, useless shape of your anger expanding inside your chest.

"Another live interview. Midday. They want me between them this time."

"Of course they do."

"Father sent me the approved answers. If they ask about you, I'm supposed to say the family remains united in its values."

Veyra picks a loose thread from the fitted sheet. "Will they ask?"

"They arranged for them to ask."

"Efficient."

"Stop doing that."

"Folding?"

"Pretending it doesn't hurt."

They look at you at last. Their face is not empty. You have simply become skilled at mistaking exhaustion for calm.

"What would you like me to do instead?" they ask. "Throw the mug? We established it has sentimental value."

"Be angry."

"I am angry. You just don't get to schedule the performance."

The machines hum around you. On the other side of the pillar, the television changes to an advertisement; a bright jingle bleeds through its damaged speaker for half a second before the sound cuts again.

Veyra releases the sheet. "Did you come to hear me, Mica, or did you come to empty your guilt somewhere it won't stain the uniform?"

Their use of your name lands more sharply than disgrace ever could. Your parents use it for introductions. Veyra uses it when they need you to stop moving.

"I defended you tonight."

"At home?"

"Yes."

"In the room with the three people who already know what happened."

"I told them they were lying. Father said I was being emotional. Mother asked if you'd put me up to it."

"I didn't."

"I know that."

"Do they?"

"What does that matter?" Your voice rises. At the front of the laundromat, a man asleep across three plastic chairs shifts and pulls his cap lower. You force the next words through your teeth. "I'm done. I won't go tomorrow. I'll quit the team tonight. They can keep the crest, the house, all of it."

Veyra puts both palms on the folding table. "No."

You had imagined resistance. You had prepared answers for worry, gratitude, even the hard relief of being believed. The flat refusal knocks them all loose.

"You don't decide that."

"No, you do. But you don't get to put the decision in my hands and call it loyalty."

"That's not what I'm doing."

"Then why are you here announcing it to me before you've done anything?"

"Because you're my sibling, and I thought you might want to know I won't stand next to them while they say those things."

Veyra pushes the quarters into two short stacks. Ten in each, edges aligned. It is what they do when they need their hands to obey.

"If you walk out tonight," they say, "they will say I poisoned you against them. You will lose your home and your work, and every time you hate it, I will wonder whether you hate me too. They'll have two exiles instead of one, and they'll still have the story."

"So I should smile tomorrow?"

"I didn't say that."

"Then tell me what you want."

"I want you to stop offering me explosions because you're afraid of doing one precise thing."

The dryers turn. A buckle taps a glass door with patient, regular clicks.

"What precise thing?"

Veyra studies you. "Say it where someone can disagree with you."

"I say it here."

"Yes. Here, after midnight, behind a pillar, with a sleeping man for a witness. You tell me I saved those people. You tell me there was no other move. Then you go home, and Crownfire says a real hero would have found a way, and Palisade says my name like it belongs on a warning sign."

"They'll destroy me if I contradict them in public."

"I know."

The answer is not cruel. That makes it worse.

Veyra picks up the mug and runs a thumb over the chip. "You are the only person I can talk to about that night. Not because you're the only one who still visits. Because you were there. You remember the whole choice. But being defended only in a locked room still leaves me alone everywhere that costs something."

Your wrist throbs in time with your pulse. You cradle it against your stomach.

"I was on the train," you say.

"I remember."

"I almost died too."

"I remember that part most clearly."

The bridge returns in pieces whenever you let it. Rain boiling against torn electrical lines. Four passenger cars tilted past the edge of the broken track. Your shoulder pinned between two seats while the windows showed nothing below but river lights, far too small.

Veyra stood on the maintenance span beneath the first car. Both hands were raised, fingers open. Their barrier was invisible except where rain struck it and flattened, drawing the shape of a bowl beneath the train. Every time the cars shifted, their knees bent farther.

Shearpoint had one hand on the surviving rail. Each pulse he drove into the steel loosened another brace. The sound came through the whole train, too low to hear cleanly. You felt it in your teeth.

There had been no duel by then. No audience for the clean exchange of blow and counterblow. There was Shearpoint at one end of the span, Veyra under the train, and your own breath counting the intervals between pulses.

"One point eight seconds," you say.

Veyra's eyes close.

Your suit had called the timing into your ear. One point eight seconds between the final two pulses. Eleven centimeters of drop after the first. The barrier had buckled under the rear carriage and then caught again.

Veyra shouted across the span. *Stop. There are people in it.*

Shearpoint looked toward the hanging windows. He saw you. You know he saw you because his head turned and held there for half a second.

Then he pressed his palm down for another pulse.

Rampart's gift had never been making walls. That was the simplified version painted on lunch tins. Veyra gave force a path. On the bridge, every path was already carrying weight. They could release the bowl beneath the train and strike him. They could keep holding it and let his next pulse shear the last braces. They could turn his force aside, but turning it required an edge, and every edge of their barrier was under one of the four cars.

There was one open path. Straight back along the rail, through the man creating the pulse.

Veyra took it.

The train settled into the barrier instead of falling. Shearpoint struck the guardrail and did not rise. By the time the first car reached solid track, he was dead.

You remember Veyra kneeling beside him after the last passenger was carried away. They did not touch him. Their hands hovered over their knees, shaking so badly they could not close them.

"Father had the timing," you say. "He saw my suit log before he gave the first statement."

"Yes."

"Mother heard the recording. She heard you warn him."

"Yes."

"Then she stood in front of the cameras and said you chose anger over discipline."

"Yes."

Each yes removes another place for you to hide.

"I should have spoken."

"You were injured."

"Not for three months. Not for the year after that."

"They told you the hearings were over. They told you speaking would reopen everything."

"And I let that be enough."

Veyra's gaze shifts to the rain tracking down the front windows. "I can live with what I did, most days. That doesn't mean I think it was good. It doesn't mean I sleep through the night. A person died because I chose where to send the force. I chose."

You start to speak, but they lift one finger.

"Don't take that word away from me. No viable alternative is not the same thing as no choice. If I call it nothing, then his death becomes nothing too."

The sleeping man coughs. A washer enters its final spin, quick and unsteady, then smooths into speed.

"What I cannot live with," Veyra says, "is them insisting the proof that I never belonged in the family is that I refused to let the train fall. That I refused to let you fall. They can hate the outcome. I hate it. But they don't get to make saving you my disgrace."

You press your left palm against the folding table until the pattern of its metal grid marks your skin.

"Why do you still use Serrin?"

The question escapes harsher than you intend. Veyra flinches anyway.

"They took the suit, the crest, Rampart. They made the name into a weapon. Why keep giving them that?"

"Rampart was theirs," Veyra says. "Serrin wasn't."

"It's Father's name."

"It was ours before it was a logo. Yours and mine. I knew you might stop coming. I knew they might make you choose, and you might choose the only home you'd ever had. I needed to keep one thing that still said we came from the same place."

They give a short, embarrassed breath, almost a laugh. "It was a foolish reason."

"No."

"It was not legally or strategically sound."

"Veyra."

Their eyes meet yours.

"You kept it for me?"

"I kept it because it was mine," they say, careful now. "But part of mine was you."

The anger in you changes shape. Until this moment, you have wanted to hurt your parents back. To leave a costume on the marble hall, break the family line in half, make them feel one fraction of the absence they assigned to Veyra.

That would still leave Veyra carrying the bridge alone.

You pull your phone from your coat and set it between the stacks of quarters.

"My suit retained the original buffer," you say.

Veyra does not touch the phone. "Father said all field records had been surrendered."

"The official set was. Mine makes a local copy for injury review. I found it when I was looking for a training sequence."

"How long have you had it?"

"Six months."

Their face tightens. You do not explain. There is no explanation that would not ask them to soothe you.

You unlock the phone and open the folder. A waveform, suit telemetry, a small view from the camera at your collar. The first frame shows rain and the torn interior of the passenger car.

"It has the one point eight seconds," you say. "The drop after the pulse. Your warning. My suit estimates what would happen if the support field shifted. And it recorded me saying I could see Shearpoint's hand on the rail."

"You could release that tomorrow."

"I could. I won't unless you want me to."

Veyra's attention moves from the phone to your face. The change is so slight another person might miss it. You do not. For the first time tonight, they are not braced against you.

"What are you asking?" they say.

"What can you bear to have shown?"

They sit on the edge of a molded chair. Together you go through the recording without sound first. At seventeen seconds, Veyra asks you to stop. The frame shows Shearpoint against the rail after the return strike, distant and still.

"Not that," they say.

"Not that."

You trim the view before impact. Keep the suit diagram and the timing. Keep Veyra's warning, but not the sound they make afterward. No footage of Shearpoint's body. No footage of Veyra kneeling. No triumphant music, no slowed replay, no caption claiming a clean victory.

"Your statement," Veyra says. "Only what you saw. Don't say everyone was saved. He wasn't."

"I will say the passengers were saved. I'll say you saved me."

Their jaw works once. "All right."

You type while they watch.

*I was in the lead passenger car. I witnessed the final two seconds. Veyra Serrin was supporting all four cars when Shearpoint initiated another structural pulse. The field record shows that releasing or redirecting support would have caused the train to fall. Veyra warned him. He continued. Veyra returned the pulse along the sole path that preserved support beneath the train. Shearpoint died. That death matters. It is also false to say Veyra acted from rage, or that another viable rescue was available in the time remaining.*

Below it, you write your full name.

Mica Serrin.

"Still yours?" Veyra asks.

You remember their answer and give it back. "It was ours before it was a logo."

This time their almost-laugh becomes real, though it lasts only a second.

You schedule nothing. You send nothing. You hand Veyra the phone and let them read every word twice. When they return it, they hold on for a moment.

"Go tomorrow," they say.

"I was planning to."

"No explosions."

"One precise thing."

"Then call me after."

"Will you answer?"

Veyra looks at the folded clothes, the chipped mug, the two stacks of quarters. "I always have."

***

At twelve fourteen the next day, you sit between Crownfire and Palisade beneath enough studio light to erase every shadow.

Your wrist is braced. The medic insisted after seeing you flex it badly in the corridor. Your mother noticed, frowned, then arranged your sleeve so the brace would not catch the camera.

The host asks the prepared question.

"After everything your family has endured, do you believe Veyra Serrin can ever return to the values you represent?"

Crownfire turns to the main camera. She does not hesitate.

"Veyra failed the people who trusted our crest," she says. "Until they accept that, inviting them back would teach every young hero watching that disgrace has no consequence."

Your father lays two fingers against your knee. A warning gentle enough for the wide shot.

You remove his hand.

"That's false," you say.

The host blinks. Your mother's smile remains in place, but all the warmth leaves it.

"Mica," Palisade says, "this is not the time."

"It became the time when you arranged the question."

You face the camera. The lens looks smaller than it did in rehearsal.

"I was on the train. Veyra was holding four passenger cars above the river when Shearpoint triggered the last pulse. There were one point eight seconds to act. Letting go, delaying, or turning the force aside would have dropped us. Veyra warned him. He continued. They returned the force through the only path that kept the train supported."

"Cut," your mother says, no longer smiling.

The red light stays on.

"Shearpoint died," you continue. "That is not easy, clean, or nothing. But Veyra did not act in rage. They saved the passengers. They saved me. Calling them a failure for that is a lie, and calling them a disgrace is something my parents do. It is not something I accept."

Your father grips the little metal crest fastened over your heart. For a moment you think he means to pull you toward him. Then the two pins tear free of the fabric.

The joined flame and wall lie in his palm.

"You no longer speak for this family," he says.

The light on your camera goes dark.

Across the set, the host's camera remains red for two more breaths.

That is enough.

By the time security walks you to the street, your statement and the selected telemetry are public. Veyra approved the final upload from the laundromat at dawn. Messages multiply across your screen too quickly to read: fury, disbelief, old accusations, people slowing the audio to measure the warning against the pulse.

None of it is justice yet. None of it gives Shearpoint his life or Veyra their sleep. Your parents have already issued a notice saying you are distressed.

The torn holes where the crest had been let cold air through your shirt.

You stand in the clear noon light and call Veyra.

It rings once. Twice. Five times.

They answer on the seventh, but neither of you speaks at first. Traffic moves past. Someone on the opposite pavement recognizes you and raises a phone. You do not turn away.

"They took the crest," you say.

"I saw."

"I kept the name."

"I saw that too."

Their voice frays on the last word. You look down at the blue laundry sack still in your hand. In the rush to leave the laundromat, you forgot to give it back.

"I have your fitted sheet," you say.

There is a pause. Then Veyra says, with grave patience, "Did you fold it correctly?"

"Absolutely not."

"Failure. Disgrace."

The laugh surprises both of you. It does not repair the bridge or the year of locked-room kindness. It does not have to.

"Don't hang up," you say.

"I wasn't going to."

You start walking. "Tell me how to fold it again."

In public daylight, with their voice clear beside you, Veyra begins.

stories.title: What the Town Owed Her
stories.prompt: The gothic witch that lives in apartment next to you looks incredible youthful but it seems like every family in town owes her something.
stories.body:
# What the Town Owed Her

By the time I unlocked my grandmother's apartment, three families had visited the witch next door.

I knew they were three families, though only five people climbed the stairs. Mirehaven had a way of making ancestry visible. You could tell which children belonged to the woman from the bakery by the flour worked into the seams of their coats, and which old man had married into the hardware family because he carried a paper parcel tied with their particular blue string. They came separately through the rain, knocked at number six, and offered up a jar of honey, a coil of copper wire, and a key without a lock.

The woman who accepted them looked no older than twenty-five.

She wore a black dress buttoned to the throat and cuffs narrow enough to make her hands seem delicate. Her hair was the brown-black of wet bark, pinned in a style I knew from the photographs in my grandmother's sitting room. Not similar to it. The same.

The old man saw me watching and lowered his voice.

“My grandfather said she'd ask when the town needed us.”

“Not today,” the young woman told him. She returned the key to his palm and folded his fingers over it. “Keep it where you can find it quickly.”

He obeyed with the relief of a man who had been refused a sentence.

Then she turned to me. Her face was lovely in the severe, improbable way of a saint carved into a tomb.

“You are the Sayer granddaughter.”

“Leonie.”

“Evadne Trell.”

Behind her, number six was lit by candles despite the gray afternoon. Bundles of drying plants hung from a brass rail. Their shadows stirred when no draft touched my face.

“My grandmother said you were a witch,” I told her.

“Your grandmother said many accurate things in an unhelpful tone.” Evadne glanced at the keys in my hand. “You should check the cellar before you sign anything.”

I had come to empty number five, sell it, and leave before Mirehaven remembered enough about me to start making demands. The buyers were due in two days. Their surveyor had already found damp in the basement, but old buildings had damp, and Rookglass House was older than most excuses. Its stone angels had lost their faces to salt. Its gutters spilled brown ropes of water down the windows. Nothing about it had ever been dry, level, or easy to heat.

Inside, my grandmother's rooms waited in perfect order. Her slippers stood under the bed. A cup with a faint crescent of lipstick rested beside the sink, as if death had interrupted her between sips and she meant to complain about the intrusion when she returned.

I began with the desk because grief could not hide inside a bank statement. Three hours later I had made piles for the solicitor, the charity shop, and the bin. The rain thickened against the glass. Water gurgled somewhere in the walls.

At the back of the lowest drawer lay an envelope with my name on it.

Inside was one line in my grandmother's square hand.

*When Evadne asks, open the east cellar wall.*

I read it twice, then carried it next door.

Evadne opened before I knocked. The honey, copper wire, and key were not in sight.

“What is in the wall?” I asked.

“Something your grandmother believed should remain closed until it was needed.”

“And when will that be?”

She listened. At first I thought the pose theatrical. Then I heard a low vibration beneath the building, too steady for thunder.

“Possibly tonight.”

I laughed. She did not.

My telephone rang inside number five. The estate agent had photographs from the surveyor: a wet fracture had appeared along the basement's eastern side. Until its cause was known, the buyers would not exchange contracts.

“There goes possibly,” Evadne said.

I shut my door in her face.

At eleven, hammering woke me on the sofa. I had fallen asleep among boxes with my grandmother's note clenched in one hand. The electric lights flickered. Something struck stone below, paused, then struck twice more.

The cellar stairs smelled of wet iron. My torch found Evadne kneeling beside the east wall, measuring a crack with a dressmaker's rule. She had changed into boots and a man's old wool coat, though the black skirt still brushed her ankles. Water shone between the floor tiles.

“You asked me to open this,” I said.

“I haven't asked yet.”

“You sent three generations of dead people to do it for you.”

On a stool behind her lay a thick book bound in scuffed green leather. Beside it sat a tin of photographs. I recognized Evadne in the top one, standing in ankle-deep floodwater among women in long aprons and men with watch chains. On the back, a date had been written more than a century ago.

The next photograph showed her outside Rookglass House when its stone angels still had faces. In the next, she held a child in a coat from the years of my grandmother's youth. Her dress changed. Her expression did not. So little as a line had appeared around her eyes.

I opened the book.

The entries began in several different hands, then settled into Evadne's narrow script. A family rescued when the old river flooded its banks: *anything in our power, whenever you name it.* A baby delivered while fire trapped the midwife across town: *anything.* Two brothers found alive in winter scrub: *we will answer you, whenever.* A widow sheltered from a violent husband. A roof held through a storm. Medicine brought through snow.

The last column on every page was marked *unanswered*.

“They tell children they owe you,” I said. “They bring offerings. They lower their voices when they say your name.”

“Yes.”

“And you stand there looking younger than their grandchildren.”

“Also yes.”

Anger felt cleaner than the fear moving under my ribs. “What do you take from them?”

Evadne rose. “Nothing they don't give.”

“Their years?”

For the first time, her composure broke. Not much; a tightening at one corner of her mouth. “Do you think I would choose to watch a century pass through this town one funeral at a time?”

She turned the ledger toward herself. Her finger rested on the first page, where rain had feathered the oldest ink.

“When the first flood came, I kept a dozen people alive in the upper rooms of this building until the water fell. I was young, frightened, and far too pleased with my own power. They promised me anything. I let the promise stand.” She looked toward the wall. “Whatever answers vows in Mirehaven fixed me at the age I was when that first one went unanswered. Each open promise added another knot. I cannot grow older, and I cannot cross the town boundary.”

“Convenient punishment.”

“There are worse faces to be trapped inside.” Her voice went flat. “That does not make it freedom.”

“Then ask for a loaf of bread from each of them. Cross out the lines. Walk away.”

“The people who spoke those promises are dead. Their descendants did not consent to them.”

“You let the descendants think they did.”

This time she had no quick answer.

Rain rattled the pavement grates outside. The vibration under our feet deepened.

“I told each household they could refuse,” she said. “I accepted gifts when refusing them would have been cruel, but I did not call the gifts payment. And I waited because the old relief channel would be needed again. When it is opened, it takes half the town to clear it and one witch to keep the roof from falling. I thought the promises might make them listen long enough to choose.”

“You kept them afraid because one day fear might be useful.”

“Yes.” She met my eyes. “I have had time to become wrong in several directions.”

The wall gave a soft crack. A thread of black water pushed through the mortar and ran over the toe of her boot.

I went upstairs to find proof.

My grandmother had kept Rookglass House's repair bills in a kitchen cupboard, sorted by year and tied with string. Behind them lay a cardboard tube containing plans drawn on waxed linen. The oldest showed a stone channel branching from the river, passing beneath the building, and rejoining the marsh below the lower streets. A red line marked a manual spillway behind the east cellar wall.

Later sheets carried my grandmother's measurements. The main culvert had bowed inward. If it collapsed during a surge, water would back through the lower drains and fill three streets. The hidden spillway could divert it, but opening the access would destroy the cellar wall, undermine two storage bays, and probably ruin number five above them.

On the final page she had listed three warning signs: dark water at the bakery drain, vibration under Rookglass House, a wet diagonal fracture in the eastern foundation.

Two were already beneath my feet.

My telephone rang before I could search for the third. A breathless voice from the bakery asked whether Evadne was with me. Black water had come up through their floor.

Downstairs, the cellar crack opened with a noise like a branch splitting. Water slapped across the tiles.

Evadne looked at me.

“Ask,” I said.

“Leonie Sayer, will you open the east wall?”

The easy sale of the apartment ended in that question. So did the fantasy that I could pack my grandmother into six boxes and be finished with every choice she had made.

“Not until everyone hears the truth,” I said. “No inherited debt. No punishment for refusal. And when tonight is over, you close every line, including the ones people decline.”

“Some will refuse if they know they can.”

“Then ask for what you need, not what their grandparents offered.”

Water covered the soles of our boots.

Evadne held out her hand. “Agreed.”

I did not take it. “No promise. Just get them here.”

The residents of Mirehaven filled the entrance hall in twenty minutes. Some arrived because Evadne called. More came because their parents had taught them never to ignore a summons from number six. They brought the things their households had preserved against an unnamed day: pry bars wrapped in oilcloth, old iron keys, coils of rope, shovels, a masonry drill, a hand winch. One driver parked a recovery truck outside. Another came with a van to move people from the lower streets.

They watched Evadne. Evadne watched me.

So I told them.

I showed them the ledger and the plans. I told them the promise-working kept Evadne young and trapped, not them obedient. No ancestor's consent had entered their blood. Anyone could leave. Anyone who left would lose nothing except the chance to help keep black water out of their neighbors' homes.

An elderly woman in a green raincoat began to cry. “My mother said our family would sicken if we refused.”

“Your mother was mistaken,” Evadne said.

“You never corrected her.”

“No.”

The woman set down the case of tools she had brought. “Then I refuse you.”

A murmur moved through the hall.

Evadne opened the ledger, found the line the woman indicated, and drew her pen through it. “Released,” she said.

The woman stared, perhaps waiting for a pain that did not come. Then she picked up the case again.

“These aren't for you,” she said. “My daughter lives downhill.”

“Understood.”

That was the moment the room changed. Not into bravery; there was too much weather beating at the doors for that. But fear loosened its grip enough for decisions to fit beside it.

Evadne asked the hardware household for their kept key to open the rear service gate. She asked the mechanic to anchor the winch outside. She asked the bakery family for every empty flour sack they could fill with rubble. She asked two households for evacuation vehicles, four for strong backs, one for knowledge of the old drains. Each time she asked, she waited for an answer. Some said no. She released them. Enough said yes.

Then she turned to me.

I took up my grandmother's mason's hammer.

The plaster broke easily. The brick behind it did not. We worked knee-deep in water while the drill screamed and grit coated our mouths. When we had opened a hole wide enough to see through, my torch found a stone gallery packed with branches, silt, and pieces of a collapsed iron screen. A wheel taller than I was stood on the far side, red with rust.

Another surge struck. The hole spat water hard enough to knock a man backward.

Evadne stepped into it.

She planted both hands on the broken edges of the wall and spoke words too low for me to understand. Pale light spread from her palms through the mortar, branching like roots under ice. The stones stopped shifting. She did not. Her shoulders shook with every impact from the water.

“I can hold the passage,” she said through her teeth. “I cannot open it.”

We widened the breach around her. The mechanic fed the winch cable through and hooked the fallen screen. Upstairs, the truck's engine roared. Iron shrieked along stone. Others dragged out branches and shoveled silt into flour sacks, passing them hand to hand toward the rear gate.

The wheel would not move.

I climbed through with my grandmother's plans inside my coat. Water reached my thighs, then my waist as the gallery dipped. Behind me, Evadne's light showed each crack she held shut. Ahead, the spillway gate shuddered in its frame.

The diagram showed a retaining catch on our side. I found it under the water, drove a chisel beneath it, and struck until my wrist went numb. The catch lifted. The wheel turned a quarter circle and stopped.

The gallery lurched.

One of Evadne's hands tore free of the wall. A seam opened overhead, pouring gravel and water. The people behind me scattered; then two came back to brace Evadne's arm while she pressed her palm into place again. The light returned, dimmer.

“There is another keeper,” I shouted.

My grandmother had drawn it on the far side of the gate.

The only way to reach it was through a maintenance gap barely wider than my shoulders. Water hammered through it. Someone tied a rope around my waist. Evadne looked at the plan, then at me.

“Your grandmother intended to do this herself.”

“She should have written better instructions.”

I went through before I could become sensible.

Cold closed over my head. For a few seconds there was no town, no inheritance, only stone scraping my coat and the rope cutting under my ribs. I pulled myself into the pocket beyond the gate and came up coughing in darkness.

The second keeper was above me, furred with rust. I fitted the chisel. My first blow glanced away. My second rang through the metal. On the third, the keeper dropped.

“Turn it!” I yelled.

The wheel groaned. The gate climbed.

Water seized my legs and dragged me toward the opening. The rope snapped taut. Hands hauled from the other side while the river battered through, carrying years of silt with it. I lost the hammer. I kept the plans inside my coat.

Then the spillway took the surge.

The water changed direction with a deep, bodily roar. It rushed away beneath the hill toward the marsh instead of forcing itself back under the lower streets. The pressure fell. One by one, the cracks around Evadne's hands went dark.

We crawled from the cellar near dawn, soaked black to the shoulders and gray with brick dust. Rookglass House had lost part of its east foundation. Number five would not be sold in two days, or two months. But when the drivers returned from below, they reported wet floors, frightened residents, and no drowned streets.

Evadne sat on the bottom stair with the ledger open on her knees.

Those who had answered stood before her while she recorded what they had freely done and crossed out each line. For those who had refused, she wrote *released*. She did not hurry. The last open promise belonged to my grandmother.

Evadne offered me the pen.

“It was never mine,” I said.

“No.” She looked at the broken wall. “But the choice was.”

She wrote *released by death* beside my grandmother's promise. Beneath it, she added, *answered freely by Leonie Sayer*, and closed the book.

Nothing flashed. No wind swept the cellar. Evadne simply bowed her head as if listening to a sound recede.

In the washed blue light after the storm, half the town walked with her to the boundary marker. Perhaps they wanted to see whether she had lied. From the care with which Evadne placed each boot, I thought she wanted to know too.

Evadne stopped with one boot in Mirehaven and one beyond it. She looked suddenly uncertain, younger in that instant than her unchanged face had ever made her seem.

Then she stepped across.

No force pulled her back. She walked twenty paces down the wet road, laughing once under her breath. When she turned, a single silver hair shone beside her temple.

I thought of number five with its cracked floor and ruined sale. I thought of the city train leaving that afternoon, and of how easily a new duty could disguise itself as a choice. I did not decide my whole life beside a boundary stone.

I decided the morning.

“Evadne,” I called. “I have tea upstairs, if the kettle still works.”

She touched the silver hair, then looked back at Rookglass House.

“What will I owe you?”

“Nothing,” I said. “It's tea.”

She crossed into Mirehaven again because she wanted to, and came home with me through the rain.

stories.title: The Kingdom That Said No
stories.prompt: You're a hero that travels the world. You've saved many regions in your day, but this new kingdom doesn't particularly WANT to be saved...
stories.body:
# The Kingdom That Said No

I knew how kingdoms asked to be saved.

Sometimes they sent riders with white ribbons tied around their wrists. Sometimes they lit three fires on a hill, or rang every bell they owned until somebody with a sword grew curious. Once, a whole fishing village had floated its doors out to sea, each painted with the same black plea. I had learned to recognize distress at a distance.

So when I crossed the eastern ridge and saw smoke rising from Aldervane in five ruler-straight columns, I did not stop to wonder whether the smoke meant something else.

Below me, the kingdom filled a narrow green valley between shelves of red stone. Houses climbed the northern slope in orderly terraces. Orchards covered the southern one. Along the valley floor ran a broad avenue of packed clay, wide enough for six carts abreast, leading from one end of the kingdom to the other.

Something enormous was coming down that avenue.

It moved beneath a bruise-colored mass of cloud. At first I mistook the ridges on its back for a line of wagons. Then it shouldered around a spur of rock, and lightning crawled from one black plate of its hide to the next.

The thunderback stood higher than a house. Its low head swung as it walked, sweeping blunt horns over scrub and stone. Each footfall puffed dust from the dry earth. Behind it, rain stitched the hills silver. Ahead, Aldervane's fields lay cracked and yellow beneath a clear sky.

Five columns of smoke. A beast. A city in its path.

I started downhill at a run.

As I descended, sections of Aldervane's outer wall toppled inward.

Not one section. Three. Then a fourth.

The blocks did not tumble like masonry under attack. They folded neatly, each wall dropping into the dust as if its mortar had vanished. People in yellow vests pulled ropes and ran clear. Beyond them, teams rolled market stalls from the central avenue. Doors swung open. Bright awnings came down. The kingdom was laying itself bare.

I had seen panic disguised as obedience before. I had seen frightened councils order their people to call surrender wisdom. By the time I reached the boundary stone, my hand was on the hilt at my shoulder and every old lesson in me was shouting the same command: do not wait for permission from someone who has decided to die.

A woman stepped into my path.

She wore a gray coat despite the heat, its sleeves rolled above brown forearms. A bundle of signal flags was tucked under one arm. The other hand was raised, palm out. She was perhaps my age, though the white beginning at her temples made her look sterner, and her eyes went first to my weapon rather than my face.

"Ulric Quist," she said.

I slowed. "You know me. Good. Who commands the defense?"

"I command the route. Neya Orm, third warden." She planted a heel against the white line painted across the road. "By authority of the valley council and the households of the passage district, Aldervane refuses your intervention. You are not to attack, divert, obstruct, bait, challenge, rescue us from, or otherwise interfere with the thunderback."

I stared at her. The beast took another step in the distance. A blue spark leaped from its shoulder to a standing stone with a crack like a breaking mast.

"You practiced that speech," I said.

"Every spring for eleven years. You're the first wandering hero we've needed it for."

"Your wall is open."

"Yes."

"Your people are abandoning their homes."

"They are moving out of the passage district until tomorrow."

"And that thing is walking toward you."

Neya glanced past me, measuring distance. "It is walking through us. It has done so three times in my life. The oldest terrace records describe twenty-seven passages. It cracks the hardpan so rain can reach the deep soil. Seeds lodge between its back plates and shake loose along the valley. The storm follows it. If you turn it aside, the western cisterns will stay empty and half our planting will fail."

As if the animal had heard her, thunder rolled behind the ridge.

"If it follows the avenue," she continued, "it will break shutters, gutters, several cheap walls, and whatever some fool forgot to move. Those things can be replaced. The occupied terraces are outside its path."

I looked at the fallen wall sections, the ropes, the bare road. There was order in it. I could see that. I could also see the thunderback's horn gouge a pale scar through a boulder I could not have moved with both arms.

"What if it leaves the path?"

"Then the horns sound three descending notes, the upper terraces evacuate, and my crews open a wider line."

"What if your crews are too slow?"

"They have not been."

"Until they are."

Her mouth tightened. "That is not consent."

The words landed harder than they should have. I told myself it was her tone.

"A title can speak for a kingdom," I said, "but it cannot speak for every frightened person in it. Let me walk your cleared streets. If no one asks for my help, I'll leave your beast alone."

Neya studied me while the smoke columns thinned in the wind. "You will keep your weapon bound. You will touch no route marker, rope, wall pin, shelter door, or signal stand."

"Agreed."

"And when no one asks, you will believe them."

I hesitated just long enough for her to notice.

"I'll listen," I said.

She led me into the kingdom.

The first person I approached was a cooper hammering wooden pegs into the brackets of a breakaway porch. His family carried hoops and staves uphill behind him.

"Do you want an escort?" I asked. "I can take you all beyond the western ridge before the animal arrives."

He squinted at the cloud. "Then who'd put my porch back up?"

"Your life is worth more than a porch."

"That's why I'm leaving the porch here and taking my life to my sister's kitchen." He struck the last peg flush. "No offense, hero, but you've made a poor bargain sound like generosity."

Neya did not smile. I wished she had. It would have been easier to dismiss her.

Farther on, two old women painted fresh white arrows at a junction where runoff channels crossed the road. They refused my offer without pausing their work. A baker loading sacks onto a handcart said the thunderback's last passage had ruined his oven and given him the best wheat crop of his life. He hoped to move the oven this time.

At a low house beneath the second terrace, a mother and two children were climbing an exterior stair. Their packs looked too small for flight.

"The ridge road is clear," I called. "I can carry the youngest."

The older child, a boy missing one front tooth, hugged a clay jar to his chest. "We're going to the viewing roof."

"You are not," his mother said.

"We brought plum cakes."

"We are going to the shelter gallery, from which there happens to be a safe view." She looked down at me. "The gallery is cut into the slope. It has two exits and stone between us and the route. We have practiced. Please don't frighten them."

The younger child was not frightened. She leaned between the rails and asked whether I had really held up a collapsing bridge while thirty people crawled over my back.

"Twenty-eight," I said.

"Did they say thank you?"

"Most of them."

"We said no thank you," the boy informed me.

Their mother herded them upward before I found an answer.

Everywhere I looked, Aldervane was taking itself apart in careful pieces. Clay pipes separated at cloth-wrapped joints. Shopfronts folded flat against stone. Fruit trees along the avenue had been trained low behind waist-high berms. White niches punctuated the red cliff at regular intervals, each marked with a painted spiral. Nothing was hidden. Nothing was abandoned thoughtlessly.

This should have reassured me.

Instead I felt the old uselessness gathering beneath my ribs.

For years I had reached places at the worst hour of their lives. People saw the sword over my shoulder and made room. They trusted me with choices they could not bear to make. In the moments after, when fires were out or floodgates shut or teeth no longer pressed at the door, I always knew exactly who I was.

Aldervane had made room, too. It simply was not for me.

The first horn sounded: one long note.

Neya snapped a yellow flag open. Down the avenue, wardens answered in sequence. On the terraces, doors closed. The last handcarts rolled behind stone barriers. I turned toward the eastern gap.

The thunderback entered Aldervane.

Up close, its size defeated comparison. It was not a house or a hill or a siege engine. It was an animal, and that was worse, because a wall did not breathe steam from four nostrils or twitch a hide heavy enough to crush a wagon. Its back plates overlapped in jagged rows, black at the roots and blue along the edges. Dry grass, thorn pods, and handfuls of dark mud clung in the gaps. Tiny white flowers grew behind one shoulder.

It followed the open road.

The ground shook. Window latches chattered on the empty houses. Static lifted my hair and filled my mouth with the taste of old coins. Rain advanced behind the animal in a gray curtain, but the street around us remained hot and dry.

Neya raised a red flag. We stood behind a retaining wall on the first terrace, high enough to see the route but well back from it. "Eastern team in shelter," she said, more to herself than to me. "Second wall clear. West gate standing by."

A runner appeared below, sprinting across the avenue.

She wore a yellow vest and carried a roll of blue cloth under one arm. The thunderback was three houses away. With every stride of the beast, stones jumped under the runner's boots.

"She's too late," I said.

"She is on count."

The runner reached the cliff side. Instead of climbing toward us, she dropped to her knees and vanished into one of the white spiral niches.

The thunderback lowered its head.

For one instant I did not see Aldervane. I saw another street years earlier, smoke turning daylight brown. I saw a cellar door jammed by falling beams and a hand reaching through the gap. The people there had told me the lower floor was empty. They had been wrong.

"Stay here," Neya ordered.

I was already over the retaining wall.

The niche sat beneath an overhanging ledge of red rock. If I brought the ledge down ahead of the thunderback, the impact would force it away from the cliff. Away from the runner. I tore the binding from my sword, drove the point into a seam, and put my shoulder against the hilt.

Neya shouted my name.

Stone resisted, then split.

The ledge came down in three great slabs and a boiling sheet of rubble. The thunderback reared. Lightning snapped across the avenue. One of the cheap walls burst outward. The animal swung its head from the noise and struck the fallen stone with one horn.

The ledge did not turn it back toward the center of the route.

It blocked the route.

The thunderback stepped sideways.

Above us, the occupied terraces clung to the northern slope.

The horns sounded three descending notes.

For a few breaths, Aldervane became all movement. Shutters banged open on the upper galleries. People streamed toward cut-stone stairs. Yellow flags flashed from roof to roof. A wall team hacked free the lashings on a second gap. Through it all, the thunderback kept edging north, seeking firm ground around the pile I had made.

Neya slid down the scree toward me. Blood striped one sleeve where a flying chip had caught her, but her signal flags remained in her hand.

"The niche has a stone roof and a rear shaft," she said. Her voice was low and terribly even. "It was built for runners. She was safe."

I looked at the rubble. "I can clear it."

"You can make more guesses, certainly."

The animal planted one broad foot on the curb. Clay blocks powdered beneath its weight.

"Tell me what to do."

Neya searched my face, perhaps for the argument I had given her at the boundary. I had none left.

"The danger is mine," I said. "At least partly. Use me."

"Entirely under my signals," she said. "You move only stones marked with blue paint. You do not chase the runner when she emerges. You do not improvise. Afterward, if there is an afterward, you answer to the district in public."

"Yes."

"Say it properly."

The thunderback's horn scraped the retaining wall. Cracks forked beneath my boots.

"I accept your command."

Neya raised the yellow flag.

Workers spilled from a side passage carrying pots of blue wash. Two dabbed marks across the fallen slabs while others threaded chains around the largest. I waited until Neya pointed to the first mark. Then I lifted.

My cracked ledge was heavier than the bridge of the old story, and no cheering crowd waited on the other side. Chains bit through my gloves. Six people hauled beside me, timing their pull to the horn blasts. We dragged the slab into the shell of an empty shop. A marked boulder followed.
