The caster gave a breath-short laugh that broke into a cough. "Your standards inspire confidence."

Ruva ignored them. Listing reasons had not changed the room. She changed tactics.

"A shield lane. A count I don't have to keep myself. Permission to abort if I lose the line."

"Yes. I drop the lane if my fingers go numb. If you lose the line, you stop. No blind cut."

"And the roof?"

"The posts carry most of it now, and the knot keeps its pressure divided. When you begin the final map, I take all four lines. About sixty heartbeats at full load."

The caster's hand closed over the clasp. "It stays. It's the only reason your people haven't killed me."

"It's also killing you," Ruva said. "Hold still and warn me when the false branch moves. I will try to separate it without cutting your shoulder. If you live, you go to treatment under ordinary guard. Not free. Alive."

"Try?"

"That's the true word."

The caster looked past her to Vekran. "And him?"

"Those are the terms," Vekran said. His voice had gone plain and thin. "Your companions have fled or fallen. Choose."

Dust spilled from a new crack overhead.

The caster released the clasp, though their fingers hovered beside it. "After each tightening, the false branch starts across on one. It lies over the living line on two and three. It clears on four. The gap after four lasts until the next tightening. I call every beat."

Ruva took chalk from her satchel and settled the edged apprentice blade in her grip. Stabilize for three breaths. Trace. Shift to guard. Turn the defensive pressure into bare floor. Part the braid. If the map blurred, stop.

Narrow enough to attempt. Too narrow for courage to improve.

* * *

Ruva tucked both hands into the warm fold of her cloak until her fingertips stung.

"Do I still have your yes to touch the shoulder?"

"Yes. The clasp stays until you cut it."

"If you pull away, I stop."

"This pass only settles the wound," Ruva told Vekran. "Keep the partial brace until I call the final map."

She cleaned the accessible skin, replaced the blood-wet cloth, and set her palms around the wound. Her warmth moved again. One breath: tissue edges, unsteady but distinct. Two: the caster's true pulse, quick beneath her little finger. Three: the imposed rhythm sliding beside it.

"Tightening," the caster whispered. "One."

Movement sounded at the broken side door.

An attacker from the courtyard lurched through, one hand braced on the frame, a short sword in the other. Their eyes found the caster.

"Traitor," they said, and drove forward.

Ruva released the healing working and stood. Six weeks had not taught her how to win a sword fight. Six weeks had taught her one short parry and how badly her guard recovered afterward.

The sword struck her bracer hard enough to bruise through leather. She caught it late, gave ground, and saw the attacker's wrist turn beneath the guard.

Inside line. The hand, not the shoulder.

Ruva cut once. The edge opened sleeve and skin shallowly across the exact disabling line. The attacker's grip sprang open. Their sword hit the floor.

She kicked it through the broken doorway. The attacker clutched the useless hand, stared at her, then stumbled after their fleeing companions rather than try Vekran's ward unarmed. Ruva did not pursue.

"Position," Vekran said.

Not praise. The thing she needed.

Ruva dropped beside the caster and raised a shield-sized hold as pressure snapped outward from the working they were still struggling to sustain. Her back foot slid in blood-damp dust. The hold buckled, flinging strain into her shoulder.

She let it go.

The pressure struck the wall above them and showered grit. Forcing the hold would have thrown it through the patients—or through Ruva.

"New count," she said. Her breath shook. "I lost the footing."

She shifted half a pace to dry stone. Her arm throbbed where the bracer had taken the sword. Vekran's hands shook now, too, but his partial brace remained fixed.

"Still yes?"

"Yes. Hurry."

"Call the branch. Nothing else."

The caster swallowed and nodded.

"The full load starts with my first breath," Ruva said.

"Ready," Vekran said.

Ruva put her palms back to the wound. Vekran drove his sword point deeper and, with one long exhale, interposed his fixed ward across all four roof lines. The ceiling settled the width of a finger as the intact posts shed their strain into him. His next breath stopped short.

"Full load," he said. "Sixty."

"First breath," Vekran counted.

Ruva found the living pulse.

"Second."

She found the false rhythm alongside it.

"Third breath. Forty-six heartbeats."

She drew chalk across the clasp where the narrow gap lay at that instant. Then she released the healing hold. The wound stayed bound by cloth and its own encouraged clotting, not cured, not safe for long.

Ruva shifted to guard.

The caster's trained reflex tightened the working as pain caught their breath. Pressure lashed from the clasp toward Ruva's chest. She met one bounded line with her bracer, set her weight through the dry back foot, and turned.

Force hammered into the floor. Tile split with a flat crack. Numbness rushed from her wrist to her elbow.

Moved, not erased.

"Thirty-four," Vekran said.

"One—moving," the caster gasped.

Ruva began the stroke toward the chalk mark, intending to land before the second beat.

"Two. Across. Stop."

The false branch slid across the living pulse.

Vekran's breath hitched. The beam above him dropped the width of a nail before his ward caught it again.

Every urgent part of Ruva wanted to finish the stroke. Faster. Stronger. Before the room chose for them.

But there was no safe line beneath her blade.

She aborted, drew back, and waited.

"Twenty-eight," Vekran said.

"Three. Hold," the caster said. Their whole body strained against the need to move. "Four. Clear. Now."

The false branch passed beyond the living pulse. In the promised gap before the next tightening, healer-sense gave Ruva the boundary her eyes could not: warm living tissue here, cold clasp there, shaped pressure crossing only the iron.

She cut on that line.

The blade passed through the edge of the clasp and the braided working with a sound like cloth tearing under water. The caster cried out but the edge cleared their shoulder.

The four roof loads released unevenly.

"Eighteen," Vekran said. He pulled his sword from the floor and turned with his whole body. He opened the ward toward the cleared strip between the doorway and the trough. Timber, tile, and force went outward through the path he chose, bursting across the empty paving in a roar of dust.

Then he dropped the hold before it could take the last warmth from his hands.

Part of the roof fell across the cleared strip, stopping short of the cart behind the rear wall. The inner beam settled onto the overturned table instead of the people behind it.

Vekran sank to one knee, conscious, his sword point resting on stone.

Ruva did not check whether anyone had seen her cut. She put the blade down, caught the caster before they slumped against the post, and pressed fresh cloth to the shoulder.

"Stay with me," she said. "The spell is over. The wound isn't."

* * *

By the time guards arrived from the road, Ruva had found six injuries, none immediately fatal. The driver needed watching for confusion. The patient with the bruised leg needed a splint for the journey. The caster needed warmth, fluids if they could keep them down, and proper cleaning before anyone considered removing what remained of the clasp.

Vekran needed stitches.

"Cloak first," Ruva told him.

"The caster—"

"Has mine and two warmed bricks. Give me your arm."

He did. His cut was shallow but longer than she had hoped, and his skin had the waxy chill of spent measurework. She cleaned and bound it; stitching could wait until there was better light and a roof that did not shed dust into open wounds.

The caster watched from a litter while a guard secured their uninjured wrist. Ruva checked the restraint for circulation, then checked the shoulder binding again.

"This isn't pardon," the caster said.

"No. It's transport. Keep that hand still."

They looked as if they had another taunt available. Exhaustion won. The litter went toward the road under guard.

The infirmary had lost half its roof. The medicine cart had a split axle and three bolts through its canvas. Those who could walk gathered blankets and unbroken jars from the dust. There would be repairs, statements, custody, more treatment. Nothing Ruva had done made those costs vanish.

Vekran sat against the wall with his bandaged arm inside the cloak. "Assessment."

Ruva was too tired to pretend not to know what he meant. "Of me?"

"By you."

She wanted one word: worthy or mistaken. He had never offered comfort where evidence would do, so she gave him the evidence.

"My recovery is weak. I failed the first hold because I didn't clear my footing. The turn worked and numbed my arm. The parting worked because the caster corrected my timing. I stabilized two patients." She looked at his bandage. "And one mentor who still needs stitches."

"Accurate."

"Is that why you chose me? To keep a witchknight alive after the work?"

"Partly. Not chiefly." He flexed his fingers, stopped when they trembled, and put the hand back under the cloak. "Anyone can be taught where to cut. I needed an apprentice already trained to ask what has to live through it."

Ruva glanced at the ruined room. "Then you should have said you wanted a healer. Not someone you meant to turn into a former healer."

"I thought bringing the satchel made that plain."

"It did not."

He considered this with the same seriousness he gave a bad map. "My error."

"The satchel stays in every field kit. Healing shifts count as witchknight training, not time away from it. Those are my terms."

"Agreed."

No ceremony. Ruva found that she preferred it.

Vekran nodded toward the broken tile where her turn had landed. "Your back foot was late."

"I noticed."

"Tomorrow—"

"Tomorrow you sleep. The day after, perhaps you may criticize my feet."

His mouth moved at one corner, too tired to become a smile.

When the damaged medicine cart finally rolled toward town, Ruva walked beside the patients. Her healer's satchel crossed one shoulder. Her edged apprentice sword crossed the other, cleaned and returned to its sheath.

The two weights pulled differently. After a dozen steps, Ruva stopped and shortened the sword strap until they balanced. Then she walked on.

stories.title: Hello, Lover
stories.prompt: A demon appears before your party, exclaiming “Hello lover!” Everyone looks at the bard, but then the cleric speaks up. “Actually, my ex is referring to me.”
stories.body:
# Hello, Lover

Emet Sarn had one hand on the stolen brass when he recognized the file mark.

Three shallow strokes crossed the lower hinge leaf, the middle one wandering crooked because Lacrixa had laughed into his shoulder while he worked. He had once known that scratch by touch in the dark. Now the leaf was bolted into an iron scaffold in a ruined roadside sanctuary, between three black loops and jars of salt-glass cloudy with someone else's stored charge.

“Familiar workmanship?” Udren asked from beneath the cracked arch. Her shield was already angled toward the doorway, the road settlement downhill, and every person who had ignored their warning to stay indoors.

Emet removed his thumb from the scratches. “Familiar principles.”

Not a lie, if one filed truth as badly as brass.

Bosk, the party's bard, crouched beside him, keeping his embroidered sleeves clear of the iron. “Can you quiet it?”

Emet pressed the stamped medallion at his throat, not for help from the inert silver but for the shelter-count cut into it. Breath in. Heat gathered behind his sternum. On the exhale, he fed a thread of his own ward-light through the stolen leaf to feel for the trap's edge.

The scaffold took everything he offered.

Heat drew an upright line in the air. The line opened hand-wide, showing red tile, white glare, and one amber eye.

Emet stopped breathing.

The opening widened. Lacrixa stepped through in a scorched traveling coat, a living demon from the far Cauterized Reach, one horn wrapped in a strip of copper cloth and her boot soles smoking against the sanctuary floor. She looked straight past Bosk and smiled at Emet with all her teeth.

“Hello lover!”

Everyone looked at Bosk.

It was, Emet had to admit, a reasoned response. On three previous jobs, Bosk's stage acquaintances had arrived through a window, a funeral procession, and a magistrate's evidence cupboard. All three had greeted him as if entering to applause.

Bosk put a hand to his chest. For once, he looked genuinely unprepared.

“Actually, my ex is referring to me.” Emet said it because collapse procedure began with correcting dangerous assumptions.

“I had a line,” Bosk said faintly. “It has left the stage.”

No one laughed. Iron slammed against iron behind Lacrixa. The first black loop cinched around the scaffold, brass reddened, and the sanctuary inhaled hard enough to lift ash from the floor.

Udren raised her shield. “Threat.”

Lacrixa's smile vanished. She caught the frame with both hands, the skin along her knuckles glowing the color of banked coals. “Three borrower loops. Freight pattern.” She looked at Emet. “What did you open?”

The pressure pulled at their clothes, toward the red seam.

Emet reached for the severing verse engraved inside his medallion. “I can close it.”

“If you want to cut a street in half.”

Lacrixa did not grab him. She stopped her hand a finger's width from his wrist and pointed instead. A shape wavered in the opening behind her: an apron, an upraised arm, a person backing away through kiln glare.

“Worker on the far side,” Udren said.

Emet lowered his hand.

“Good,” Lacrixa said. “The cleric can still be taught by evidence.”

“The frame is holding your passage open.”

“Our passage.” She tapped the brass with one claw. “This leaf has your keying. Mine signaled a forced expansion, so I supplied heat and breath to inspect it. You supplied ward-work here. The loops stored both contributions and bent them into this.”

The iron and glass had not invited her, chosen her, or made power of their own. They had redirected what two living people deliberately put in. That distinction would have comforted Emet if the redirect were not trying to tear two buildings together.

Ordinarily, their courtesy hinge admitted one traveler or stayed open eighty heartbeats, with fresh assent and living power at both ends. Mounting the stolen leaf in a new frame had not opened a road; the fence's work remained inert until its keyed bearer supplied a fresh living opening. By recognizing the leaf and powering the rig, Emet had knowingly met that condition, and Lacrixa had answered from her side.

Bosk edged toward the wall, out of the suction's straight path. “For the record, I prefer entrances with a rehearsed exit.”

Lacrixa did not glance at him.

His mouth shut. “What beat do you need?”

“Not yet.” She leaned close to the scaffold. Ember-light moved from her palm into the metal; her own, spent by choice. The black loops answered by brightening at three separate joints. “North jamb. Under the floor. Behind the throat. Remove them in that order, bleed each charge into stone, and then we withdraw together after I'm home.”

Emet watched the salt-glass turn milk-white. “Or sever before the next pulse and accept damage to an empty endpoint.”

“It isn't empty.”

“We evacuate it.”

“In the time you took to say that, the scaffold pulled another six feet of my kiln court into alignment.” She pointed to the stolen leaf. “Why is your private half in a freight rig?”

Udren's gaze moved to him. “Compromised?”

“The leaf was stolen with other brasswork. We caught the fence. We followed the components here.”

All true. None sufficient.

“And you recognized it,” Lacrixa said.

Air reversed.

The first pulse struck with a sound below hearing. Emet's teeth rang. The opening flared wider, revealing a crowded court of red tile and copper awnings. Two workers dragged a third away from a rack of cooling vessels. A tool cart rolled toward them without anyone touching it. Here, a crack raced through the sanctuary arch, and hot wind poured downslope through the broken wall.

“Answer,” Udren said.

Emet looked at the arch, the road, the widening seam—every exposure except Lacrixa. “After the first loop.”

Lacrixa's tail struck the floor once, a hard refusal.

“We lose both sites if we debate provenance now,” he said. Formality settled over his voice like ceremonial cloth. “Give me the discharge order, and I will answer after the first loop is safe.”

“One loop,” Lacrixa said. “Then no more careful fractions.”

Udren wedged her shield under the sagging arch. “Deadline accepted. Move.”

* * *

The north-jamb loop hung twelve feet up, its iron collar sunk behind rotten stone. Udren planted her boots and took the arch's weight on her shield while Emet climbed the scaffold. Below, Bosk unhooked the small frame drum from his pack.

“Eight beats,” Lacrixa said. “We feed on one and five. Pull the pin on seven. Stone takes it on eight.”

“A sparse arrangement,” Bosk said. He struck the drum once, listened to the sanctuary answer, and adjusted his grip. “Again.”

The second beat came clean and low.

Emet set his palm against one side of the brass. Lacrixa took the other. They had done this hundreds of times in two years: her heat rising as his breath left, his ward steadying when hers flared. His body found the old timing before his pride could object.

One. He fed the smallest possible thread.

Five. Lacrixa answered. The brass warmed between them.

Seven. Udren drove out the inert pin with the boss of her shield.

Eight. Emet turned their joined charge down through the scaffold's foot. Foundation stone flashed white. The loop dropped, empty and ordinary, and shattered a floor tile.

The sudden relief made his knees loosen. Lacrixa's glow had faded around her knuckles.

“Question,” she said.

“Second loop first.”

She stared until he added, “Please.”

Udren did not look up from the arch. “He bought one loop. Debt's due.”

The floor bucked beneath them. The second collar tightened under a fractured paving slab, dragging its iron staples deeper. Bosk moved his drumbeat faster at Lacrixa's signal while Udren lowered the arch onto a surviving pillar and crossed the room. Emet knelt, hooked numb fingers beneath the slab, and lifted with her.

“Cut?” Udren asked.

“No,” Emet said.

“Not the leaf. The staple.”

“Left one only.” Lacrixa was already bracing the opposite edge. “Right carries the throat.”

Udren struck left. The staple split. Emet and Lacrixa breathed on one and five, and the old coordination returned in humiliating details: the slight turn of her wrist that meant hold; the way his thumb shifted before he sent power; the shared half-breath they had used when a hearthframe caught in wet weather.

He remembered her bare feet on the table in their rented room, polishing hinge pins while he wrote shelter reports. They had been twenty-eight and thirty-one when they began, adults with separate work and keys and the belief that asking clearly would keep them from hurting each other. For a while, it had.

The second loop came free.

The second pulse caught its stored charge before it could discharge. The salt-glass flashed.

The kiln court disappeared. In its place stood their old room: narrow bed, blue washbasin, rain stippling the window. On the table lay two unfinished cups and the little file Lacrixa had jostled when she laughed. The image was no memory Emet had meant to offer. But the charged metal had been shaped to widen whatever route-impressions its living bearers supplied, and his trained intent had reached for safety as it had once looked.

Lacrixa went very still.

Then she saw the repaired corner on his leaf, the bright solder line made after the last winter they shared.

“You kept it keyed.”

A roof slab broke loose.

Udren shoved Bosk clear and caught the worst of it on her shield. Stone struck stone. Dust erased the room, the court, and half the sanctuary. Emet fell into the side alcove with Lacrixa. A tilted pillar blocked them from the others, though Bosk's drum continued through the dust—slower now, a pulse they could follow.

Lacrixa's eyes found him in the red gloom. “You kept it keyed.”

Emet put his shoulder against the pillar. It did not move. “Yes.”

“The letter said your oath required a clean severance.”

His silence had once passed for dignity at council tables. Here it was simply an answer.

“I won't trust final withdrawal to another silence,” she said. No endearment now, no ceremony. “Tell me what I am trusting.”

* * *

Ash blew through the alcove. Each breath scraped. Emet's right hand shook against the frame, and Lacrixa's skin had cooled from ember-red to dull brown at the fingertips. Beyond the pillar, Udren cursed once, concisely, while stone ground over metal.

“I was offered the permanent circuit,” Emet said. “Six shelters. Twenty years.”

“I remember your chronology.”

Of course she did. He had used dates in the letter the way a mason used rubble: to fill the space where a proper stone should go.

“The House of Common Shelter did not forbid us,” he said.

Lacrixa stopped examining the frame.

The third pulse gathered in the salt-glass, a cloudy brightness that grew with every breath they lost.

“They did not ask me to choose the circuit over you,” Emet continued. “You asked whether I wanted a shared home. I was afraid to leave my work. I was afraid to ask you to leave yours. And I was more afraid to say that I didn't know which fear mattered more.”

“So you invented a prohibition.”

“Yes.” The word hurt less than the long explanations had. That was no credit to him. “I made myself obedient instead of cowardly. I let you believe the institution I served had judged you unfit. Then I kept the leaf because calling uncertainty a safety precaution sounded better than admitting I wanted a door I had refused to walk through.”

“And today?”

“I recognized the file marks before I powered the rig. I did not tell them.”

Her face changed by almost nothing. It had always been dangerous to mistake her stillness for absence.

“I spent three years preparing arguments,” she said. “Rules of residence. Kiln-court protections. Precedents from mixed households in the Reach. I had an answer for every objection your House never made.”

The charge brightened behind her. Bosk's beat came through the pillar: steady, asking nothing.

“I am sorry,” Emet said. “For the lie then. For the concealment now. Both were choices. Neither protected anyone.”

He did not add that he had loved her. That fact was visible in the danger around them and useless as a claim.

Lacrixa crouched beside the second loop and worked a claw under its split edge. “I kept my leaf locked away because breaking one half without neutral de-keying can leave a dangerous echo. That was the technical reason.” She pried. Iron screamed. “The other reason was that I wanted you to have to answer me someday. Pride can wear procedure too.”

The admission did not divide fault equally. It was not offered to do so.

“Do you forgive me?” Emet did not ask.

Instead he said, “Will you trust me for one synchronized withdrawal?”

“I will trust the count. I will trust what you do on it.” Her eyes held his. “We are finishing the road, Emet. We are not beginning again.”

“Understood.”

The third pulse broke.

He and Lacrixa threw their remaining power down together. The second loop released its charge into the foundation, and the tilted pillar jumped aside. Udren hauled Emet through the gap by his collar. Bosk caught Lacrixa's forearm, failed to hide his surprise at how cold her skin had become, and adjusted his grip without comment.

No one had time for relief. Behind them, the third loop glowed white.

* * *

“Full account,” Udren said.

Emet forced air into his lungs. “The leaf is mine. I kept it keyed. The last loop sits behind the throat. Once it's removed, Lacrixa crosses, and we both revoke future access on Bosk's count.”

Udren compressed everything she wanted to say into three questions. “Other traps?”

“None I know.”

“Can she close her side?”

“Yes.”

“Will you release on count?”

The honest answer arrived before the respectable one. “I am afraid I won't.”

“Then I stand with you.” She turned to Lacrixa. “Shield before or behind?”

Lacrixa pointed into the widening seam. “Behind me until I clear. The court roof is shedding tile.”

Udren moved without hesitation, placing her shield between Lacrixa and the falling stone of her own home.

Bosk tightened the drum strap around his burned fingers. “Eighty heartbeats until this tries freight width?”

“At most,” Lacrixa said.

“One tempo. On sixty, Udren takes the pin. On seventy, Lacrixa crosses. On seventy-eight, the leaves break. On eighty, nobody is between.” He looked from face to face. “That is the arrangement. No solos.”

Emet nodded.

“Good,” Bosk said, and began.

* * *

At twelve, the opening widened to the height of the arch.

At twenty, kiln wind struck sanctuary air. Heat blasted one way while tools, roof tiles, and loose stones skidded the other. Emet held the near edge with both palms, feeding ward-light through muscles that no longer wanted to close. Lacrixa held the far edge. Her coat snapped in the crossing wind; her horns were dark against the furnace glare.

At thirty-four, Udren advanced behind her shield. The third loop lay behind the throat, visible whenever the opening shuddered: black iron, a hot clasp, one pin driven through the scaffold's rear brace.

At forty, the sanctuary roof began to peel.

Bosk's beat did not change.

Emet's ward-light had once illuminated whole refuge halls. Now it barely silvered his fingers. The scaffold held no strength of its own, but its salt-glass reservoirs returned his earlier contribution in distorted surges, each one demanding that he spend more to keep the person-wide center clear.

At fifty-two, Lacrixa missed her handhold.

Emet shifted as she recovered, matching the old half-breath. Intimacy lived in the body longer than permission. It told him what she would do. It did not entitle him to decide for her.

“Clasp won't lift,” Udren called.

Lacrixa pressed both cooling hands around the hot iron. A last ember-glow moved out of her skin by choice. The clasp softened, then sagged around the pin.

“Foundation,” she ordered.

Emet took one hand from the edge. The throat narrowed, throwing a strip of kiln light across Udren's shield. He drove what remained of his ward down the rear brace. The foundation stone whitened, ready to receive the stored charge.

Sixty.

Udren hit the pin.

It moved the width of a thumbnail and jammed.

She hit it again. The shield slipped in the suction. A tile from the kiln court struck its rim. Lacrixa caught Udren's shoulder before she pitched into the throat, and the three of them lost the count beneath a roar of moving air.

The drum tore free of Bosk's hands. It sailed through the breach and vanished among the copper awnings.

“Sixty-four!” Bosk shouted. His voice cracked, but his tempo did not. “Sixty-five! Sixty-six!”

Udren planted one boot against the scaffold and drove her shield boss into the pin.

At sixty-nine, it came free.

The final loop dropped. White fire ran harmlessly down the prepared line into dead stone, but the throat convulsed around the sudden absence of its brace.

“Cross!” Emet shouted.

Lacrixa backed through first, facing them. Udren followed just far enough to keep the shield over her while remaining on the sanctuary side. At seventy-three, falling tile struck the top edge. At seventy-five, Lacrixa stumbled.

Emet poured more of himself into the leaf.

“Seventy-six!” Bosk called.

Lacrixa rolled, rose on the red tile, and turned. One boot was visible. The other vanished behind the warping edge.

Emet held.

“Seventy-seven!”

The opening drank his breath. Red spread through the brass again. The empty loop sockets began to shine as his continued supply recharged the route.

“Emet.” Lacrixa's voice crossed the narrowing distance. “Both feet clear.”

He could not see them.

He held.

Udren abandoned the pin. She caught his forearm in both hands and planted his palm flat against the stone beside the leaf. She did not tear him away. She made him feel something that was not the open road: grit, weight, the shaking of his own muscles.

“Off,” she said.

Across the breach, Lacrixa reached her hearthframe. “You do not keep me safe by keeping access.”

No ornament. No technical argument. A command he had spent three years earning.

“Seventy-eight!” Bosk shouted.

Emet withdrew.

The loss of power struck like a missed stair. He sagged against Udren, but his right hand found the stolen leaf. He wrenched it from the loosened bolts, set its keyed edge against the foundation, and bent with what little strength remained.

Across the narrowing sight-window, Lacrixa pulled her leaf from its hearthframe. Embercraft lit one fingertip. She melted the keyed edge into a bright, useless curve and let the ruined brass fall onto the red tile beside the frame.

Emet's brass folded under his weight.

“No future invitation,” Lacrixa said.

“None,” he answered.

The opening shrank to hand-width. Behind her, people lifted the fallen kiln worker. Here, the sanctuary settled by inches instead of collapsing. Both places remained themselves.

For one beat, Lacrixa's face filled the small square of light.

Emet did not ask if they would meet again.

“Goodbye, Lacrixa.”

She studied him as if accuracy still mattered, because it did. “Goodbye, Emet.”

The window closed.

* * *

At first light, the road settlement still stood. Smoke marked one scorched field below the sanctuary, but no freight breach had opened above it, and no one had been pulled from the kiln court.

Before dawn, they spent an hour shoring the wounded arch with salvaged beams. Emet could lift only with his left hand. Bosk worked without turning the labor into a performance, and Udren accepted no assurance about a brace that she could not test with her own weight. Each time the wind stirred ash through the scaffold, Emet looked at the warped loops. The iron stayed cold.

Bosk wrapped his burned fingertips in strips torn from the lining of his least embroidered sleeve. Udren bound Emet's strained wrist with considerably less tenderness and considerably better tension.

Emet gave them the fuller account: the two adult years he and Lacrixa had chosen together, the false letter, the retained leaf, the moment he recognized it and said nothing. He kept his sentences plain. Neither oath nor magic received the blame.

Udren tied off the bandage. “We discuss field trust after we deliver the evidence.”

“Yes.”

Bosk glanced at the dead scaffold. There was room for a joke in his expression. He let it pass. “Can you walk?”

Emet tested his legs. “Slowly.”

“A tempo I can manage.”

They left Emet's folded leaf, the three warped loops, the spent salt-glass, and the dead iron scaffold for the local authorities. Udren propped the sanctuary's ordinary door open with a fallen stone. Cool morning moved through it, and Emet followed his companions outside.

stories.title: Transitions in Common
stories.prompt: Your friend got so excited when you said you're trans like them. You just figured out too late they meant transgender, not actually a shapeshifter like you. - update the rate for this story to YA-14+ - male vs female identity play
stories.body:
# Transitions in Common

The black jacket was going to betray me by fitting perfectly.

I stood in the costume-room mirror late Friday, one arm through a sleeve, and watched the shoulder seam land exactly where it should on the masculine body I wore to school. On my practiced feminine body, the same seam would slide down my arm and the button would pull. The jacket didn't know that. Clothes were loyal to measurements, not people.

"Are you planning to return that," Hugo asked, "or form a permanent attachment?"

"I'm waiting for it to admit it has limitations."

He usually would have told me the jacket's greatest limitation was me. Instead, he checked the corridor, shut the costume-room door, and tested the latch twice.

"I need to ask you about the portrait," he said.

Monday's arts-night display required a self-portrait. Hugo had been avoiding his with the dedication of someone studying for an exam in avoidance. I pulled my arm free and rehung the jacket.

"I can take it. You can veto every shot."

"That's part of it." He flattened a crooked paper label on a box of gloves. "I want to control the clothes and who sees it. And I want you to understand why."

The room held its usual smells of dust, hot stage lights, and fabric that had survived too many imaginary centuries. Beyond the door, a rack squeaked along the auditorium floor and faded away.

Hugo said, "I'm trans."

I knew the common meaning of the word. Of course I did. But he had locked the door. He had mentioned photographs and clothes and being seen as the wrong version. For years, I had shortened my own impossible secret to the same four letters inside my head, because naming a thing privately was safer than explaining it aloud.

Hope reached the sentence before sense did.

"Me too," I said.

His whole face changed—not into another face, which should have warned me, but from braced to bright. "You're serious?"

"Completely. Nobody at school knows."

"I had no idea." He laughed once, mostly breath. "I thought maybe, because of the they/them, but I wasn't going to decide for you."

I heard *decide for you* and thought of body maps held behind my teeth, each one mine and none safe to show. "Thank you."

"How long have you known?"

"I started changing a few years ago. I got better at it slowly."

His excitement softened. "Yeah. Slowly sounds familiar."

That could have been the moment. So could half a dozen moments after it. Instead, we traded truths with the important noun cut out. He said photographs could pin other people's expectations to you. I said one version of me had ended up on every school record, so I kept using it even when another fit better. He said telling parents could be complicated. I said mine expected consistency.

Neither of us asked the question that might demand an answer we weren't ready to give.

"This stays here," Hugo said at last. "You don't tell anyone about me."

"Never. Same for me?"

"Obviously." He looked offended that I needed to ask, which made me trust him more. "Will you help me find something tomorrow? For the portrait. Then Sunday, we can change here and take it before anyone arrives."

I looked at the jacket, then at my friend, and imagined opening one locked door in my life.

"Yes," I said.

We meant different doors.

* * *

At the secondhand shop on Saturday, Hugo rejected three vests for being too shiny, too square, and "designed for a child magician with tax problems."

The fourth was charcoal gray and plain enough that he went quiet when he saw himself in it. He rolled the sleeves of an open-collar shirt beneath it and shifted under the fitting-room lights, checking the line from shoulder to waist.

"That one," I said.

"You didn't even make a joke."

"I respect the vest."

"Terrifying."

I had kept my school body for the trip. It matched the face people knew, and shopping already required enough arithmetic without changing height halfway through. Still, I took a soft blue blouse from the next rack and pulled it over my T-shirt. Its narrow cut sat oddly across my current shoulders, but I liked the drape of the sleeves.

Hugo glanced over. "Also that one."

"It doesn't fit."

"It doesn't fit *like that*."

I stared at him. The sentence was so exactly right under my meaning that it felt like a hand offered in the dark.

I added the blouse to our basket, then found a sharply cut jacket one size larger. The jacket worked over the blouse. Neither garment changed who was inside it, but together they made my reflection feel less like a form waiting to be filed under one heading.

Hugo watched me gather trousers in two sizes and another shirt in a third. "Planning several lives?"

"Same life. Unreliable measurements."

"Bodies are inconsiderate that way."

"Do your shoulders take long to settle?" I asked.

His attention snapped from the mirror to me. "I'm not discussing my body in detail. Or medical decisions. If I bring something up, fine. Otherwise, no."

Heat reached my ears. I had been trying to ask how quickly he transformed without making him prove anything. I had managed to be invasive under either interpretation.

"Right. Sorry. You don't owe me mechanics."

He studied me for another second, then tugged the vest straight. "Bodies don't move on command just because someone wants them to. That's all I'm saying."

I nodded, privately impressed by what I mistook for discipline. My own first changes had taken months of failed concentration before I learned the trick of holding a body-map and releasing my breath into it.

At the shop's little counter, Hugo paid for the vest and shirt. Outside, we divided the bags and reviewed Sunday as if precision about logistics could compensate for the noun neither of us had supplied.

"No portrait gets displayed unless I approve the exact picture," he said. "No posting it."

"Agreed. And when I'm changing: no camera, no coming in, no touching."

"I wasn't planning to tackle you into your trousers."

"Good. They're fragile."

The joke landed badly enough that I hurried on. "We could each show the other a version not many people see. If you want."

Hugo adjusted the paper handles cutting into his fingers. "You first or me first?"

"Same time? Screens between us."

"Then we come out when we're ready."

"Yes."

"Okay," he said. "I trust you."

That should have slowed me down. Instead, it felt like permission to run.

* * *

On Sunday, I put a PRIVATE FITTING sign on the costume-room door, checked the latch, and turned Hugo's instant camera facedown on a table. I set my water bottle and two oat bars beside it. A full change always left me thirsty, hungry, and weak in the muscles, and it made another full change unreliable for twenty minutes. Preparation was how I made danger look like tidiness.

Hugo arrived carrying the vest and shirt. "You brought emergency rations?"

"Wardrobe is strenuous."

He gave the food a puzzled glance but took his clothes behind the left screen. I went behind the right in loose trousers and a sweatshirt with enough room to forgive several versions of me.

Fabric rustled on his side. A button clicked against the floor, followed by a quiet, heartfelt complaint. Then Hugo said, "Ready."

I put my hand on the screen's wooden edge. "Ready for me to change?"

"Yes."

He had agreed to witness a change of clothes. I had asked permission to do something I had never named. My excitement called the difference unimportant.

I chose the familiar map of my feminine body. I held it whole: shorter reach, lighter frame, a different line to my face, longer hair, a voice that resonated higher without becoming anybody else's. Then I let out the breath I had been holding.

Warmth spread from my ribs through my shoulders and down my legs. The sweatshirt loosened, then caught at one hip as my balance shifted. My heels pressed differently into the floor. The top of the screen rose in my vision as I lost a few centimeters of height. I kept breathing. My jaw eased under my fingertips; hair brushed my neck, then the cloth between my shoulder blades. Every few seconds, the remembered map tugged against the body I was leaving, not painfully, but with the deep fatigue of holding a difficult pose.

At thirty seconds, my hands were trembling from effort. At forty, the warmth settled. I was still Cody. I had the same scuff on my left knee, the same promise to protect Hugo's secret, and the same terrible habit of believing preparation made me careful.

I stepped out.

Hugo emerged at the same time in the charcoal vest and open-collar shirt. It was exactly the look he had chosen: simple, sharp, entirely his.

Then he saw me.

My hair was still shortening by a final fraction around my face, and the last warmth was leaving my throat. His hand tightened on the screen.

"Hey," I said. My changed voice made the ordinary word unmistakably strange. "It's me."

His gaze went from my face to my unchanged sweatshirt to my face again. "Cody?"

"Yes." I waited for astonishment to become delight. "So. When do you change?"

He looked down at his vest. "I did."

"No, I mean—"

"I changed my clothes."

We stood there, each waiting for the other to catch up.

Hugo said, very carefully, "When I told you I was trans, I meant I'm a transgender boy."

Every double-edged sentence from the last two days turned at once. Not magic. Not body maps. Not a secret ability. Hugo had trusted me with himself, and I had answered from a private dictionary he had never seen.

"Oh," I said.

His face closed. "Did you understand what I told you?"

"I thought you meant—what I can do. I use it as a shortened word. For transmutable. Only in my head, mostly, but everything you said about changing and pictures and—"

"Did you know I might mean transgender?"

The technical defense crowded my mouth. I hadn't lied. I had told him something true. We both had secrets and complicated clothes and versions other people expected to see.

"I knew that was one meaning," I said.

"The usual meaning."

"Yes. But with the locked door, and you said—"

"You let me keep talking." His voice narrowed rather than rose. "You said 'me too.' I told you more because I thought you understood that part of my life. Did you?"

"I understand hiding. And people deciding what they see. There are similarities."

"That's not what I asked."

I reached for the body-map of my school form. If I changed back, maybe the room would contain one less impossible thing. I pulled in a breath.

"Stop," Hugo said. "Don't turn into someone else to win the argument."

"It's not someone else. It's all me. I can show you."

"I said stop."

I should have listened. Panic made the choice for speed, though the power still waited for me to initiate it. I released my breath too soon.

Heat lurched through me and stalled. My shoulders shifted wider; my height returned halfway; my face found a stable line between two practiced maps and refused to move farther. Dizziness tipped the room. I caught the screen, but my hand shook hard enough to knock a hanger from its hook.

The metal clattered across the floor.

Three knocks struck the door. "Hello? I need the rolling rack."

The handle pushed against the latch.

My school face was gone. The feminine one was gone too. The mixed body I had once imagined showing Hugo with a ridiculous flourish now felt like evidence under a bare bulb. Another full change wasn't available. The camera was facedown, but memory needed no lens.

Hugo stared at the door, then at me. He could have picked up his bag and left the problem with its owner.

Instead, he stepped into the corridor, pulling the door shut behind him.

"Private wardrobe fitting," he said through the thin panel. His voice had gone calm in the way it did when calm was work. "I'll bring the rack out. Give us ten minutes."

Wheels rattled. The other student said something too muffled to catch. A minute later, Hugo returned alone and locked the door.

"Thank you," I whispered.

He picked up the camera and capped its lens. "I protected your secret. That wasn't forgiveness."

"I know. I'm sorry, I just thought the word meant the other thing, and you have to understand I've never told anyone, and—"

"You're doing it again."

The sentence stopped me more cleanly than the cooldown had.

Hugo folded the charcoal vest with exact, angry care. He put it beside the reflector and spare film instead of in his bag. "I don't want your explanation right now. I don't want to take a portrait. I want to leave."

This time, I listened.

He took his camera and shirt. The vest and the rest of the gear stayed behind. The latch clicked after him.

I sat on the floor in the body I had wanted him to see, drank water with both hands around the bottle, and waited until I was strong enough to go back to the face on my school records.

* * *

Twenty minutes later, the familiar map held. I ate both oat bars before walking home with Hugo's vest, the reflector, and the spare film in a shop bag.

That evening, I wrote him four explanations and deleted them. One described body maps. One explained why *transmutable* was technically accurate. One listed all the things I thought we had in common. The fourth was six paragraphs long and contained the word *but* nine times.

I deleted that one twice.

What I sent was shorter.

*I assumed what you meant instead of asking. I said "me too" and let you believe I shared an experience I did not understand. I accepted more of your private disclosure because of that claim. Today I asked if I could change, but I did not say shapeshift, and you did not give permission to witness that. I'm sorry.*

*What you told me stays private. My ability is a separate secret, and you can decide whether you want to keep it; you do not owe me a reply, forgiveness, or an explanation of being transgender. Tell me where to return the vest and portrait gear.*

Nothing came back Sunday night.

On Monday, at lunch, my phone buzzed.

*Costume room after school. Bring the gear. No shifting until we've talked. I still want my portrait.*

It was not forgiveness. It was an appointment, which was more than I had earned the right to expect.

* * *

I arrived in my masculine school body because Hugo had named the limit plainly. The vest lay folded over my arm. The reflector and film were in the bag. I set all of it on the table and left the camera where he had placed it.

Hugo locked the door, but this time the sound offered no secret meaning.

"I'm sorry," I said. "For all four things in the message."

He leaned against the table, arms folded. "What do you think we have in common?"

My mind produced a careful twelve-part answer with definitions. I let it pass.

"People make guesses about us," I said. "We both care who gets private information and what words people use. That's some common ground. My body changing is not the same thing as you being a transgender boy. I don't know your history or what you need, and I shouldn't have claimed I did."

"And what you can do doesn't tell me your gender."

It was not a question, so I didn't treat it like one. "Right."

He watched me long enough that I noticed every piece of lint on the vest.

"Can I ask what your gender is?" he said. "You can say no."

"You can ask." I looked at my hands, familiar in this form because school had made them routine. "I don't have a finished answer. Cody is right. They and them are right in every body. Masculine feels good sometimes. Feminine feels good sometimes. Mixed feels good sometimes. None of that hands me a label. Questioning, maybe. Genderfluid, maybe. I'm not choosing today."

Hugo nodded once. He did not tell me what I was.

"I don't want questions about anatomy or medical history," he said. "If I decide to talk about something, I start it. You don't tell anyone I'm trans."

"Agreed. I don't want anyone told I can shapeshift. No filming a change, no touching me during one, and no demonstrations unless I say yes to that exact thing."

"And 'changing' means clothes unless somebody supplies a better noun."

"Yes." A weak joke presented itself. I put it down before it could hurt anyone. "I'm retiring my private shorthand. Transmutable was never useful enough to cause this much damage."

"Can I ask one question about the shapeshifting?"

"You can ask. I might not answer."

"Can you look like anyone?"

"No. Only human versions of me. I can adjust them, but I can't copy another person. And fear can ruin a change; it can't start one unless I choose it."

"Okay." Hugo nodded and did not reach for a second question.

Hugo reached over and turned the vest so its buttons faced upward. "I'm willing to keep being friends. I'm not willing to pretend this didn't happen. I may ask extremely literal questions for a while."

Relief tried to make me promise everything forever. "Okay," I said.

"Good. I still need a portrait."

"Can I ask what you want the display to tell people?"

"That the vest was worth twelve." His mouth shifted, almost a smile. "Nothing about what I told you on Friday. If that changes, I decide."

That was how Hugo chose to continue: not with a speech, but by putting on the shirt and vest he had selected and standing on the strip of faded tape that marked the portrait corner.

I checked the latch. I asked whether he wanted the curtain in frame. He said no. I asked whether I could raise the camera. He said yes.

The first print caught him glancing toward the door. He studied it while the image developed, then handed it back.

"Again. Move left so the light isn't flattening the vest."

I moved. Hugo reset his shoulders, lifted his chin by a fraction, and looked into the lens because he had chosen to. The second picture emerged slowly: open collar, dark vest, steady expression.

"That one," he said. "That one can go in the display."

I wrote nothing on it. It was his image.

Hugo took the camera from me and set it down on the table. "Do you want a portrait?"

"Yes."

"Do you want to change first?"

"Yes. Specifically, shapeshift."

"May I stay in the room?"

"By the door. Don't touch me. Camera down and capped until I say I'm finished."

He placed it facedown, clicked on the cap, and moved to the door.

I changed with water and food ready, though Sunday was far enough behind me that the cooldown had long passed. I held the feminine map first. Warmth loosened my jaw and shortened my reach; the blouse settled closer as my shoulders changed. Then I chose deliberately between the practiced maps—not a truest body, not a compromise, simply the one I wanted for this picture. I stopped with my height and face in their mixed range. The same old scuff marked my knee. The same nerves made me check the jacket seam twice.

I put the sharply cut jacket over the soft blue blouse.

"Finished," I said.

Only then did Hugo lift the camera.

"Name?" he asked.

"Cody."

"Pronouns?"

"They and them."

"Can I take the picture?"

"Yes."

He waited until I chose how to stand. The shutter clicked.

As the print darkened between us, Hugo asked, "May I keep this?"

"One copy. Private. No display, no sharing."

"Okay."

We sat at the costume table with the two approved prints between us. Beneath the portrait in the charcoal vest, Hugo wrote **HUGO — DISPLAY**. Beneath the face no school record knew, I wrote **CODY — PRIVATE**.

We left them side by side while the images finished developing, each label in its owner's hand.

stories.body:
# What I Hate Most

Stormglass reached Vantress before Queen Draxenne did.

It lay across the northern dark like a bruise: violet at the advancing edge, black behind, dense with mineral grit torn out of the Cinder March. The last evacuation wagons labored through the gate beneath her while she climbed the parapet. Wet ropes slapped stone. Wheels struck cracks that should have been repaired three seasons ago. On the road behind them, people ran with cloth bound over their mouths and one hand on whoever could not run as quickly.

Draxenne had brought twelve ceramic plates, four carts of powdered stone, and a channeling plan that could keep that road alive. At thirty-nine, she had learned not to arrive at a border dispute with only an argument.

Night-Sovereign Ombria stood at the central pylon with one bare hand spread upon its palm-worn surface.

Five brass pressure studs knocked beneath her fingers, each carrying the mechanical pulse of a different ward district. Ombria listened to all five, but gave active shadow to four: four thin planes rose beneath her boots, barely visible except where the lamps broke against their edges. The fifth stud carried pressure only until she chose to answer it. Her black coat streamed in the grit. Her face was composed, severe, and much too pale.

Forty-two years old, and still determined to spend herself as if the city had appointed her an inexhaustible resource.

“The Ninth Conduit is split,” Ombria said without looking around. “I am pulling the lattice inward.”

On the slate pressure map, a fresh white fracture crossed the border junction. The inward seal would keep the crowded inner streets behind layers of angled shadow. It would also strip the March road and the outer settlements bare.

“No,” Draxenne said.

Ombria's smallest finger twitched as a southern district called. The nearest shadow plane flexed. “An unusually concise objection.”

“I save my ornament for listeners.” Draxenne laid one prepared plate over the conduit housing. Its clay surface was grooved for venting, its edges already dusted with mineral fuel. “The old spillway is empty. Give me the Ninth. You baffle the gale; I fuse the glass and drop it before it reaches either side.”

“Your heat passes below the inner market.”

“Contained heat.”

“A phrase beloved by people standing outside the container.”

Another stud struck Ombria's palm. Her shoulders did not move, but the words came a fraction slower. Draxenne touched the back of Ombria's wrist. Cold bit through her glove.

Ombria withdrew before the touch could become anything but evidence. “Do not make my body your argument.”

There it was: a fault line cleaner than the one on the slate. Draxenne could press it, or she could save the people choking on her road.

“Thirty breaths,” she said. “Whoever holds the conduit at the end commands it for this breach.”

At last, Ombria turned. She released one district plane long enough to face Draxenne fully, and darkness fell flat behind her. “A spoken yield, a spoken withdrawal, or loss of contact with the housing ends a claim. No cast enters a body. No strike touches a ward sheltering civilians.”

“Agreed.”

“The winner gains the Ninth Conduit for this breach. Nothing else. No office, no territory, no future audience, no touch.”

Draxenne smiled despite the storm crawling toward them. “You make victory sound dreary.”

Ombria put her free hand on the housing. “The first breath has begun.”

* * *

Draxenne locked her left hand around the lower lip of the housing and opened her right fist.

Blue-white cinders ran from the plate beneath her palm, thin as wire and hot enough to paint both women's faces in hard light. She sent the stream for the conduit latch. Ombria folded her own shadow up between them. Flame struck the dark plane, compressed, and spat backward through the plate's vents.

Draxenne turned her head before the flare took her eyes. Four breaths.

She dragged the stream sideways through grit lodged in the parapet seam. The cinders obeyed her attention, eating a bright path through mineral dust toward the housing's western edge. Ombria changed the angle of her wrist. Her plane changed with it, shunting the heat toward open air.

She could have angled it into Draxenne's ribs. She did not.

Draxenne could have let the stream lick across Ombria's bare hand. She broke it around her fingers instead, a white fork close enough to raise steam from damp stone.

Ombria's mouth curved by the smallest treacherous amount.

Eight breaths.

Draxenne drove a second stream through a ceramic groove. Ombria let one quiet district plane flatten into ordinary darkness, stepped onto the maintenance bridge, and drew a second contesting plane from the shadow of her moving body. She crossed the two like shears across Draxenne's route, four planes active in all. The bridge shuddered beneath the approaching gale. Ombria's dark silhouette held at its center, coat snapping, one hand shaping the planes while the other kept contact with the iron-rimmed housing.

Dark-queen nonsense, Draxenne thought. Appointed by a council, worked to numbness, answerable to half a million complaints, and still somehow composed like night had dressed itself for her.

Draxenne advanced.

Her first stream curled low. Her second climbed. Ombria constricted them between two shadow planes, stealing the open air cindercraft needed. Heat flashed back along the mineral path. Draxenne snapped her hands open, ending both streams before the ceramic burst.

The planes passed an inch from her throat as Ombria repositioned them. No contact. No claim beyond the conduit.

“Twelve,” Ombria said.

“You count beautifully.”

“You breathe loudly.”

“You have noticed.”

The provocation went unanswered. A pressure stud hammered beneath Ombria's distant hand on the housing, and her gaze cut past Draxenne toward the eastern roofs. One plane turned grainy at its edge. Ombria stiffened it, pulling more heat from her own body.

Draxenne hated that precise, disciplined choice. Hated the five demands in one hand. Hated every ward that could reach into this woman and receive an answer, while Draxenne got a visit between council sessions, a duel between crises, one almost-kiss on a rain stair two years ago before a messenger had come pounding up it.

Sixteen breaths.

She drove her right palm against the parapet. Cinder flashed through three hairline cracks at once, not three streams but one divided path. Ombria caught two. The third fused the grit beneath her heel into slick glass. Draxenne kept her left hand fixed on the housing rim.

Ombria shifted exactly as Draxenne knew she would. Draxenne rose inside her guard, close enough that heat met cold between their faces. Ombria's back stopped one handspan from the conduit housing. Her shadow pressed around Draxenne's flame, neither able to close without violating the terms.

Twenty breaths.

Draxenne could smell rain on Ombria's coat and the clean scorched-clay scent of her own gloves. Ombria looked at her mouth, then at the flame threaded between them.

Another district pulse struck.

“You know what I hate most? That I have to share you~.” Draxenne let the cinder brighten, a dangerous promise pointed safely into stone.

Ombria's brows lifted. She was still crushing Draxenne's hottest route between two planes, still keeping two other districts intact, still cold enough that her next breath shook. “Wait are we fighting or flirting because I’m getting mixed signals here.”

There were a dozen answers Draxenne might have given on an easier night. Each was polished, possessive, and useless.

The eastern stud struck again.

Draxenne cut her flame to a dull line and leaned back as far as her grip allowed. Ombria watched her, waiting perhaps for the joke, perhaps for proof that Draxenne could hear an uncertainty without turning it into permission.

Draxenne gave her neither pressure nor reassurance. She drove the dull cinder line into the bridge seam, then flared it against the western rim as if she meant to circle the housing.

Ombria blocked west.

The attack was a feint. Without releasing the housing, Draxenne snapped her right hand across and slapped it against the eastern ceramic plate.

The district pulse struck a third time.

Ombria chose.

Her housing hand tore free. The agreed rule ended her claim the instant her palm left iron. With that freed hand Ombria released the western contesting plane and used the freed capacity to raise a district plane toward the eastern roofs, while Draxenne's safe feint ran over the empty edge of the housing. Draxenne closed both hands around the conduit rim.

“Twenty-nine,” Ombria said.

The eastern roofs settled on the pressure map.

“Thirty.”

Draxenne held the Ninth. Ombria stood exposed beside her, shadow stretched elsewhere, throat bare to any cruelty the rules forbade.

Draxenne opened her casting hand. The flame vanished. Residual heat hissed harmlessly through the plate vents.

“Mine for the breach,” she said.

Ombria's gaze moved from Draxenne's empty palm to her face. Whatever answer lived there, she kept it. “Then command it.”

* * *

For eleven breaths, Draxenne was right.

Ombria kept four costly planes active: two angled into baffles without contesting Draxenne's grip, and two covering the districts still under load. The storm front struck the outer lattice. Violet-black dust plunged into the Ninth, compressed between Ombria's baffles, and met Draxenne's cinder in measured bursts. Each burst fused a cloud of razored grit into heavy black beads. They fell rattling into the empty spillway.

On the pressure map, the March road remained a steady gray line. The last wagons cleared the gate.

“You may say it,” Draxenne told her.

“The eastern baffle needs four degrees more pitch.”

“Not that.”

“Your second vent is narrowing.”

The old stone gave a thick internal knock.

Draxenne felt the wrongness through the housing: pressure returning from below instead of leaving. A buried crack opened across the spillway wall. The gale struck it, climbed, and began forcing Draxenne's cooling beads toward the inner market.

Ombria had seen the shift half a breath earlier. “Drop your heat.”

“I can clear it.”

Draxenne opened a third stream. Her vision haloed white. The air thinned inside her chest as cindercraft consumed what her body could give it. She melted the first clot of stormglass, only to send it deeper into the outlet, where it hardened across the crack like mortar in the wrong wound.

Pressure doubled. The ceramic beneath her palms whined.

Brute force would seal the route completely. Then the trapped heat would flash back through the housing and burst into the street.

Her winning plan had become the weapon Ombria warned her about.

Draxenne closed all three streams. Darkness crashed back into her sight. She kept one hand on the housing because she had won it, because surrender tasted worse than blood, because queens did not release a wall while their people stood behind it.

Ombria could have invoked the failure. She could have taken the Ninth and sealed the city, leaving the outer road to the storm.

Instead she asked, “What do you need?”

No triumph. No rescue disguised as command. The choice remained Draxenne's long enough to become a better one.

Draxenne lifted her hand from the housing. With the other, she pried the vented plate free and tucked it beneath her arm; it was warm, but no longer molten.

“Vents inside the channel,” she said. Without heat to sharpen her, the words came plain. “Three angled baffles. I can carry the eastern load through the ceramic. You would hold three planes, not four. Which two anchors can you give up?”

Ombria stared at her. Then another crack sounded below them.

“Come down,” she said. “We decide on the bridge.”

* * *

The storm reached the wall as they descended.

Grit shrieked across the stone. Ombria held four planes, turning one above the stair so stormglass streaked along its angled surface in luminous purple threads while the other three strained toward their anchors. The maintenance bridge dropped into the conduit throat, narrow, wet, and crowded with ceramic braces that Draxenne's crews had fixed to the old masonry. Draxenne dropped the recovered housing plate atop the eleven waiting along the bridge wall. Below, the clogged spillway boiled with dust.

“I release road east,” Ombria said. Cold had shortened her words. “You take its pressure in the braces. I keep three.”

“And lower east?”

“It is open. To put its load into your brace cleanly, I must catch it first.”

“With a fifth plane.”

“For no more than three breaths.”

The plane above them rippled. Ombria's fingers had gone gray at the tips.

Draxenne fastened both hands around a ceramic brace. Heat cracks opened across her skin beneath the gloves. “The parapet is empty.”

“The transfer may burn through your hands.”

“They are my hands.”

“An argument you found objectionable when applied to mine.”

Draxenne nearly ordered her. The old impulse rose hot and regal: give it to me, let me decide, stop making me watch you die by fractions. Command would be quicker. It would also prove Ombria right to resist.

She swallowed smoke and pride together. “Which two anchors can you live without?”

Ombria studied her grip, her breathing, the open vents behind her. “Lower east and road east. I catch the first, then taper both. The remaining three become baffles. You hold two streams, no more. If either of us says stop, I turn the three inward and you vent into the spillway.”

“And if the spillway closes?”

“We stop anyway and get off the bridge.”

It would cost both sides of the wall. It was still a real exit.

“Accepted,” Draxenne said.

Ombria lifted her smallest finger. A fifth plane sprang across the unshielded lower-eastern gap and caught its loose pressure. Cold stripped the composure from her face.

On the first breath, Ombria bent that emergency plane toward the first ceramic brace.

On the second, Draxenne fed a narrow cinder stream through the prepared brace. Ceramic glowed red, softened, and locked against the masonry. Ombria released the fifth plane. It became ordinary shadow, and the physical load hit Draxenne's brace. Her shoulder slammed into stone.

On the third, Ombria released the road plane. It became shadow and nothing more. Draxenne ignited the second brace.

The bridge lurched. Her boot skidded to its outer edge.

The fifth plane had existed for two breaths. Even so, Ombria swayed before she reached for Draxenne, then stopped rather than take either of her casting hands. “Can you hold?”

Draxenne's first instinct was to make the flame broad enough to blind the night.

Instead she made it smaller.

The braces cooled from white to a sustainable red. Her muscles still shook, but the mineral paths held. “Yes. Three planes. Now.”

Ombria stepped to the bridge rail. With one hand braced on basalt and the other cutting exact positions through the darkness, she changed the angles of her three remaining planes and anchored them across the broken channel. Not a wall. A descending series of blades turned sideways, each with a deliberate gap.

“First vent,” Ombria said.

Draxenne pulsed heat through it. A dense ribbon of dust whitened, rounded, fell.

“Second.”

The next pulse staggered Draxenne. Ombria widened the gap before the flame could choke. She did not take the work away. She changed only what was hers to change.

Stormglass fell around them in hot black beads, bouncing off the bridge and clicking into the spillway. Ombria advanced one step. Draxenne followed, dragging the load along the braces through molten seams.

They moved into the breach together.

There was no elegance left for flirting. Ombria's instructions broke into nouns. “Upper gap. Wait. Now.”

Draxenne had no breath for wit. “Wider.”

“Too much draws gale.”

“I need air.”

Ombria widened it.

Draxenne drank one harsh breath and cast. Her cinder changed the storm one handful at a time: knife dust to liquid, liquid to bead, bead to weight. Ombria made the paths that let each change happen without killing them. When numbness made Ombria's third finger fail to lift, Draxenne called the timing. When the tremor in Draxenne's arms sent her flame high, Ombria vented the pressure into bare stone.

The cracked section came into reach.

A slab above the outlet shifted.

Draxenne saw the load path before it fell: fractured edge, failing brace, the last open spillway directly beneath. If the slab closed that mouth, the conduit would burst toward both the market and the March road.

Her twelve prepared plates were stacked along the bridge wall. Enough fired ceramic to replace the failed brace, if she melted every one into the gap. The Cinder March would have no fitted plates for its own defenses when the next front came.

Ombria saw her look. “I can take the east anchors back.”

Her voice dragged with cold. A fourth plane would make her slower; a fifth might stop her heart. She offered it anyway, not as a sovereign issuing terms, but as a woman willing to carry the cost Draxenne had not yet chosen.

“No,” Draxenne said. “Keep the vents open.”

She tore the first plate from the stack and drove cinder through it. The ceramic slumped into the fracture, bright as a piece of fallen noon. A second plate followed, then a third. Each one drank water and oxygen from her body. Each one hardened into an ugly, load-bearing mass beneath the slab.

Ombria held three planes. She did not reach for a fourth.

Draxenne melted the last plate.

The slab dropped.

The new brace caught it.

All the trapped pressure found Ombria's three gaps at once. Her planes turned grainy, edges shivering under the load.

“Final pulse,” Draxenne said.

Ombria's hands were nearly still. “On you.”

Draxenne set both feet against the bridge lip. She opened two streams and no more. Ombria angled. Draxenne fired.

Blue-white cinder crossed load-bearing shadow. The stormglass front folded through the vents, fused, and came down in a black glittering fall that filled the spillway without sealing it. The last of the gale went over the wall as ordinary wind.

For one breath, neither woman moved.

Then Ombria lowered her first plane through a three-count. Draxenne opened her casting hands and let the braces cool. Ombria lowered the second, then the third. Shadow became shadow. Ceramic ceased to glow. The pylons held only the harmless residue of their charge.

The ward was inert.

The road and the market remained standing.

Draxenne sat down hard on the bridge because remaining upright had become a vanity she could no longer finance.

Ombria sat beside her, shoulder against shoulder, and laughed once without grace.

* * *

Before dawn, they occupied a ward room that smelled of soot, wet wool, and boiled water.

Unnamed crews moved beyond the open door, shoveling cooling beads from the channels. Each scrape proved another route remained open. Draxenne's fingers were wrapped in clean linen. Ombria held a steaming cup between both palms, though she seemed to take warmth more readily from the shared cloak over their shoulders.

The pressure map lay across their knees.

“One moon cycle,” Draxenne said. “I take personal casting responsibility at the two eastern stations, holding their pressure through rebuilt ceramic braces, and I supply the maintenance crews. I replace the plates as soon as my kilns can fit them. You retain the other three anchors and your office.”

“Your veto remains yours,” Ombria said. “Mine remains mine. Either may end the compact after a safe transfer.”

“Either may withdraw immediately from unsafe casting.”

Ombria marked the terms in chalk at the map's margin. Her handwriting was usually architectural. Tonight it leaned drunkenly downhill.

“No magical bond,” Draxenne said. “No penalty beyond the ordinary consequences we arrange for.”

“And no pretending this is permanent because permanence saves us another conversation.” Ombria drew two small blocks on the weekly duty slate. “These hours are private. The ward office does not summon me except for immediate danger to life.”

Draxenne looked at the blocks. “Private for whom?”

Ombria gave her a cold, level glance over the cup. The effect was impaired by the cloak, which had slipped over one eyebrow. “Administration first.”

“Cruel woman.”

“You did fight me for my conduit.”

“And won.”

“Then clogged it.”

There was the late humor, quiet and exact. Draxenne could have hidden in the familiar exchange all the way to sunrise.

She touched the chalk marks instead.

“What I said on the bridge was true,” she said. “Badly shaped. Still true.”

Ombria waited.

“I don't hate the city for needing you. I don't hate that you answer. I hate being given whatever remains after you have answered everyone until your hands cannot feel mine.” Draxenne looked down at her bandages. “And I have behaved as if the remedy were to make your attention mine. It isn't.”

“No,” Ombria said.

The word landed without softening. Draxenne respected it enough not to flinch.

“I want time you choose before there is nothing left of you to choose with,” Draxenne said. “Emergencies will interrupt it. Your duty will remain yours. I will be angry sometimes, and I will try not to make the anger a claim.”

Ombria set down the cup. “Vantress cannot grant me to you. Your victory cannot. Your crown cannot.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

Two years of almosts stood between them: rain stairs, council corridors, visits cut to pieces by pressure calls. Draxenne had always thought clarity meant losing ground. Tonight she had learned what happened when one kept exclusive control of a broken channel.

She turned beneath the cloak until she faced Ombria fully.

“May I court you?”

Ombria's expression changed by degrees. Weariness remained. So did authority, and the aggravating precision with which she inspected any proposal likely to affect her city. Underneath them, desire arrived without disguise.

“Yes,” she said. “I would like that.”

Draxenne let out the breath she had been rationing. “May I kiss you now?”

“Yes.”

Ombria closed the distance.

Her mouth was warmer than her hands and less careful than her speech. Draxenne tasted boiled water, smoke, and the sharp little sound Ombria made when Draxenne touched her jaw. She kept the kiss brief because they were injured, exhausted, and still sitting under a municipal duty slate. Brief did not mean uncertain.

A brass stud knocked beneath the pressure map.

The eastern ward.

Ombria began to reach from habit. Draxenne's bandaged palm was already waiting on the contact point. The signal traveled into her hand: weight, direction, an ordinary public need passed through ordinary metal. She took it. Ombria watched the signal settle beneath Draxenne's palm and did not reach again.

Outside, cooling stormglass clicked beneath the first gray light. Ombria used her free hand to pull Draxenne closer.

stories.title: The Last Monster
stories.prompt: you don’t know how long you been lost in this dungeon but you are losing your mind and just want to get out. You can’t tell what a monster or an adventurer anymore so you just been killing anything in sight. It gotten to a point where the dungeon monsters are now scared of you
stories.body:
# The Last Monster

The shape comes around the corner carrying a lantern, and you kill it before the light reaches its face.

Your sword catches first on something hard, then goes through. The lantern swings. In its orange pass you see a hand wrapped in clean cloth, worked leather at the shoulder, a metal buckle stamped with a curling line. You also see a jaw too narrow, perhaps, and teeth too many, perhaps. Then the shape folds against the wall and the lantern settles upright between its knees.

It had been turning away.

Movement means attack. You know this. Waiting is how the others died.

Still, it had been turning away.

You take the lantern and fasten its strap at your shoulder with the stamped buckle. The dead shape's bag contains four strips of dried meat beside a wad of pale cave growth, food gathered by an adventurer or carried by a monster. Its flask gives you three swallows. You take all three too quickly. The corridor tilts, the flame divides into twins, and the next thing you know you are crouched with your shoulder against the wall and your sword lifted at the sound of pursuit.

Water drips into water. Nothing else moves.

Your gear keeps the count that your mind cannot. There is rust on the lower half of the blade. Your belt closes through a hole punched with the knife point, two holes beyond the last proper one. Cord holds both soles to your boots. A white seam crosses your forearm beneath three newer cuts. You remember receiving that shallow wound yesterday.

You remember several yesterdays. They cannot all have been yesterday.

The lantern gutters. When you cup a hand around it, the flame leans toward the left-hand passage and stays there. You hold still. A loose thread at your cuff lifts the same way. Against your wet fingertip, the air is cold.

Air goes somewhere.

From the left passage comes a measured sound.

Knock. Knock. Knock.

A pause. Farther ahead, three knocks answer. The signal travels away through the stone.

A hunting call, you think.

But the flame bends left. The thread lifts left. Cold touches the wet side of your finger. For the first time since counting stopped, three things agree.

You step over the body and follow the light it carried.

* * *

At every branching you make the same tests.

You shield the flame. You watch the thread. You wet one fingertip with water you should be saving. When your eyes insist that one corridor rises and your knees insist that it falls, you trust the air instead. The draft strengthens by degrees. Enclosed rot thins. Beneath it comes the smell of leaf mold, so faint you almost mistake wanting for evidence.

Then the flame bows, the thread trembles, and the damp of your finger turns cold. Evidence enough.

Something scrambles ahead.

You raise the lantern. A long-limbed figure crouches at a wall crack, hauling a smaller shape through by two of its four—or perhaps merely bent—arms. Its eyes catch the light. It bares its teeth.

No. The teeth are already bare. The lips may not close over them.

The figure shoves the smaller one into darkness, tears down a woven sleeping mat, and stuffs it into the crack between you. It never advances. It never reaches for you. When you take one step, it disappears after the smaller body.

Knock. Knock. Knock.

The warning races ahead. Claws answer it from a ceiling niche. Feet answer from below a broken stair. A cluster of low, gray scavengers abandons a fresh carcass without feeding and squeezes beneath a slab, the largest going last. Points of reflected light vanish whenever your lantern turns toward them.

They are taking positions. They are drawing you on.

The corridor ahead goes silent.

You slash at a dark shape hanging in a niche. Hide parts beneath the sword. The thing gives no cry because it is an empty sling, still warm where a body lay in it. The stroke pulls pain down your ribs and bursts sparks across your vision. For several breaths you cannot make the two lanterns become one.

At the next narrow place, stones and cracked boards fill a side opening. Their rough ends point toward you. Beyond them, tracks lead away: narrow feet, broad pads, dragging knuckles, a sweep like bundled reeds. They all overlap in one direction. A sack has split in flight, spilling cave bulbs and scraps of bedding. There are no spear points waiting through the barricade. It has been built from the far side to keep you out.

The word ambush remains ready in your mouth. The facts will not fit inside it.

Behind you, a stone grinds across stone. One of the passages you passed has been sealed. The creatures are closing the route after themselves, and if they close the airy route ahead, you will be left with the drip, the dark, and however many yesterdays your body has survived.

You begin to run.

The warning runs faster.

* * *

The passage spills you into a cistern chamber broad enough to swallow the lantern light. Bedrolls huddle near old fire pits. Gear lies scattered where a waiting party has dropped it for quick hands. Cuts score the wall in groups you cannot count at this distance.

You stop at the threshold, sword forward.

Nothing charges.

The flame shows a soot patch on the floor. Beside it sits a cup fashioned from the cheek plate of a helmet. Its rim bears one square dent.

Your thumb knows the dent before you do.

You made the cup. You slept beside that soot. At arm's height on the wall, one of the counting marks has a crooked tail because the notch in your knife catches when you pull it downward. You fit the knife to the groove. Stone dust flakes out.

The last time you stood here, the cut along your forearm was open. Now that cut is the white seam beneath the newer ones.

You have not found a new chamber. You have found a place that already survived you.
