Kethra nodded and signed, *Immediately. No penalty. No argument.*

The apprentice signed **yes**. So did the other.

Ulan rubbed his throat. “Two safe calls left,” he said. His opening call had been clean, but Kethra heard the rough edge beneath it. “No more than two.”

Dorram glanced toward the panel. “A substitute caller is available.”

Kethra kept her hands still. The choice was not his, and it was not hers. She looked at Ulan.

He considered the rails, then signed, *I stay. Two.*

She wrote the limit beside his name on her caller roster and showed it to him before he initialed the mark. Two meant two, even if the examination turned on a third.

On the emergency edge of her slate she reviewed *Crown Release* and *Safe Descent*. Neither belonged in the ceremonial sequence. Both had been tested on stone frames in the court below, because preparation that assumed nothing would break was decoration, not safety.

As Kethra turned toward the first cell, a pale line near the western joint caught her eye. A crack no longer than her smallest finger crossed the old mortar.

She signed for a manual check. Dorram climbed the short stair, pressed both palms to the joint, and sighted along it while wind worried the high shutters.

“No movement,” he reported. “The masonry is within tolerance.”

It was. Kethra still erased the upper third of her planned load.

Dorram’s stylus hovered, then marked down her impressiveness score.

The loss stung. She had wanted the panel to see the lattice at its fullest: three spells held separately by one living mind, not a choir dragging her power behind their voices. Yet the hairline remained in her thoughts, a tiny white refusal.

She showed the revised loads to every caller. One by one, each touched a node and signed **yes**.

* * *

Kethra opened the first cell, then the second, then the third.

Three patterns pressed against the limits of her attention. The lattice kept them isolated, each aligned to its own caller and sound path. It did not make the work light. A tremor began deep in her left wrist as she placed the ceremonial loads.

Dorram raised one hand. The resilience trial would begin with the planned loss of a caller.

Wind struck the shutters.

The pale crack flashed across Kethra’s memory an instant before a grinding blow shook the floor.

This was not the trial.

The western joint split under the occupied gallery’s ordinary weight. Stone lurched. Kethra slashed the abort sign before the next spell name could be called, collapsing its pattern unspent. Pain bit up her arm anyway. Dust burst from the wall and erased half the room.

Somebody screamed. The long speaking rail tore from its brackets with a metallic shriek.

Through the dust, one apprentice found Kethra’s eyes and crossed both hands: **stop**.

Kethra dropped that cell at once.

The failed pattern struck her like a missed step in darkness. Her knees dipped. With the rail broken and a caller withdrawn, the rehearsed three-cell solution was gone. The lattice held no stored commands to play back. Even if it had, old sound could not complete a living link.

A slab broke free above the gallery.

Dorram moved before Kethra could finish mapping its fall. He planted his staff against the floor—not for power, only to mark the roof’s geometry—then caught the nearest brass node between his hands. With one hand he marked the registered shape for *Roofstay*; with the other he signed **yes** against the node, authorizing himself as both living shaper and living caller for that one cell. Amber lines climbed his arms as he gathered the familiar pattern into his body and selected the sagging ribs. When the shape was ready, he gave the two-finger ready sign to open the same twelve-heartbeat window Kethra used. One heartbeat later, he drew a single breath and called his own spell.

“Roofstay!”

The live name closed his pattern. The falling slab stopped with a crack that shivered dust from every seam. Around it, the roof ribs burned amber, sustained by Dorram’s power.

The gallery occupants stumbled toward the central exit. Then the exit arch buckled inward and jammed.

Dorram had caught the roof. He had caught it fast, alone, and wrong.

Kethra saw the load pouring down his target lines. *Roofstay* had concentrated the western weight on the central exit column. A black fracture was already climbing its face.

She seized his sleeve and pointed.

His expression changed as he followed the crack upward.

The examination was over. The rescue had begun.

* * *

Kethra swept dust from the floor and sketched in chalk: roof ribs, tower crown, trapped gallery, central column, broken rail. The map made the choice plain and terrible. If Dorram released *Roofstay* now, the roof would drop. If he sustained it, the exit column would split. They could preserve the tower or clear the people below it, but not both.

Coughing filled the chamber. Before anyone could follow her plan, they needed air.

Ulan stood beside the mouth of the one short rail still fixed to the central node. Kethra met his eyes, touched the brass, and marked *Airclear*. The previous link was gone; consent could not be assumed from it.

Ulan touched beside her and signed **yes**.

Kethra shaped one narrow corridor from the gallery to the open court. She could not clear the whole tower. She could not spare the power to try. When the pattern was ready, she raised two fingers.

“Airclear!” Ulan called.

His living breath traveled the short rail. Kethra’s power released in a cool spiral, and dust peeled away from the mapped corridor as if drawn through a glass tunnel. Trapped students bent into the cleaner air.

Ulan coughed hard afterward. When Kethra looked to him, he signed **wait**.

Every part of her wanted the final cell ready now. She closed her hand and waited.

Dorram stared at her chalk map. “*Crown Release* would destroy the upper ring.”

Kethra nodded.

“And your lattice with it.”

She nodded again. Four years of measured brass, revised diagrams, and evenings spent proving that a caller’s sound did not own the shaper’s art. Her masterwork shone above them through the dust. She wanted the title badly enough that the thought of tearing it apart felt like tearing out a bone.

The exit column cracked loud enough to silence the room.

Kethra drew three load arrows. She showed how *Roofstay* pinned the crown joints and drove force into the column. She crossed out every sustaining route. Then she marked the only sequence that left time for descent: ground the gallery; end *Roofstay*; separate the crown; lower the occupied platform and loose stone into the cleared court.

Dorram began to object. Kethra struck the chalk against the point where his spell met the column and signed in the standard field language, *Your sustain lasts until your strength fails or the exit does. Either failure kills the route.*

Another chip sprang from the column.

Dorram looked from the map to the people pressed inside the air corridor. Then he laid his staff down.

“Kethra has incident command,” he told the room.

She did not waste a heartbeat on relief. She climbed onto the examination table and tore the first ornamental rail free.

Her beautiful lattice became raw brass in her hands.

* * *

Kethra rebuilt for survival.

She bent one speaking rail down to the gallery footing and anchored it against sound stone. She ran another across the crown joints, following every fracture she wanted *Crown Release* to open and none she wanted spared. From the central node she mapped a descent field around the stranded platform and the loosened upper stones.

The rails chose nothing. Her diagrams powered nothing. Kethra held the three spell cells in her body and attention until her teeth ached.

An adult volunteer from the lower gallery stepped into the court and raised a hand. “I know *Weightward*. I can call.”

Kethra showed the volunteer the grounded path and its danger: the spell moved existing weight; it did not create support. A bad map could drive the load through the floor. The volunteer studied the chalk, touched the first node with her, and signed **yes**.

At the second node, Kethra marked *Crown Release*. Dorram checked the traced joints himself, then placed his fingers beside hers. He signed **yes**.

Ulan had rested against the wall with a wet cloth over his mouth. One safe call remained. Kethra showed him the descent target, the short duration, and the place the platform must reach before her power failed. She pointed to **wait** and **stop** as deliberately as she pointed to **yes**.

Ulan lowered the cloth. He touched the third node and signed **yes**.

Three living choices. Three isolated cells. Kethra’s maximum.

Her hands had begun to shake visibly. Holding the gallery’s map while tracing the crown and enclosing the descent field made each movement slow, as if the air had thickened around her. If one call failed, its collapsing pattern could tear the sequence out of her grasp. She looked at the volunteer.

The first ready sign.

“Weightward!”

The full name rang out at conversational strength, each syllable clear. The live call closed Kethra’s first pattern. Power surged from her into the grounded rails. The gallery settled with a deep stone knock as she moved its load away from the cracked exit and into the tower footing. She held the map until every gold line reached sound foundation.

One major release. Her left arm shook from shoulder to fingertips.

Kethra faced Dorram and made the cutting sign.

He ended *Roofstay*.

The amber ribs vanished. For one plunging instant the unloaded crown shifted above them. Kethra maintained the grounded gallery and thrust her second cell toward the joints. Two fingers rose.

“Crown Release!” Dorram called.

His voice was living and chosen; the spell was Kethra’s shaping, Kethra’s power, Kethra’s exact target. White light snapped along the repurposed rails. The upper ring split at its joints in a thunder of shearing mortar. Blocks peeled outward instead of crushing the exit column.

The tower crown—and the ornate lattice fixed across it—came apart.

Two major releases. Kethra’s vision narrowed. The second pattern tried to pull her down with the falling stone, but she held its separation long enough for the crown to clear the gallery.

Then the platform dropped.

Kethra turned to Ulan and gave the final ready sign.

The remote speaking rail snapped.

Its broken end lashed through empty air. Ulan’s call position was cut away from the shaped field. No matter how loudly he spoke, no living sound could reach the active node through a severed tube.

Twelve heartbeats.

Kethra could not call the name herself. Her throat could make no ordinary words, and neither terror nor magic changed that. The incomplete pattern burned inside her, draining strength with every beat.

She wrenched the third cell’s small brass node from its rail and carried it.

Eleven.

The target geometry pulled against her grip. She kept one hand shaped around the falling platform and ran with the other clenched on the node.

Ten. Nine.

Stone struck stone behind her. A fragment clipped her shoulder and spun her sideways. She stayed upright.

Eight. Seven.

Ulan saw what she was doing and pushed away from the wall. His face was gray beneath the dust.

Six.

Kethra reached direct speaking range. She could have ordered with her eyes. She could have treated his earlier assent as permanent because people were falling.

Instead she showed him the node, pointed once to his throat, and opened her hand in a question.

Five.

Ulan looked at the descending platform. Then he looked at her and chose **yes**.

Four.

“Safe Descent!”

The words came hoarse but complete on one living exhalation. The nearby node caught and modestly carried them into Kethra’s active field. Her third pattern closed.

Power tore through her. She spread it beneath the platform and falling crown stones, slowing rather than stopping them. The spell could not hold them aloft. It bought only a few breaths, and Kethra spent those breaths steering.

The platform sank into the cleared court. People jumped away as its edge touched down. Crown blocks followed in a grinding curtain, slow enough for rescuers to pull the last apprentice clear. Kethra guided the largest slab aside by half a pace—only half, but enough.

Three major releases.

Her legs stopped obeying. She remained standing until the platform rested on stone and the final white line faded. Then her knees struck the dusty floor.

For a moment she could hear nothing but her own pulse.

Then came crying, coughing, and the astonished noise of people discovering one another alive.

* * *

By dusk, the open court had become a place of cups, bandages, and blankets. The injuries were bruises and shallow cuts. The tower crown lay in ordered wreckage around the platform, its broken brass rails dull in the fading light.

The apprentice who had signed **stop** sat with a cup between both hands. No one blamed the apprentice for withdrawing. Kethra made certain of that before she allowed anyone to look at her shoulder.

The volunteer received water and thanks. Dorram’s voice had roughened on *Crown Release*, and a healer wrapped a warm cloth around his throat. Ulan declined every spoken question. He rested his voice and answered in sign, with his usual sharp precision.

Kethra sat before the panel with a blanket around her and her ruined masterwork behind them. She knew what they had seen: three voices where she possessed none; an examiner forced to intervene in her trial; a tower sacrificed on the day she was supposed to prove she could be trusted with one.

Dorram set the office seal on the table.

“The examination has four requirements,” he said, his voice quiet. “Original architecture. Precise control of power and consequence. A method others can learn safely. Discretionary command that values lives above prestige, property, and the candidate’s own work.”

He touched the first mark. “You designed the voiced lattice, then proved you understood it well enough to dismantle it.”

The second. “You diagnosed my error, mapped every load, and ordered three effects so none destroyed what the next required.”

The third. “Your callers understood their tasks, named their limits, stopped, waited, and chose again. That cost time. It also kept them people.”

The fourth. “You destroyed the work meant to win this seal, because keeping it would have killed those we teach.”

Kethra looked at the broken crown. She had spent years trying to make interdependence look like independence, afraid that any visible need would be counted as someone else’s mastery. Today the need had been visible, dangerous, and real. So had the limits of Dorram’s solitary spell.

“The calls were not yours,” Dorram said. “Their courage and labor belong to the callers. The architecture, power, diagnosis, sequence, and command were yours. I mistook resilience for self-sufficiency. The evidence corrected me.”

He pushed the seal across the table.

“The panel finds Kethra qualified for the office of archmage.”

Ulan grinned and applauded silently, striking one palm against the back of his other hand. Kethra laughed without a voice, shoulders shaking until it hurt. Nothing opened in her throat. No hidden word arrived. The rules of the practice had not bent for her, and neither had she been diminished by them.

The next morning, the office seal rested beside a fresh caller roster. Kethra had drawn spaces for voluntary assignments, individual voice limits, and the signs for **yes** and **wait**. The crossed hands of **stop** stood at the top, where no one could miss them.

Students gathered around the scarred court. Ulan sat among them, still resting his voice.

Kethra raised her hands and began her first safety briefing as an archmage.

stories.title: The Five-Minute Warranty
stories.prompt: Goblin's aren't terrible engineers, they can make anything work. And I mean anything. Just... not for very long.
stories.body:
# The Five-Minute Warranty

The North Rise died in three sounds.

First came the kiln-shed blast, a flat blow that struck soot from the upper landing's rafters. Then the lift cables sang as the lower terrace jumped beneath them. Last came a crunch so deep and expensive that Kezli, standing two streets away in her workshop yard, knew a crown gear had lost more than one tooth.

In the echoes, she reconstructed the likely sequence: broken teeth punching through the inspection cover, the cable drum lurching half a turn, the ratchet brake catching with a crack. If one cage had been at the upper landing, its twin would be stranded somewhere in the smoke below.

By the time Director Nalda Vick's runner reached the workshop, Kezli and Olbit had already packed gauges, oakcloth, and every wrench that could be carried at a trot.

When they arrived, Kezli found the failure she had heard. Two iron wedges lay on the Rise's landing stones beside the holes they had punched through the inspection cover. The cable drum stood half a turn out of position, held fast by its ratchet brake.

Four signal flags hung from the lower station: ten people ready, ten behind them, ten more behind those, and a fourth group still coming out of the quarry sheds. Forty in all. A bruised lift attendant below worked the speaking wire with one arm. Beyond the flags, black smoke moved across the kiln yard toward the station. The stair road had vanished under a spill of rock and brick.

Two human lift mechanics knelt beside the opened gear housing. One held up half a tooth as if the rest might apologize and come back.

"The crown is finished," he said. "Casting and cutting another takes six days. Resetting that pedestal may take ten."

"You have minutes," Nalda told Kezli. Her gray coat was powdered white from the blast. "I need a proper repair. Permanent."

Kezli looked at the drive pedestal. A hairline crack ran through its masonry footing exactly where her rejected maintenance bid had warned it would. *Excessive short-term work,* Nalda had written across that bid. *The lift office requires lasting solutions.*

All around the upper landing, people were watching Kezli as though goblin pride might be hammered flat enough to fit where the gear had been. She wanted the civic contract. She wanted Nalda to regret every word of that rejection. For one hot, foolish moment, she wanted to say yes before she knew what yes would cost.

Olbit crouched beside the cable drum and put two fingers against the brake pawl. "Still holding," he said. "That is one useful fact. Shall we collect more before making promises?"

Kezli let out the breath she had been saving for a boast.

"A permanent repair? No," she said. Nalda's face tightened. Kezli pointed past the wrecked teeth to the smooth iron collar left on the engine shaft, then to the clean outer rim of the cable drum. "But the boiler still turns, and the drum can still turn. They can't mesh anymore. They might be persuaded to touch."

***

Kezli checked the engine while Olbit checked the load path. They worked separately because agreement was useful only when it survived two sets of hands.

Boiler pressure held steady. The piston rods ran true. The engine-side shaft had gained a bright score but no bend. Kezli chalked a line on the flywheel and watched three slow revolutions under steam. Across the housing, Olbit measured cable lay, tested both landing brakes, and sent an empty cage two handspans down and back on the emergency windlass.

"Cables pass," he said. "Cages pass. Brakes engage. Drum collar is sound. Pedestal offset is eleven fingers at the crown and worsening under weight."

One of the lift mechanics proposed welding the broken teeth into place.

"The crown is brittle," Kezli said. "The first passenger load would pull the welds out with larger pieces attached."

The other suggested a leather belt around both rims.

Olbit stretched a cord between the misaligned shafts. It wandered to the edge before he had pulled it taut. "The belt would walk off before the first cage cleared the lower roof."

"Then couple the drum directly," Nalda said.

"The engine turns six times too fast," Kezli said. "Direct drive would bring the cage up promptly. It would not stop at the landing, which is where passengers generally prefer to leave it."

Nalda pressed her mouth shut. Below, the speaking wire clicked twice: smoke had crossed the kiln yard.

Kezli sighted along the two bare rims. Rigid teeth demanded alignment. Friction did not, if the contact could follow the offset and if something gentler than iron carried the heat. She drew two circles in the soot on the housing, then a smaller circle pinched between them.

"A contact roller," she said. "Spring-mounted. Sleeve it in oakcloth so it grips both rims."

"One roller will climb," Olbit said. He drew a second small circle under hers. "Two will share the side thrust. Put them in a flexure brace so they can follow the shifted axis instead of arguing with it."

"The piston pulse will eat the cloth."

"Sorter flywheel. The cracked ore sorter behind the coal shed still has one."

"Too heavy."

"Which is why it will smooth the pulse."

Kezli grinned despite the smoke. That was the pleasure of working with Olbit: he disagreed in completed calculations.

They measured the shaft speeds and chose roller diameters that reduced the engine's turns to the drum's safe rate. Olbit took two brass weights from a platform scale and sketched a ball governor to hold that rate under load. Kezli cut a strip from a standard resin-bound oakcloth leaf, clamped it to a test roller, and pressed it against the powered engine collar for ten counted seconds.

The sample emerged hot, glazed, and thinner by a measurable shaving.

They ran it again at the pressure required to lift the heaviest declared cage. Kezli marked wear against time. Olbit measured the available collar clearance.

"Five standard leaves," he said.

Kezli stacked them around the test roller: white, blue, yellow, orange, red. Five fitted snugly. A sixth made the roller too fat to engage. She tried six thinner strips; the test heat burned through the outer pair so quickly that iron would meet iron before the fourth load arrived.

Nalda watched the red layer disappear beneath the others. "How long?"

"Under a declared load, at governed speed, five minutes from clutch engagement to bare iron," Kezli said. "Not six. Not five and a favorable opinion. Five."

"People say your workshop can make anything work."

It was a local joke, usually told when someone wanted a miracle at the price of a hinge. Kezli rolled the ruined test strip between her fingers.

"We can make these parts agree," she said. "For five minutes. If you want anything else, call someone who lies."

***

The apparatus looked improbable only to anyone who could not see what each piece did.

Cart springs became the flexure that kept the rollers pressed against both offset rims. A straight length of ore rail braced the frame. The salvaged sorter flywheel went on the engine side to swallow the pistons' hammering pulses. The scale weights spun on hinged arms above it, opening the steam throttle linkage when speed fell and closing it when speed rose. Five resin-bound oakcloth leaves wrapped the main contact roller, each dyed a different color and chalked with a wear line.

Olbit riveted a copper tab into every layer. As each leaf stripped away, its tab would strike a hanging clapper. Kezli notched a bronze shear link to part at the force expected when compliant cloth gave way to bare iron. The parting link would release the spring brace, pull the rollers clear, and trip the steam-dump latch. After that, the Rise's own tested ratchet brake would hold the drum.

Nothing in the chain was decorative. Even the shield of dented boiler plate had one purpose: keeping curious people away from the harmless but alarming pieces.

Nalda returned with a passenger sheet while Kezli fitted the final pin.

Olbit read it and frowned. "It says 'forty, roughly adult.'"

"There are also three children," Nalda said.

"Then they are remarkably roughly adult. Any tools? Ore samples? Family trunks?"

"One hand bag each."

"A hand is not a unit of mass."

Smoke rolled above the lower terrace roof. Still, Olbit would not sign for a mystery. They weighed upper-landing volunteers with ballast, established ten marks on the cage floor, and sent instructions down the speaking wire: four balanced groups of ten, bags on laps, quarry tools left behind. The bruised attendant confirmed each group against the marks.

Kezli wrote the operating ticket on a board and read every line aloud.

"Four passenger loads. Governed speed at the painted line. Five minutes beginning at clutch engagement. White, blue, yellow, orange, red, then bare iron. Smoke expected. Clatter expected. Copper strike at every cleared leaf. Everyone behind the shield line when red appears. Terminal sequence: shear, roller withdrawal, steam dump, brake engagement. No restart after terminal shear."

At the bottom waited signature lines for engineer, loadwright, director, and use priority.

Five minutes looked miserable in ink. Six looked almost generous. Six might look like confidence to Nalda, and permanence's smaller, respectable cousin to the council.

Kezli's pen hovered.

Olbit glanced at it. "Will the extra minute be made of ink?"

She scratched out the beginning of a curve before it became a six, wrote a hard-edged five, and stamped the ticket in red.

"Five," she said.

Director Vick signed beneath her. "Five."

The speaking wire bell rang before Nalda could fill in the use-priority line.

The council courier bent to the mouthpiece, listened, and went pale. "Order from the council. Two guards take the first empty cage down. The returning cage carries the civic strongbox. Passenger evacuation follows."

Nalda stared toward the smoke. "The strongbox holds the quarry receipts and the reserve for wages. Without it, half the lower district may not be paid. We may not be able to rebuild this lift."

The order was not foolish. That made it worse.

Olbit laid four square washers on the ticket, one for each passenger group. Then he set a brass nut beside them for the strongbox cycle. There was no room for the nut.

"Find another minute," Nalda said to Kezli. Quietly, as if quiet words weighed less. "Or slow the lift and stretch the five."

"Slower means the cloth sits under pressure longer and cooks," Kezli said. "Faster means the landing brake takes more speed than we tested. The four passenger loads use the travel and loading time we have. Send guards and retrieve the strongbox, and ten people remain below when red clears."

"Then tell me what to do."

Kezli felt the invitation inside the demand. If she chose, the director could later say the goblins had forced her hand. If Kezli invented a sixth minute, everyone could pretend the machine had erased the choice.

She moved the washers and nut apart.

"I can price your choices in loads and minutes," she said. "I cannot decide whose future counts. That line is yours."

For one breath Nalda looked furious. Then she took the pen.

On the use-priority line, she wrote: **PERSONS BEFORE PROPERTY. FOUR PASSENGER LOADS. STRONGBOX REMAINS BELOW.** She signed the addition and made the council courier witness it. Then she took the speaking-wire mouthpiece herself and transmitted the order to the bruised attendant.

The four lower flags dipped in acknowledgment.

"Engage," Nalda said.

***

White showed on the roller. Five minutes remained.

Kezli opened the boiler feed, watched the governor weights lift to their painted line, and pulled the clutch lever.

The roller train gripped.

For a terrible half second, every piece merely strained: engine collar against white oakcloth, cloth against rollers, rollers against the hoist rim, drum against forty lives' worth of cable. Then the empty upper cage descended. Out of the smoke, its loaded twin began to rise.

The impossible connection worked because every part was doing exactly one possible thing.

"Speed on line," Kezli called.

"Contact pressure true," Olbit answered.

Nalda read the first ten names from the passenger sheet, then caught herself and called, "First load rising."

The drum turned steadily. Resin warmed into a bitter smell. At the first chalk line the white leaf frayed, tore into smoking ribbons, and flung itself against the shield. Its copper tab struck the clapper once.

Several onlookers cried out.

"Expected transition," Kezli said. "Blue exposed. Four minutes. Keep the landing clear."

The first cage settled onto the upper stops. Ten soot-streaked people spilled out while the other cage reached the lower station. Nalda counted them herself. Below, the second group loaded according to the marks.

The council courier appeared at her shoulder. "The council repeats its order. The strongbox—"

"Remains below by my signed direction," Nalda said, loudly enough for the arriving passengers to hear. "Send the cage back."

The blue leaf darkened along Kezli's chalk line. The governor weights held steady. Kezli reversed the drum for the empty cage's exchange, then took up the second load. The connection changed direction without wandering off the rims. That had been Olbit's second roller. She glanced at him; he was already watching the brace, not seeking thanks.

The clapper rang. Blue strips snapped away, and yellow appeared with three minutes remaining.

The second load climbed. Halfway up, heat widened the engine collar. The contact roller edged toward the limit mark. The flexure brace kicked hard enough to dent its wooden stop.

The crowd recoiled.

"Expected brace correction," Olbit said.

He did not improvise. He pulled the premeasured second fulcrum pin from his belt, drove it into the waiting hole, and shifted the spring weight one notch. Contact pressure dropped. The roller recentered between its chalk lines.

"Pressure true," he called.

Kezli kept her hand off his work. Trusting a partner was another form of accuracy.

Ten more people reached the upper landing. Twenty safe. Yellow glazed, blistered, and peeled away. Its tab hit the clapper. Orange emerged with two minutes left.

The third cage rose through resin smoke and a shower of black scale. The bruised attendant stood inside, one arm strapped to their chest, while another worker below organized the final group. The apparatus looked as though it were burning itself apart because it was, in the measured and useful way stated on the ticket.

"Governor still on line," Kezli said.

"Drum steady," Olbit said.

Nalda no longer watched their hands. She helped the third group off the cage, supported the attendant by the good arm, and cleared all ten behind the shield line.

Orange reached its final chalk mark. The orange tab dropped against the clapper, and red turned on the roller like a warning lamp.

"One minute," Kezli called. "Operating trio only. Everyone else behind the shield."

The final cage began to rise.

The lower signal flag fell. No people remained at the station. Through a gap in the smoke, Kezli saw the squat civic strongbox still chained beside the speaking-wire desk.

"Final wear mark approaching," Olbit said.

The red leaf looked thicker than it had on the bench. For one treacherous instant, Kezli imagined it lasting another passage. Perhaps the measurements had been conservative. Perhaps she could wrap on another leaf, fetch the strongbox, save Nalda from the inquiry, and turn five good minutes into six glorious ones.

Then she saw the heat score spreading across the shaft and the flexure spring sitting at the end of its useful travel. Hope was not a measurement.

"Cut fuel," she told the boiler tender. "Dump ready."

The council courier gripped the edge of the shield. "The sleeve can be packed again. When they arrive, send it down once more."

"No," Kezli said. "After shear, the shaft is scored, the brace is spent, and the lower station will be inside the fire. The warranty includes stopping."

The fourth cage broke through the smoke. Nalda and the lift mechanics hauled it onto the upper landing. Ten people crossed the stop line with seconds left.

Forty.

Red vanished.

Bare iron caught against iron instead of slipping compliantly. The jolt loaded the notched bronze link past its threshold. It parted with a clean metallic crack. Released springs snapped the contact rollers away. The same motion tripped the steam-dump latch, and white vapor burst above the housing. The ratchet brake dropped into the drum and caught it against the landing stops.

Sparks scattered across the boiler-plate shield. Scale pattered onto the stones. The clapper rang one last time, nearly lost beneath the hiss of vented steam.

People screamed.

Then nothing moved.

Kezli looked down the sequence on the ticket. Bare iron. Shear. Withdrawal. Dump. Brake.

"Terminal behavior as warranted," she said, and discovered that her voice was shaking only after the words were out.

Olbit checked the brake pawl and held up his thumb. "Forty passengers. Five minutes. Zero unpriced adults."

The upper landing laughed, a thin and astonished sound that became cheering.

A second rumble rolled up from the terrace. The roof of the lower station folded into the fire, and rock swept across it from the broken stair road. When the dust cleared, the speaking-wire desk and the strongbox were gone.

Nalda watched the place where they had been. She did not look away from the price she had signed for.

***

By noon, the North Rise was quiet enough to hear cooling iron tick.

Kezli and Olbit inventoried what remained: five stripped oakcloth leaves, one cleanly parted shear link, one heat-scored shaft, a flexure spring with no safe travel left, and a brake still locked around the drum. Olbit punched each completed color on the ticket as they checked it. Beneath all of it, the pedestal crack remained. The crown gear was still ruined. Their success had not repaired a single permanent fault.

It had only kept every one of those faults from mattering for five minutes.

At a makeshift desk, Nalda dictated two records. The first admitted that she had deferred the pedestal work after Kezli's maintenance bid and recorded her decision to leave civic funds below. The second listed the emergency rig's declared duration, four-load capacity, five warning colors, and terminal sequence. Every item had occurred within its stated bound.

"The council will hold an inquiry," she said.

"Probably several," Olbit said. "Committees multiply when stored near missing money."

Nalda gave him a tired, unwilling smile. Then she paid the emergency invoice in full from the lift office's upper reserve. On a fresh work order, she commissioned a new pedestal and crown gear, named Kezli's workshop as paid lead, and assigned the ordinary lift mechanics as independent inspectors.

"A permanent repair," Nalda said, offering Kezli the pen.

This time the phrase did not sound like a verdict on everything temporary.

Kezli signed.

They pinned the red-stamped warranty to the silent lift housing beside the rebuild order. All five colored boxes had been punched through, exactly as promised. Below them, in the space for witnesses, forty soot-marked fingerprints crowded one another nearly off the board.

Kezli looked past the spent leaves to the cracked pedestal they would set right next. The five-minute machine had not lasted.

Its consequence would.

stories.prompt: "So if you win the duel, you get to take her on a date." They both nodded. "And if she wins the duel, she gets to take you on a date." They both nodded. "So why don't you both just... Skip that and go on a date?" They both glared.
stories.body:
# The Courtesy of Blades

Fiora Halwick set her travel case beneath the spectator rail, where it looked
like an accusation.

The buckles were fastened. Her teaching coats were rolled around two pairs of
boots. At dawn, a hired cart would carry her upriver to East Weir and the yard
that had trusted her with its head instructor's keys. Everything about the case
said *settled*. Everything about Fiora standing in the Lacebridge civic blade
yard in a padded practice coat said otherwise.

Across the strip, Jasper Renlow tightened his throat guard. He caught her
watching and lifted his chin in question.

Fiora lifted hers back. If he wanted reassurance, he could earn it point by
point.

Between them, Quade inspected the flex of one chalk-edged blade, then the other.
Evening light slanted through the open side of the yard and turned the chalk
dust pale gold. Beyond the wall came the river's slap against pilings and the
more persuasive hiss of onions hitting hot iron at the supper stalls.

Quade sighted along Fiora's blunt blade. “No cracks. Edge freshly chalked. Eye
guards down when I call ready. Marks count only on the dark torso and upper-arm
panels. Head, throat, hands, and joints are out. Either of you may halt or
surrender. I may halt you whether you like it or not.”

“You've been waiting years to say that to us,” Jasper said.

“I've been saying it to you for years. Tonight I have witnesses.” Quade handed
the blade to Fiora. “First to three. Clear touches are mine to judge. If you
both land and I cannot see the order, you call your own truth. Understood?”

“Understood,” Fiora and Jasper said together.

That earned a ripple of amusement from behind the rail. Fiora did not look
toward it. The bronze trial badge pinned inside her case had been won in this
same strip, three points to two. For six months, people had admired it by asking
whether Jasper had let her have the last touch.

Quade opened the yard ledger. “Now the personal stake. So if you win the duel,
you get to take her on a date.”

They both nodded.

“And if she wins the duel, she gets to take you on a date.”

They both nodded.

Quade looked from one of them to the other. “So why don't you both just... skip
that and go on a date?”

They both glared.

Quade waited a beat. “Yes, very frightening. For the record, *take* means the
winner gets the first invitation and chooses the place. The loser may decline.
The winner may decide not to ask. Nobody owes anyone a hand, a kiss, a change
of town, a second evening, or even dessert. This is a courtesy-bout stake, not
custody. Do you each enter freely?”

“Yes,” Jasper said.

“Yes,” Fiora said.

“Do you understand that this entire business could have been accomplished with
two sentences and clean shirts?”

“Ready, Quade,” Fiora said.

Jasper lowered his eye guard. “Very ready.”

Their mutual glare had been agreement of a kind. The absurdity was admitted.
The necessity was not. Fiora raised her blade and stepped onto the strip.

***

Jasper saluted with the crisp economy that made him infuriating on patrol and
worse in a fencing yard. He had the sort of balance that never looked hurried,
even when Fiora knew perfectly well she had him worried.

She intended to worry him quickly.

“Ready,” Quade called. “Fence.”

Fiora advanced behind two small testing cuts. Jasper yielded half a step, blade
quiet, his gaze fixed through the guard on the center of her coat. She pressed.
His retreat put him exactly where she wanted him: weight shifting back, right
side open, attention dragged low.

She snapped her blade high.

Jasper was already there.

His parry turned her familiar feint aside. Before she could recover, his blade
flexed against the padded panel of her upper arm and sprang away, leaving one
clean white bar.

“Halt.” Quade stepped between their lines before either could continue. He
examined the mark. “Touch, Jasper. One to nothing.”

The yard murmured.

Fiora stared at the chalk on her sleeve. Jasper had known the attack. Not
guessed—known. He had remembered the hitch of her shoulder, or the fraction by
which she shortened her second step, and he had trained an answer precise
enough to make the point look simple.

It was deeply annoying.

It was also the first thing she had wanted from him all evening.

Jasper returned to his mark without smiling. “You still announce the high line
with your left eyebrow.”

“My eyebrow is a master of deception.”

“It told me everything.”

“Then do keep listening.”

Quade checked the chalk edge, backed away, and called them on.

Fiora gave Jasper the same two testing cuts. This time his mouth twitched. He
settled to meet the high feint again.

She sank instead.

The new pivot had been born from three weeks of preparing lessons for East
Weir, where the shortest practice strip was hemmed in by two inconvenient
pillars. Fiora folded low without surrendering her balance, turned beneath
Jasper's parry, and came up past his outside shoulder. Her chalk edge kissed
the dark panel over his ribs.

Quade's “Halt” arrived on the same breath as Jasper's startled laugh.

The mark was a bright crescent.

“Touch, Fiora. One to one.”

Jasper looked down at it, then across at her. There was no embarrassment in his
face, only sharp interest. “That's new.”

“East Weir.”

“You developed it for the new yard?”

“I developed it because the new yard has pillars, and pillars refuse to adjust
their style for my convenience.”

“I always said you should train with more reasonable opponents.”

“You have never been evidence for that argument.”

This time he did smile, quick and unwilling and much too handsome. Fiora's
heart made a tactical error. She covered it by returning to her mark.

One to one. He knew her, but not all of her. She could work with that.

***

On the next call, Jasper came forward.

The lazy-looking patience vanished from his feet. He drove Fiora down the strip
with compact attacks that made her give ground honestly. Chalk whispered once
past her shoulder without touching. She caught his next blade and turned it,
but he was already angling for her ribs.

He was not easing against her. The realization warmed something under her
breastbone at the least convenient possible time.

Fiora broke his rhythm with a stop, then another. Jasper adjusted. She let him.
On his third advance she offered the opening he had been trying to create, a
sliver of dark panel under her arm.

He took it.

Her blade was waiting on the line he abandoned.

She rotated out, struck his upper-arm panel with a flat white line, and was
already clear when Quade called halt.

“Touch, Fiora. Two to one.”

The cheer behind the rail came fast enough to lift the rafters. Fiora stepped
back, breathless and grinning despite herself.

Jasper rubbed a thumb near the mark, careful not to smear it. “A trap.”

“A lesson plan.”

“Your pupils are doomed.”

“My pupils will learn.”

“I am learning.” His gaze held hers. “That's the trouble.”

It would have been easier if he had sounded flirtatious. He sounded sincere.

Then a voice behind the rail said, not quite softly enough, “Still easing off,
then.”

The grin left Fiora's face.

Quade turned toward the onlookers. “The next person who offers an unofficial
judgment may enjoy the rest of the bout from the street.”

Silence followed, but the words had found the old bruise.

Still easing off. Still giving her room. Still letting the ambitious assistant
instructor leave town with a badge she had not properly earned. She could
already hear the story traveling upriver ahead of her: Jasper had indulged her
again, out of affection this time, and East Weir had appointed the beneficiary
of his gallantry.

Jasper returned to his mark. His shoulders were loose, his attention on her,
as if the rail did not exist.

“You're not going to answer that?” Fiora asked.

“I can argue with the rail,” he said, “or I can fence you. Which do you want?”

“I want your best.”

“You have it.”

Quade studied them. “Do either of you need a halt?”

“No,” Fiora said.

“No,” Jasper echoed.

“Then leave the rail outside the rail. Ready. Fence.”

Fiora attacked before the last word had settled.

Anger lent speed and stole judgment. Her first advance forced Jasper back; her
second beat his blade wide. She saw the opening at his ribs and chased it with
the fierce satisfaction of a door flying open.

It was too wide.

Jasper dropped his point under hers, turned, and let her own forward drive
carry her onto the flex of his blade. Chalk struck squarely across her rib
panel. The padded coat absorbed the touch with a firm thump.

“Halt!” Quade was already moving between them, one arm extended until both
blades were safely down. His eyes went from Fiora's panel to Jasper's edge.
“Clean touch. Jasper. Two to two.”

Fiora's lungs objected to every part of the situation.

Jasper did not apologize. He did not soften the point by calling it luck or
looking ashamed of the mark. He only waited while she found her breath.

She had asked for his best. He had respected her enough to make the request
cost something.

“That,” she said, “was obnoxiously clean.”

“Your eyebrow told me nothing.”

“It was distracted by your personality.”

Quade pinched the bridge of his nose. “Mandatory pause. Re-chalk. Water. Try
not to court each other into heatstroke.”

***

Fiora pushed up her eye guard. The evening air cooled the sweat at her temples.
Across the strip, Jasper did the same.

Quade ran a practiced hand along each blade for damage, then worked fresh chalk
over their edges. “Two to two. Final point decides. Before it does: hands?”

“Sound,” Fiora said.

“Sound,” Jasper said.

“Vision?”

“Clear.”

“Clear.”

Quade gave them water and moved several paces away. Close enough to intervene,
far enough to offer privacy that fooled no one in a yard full of listeners.

Fiora drank, then stared at the old chalk on Jasper's arm. “At the trial,” she
said, “did I land first?”

Jasper lowered his cup. “Yes.”

The answer came without decoration. That almost made her angrier.

“Then why did you never say so afterward?”

“I called your touch in front of Quade and half this yard.”

“And when they said you gave it to me?”

“I thought the call was the answer.” Jasper looked toward the strip rather than
the rail. “I was wrong. I should have said it again when the story changed. I
should have said it every time someone made my honesty into your humiliation.”

Fiora had prepared for denial, chivalry, or some noble nonsense about wanting
her to leave with the badge. An admission fitted nowhere in her defenses.

“If I simply went to supper with you,” she said, “they would call that proof.
They would say you wanted me, so you spared me. And I wouldn't know which
version you believed. I would sit across a table wondering whether you saw me
or someone you had to be gentle with.”

Jasper met her eyes. “I do want you.”

Her fingers tightened around the cup.

“I also wanted to win that trial,” he continued. “You touched first. Both are
true.”

“And tonight?”

“Tonight I want to win. If I do, I get to ask one question and choose where we
eat. You can say no. You leave for East Weir at dawn. I have no claim on that,
or on a second supper, or on any day after tonight.” His expression shifted,
not quite a smile. “Though I reserve the right to be intolerably hopeful.”

It was, Fiora thought, remarkably unfair to become more attractive while
renouncing all rights to her.

Quade returned and offered Fiora her blade hilt-first. “You may agree to a draw.
You may surrender. You may continue. Separately, please, so neither of you can
hide inside the other's answer. Fiora?”

The easy refuge waited. A draw would leave her badge technically untouched and
her doubt perfectly preserved.

She took the blade. “Continue.”

Quade turned. “Jasper?”

Jasper took his. “Continue.”

Fiora lowered her eye guard. The truth of the old match could no longer be
proved by winning this one. It could only be tested by what they did when the
truth hurt.

***

They returned to their marks with two white scores on each coat.

Fiora heard the crowd settle behind the rail. She heard the river and the
supper fires and the faint clink of the buckle on her waiting travel case. The
world had become offensively full of things that would continue after the next
touch.

Quade raised one hand. “Ready.”

Fiora set her feet.

Jasper's blade hovered on the line that had defeated her high feint at the
opening. But his weight had shifted a degree lower. He was preparing for the
East Weir pivot now.

Good.

“Fence.”

Neither moved.

Jasper's eyebrows rose behind his guard.

“Mine say nothing,” Fiora told him.

“They say you intend something unkind.”

“That's not prediction. That's experience.”

He advanced.

The last exchange began almost quietly: blade to blade, a light scrape, two
measured steps. Jasper tested her outside line. Fiora gave him no answer. He
pressed again, quicker, and she turned the attack without taking the opening
that followed.

He knew her patience was borrowed. She knew his was a weapon.

Jasper changed pace. Fiora retreated once, twice, until the end mark brushed
beneath her heel. He expected her to spring high rather than be crowded off the
strip. She saw it in the angle of his guard, the answer waiting where it had
waited for her first attack.

So she began the new pivot.

She dropped her center. Jasper adjusted at once, blade falling to catch the low
turn that had scored against his ribs. Fiora let the motion carry halfway—then
drove upward, unwinding the pivot into the old high attack.

Surprise flashed across his face.

Not enough surprise.

Jasper recovered with brutal neatness. His low parry swept up as Fiora's point
cut toward his upper arm. Their shoulders crossed. For one compressed instant,
his body blocked Quade's view of both target panels.

Two chalked blades flexed.

Quade called halt.

Fiora froze with Jasper so close she could hear the catch in his breath. Her
blade rested against his upper-arm panel. His rested against the dark padding
over her ribs.

To the rail, the touches had been one sound.

To Quade, hidden by their crossing bodies, they had been one motion.

To Fiora, they had not.

She had felt Jasper's blade bow against her coat. She had seen white chalk
bloom at the lower edge of her vision. Half a beat later, her own edge had
drawn its line across his arm.

Jasper eased his blade away but said nothing. He looked at her, waiting.

Six months earlier, in this strip, he had stood where she stood. He had owned a
fraction of knowledge that could cost him the match, and he had spoken it.
Courtesy, Fiora understood at last, was not making the world painless for
someone. It was trusting them with the truth and trusting that they could bear
what came next.

She could say she did not know. Quade would order the point refenced. She might
win. The badge in her case might feel defended for an hour, perhaps even a
week.

And every time she looked at it, she would know what she had withheld.

“Jasper's touch landed first,” Fiora said.

The words passed through the yard with more force than a shout.

Jasper glanced once at the white mark on her ribs. He could have disputed her.
He could have performed generosity and handed the point back until neither of
them knew what anything meant.

Instead he nodded. “My touch first.”

Quade inspected both marks. He looked at Fiora, giving her room to correct or
withdraw the call.

She held his gaze. “The point is Jasper's.”

Quade straightened. “Touch, Jasper. Match to Jasper, three to two.”

For a moment no one behind the rail spoke. Then the applause came, less like a
victory roar than a release of breath.

Fiora lifted her guard. Jasper did the same. He was smiling, but not as a man
who had been awarded her company. He looked as she must have looked at the old
trial: astonished, relieved, and fiercely proud of the person who had beaten
him to the truth.

They saluted.

Quade carried the ledger to the rail and wrote the result in a firm hand:
Jasper, three; Fiora, two. Beneath the notation, he added the final touch as
self-called by Fiora. The old trial remained in its own place in the book:
Fiora, three; Jasper, two, with Jasper's call beside it.

Quade studied the two entries. “I withdraw my objection to the rematch.”

“Thank you,” Fiora said.

“I maintain every objection to your methods of conversation.”

“Also fair,” Jasper said.

***

The onlookers drifted toward the supper stalls, already arguing cheerfully
about the final exchange. Quade made Fiora and Jasper return their blades,
remove their guards, and submit to one last inspection before he would let
either of them near food.

“No damage except to judgment,” he pronounced.

“Whose?” Fiora asked.

“Mine, for officiating.” Quade shut the ledger. “The match is recorded. What
happens now is not.”

He walked away with enough determination to prove he was not about to arrange
the rest for them.

Fiora knelt by her travel case and checked the nearest buckle. Still fastened.
The cart would still come at dawn. East Weir's yard would still be hers to
lead. Losing had altered none of that.

Jasper stopped beside her. The chalk marks on his coat made him look like a
particularly elegant piece of disputed arithmetic.

“The bout is over,” he said. “Your answer belongs to you.”

Fiora stood.

He took a breath. This, apparently, frightened him more than facing her blade.
The discovery was so charming she almost rescued him, then decided equality
required letting him suffer properly.

“Fiora Halwick,” Jasper said, “would you have supper with me at the riverside
stalls tonight? One supper. I choose the place; you choose whether to come. You
leave for East Weir at dawn either way.”

There it was: no ritual left to speak for him, no point pretending the question
was anything but a hope placed carefully in her hands.

“Yes,” Fiora said. “Because I want to.”

His whole face changed.

“You may choose the stall,” she added, “but if you choose the one that burns
the onions, I reserve the right to regret my consent.”

“Continued consent was explicitly covered.”

“Good. You were listening.”

They left the yard in their chalk-marked practice coats, Fiora carrying the
travel case and Jasper carrying both guards. At the riverside, canvas awnings
snapped above iron cooking plates. Warm bread steamed in baskets. The lamps
along the pilings laid wavering paths across the dark water.

Jasper selected a stall where the onions were merely browned. He bought two
folded breads full of vegetables and sharp cheese, then waited until Fiora had
chosen a bench before sitting beside her.

The date began with her stealing one of his crispest onions.

“When may I visit East Weir?” he asked.

Fiora chewed thoughtfully. She could picture the new yard's narrow strip, the
awkward pillars, the rack waiting to be filled. She could picture herself at
its center in the head instructor's coat she had earned. Jasper belonged
nowhere in that picture unless invited, which made room for wanting him there.

“When you've devised a respectable counter to my pivot,” she said.

“I countered it.”

“Eventually. After it scored.”

“Then I may need a rematch.”

“You may need several.” Fiora raised her supper in salute. “Come prepared to
lose three to two.”

Jasper touched his folded bread to hers with grave courtesy. “I'll come
prepared to call what lands first.”

Fiora smiled and took another bite. Dawn would carry her east. Tonight, beside
the river, neither of them asked it to wait.

stories.title: The Last Thing I Could Fix
stories.prompt: You are a legendary blacksmith, sought out for your ability to fix anything. Talking swords, obsidian breastplates, staves made of crystal, daggers forged from dragon scales, you've done it all. The real challenge today is a young hero asking you to fix what they call their 'plot armor'.
stories.body:
# The Last Thing I Could Fix

I had corrected the manners of talking swords, which is harder than sharpening them and only slightly easier than convincing their owners to pay. I had mended obsidian breastplates without turning their wearers into pincushions of black glass. I had spliced crystal staves whose two halves disagreed about the direction of lightning. I had even reset the scales on dragon-scale daggers, a task best undertaken after establishing whether the dragon was finished with them.

In short, I was Hadrik, and I fixed anything.

The sign over my forge said so. The words were cut deep enough to outlive me and gilded thick enough to suggest they might. Travelers came up the valley to point at it, then at some impossible wreck in a velvet box. Nothing left my bench until it did what its maker had intended.

That last part was not on the sign. At the time, I thought it too obvious to carve.

Aven arrived in a thunderstorm with a bundle under one arm and bloodless determination holding their young face together. Water ran from their hair, their sleeves, and the toe of one split boot. They put the bundle on my bench. Scorched metal showed through the wrapping.

“I need you to fix my plot armor.”

I waited for the grin. Aven did not provide one.

“That is what the court chroniclers call it,” they said. “Because it keeps the hero alive for the next great deed.”

“Chroniclers,” I said. “Of course. Smiths call things by what they are. Chroniclers call them by what rhymes with the wine.”

I unwrapped a close-fitted under-harness: small overlapping plates, a mesh of silver-gray response wire, and enough scorch marks to trouble me. Then the reservoir bell sounded uphill, one iron note rolling beneath the thunder.

Aven told me the relief gate had jammed. The reservoir was climbing toward the rim. On their first attempt, a gate bolt had torn loose above them. Their guide had reached out—and the harness had dragged the guide beneath the falling iron. The bolt broke the guide’s leg instead of Aven’s back.

“They told me to try again alone,” Aven said. “Nothing near me for the armor to hurt.”

“A practical solution, if one is a wheelbarrow.”

“I am not wearing it again until I understand what it does.”

That was the first sensible thing anyone had said about the harness, myself included. I still gave the answer expected of a legend.

“You will have it by midday.”

The reservoir bell sounded again before the echo of my promise had died.

Off Aven’s body, the harness was as magical as a soup pot. I laid it in salt, passed a lodestone over every plate, warmed it by the forge and cooled it in rainwater. Nothing answered. The response wire held a faint stored tension, but no heat, pulse, or motion of its own.

“It needs someone living,” I said. “Likely you. Put it on.”

Aven’s hands stopped at the buckles.

“We test with cloth, not gate bolts,” I said. “And I stop when you say.”

They searched my face long enough to make me glad I had said it plainly. Then they stripped off their wet coat and fitted the harness over their shirt.

I blackened every wire junction with soot and hung a sack of rags from a ceiling chain. It made a gentle pendulum, by heroic standards. By mine, it was still a weight moving toward a client.

“Do nothing,” I told Aven. “I will catch it.”

I drew the sack back. Aven nodded. I let go.

The sack swung. Nothing warmed in advance, no invisible hand tipped it aside. The canvas touched the center plate with a padded thud.

Only then did the wire tighten.

A rivet at Aven’s sternum flashed hot. A line of lampblack leapt outward along one narrow hook. I had planted my boots and sworn to hold still, but some older part of me saw a young person in danger and reached before pride could stop it.

That reach completed the open circuit.

My arm jerked across Aven’s chest and into the sack’s path. I caught the chain with my other hand before the returning weight could crack my elbow. The pendulum had not swerved by a finger’s width. I had.

Aven went pale. “That was how the guide moved.”

I examined the hot center rivet under a lens. A hairline split ran through the metal and left its tiny assent gate jammed open. The outward hooks were made to take the intention of a nearby protector, but the choice rivet was supposed to admit only someone who actively joined the circuit. Cracked, it could turn a flinch, a reach, the bare wish that Aven not be hurt, into a bodily pull.

The wire had not foreseen the sack. It stayed cold until contact. Then Aven’s alarm and my protective reflex supplied the current, and the open circuit routed the pull through me as the nearer shield.

I drove ceramic wedges beneath the witness hooks and swung the sack again. It struck. The plates cinched hard around Aven; the split rivet heated; but the soot stopped at the blocked hooks, and I did not move.

There are diagnoses one enjoys being right about. This was not one of them.

“The central rivet is split,” I said. “I can drill it out, forge another, and reconnect the hooks. With the assent catch sound, it will take only a willing protector. Two hours.”

I reached for my smallest punch.

“No.”

“It is the proper repair.”

“It is the same purpose with a better latch.” Aven touched the reddened cloth over their sternum. “The latch broke once.”

“Everything breaks once. Most things make a career of it.”

“Then I won’t wear a thing whose failure turns people into shields.”

Outside, rain hissed on my chimney cap. I looked at the sign through the open forge door, its gold letters blurred by water. Anything fixed. A promise is an excellent servant until it hears a deadline; then it becomes a magistrate.

“The adults below expect that harness to bring their hero back,” I said.

“They expect me to go where they won’t because they think it has always brought me back.” Aven swallowed. “I don’t know how many times somebody else moved because of it. I don’t know which victories were mine.”

That landed harder than the sack had.

“The armor did not climb the road for you,” I said. “It did not learn the gate or decide to return here. But it changed who paid when things went wrong.” I put down the punch. “Tell me what fixed means.”

Aven looked surprised. So was I.

“It means I choose what I do,” they said. “It means nobody else pays unless they know the price and say yes. It means if it can’t save me honestly, it doesn’t pretend it can.”

The reservoir bell began ringing in strokes of three.

“That,” I said, “is a much slower repair.”

“Can you do it?”

“I did carve the sign very deeply.”

I cut away the witness hooks. One curved piece—the old bypass hook—could bridge an assent gate without a rivet and leave the outward path permanently open. I coiled it and dropped it into my tool roll, because smiths save dangerous scraps with the faith that labeling them dangerous makes us wise. Then I unfolded the response braid, turned every other outward path inward, and stitched it back through the plates.

The split choice rivet came out under my drill in bright curls. In its place I forged a will-catch: one contact beneath Aven’s sternum, one beneath the palm of their working hand. Aven stood beside the quench trough with their fingers on both while I tempered the fitted circuit. Their intent ran warm through the wire; my tongs and fire shaped it but supplied none of their own.

Last, I forged three rivets from soft iron, heated them to straw, then violet, then the blue of deep water. I set them where overload would break them before the braid could seek another body or hide the strain.

“Three hard uses,” I said. “Visible ones. After the third, this becomes rather uncomfortable ordinary armor.”

“What counts as a use?”

“First, danger must actually touch you. No warning. You must be conscious, understand the motion, press the will-catch, and say what you choose to do. One verb. One direction. The braid will brace that line for about one breath.”

“And the force?”

“Still exists. It spreads through the plates and through you. A blow from the side remains a blow from the side. Too much force will injure or kill you, whether the rivets have admired your courage or not.”

Aven gave the three blue heads a sober glance. “Better.”

I retained one outward loop of copper, isolated from the rest. “A second person may share the load by taking this consent ring with bare skin and saying yes, then and there. Let go, and the join ends. No stored permission. No borrowed reflex.”

We tested the redesign before trusting a town to it.

First I swung the padded sack slowly. Aven watched it come and stepped aside. It passed them. Nothing warmed; nothing pulled. They laughed once, mostly from surprise.

Then they returned to the mark. The sack touched the breastplate.

Aven pressed sternum and palm. “Stand.”

The inward braid lit beneath its soot. The plates drew tight along the line from their boots to their shoulders. The sack drove them back half a step and left a bruise they would feel by supper. It did not throw them. One blue rivet snapped with a crack like a seed in flame.

My arms remained entirely my own.

For the consent check, I gripped the copper ring while Aven leaned into a lightly padded press. They said, “Stand.” The mesh warmed around them. The ring stayed cold in my hand.

“Yes,” I said.

Heat crossed my palm, mild but unmistakable, and the resistance divided between us until I let go. The remaining two rivets stayed blue.

The bell above us rang three strokes again, with less silence between each set.

I packed my hammer, wedges, and tool roll.

“You said I would have it by midday,” Aven said.

“You have it.” I tied on my rain cloak. “I did not say you would have the poor judgment to field an unproven redesign without its smith.”

I had serviced the spillgate years before, an ordinary job of rust, hinges, and a locking wedge that swelled every wet season. Less glamorous than dragon scales. Considerably more useful that morning.

The path climbed beside the relief channel. Rain had turned its stones black and slick, and water boomed behind the reservoir wall like something enormous objecting to architecture. Aven led. They knew where the first attempt had torn loose railings and which stair had split.

Halfway across the upper catwalk, a support gave way under me.

There was no omen. One moment I had iron under both boots. The next, the bracket peeled from wet stone and the walkway dropped. I caught the rail with one hand. My hammer dragged at my belt while the relief channel hammered below.

Aven turned. For one naked instant, they stood perfectly still.

They were waiting for rescue to happen.

Nothing did. The wire could not choose. The old hooks were gone. The harness offered no warning and took no one’s body.

Then Aven saw me, saw the intact support behind them, and made a decision.

They dropped flat, hooked one knee around the support, and caught my wrist. The load struck their shoulder. They pressed the will-catch against the rail with their free hand.

“Catch.”

The braid braced backward along their chosen pull. Aven hauled; I kicked against the wall; together we got my chest over the broken edge. The second rivet sheared.

When the breath ended, Aven rolled onto their back with their injured arm clutched close.

“Shoulder?” I asked.

“Strained.” Their face said more than the word did.

I checked the joint as gently as my hands allowed. Painful, still placed. I looked at the single blue rivet remaining.

“We can go back,” I said.

Below the clouds, the valley town was a huddle of slate roofs beside a river already too broad for its banks. Aven stared down at it.

“The armor didn’t make me catch you,” they said.

“No.”

“And it didn’t make me freeze.”

“No. That habit came from people teaching you rescue was automatic.”

They flexed their good hand. “Then I can learn a different one.”

We went on.

The relief gate shuddered in its stone throat. Water sprayed through every seam. The release bar had jammed halfway, exactly where rust had always loved it, and the locking wedge beneath it had swollen fast. Worse, the final retaining bracket was peeling from the wall. Each surge bent it farther. When it tore free, the bar would kick loose and the gate would stay shut until the reservoir overtopped.

I laid out the work. Aven would brace beneath the release bar while I drove the wedge through its lock. When the wedge seated, the gate would fall open toward the empty relief channel. We would both drop left, behind the stone pier, before the first water struck.

“One rivet,” Aven said.

“One breath,” I agreed.

“Will it work?”

The old answer rose easily. Of course. Hadrik fixed anything. The words even sounded like courage if one did not inspect them closely.

“It can work,” I said. “The upward load is within the design. The bar may twist. Your shoulder is already strained. I cannot promise either of us leaves unhurt.”

“Can we retreat?”

“Yes.” The bracket shrieked. “We would probably live. The lower town would flood.”

Aven shut their eyes. When they opened them, there was fear in them and room beside it for thought.

“I’m not doing this because the court called me a hero,” they said. “I’m doing it because I know what happens if we leave, and because you told me the truth.”

“You may still say no.”

“So may you.”

That was the soundest safety rule either of us had made.

We took our places.

The release bar slammed down until it met Aven’s raised hands. Contact first. Metal groaned against metal. Aven perceived the direction and set their boots. They flattened their working palm beneath the bar, compressing that contact against the iron, and leaned into the breastplate until the second contact seated beneath their sternum. Their other hand never left the bar.

“Hold.”

The last blue rivet began to whiten at its edge. The inward braid tightened from Aven’s palms through their back and legs. They cried out as the real weight spread through them, but the bar stopped descending.

I swung my hammer.

The first blow cracked rust. The second moved the locking wedge the breadth of a thumbnail. The gate shifted under water pressure—not down, but sideways.

Aven’s protection held the upward line they had chosen. It did nothing about the lateral wrench. Their strained shoulder buckled toward the wall.

One breath was not enough.

My tool roll lay open at my knee. The old bypass hook gleamed among the wedges. I could jam it across the empty assent seat in a heartbeat. The open path would seize the nearest protective impulse—mine—and turn my body into whatever brace the harness required. It was the old guarantee, close enough to touch. I could preserve the legend and call the coercion sacrifice afterward.

I dropped the hook.

Instead I tore off my glove and seized the copper consent ring.

“Yes,” I said. Not forever. Not for the court. “Yes, now.”

The ring burned into my palm.

My living intent joined Aven’s for that single hold, and the fitted wire divided the upward strain between us. It did not erase the sideways force. Aven’s shoulder still took that; my hand took heat enough to make the hammer swim in my vision. But their knees stopped folding. The whitening rivet endured one moment longer.

I struck the wedge a third time.

It seated.

The release bar leapt. The gate dropped open. Water roared into the empty channel, exactly where stone and old iron had directed it, not where luck preferred. The third rivet sheared. The response braid flashed once and fused black against the plates.

“Left!” I shouted.

We fell behind the pier as planned. The first wall of water tore through the place where we had stood, carrying rust, branches, and the discarded bypass hook down the safe channel.

For some time there was only stone under my cheek, rain on my back, and Aven’s breathing beside me.

Then the reservoir bell changed to the long, steady toll for water falling.

We had opened the gate. The lower town remained a town rather than becoming a shallow and badly planned lake. Aven could walk, though their shoulder needed a sling. I kept my burned hand wrapped against my chest. The harness hung from them as dead weight: all three blue rivets broken, the response wire fused, no warmth left anywhere in it.

Back at the forge, I laid the harness on my bench.

“Failed repair,” I said.

Aven, pale with exhaustion and dry at last, looked at me as if I had announced that anvils were migratory birds.

“It did exactly what I chose,” they said. “It stopped when you said it would. It charged nobody who hadn’t agreed.”

“The wire is ruined.”

“Then it spent itself honestly.”

I had spent my life returning objects to what their makers intended. It had never occurred to me that an intention might deserve refusal, or that a thing could be fixed by giving it an honorable way to end.

“I could make another,” I said. The offer came from habit, but not entirely. “More rivets. A stronger braid.”

Aven shook their head. “Ordinary mail. A crew. A plan. And the right to refuse the next great deed before anyone starts writing about it.”

“Ordinary mail I can guarantee against reasonable stabbing.”

“Reasonable stabbing?”

“The sign is under revision.”

The next morning, with my good hand and a narrow chisel, I climbed a ladder outside the forge. The gilding came away first. Then the wood. I cut the word *anything* out of the promise I had made so deeply.

In the space beneath, in smaller letters because truth is seldom brief, I carved: *Before I take the job, I will tell you what the repair can do and what it will cost.*

The new sign brought fewer velvet boxes. It brought better questions.

I remained Hadrik. I remained a blacksmith. I fixed many things after that, though never everything, and never by myself merely because my name was over the door.

The plot armor was the last thing I ever claimed I could fix alone.

stories.title: The Attendance Ledger
stories.prompt: A school teacher moonlights as a handler for magical girls, looking after their wellbeing in battle and the classroom, even protecting the girls' secret identities without alerting them.
stories.body:
# The Attendance Ledger

By the third name on the paper attendance ledger, Gideon Tolland knew exactly
how much sleep three of his students had not had.

Northbridge Secondary’s network had chosen community-showcase day to display a
spinning circle instead of the online register, so Gideon was using the paper
backup. The ledger was a grey administrative object with coffee feathered
along one corner. It possessed no insight. Gideon supplied the dangerous part
himself.

“Drita Ademi?”

“Present.”

Drita held her left wrist close to her body. The cuff of her uniform jumper
covered most of the bruise, but not the careful way she turned each page with
her right hand. Her fingertips were pale with cold.

“Bryn Ahn?”

“Here.”

Bryn had already drawn two routes out of the problem on the lab sheet, although
the problem concerned mineral samples and neither route was required. Her
pencil trembled once, stopped under the pressure of her thumb, then continued.

“Cassia Dominguez?”

“Physically.”

The class laughed. Cassia offered them a thin grin and lowered her face over
her folded arms.

Gideon marked all three present. At one seventeen that morning, in the
voice-scrambled privacy of an encrypted radio relay, Kiteglass had reported a
bad wrist and loss of body heat. Pulsewire had said that lights still had halos
after two difficult severances. Mothlight had joked twice as fast as usual,
which had been the clearest report of all.

Night Clerk had recommended a recovery day. The three girls had chosen school.

Mr. Tolland, who had no legitimate way to connect those reports to these
students, had prepared accordingly.

“Before anyone asks,” he told the class, “the revision token on the board is
for everyone. One deadline, moved once, no justification required. Lab roles
rotate every twelve minutes. The snack box is not charity; it is protection
against the paperwork generated by fainting.”

That earned a better laugh. He passed the box along the benches. Cassia took
two oat bars without looking up. Drita accepted one after seeing three other
students do it. Bryn chose the role nearest the door.

Kindness was easiest to disguise as policy.

Gideon had not meant to learn their secret. Six months earlier, three
voice-scrambled strangers had asked for practical help over an emergency-radio
frequency: routes, weather, first-aid supplies, someone to notice when brave
became reckless. They had named him Night Clerk as a joke, and the name had
stuck.

Then he had seen three transformed figures disappear into an alley and Drita,
Bryn, and Cassia emerge moments later. After that came matching absences,
matching injuries, Drita’s angle-cutting hand signal, Bryn’s insistence on two
exits, Cassia’s habit of making a joke before admitting fear. No single clue
had proved anything. Together, they left almost no room for him to be wrong.

He had kept that knowledge to himself. Their anonymity was not a puzzle he had
earned the right to solve.

“Feet on the floor,” he said. “Before we begin, five things you can see, four
you can feel, three you can hear. Yes, this is educational. I have declared it
so.”

The room settled by degrees. Cassia’s shoulders lowered. Gideon reached the
next line of his ledger.

From the ventilation grate above Drita came a papery whisper.

“Kiteglass?”

Drita’s head began to turn.

Gideon let the ledger fall.

It struck the floor flat, loud as a slammed door. Pages slewed beneath his
desk. Twenty-eight students looked at him instead of at Drita.

“A compelling demonstration,” he said, crouching, “of gravity’s refusal to
respect staff authority.”

In the shadow behind the grate, something black and thin withdrew. Not wire.
Not a shadow. A living filament, wetly quick, vanishing after it had enjoyed a
clear view of the page.

The Rollcaller had survived the night.

Gideon gathered the papers without hurrying. “Change of method. Mark yourselves
present on the silent check-in slips. Apparently I am no longer qualified to
hold a book.”

The class bent to the slips. Drita did not look at the grate again.

At the time, switching the register felt like protection. Gideon would later
understand that the Rollcaller had watched him protect exactly one reaction.

* * *

At lunch, Gideon locked himself in the equipment room behind the lab and
plugged an ordinary headset into an ordinary phone. The voice scrambler made
him sound like a courteous cupboard.

“Rollcaller survived,” Night Clerk said. “It entered the school ventilation,
heard me call one civilian name, and tested the alias Kiteglass. It had sight
of the paper register. I saw living filament.”

Silence held on the relay. Their health and location channels showed only what
each girl had chosen to share: three rough status lights, no names, no map
points.

“How many people reacted?” Kiteglass asked.

“One nearly did. I interrupted. The room did not appear to notice.”

“Nearly,” Kiteglass repeated, annoyed with herself.

“The creature engineered surprise. That is information about its method, not a
failure on your part.”

Pulsewire’s scrambled voice cut in. “It needs correlation. The ledger gives it
possible civilians, reactions narrow them, cameras prove them.”

“Agreed. My recommendation is evacuation and cancellation. Available
alternatives: separate departures, remaining in public view, or a contained
trap using the building map. You decide whether you engage at all.”

“Three of us leaving together would be a confession with backpacks,”
Kiteglass said. “And we built that presentation.”

“For six weeks,” Pulsewire added.

Mothlight had said nothing.

Gideon resisted the urge to fill the quiet with instructions. “Mothlight, do
you want options, quiet, or a grounding count?”

“Count. Then options.”

He counted five slow breaths. He could hear her match him by the faint hiss of
the microphone. No one hurried her.

“I’m scared,” Mothlight said at last. “That is not the same as voting no.”

“Understood.”

“I vote we stay,” she said. “I also vote we don’t improvise in front of a
guardian livestream, because I do have standards.”

Kiteglass proposed drawing the Rollcaller toward the empty rehearsal corridor
during showcase setup, away from the auditorium audience. Pulsewire requested
